28:
It is also called suffering (dukkha). All these feelings are called suffering because of the nature of suffering in formations (saṅkhāra-dukkhatā). The Buddha said, "Whatever feeling there is, it is included within suffering." This is because all these feelings cannot transcend the nature of suffering in formations. It is understood that these feelings should be repeatedly contemplated as suffering, both in terms of pleasure and pain, and because of what is said regarding the nature of pleasure and the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-dukkha). The seven contemplations have already been explained below. The remaining divisions, such as carnal (sāmisa) and spiritual (nirāmisa), should be explained in the contemplation of feeling (vedanānupassanā).

"By way of the diversity of objects, etc." means it should be understood that contemplation is to be done by way of the diversity of objects like visible forms, the diversity of types like blue, etc.; the diversity of predominances like desire (chanda), the diversity of types like inferior, etc.; the diversity of co-nascent states like wisdom and jhāna, the diversity of types like prompted (sasaṅkhārika), unprompted (asaṅkhārika), with initial thought (savitakka), etc.; the diversity of planes like the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), the diversity of types like excellent, medium, etc.; the diversity of kamma like wholesome kamma, the diversity of types like leading to the deva realm, etc.; the diversity of results like black and white, the diversity of types like to be experienced in the present life, etc.; the diversity of functional states (kiriya) in the limited plane (paritta-bhūmi), and the diversity of types like those with three roots (tihetuka), etc. By the word "etc." (ādi), the diversity of those with or without physical bases (savatthuka/avatthuka) and the diversity related to the three types of individuals should be included. "By way of individual and general characteristics" means it should be understood as contemplating by way of individual characteristics like touching (phusana), etc., and general characteristics like impermanence (aniccata), etc. "Of the nature of emptiness" (suññata-dhamma) means by way of the nature of emptiness known as non-self (anattā). To clarify this nature of emptiness, the teaching on the section of emptiness (suññatā-vāra) was given in the Abhidhamma, stating, "At that time, there are states (dhammā), there are aggregates (khandhā)," and so on.

That covetousness and grief (abhijjhā-domanassa) have already been abandoned since the previous contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā), and thus they are indeed abandoned. Therefore, it should not be said that those particular defilements are abandoned again. This is because, in abandoning defilements, they are not abandoned by distinguishing objects, but rather those defilements that are liable to arise in the future are abandoned. Therefore, having stated the abandoning of covetousness, etc., in one state, it should not be stated again in another state. This meaning is shown by the words beginning with "Granted that here" (kāmañcettha). Alternatively, at the moment of the path-consciousness (magga-citta), a defilement abandoned in one mindfulness meditation is abandoned in all mindfulness meditations. Therefore, separate abandoning in each path-moment should not be stated. In truth, it should only be said that they are abandoned once by the path. Between these two answers, the former is an explanation regarding various individuals. The abandoning by one individual is not the abandoning by another. The latter is an explanation regarding various thought-moments of mindfulness meditation. "Various thought-moments" refers to the moments when the mundane path-consciousness of mindfulness arises. Here, the mundane path (pubbabhāga-magga) preceding the supramundane path is intended. Covetousness and grief abandoned in the physical body through mundane development are not yet abandoned in feelings, etc.

If they are not yet abandoned, it should only be said that covetousness and grief no longer arise in those feelings, etc., because they have been well-suppressed by the opposing development (bhāvanā). Therefore, it is appropriate to speak of abandoning those covetousness and grief once more. The teacher said the words "abandoned in one place" (ekattha pahīnaṃ) with reference to the supramundane development of mindfulness. Or, it was said with reference to the mere non-arising of covetousness and grief in all objects due to mundane development. It should be understood that the Buddha taught in the four foundations of mindfulness—contemplation of body, feeling, mind, and mental objects—in the Vibhaṅga Pali that "the five aggregates and the five aggregates of clinging are the world." This is the sub-commentary (ṭīkā) explaining the hidden meaning of the commentary on the summary section (uddesavāra).

## Commentary on the Section on Mindfulness of Breathing in the Contemplation of the Body

One understands well by way of the diversity of objects such as the body, which should be repeatedly contemplated. This is the summary of the divisions of the foundations of mindfulness.
29:
Although covetousness and grief are abandoned in the body, they are not yet abandoned in feelings, etc. Even if they are not yet abandoned, it is not that it should not be said, but rather it should be said that covetousness and grief do not arise in those feelings, etc., because they have been well-suppressed (vikkkhambhita) by the opposing development. Therefore, it is appropriate to speak of abandoning those covetousness and grief once more. The teacher said the words "what is abandoned in one place is abandoned in the remaining places" with reference to the supramundane development of mindfulness, or with reference to the mere non-arising of covetousness and grief in all objects during mundane development. It should be understood that the Buddha taught in the four instances of the Vibhaṅga Pali that "the five aggregates of clinging are the world."

## Illumination of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Summary Section

## Contemplation of the Body

## Commentary on the Section on Mindfulness of Breathing

"By way of the object" (ārammaṇavasena) means by way of the objects such as the body which should be repeatedly contemplated. "Having divided into four" (catudhā bhinditvā) means having divided into four by way of the summary (uddesavāra). Taking each foundation of mindfulness from those four foundations of mindfulness, the remaining text intends to analyze the body (the group of form) in detail.

In the word "And how?" (kathañca), "how" (kathaṃ) is a word asking about the manner. By that word, he asks about the various ways of the contemplation of the body being pointed out. The word "and" (ca) shows a distinction. By that word "and", he highlights the distinction that is not clear in the summary (uddesavāra) but is clearly explained in the detailed exposition (niddesavāra). Because even in external systems, a small portion of this might exist, the phrase "of one who produces the contemplation of the body in all its modes" (sabbappakārakāyānupassanānibbattakassa) is used to include all modes. By that statement, the fourteen modes that come by way of the section on mindfulness of breathing, etc., are included; also included are the modes of contemplation such as internal, etc., which are contained within those modes; likewise, the modes of the four jhānas having the kasina objects of the color and shape of hair, etc., as taught in the Kāyagatāsati Sutta, as well as mundane modes, etc.—all these are included without exception. These modes exist only in this Dispensation (sāsana) and not outside of it; therefore, it is said, "all modes... and the negation." In that phrase, "negation of such a state" (tathābhāvapatiṣedhano) means the negation of the reliance on other dispensations for a person who produces the contemplation of the body in all its modes. By this, he shows that in the Pali "Here, monks" (idha bhikkhave), the word "here" (idha) has the meaning of the word "only" (eva) contained within it. There are indeed single words that have a restrictive meaning, such as "one who eats only air" (vāyubhakkho). Therefore, he said, "Only here" (idheva).

## 4. Commentary on the Mahāsudassana Sutta
## Commentary on the Royal City of Kusāvatī
'Sovaṇṇamayā' means made of gold (consisting entirely of gold). 'This wall' refers to the wall made of all kinds of jewels. 'Three by three' means three walls on the inside and three walls on the outside, thus three each.

'Esikatthambha' refers to the gatepost (indakhīla), which is an ornamental pillar that beautifies the city. Since the extent of its width is known by this (circumference), it is called 'aṅga'; this 'aṅga' is indeed the circumference (parikkhepa). This gatepost is called 'tiporisaṅgā' because it has a circumference of three men's height. Therefore, the commentator said 'tena' and so forth. It is planted with a circumference of five cubits, which is the measure of three men's height. 'In the leaves and fruits as well' means that in the leaves and fruits of the palm trees made of all kinds of jewels, they are also made of jewels. 'In this same manner' means that among the leaves, one leaf-blade is made of gold and one is made of silver. Among the fruits as well, one stripe is made of gold and one is made of silver; this meaning has been very clearly demonstrated. 'Between the walls' means there are rows of palm trees standing individually between every two walls.

'Cheka' means clear and distinct, as if played skillfully; because that clarity of sound is attractive to the mind, it is called 'sundara' (beautiful). 'Rañjetum' means to arouse passion (rāga). 'Khamateva' means it is simply pleasing. 'Na bībhatccheti' means it does not threaten (does not cause fear); because it is pleasant to the ear, it is also to be cherished. Instruments such as the pot-drum (kumbhathuṇa) and daddarika are one-sided percussion instruments. Two-sided drums are already well-known. There are also the square ambaṇa drum and the paṇava drum, which are covered on all four sides. In the word 'vaṃsādi,' the word 'ādi' includes instruments such as the conch shell. 'Sumucchitassa' refers to playing that is well-mastered and completed. 'In measure' (pamāṇe) refers to the medium measure of playing, which is neither too tight nor too loose. 'Moving the hands or the feet' means preparing and performing the rhythm (laya) of the hands and feet. 'Dancing' means performing the dance of the branches.

## Commentary on the Wheel-Treasure
Virtue (sīla) endowed with eight factors that should be constantly observed by laypeople is called Uposatha. Because the king possesses that Uposatha virtue through undertaking it, he is called 'Uposathika'; the meaning of that Uposathika king will be explained. Therefore, the commentator said 'samādinnuposathaṅgassa.' 'Tadā' means at that time (he was sitting).
194:
At that time. If one asks, 'At what time?'—it is at the time when he has reached the fulfillment of the accumulation of merit such as giving (dāna) and virtue (sīla) that leads to the state of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti); when he has performed the duties of a Cakkavatti; when he is born in a specific time, island, and region suitable for a Cakkavatti; and when he is established in an existence (attabhāva) appropriate for that state, being endowed with special qualities such as lineage, physical appearance, wealth, and sovereignty. At such a time, the exceptional person who is to become a Cakkavatti, a Khattiya king, consecrated on the head (muddhāvasitta), endowed with the aforementioned qualities and pure virtue, practices the right conduct such as distributing a hundred thousand coins on the Uposatha day. It is not only when the Wheel-Treasure appears (that he practices this, but even before). These special qualities are stated in common for all Cakkavatti kings. Therefore, it is said, 'Early in the morning... it is the natural law (dhammatā).' The qualities of Bodhisattas that bring about the state of a Cakkavatti, as well as the qualities of a Cakkavatti, are indeed superior to others.

'Having as its cause the merit of the described nature' means having as its cause the merit such as giving (dāna), self-control (dama), and restraint (saṃyama) that lead to the state of a Cakkavatti. 'Similar to a mass of blue sapphires' means similar to a heap of Indanīla gems. 'Because of being endowed with celestial power' means because of being endowed with powers similar to those of devas, such as being beautiful to behold, having a pleasant sound, being able to travel through the air, emitting radiance, being unobstructed, and fulfilling the king's wishes. Thus, because it is like celestial power, it is called 'dibba' (celestial). That Wheel-Treasure does not belong to the deva world. Because this Wheel-Treasure has a thousand spokes, it is called 'sahassāra.' 'In all aspects' means with the desired aspects in a wheel that is complete in all beautiful parts and endowed with marks. 'Paripūra' means completeness; the details of its completeness will now be elaborated.

'Panāḷီ' means a hole. It means a hole without gaps, like a clean and smooth row of teeth. Because the sides around that hub-hole are made of silver, it is said to be 'made of heart-silver.' Since the Wheel-Treasure does not have an 'inner side' like a chariot wheel, it is said 'on both outer ends.' The hub-hole should be connected with 'having a surrounding covering.' 'Nābhipanāḷiparikkhepapaṭṭesu' means on the plate that is the covering of the hub and on the plate that is the covering of the hub-hole.

'Tesaṃ' means of those spokes. 'Ghaṭaka' refers to small full-vases that serve as ornaments. Likewise, 'maṇika' refers to strings of pearls. 'Paricchedalekhā' are the demarcating lines that exist to show the boundaries of the various spokes. By the word 'ādi,' floral designs and so on are included. 'Suvibhattāneva' means they are well-distinguished without being confused with one another.
195:
In the words beginning with "surattā," the term "suratta" (well-reddened) excludes the state of having a pale color caused by mixing various dyes for cloth. The term "suddha" (pure) excludes the state of being soiled, and the term "siniddha" (glossy) excludes the state of being coarse. Although the rim of that Wheel Treasure (Cakkaratana) is produced by kamma without any joints, all the parts within the rim appear beautiful with a young-leaf color, without any other colors. Because it appears as if it has joints due to the well-defined circular lines made of bright red gold bands at the places where a natural wheel would have joints, it is said, "sandhīsu panassa," and so on.

"Nemimaṇḍalapiṭṭhiyaṃ" means on the back surface of the rim. Since that Wheel Treasure travels in the sky, there is a coral handle on the back of the rim that catches the wind. "Dasannaṃ dasannaṃ arānaṃ antare" means in the space near every ten spokes. "Chiddamaṇḍalakhacito" means adorned with circular holes. "Sukusalasamannāhatassa" means well-played by a highly skilled artist. "Vaggū" means pleasant to the mind. "Rajanīyo" means causing passion to arise in those who hear it. "Kamanīyo" means lovely. "Samosaritakusumadāmā" means having hanging garlands of fragrant flowers. "Nemiparikkhepassa" means having a boundary covering the edge of the rim. Regarding the two sides of the hub-opening, it is said, "dvinnampi nābhipanāḷīနံ." That hub-opening is indeed only one. "Yehi" means by the two openings. Again, "yehi" means by those strings and clusters of pearls.

"Odhāpayamānaṃ" means causing them to incline their ears to listen.

The moon goes in front and the Wheel Treasure follows behind; thus they fly in this sequence of front and back.

"Antepurassa" means of the King's palace in the city of Anurādhapura. The phrase "uttarasīhapañjarasadise" is said because at that time, such a lion-window facing the north was available in the King's palace. "Sukhena sakkā" means that it is possible to worship easily by throwing handfuls of flowers with the hand in its natural position, without climbing anywhere and without jumping.

"Nānāvirāgaratanappabhāsamujjalaṃ" means radiant with the brilliance of various multi-colored gems. "Ākāsaṃ abbhuggantvā pavatte" means when it ascends into the sky from the place where it arrived and stayed, and then revolves.

"Rājāyuttā" refers to the officials who are engaged in the King's affairs.
196:
Keeping Mount Sineru on the left side and moving directly east of that Mount Sineru, the commentator said, "leaving Mount Sineru on the left side," referring to the Wheel Treasure.

"Vinibbedhena" means by way of piercing through. "Sannivesakkhama" means a place suitable for establishing a military camp. "Sulabhāhārupakaraṇa" means a place fully equipped with food and drink such as alms-food, snacks, dairy products, firewood, and grass, which can be easily obtained.

"Paracakkaṃ" means the army or the authority of another king.

"Āgamananandano" means one who causes joy by his arrival. He is called "gamanasocano" because he causes sorrow by his departure. "Upakappetha" means "arrange or offer taxes and tributes in the future." "Upaparikkhitvā" means having investigated and reflected through causes, nature, results, and the faults of the present and future lives. Those who make the meaning clear through wisdom are called "vibhāvino" (the wise). "Anuyantā" means followers or retinue. It should be understood that although some of those followers do not refrain from evil out of disgust, either because they are followers or because of the King's great power, they do refrain from evil out of dread (ottappa).

"Ogacchamānaṃ" means descending downwards. "Yojanamattaṃ" means a place measuring one league in width. It descends in such a way that the ground can be seen because of the depth. Therefore, the commentator said, "the surface of the great ocean," and so on. In the end, the Wheel Treasure stands so that the water does not overwhelm the army. Because the great ocean is the boundary to the east of this Wheel Treasure, it is called "puratthimamahāsamuddapariyanta." It means making the eastern great ocean the boundary.

"Cāturantāya" means having the four oceans as its boundary, or having the four directions such as the east as its boundary. In the phrase "sobhayamānaṃ viya," the word "viya" is merely an expletive particle without specific meaning. In reality, that Wheel Treasure stands beautifying itself with its own wonderful qualities. In the Pali text, it is simply stated as "upasobhayamānaṃ."

## Hatthiratana-vaṇṇanā

In the phrase "haricandanādīhi," the word "ādi" includes the four types of fragrances and so on. They submit the request, "Please consider coming," because they have fulfilled and are familiar with the duties of a Universal Monarch. It has a pure white body because it lacks black spots and such. "Sattapatiṭṭho" refers to the Elephant Treasure that stands on the ground with seven parts: the tail, the genitals, the trunk, and the four legs.

It is called 'Sattapatiṭṭha' (sevenfold support) because it stands on the ground with seven parts: the tail, the genitals, the trunk, and the four legs. 'Sabbakaniṭṭho' means it is of a lower grade compared to all elephants of the Chaddanta clan. 'Uposathakulā sabbajeṭṭho' should be construed as: when coming from the Uposatha elephant clan, the elephant that comes is the most supreme and principal among all in that clan. 'Vuttanayena' means according to the method already stated, such as 'having given a great gift,' and so forth. For the sake of Universal Monarchs (Cakkavatti) and the sons of Universal Monarchs who aspire to the status of a Universal Monarch, that Elephant Treasure arrives. 'Apanetvā' means arriving after having driven away other elephants by its own power. Indeed, other elephants cannot even endure the scent of that Elephant Treasure.

'Gharadhenuvacchako viya' means like a calf born and raised in the very same house as a tame domestic cow. 'Sakala-pathaviṃ' refers to the entire earth known as Jambudīpa.

## Description of the Horse Treasure (Assaratana-vaṇṇanā)
'Sindhavakulatō' means it is born from the Sindhu thoroughbred (ājānīya) clan.

## Description of the Gem Treasure (Maṇiratana-vaṇṇanā)
'Sakaṭanābhisamapariṇāhaṃ' means having a circumference equal in size to the hub of a large chariot. 'Ubhosu antesu' means at both ends, the lower and the upper. 'Kaṇṇikapariyantato' means from the edges of the pericarps of two golden lotuses. 'Mutta-jālake ṭhapetvā' means being placed within a very pure net of pearls. By the phrase 'aruṇuggamanavelā viya' (like the time of dawn), it indicates the time of sunrise, taking the rising of the dawn as the primary sign.

## Description of the Woman Treasure (Itthiratana-vaṇṇanā)
After saying, 'The Woman Treasure appears,' the phrase 'Maddarājakulato' (from the royal family of Madda) and so forth is stated to show from which family she arises. It is said that the kingdom of Madda is the place of birth for extremely beautiful women in Jambudīpa. This is true because the Woman Treasures such as the Queen of King Siñcaya, the Queen of King Vessantara, and Bhaddā Kāpilānī were born only in the kingdom of Madda. 'Puññānubhāvena' means due to the power of the merit of the Universal Monarch.

'Saṇṭhānapāripūriyā' means due to the well-proportioned nature of the limbs of the body, such as the hands and feet. Because of the perfection of the parts, the perfection of the whole body is achieved. 'Rūpaṃ' refers to the body, as in the Pali passages like 'rūpaṃ tveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati' (it is just called 'body'). 'Dassanīyā' means endowed with a state worthy of being looked at because of her beautiful form.
198:
Therefore, he said 'dissamānā vā' and so forth. For those who reflect wisely, she gladdens the mind through the power of faith in Kamma and its results, which leads to joy. By the causal statement 'because of bringing clarity to the mind,' he shows the method: just as being inspiring (pāsādika) leads to the perfection of beautiful complexion (vaṇṇapokkharatā), so too being pleasant to behold (dassanīya) leads to being inspiring, and being extremely beautiful (abhirūpa) leads to being pleasant to behold. Alternatively, in reverse order, the connection should be made: because of beautiful complexion, she is inspiring; because she is inspiring, she is pleasant to behold; and because she is pleasant to behold, she is extremely beautiful. Having thus shown her extreme beauty through the perfection of the body, he now says 'abhirūpā vā' and so forth to show those qualities also through the absence of bodily defects. In that passage, just as she is endowed with proper proportions, so too, because of her height and girth, she is inspiring and not too tall, etc. Thus, the perfection of human form that is like that of the devas is described by the words 'though not reaching the divine complexion.'

Perfection of height is stated because she is inspiring in her stature. Perfection of girth is stated because of the absence of the defects of being too thin or too thick. Perfection of complexion is stated because of the absence of discolored skin. 'Kāya-vipattiyā' refers to bodily defects. 'Satavāravihatassa' refers to cotton that has been beaten or carded a hundred times (or seven times according to the Burmese gloss). This phrase 'satavāravihatassa' is said in terms of tree-cotton (kappāsa); however, silk-cotton (tūla) does not need to be beaten at all. Saffron (kuṅkuma), tagara, turukkha, and yavanapuppha are the four types of perfumes. Other teachers say 'tamāla, tagara, turukkha, and yavanapuppha.'

'Aggidaddhā viya' means as if burnt by a fire that has reached one's place. 'Paṭhamam eva' means even upon seeing the King, she is not occupied with other matters, but attends to him before any other business, meaning simultaneously with seeing him. She is called 'pacchānipātinī' because it is her nature to sit down (or retire) only after the King has sat down. She is called 'kiṃkārapaṭissāvinī' because she makes known her readiness to serve by asking, 'What shall I do?' regarding the King's various duties.

Women are generally of a deceitful nature, but to show that the Woman Treasure does not have that deceitful nature, he said 'svāssā' and so forth.

'Guṇā' refers to the qualities of beauty and the qualities of conduct. 'Purimakammānubhāvena' means by the power of past merit, by the power of past merit that brings about the state of being a Woman Treasure. The meritorious Kamma of the Universal Monarch that brings about the perfection of his retinue is also a powerful supporting condition for such a special result. Therefore, he said this.
199:
By the phrase "depending on the merit of the Cakkavatti," it should be understood that although the remaining sentient treasures also arise due to their own kamma, their distinctive qualities are clearly shown to have that king's merit as their powerful support. The perfection that was previously obtained in part (before becoming a Cakkavatti) reached full completion in every aspect from the time the king attained the status of a Cakkavatti.

## Explanation of the Gem of the Householder

Naturally, or even in the time before the appearance of the Wheel-treasure, he was a wealthy person. Just as the appearance of the Wheel-treasure's power occurred depending on the power of the Cakkavatti's merit as previously described, so too, depending on the power of that Cakkavatti's merit, the eye similar to the divine eye arises due to the kamma-result of the Householder-treasure; thus [the commentator] said, "accompanied by the power of the Wheel-treasure." This is said because the cause (merit) falls within a single continuity and the effect (divine eye) arises simultaneously with the cause.

## Explanation of the Gem of the Counselor

He is called "wise" (paṇḍita) because he possesses the state of a wise man characterized by the understanding of ownership of kamma, such as "this is wholesome, this is unwholesome." He is called "skilled" (byatta) due to the quality of great learning. He is called "sagacious" (medhāvī) because he possesses natural wisdom, known as medhā, which is accomplished by nature. He is called "discerning" (vibhāvī) because he is capable of clarifying and explaining the meaning he has correctly understood to others. "To determine" (vavatthapetum) means to be able to decide.

## Explanation of the Possession of the Four Psychic Powers

'Vipaccana' means digestion; 'vipāka' also means digestion. 'Vipāka' itself is called 'vepāka', like the example "what is vikata is vekata." Because that kamma-born heat element is even, being neither too cold nor too hot, there is digestion of the food eaten; therefore, that kamma-born digestive heat is called 'samavepākinī'. He is endowed with that kamma-born digestive heat which digests food evenly.

## Explanation of the Lotus Ponds of the Dhamma Palace

He did not create the lotus ponds by gathering a crowd and having them dig. As for why he did not have them dig with a crowd, [the commentator] said "But of the king..." etc. The reason for not needing to dig with a crowd will come later. The lotus ponds were surrounded by a single railing. In the phrase "at the boundary of the precinct's limit," "precinct" (pariveṇa) refers to the bank of the lotus pond which is an open space all around; at the end, which is the limit of that pond's bank, there were lotus ponds surrounded by a single railing. "Such as in these lotus ponds..." etc., such a thought arose. They bloom in all seasons. They planted various colored flowers and lotus seeds that would bloom. "Water-born and land-born garlands" refers to flowers born in water and flowers born on land.

## Explanation of the Bodhisatta's Past Deeds

"Assa" refers to King Mahāsudassana. "Eko thero" refers to an ordinary monk (puthujjana) whose name and lineage are unknown. "Theraṃ disvā" means seeing the elder sitting at the foot of a certain tree. "Kaṭṭhattharaṇaṃ" means a wooden mat or a wooden plank.

"Paribhogabhājanaṃ" is a vessel suitable for use, such as for drinking water or utility water. "Ārakaṇṭakaṃ" is a tool for piercing the eye of a needle. "Pipphalikaṃ" is a small knife. "Udakatumbakaṃ" is a water pitcher.

"Kūṭāgāradvāreyeva nivattesi" means that from the moment of entering the gabled chamber, he gave no opportunity for those unwholesome wrong thoughts to arise.

The kasina-disk (kasiṇamaṇḍala) becomes apparent because the Great Being (Mahāpurisa) had performed excessive merit in various lives and because those places were like well-prepared kasina-disks.

"Cattāri jhānāni" refers to the four kasina-jhanas. The reason for mentioning only the kasina-jhanas and the immeasurables (appamaññā) is that they were developed with great respect and reverence at that time. In truth, Great Bodhisattas have no special regard for formless jhanas (arūpajhāna), but they develop them as a basis for higher knowledge (abhiññā). Therefore, whatever mundane qualities the Great Being developed during his time as an ascetic or wanderer, he developed all those same qualities when he was King Mahāsudassana. Thus, it was said "Maha-puriso pana," etc.

## Explanation of the 84,000 Cities, etc.

"Abhiharitabbabhattaṃ" means food to be offered. "Nibaddhavattaṃ" means the regular cooking and feeding duty established previously.

## Explanation of Queen Subhaddā's Approach

"Āvaṭṭetvā" means having approached very closely. She specifically praised the fulfillment of whatever gifts, buildings, and luxuries the King desired, exactly as he wished.

If the King were to generate a desire for life, he might remain for a long time with great power and majesty. With such a noble wish, the Queen tried to make the King have regard for his luxuries and life. Thus, it was said:
202:
"Mā heva kho rājā," etc. Therefore, "Tassa kālaṅkiriyaṃ anicchamānā," etc., was said. In the phrase "Chandaṃ janehi," the word 'chanda' is a synonym for craving (taṇhā), so it means "generate affection (pemaṃ uppādehi)." By this nature, one has regard for the object and does not let go; therefore, it is called 'apekkha' (craving).

In the word "Garahitā," answering the internal question "By whom is it censured, and why?", it says "Buddhehi," etc. By this, it shows that death with attachment (sāpekkhakālakiriya) should be avoided because it is censured by the wise and leads to a miserable destination (duggati).

"Ekamantaṃ gantvā" means moving away from the King's sight.

## Explanation of Reaching the Brahma Realm

"Soṇassa" refers to Soṇa, the son of a wealthy man named Koḷivīsa. "Ekā bhattapātī" means a single serving of food prepared for the King. "Tādisaṃ bhattaṃ" means such a meal worth two hundred thousand, which is heavy, sweet, nutritious, and soft. "Bhuttānaṃ" refers to those who have eaten.

"Dāsamanussā" refers to slaves and royal servants.

Now, wishing to show that King Mahāsudassana's attainment of wealth is a result similar to the merit performed, it says "Etāni pana," etc. This statement is easy to understand.

"Ādito paṭṭhāya" means starting from the beginning of the attainment of wealth. It starts from the life of the third householder (gahapati) who performed the merit that caused this wealth. The Buddha taught the Mahāsudassana Jātaka starting from that initial third gahapati life.

The simile "Paṃsuvāgārakīḷaṃ viya" shows: just as children make ponds, houses, and pots out of dust, play as much as they like, and then destroy everything when they leave; similarly, the Buddha showed in detail the inconceivable majesty and wealth similar to divine bliss that He Himself experienced in the life of King Mahāsudassana, and then, turning the teaching towards Nibbāna (vivaṭṭa) by showing the danger and the escape, He said "Passānanda," etc., to show that "all that wealth has changed and perished because it is impermanent."

"Vipariṇatā" means changing, the disappearance of the original nature. Therefore, "Pakativijahanena," etc., was said. "Pakati" means the nature of phenomena as defined by arising and passing away...
203:
The nature of hardness, touch, and so forth, is cut off. That nature has been abandoned starting from the moment of dissolution (bhaṅgakkhaṇa); when it is completely relinquished, it simply no longer exists. Therefore, it is said, "Like an extinguished lamp, they have reached the state of being beyond designation (apaññattikabhāva)."

"Ettāvatā" means by this much of the course of the teaching that has proceeded from the beginning. Because the height (duration) is only many hundreds of thousands of crores of years, it is called "anekavassakoṭisata-sahassubbedhā." "Aniccalakkhaṇaṃ ādāya" means taking the mark of impermanence occurring in that prosperity and making it clear through the teaching. Just as an ordinary person cannot climb a tree a hundred cubits high if the ladder is removed, so too, by revealing impermanence, the ladder of attachment to that prosperity is removed, and thus no one can climb (cling to) it; to show this, it is said, "Like one who takes the mark of impermanence and releases the ladder."

"Teneva" means for the very reason already stated. Although at the beginning the sweetness of the cords of sensual pleasure was shown excessively, later, by showing the fault, baseness, and defilement of those pleasures with "passānanda" and so forth, and the benefits of renunciation (nekkhamma), the teaching was concluded. "Pubbe" means in the past. "Vasabharājā" refers to the great king of the island of Sīhaḷa named Vasabha.

In the word "udakapupphuḷādayo," the word "ādi" includes dew drops on the tips of grass and so forth. In the phrase "Mahāsudassanassa pana," the word "pana" highlights a special meaning. By that word "pana," it is shown that the great king Mahāsudassana produced the attainments of jhāna and higher knowledge (abhiññā), and through that supreme state, he was established in the pure state of a recluse (samaṇabhāva). Having removed the defilements of the recluse's state, such as sensual thoughts (kāmavitakka), he entered a secluded dwelling; yet, on the seventh day after that king passed away, all the prosperity of the Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) disappeared. There was nothing after that. "What an amazing human being, one with extraordinary qualities not shared by others"—this is the distinction shown.

"Anāruḷhaṃ" is said with reference to the previously mentioned meaning, such as "The king, it is said, was formerly born in a wealthy house," and so forth. For that matter was not included in the communal recitation (saṅgīti) in this sutta, but it appears elsewhere as a supplement to this teaching. Whatever is not analyzed here in terms of meaning is indeed easily understood.

## Mahāsudassanasuttavaṇṇanāya Līnatthappakāsanā.
204:
## 5. Janavasabhasuttavaṇṇanā
## Nātikiyādibyākaraṇavaṇṇanā
273-275. Just as the word 'parito' expresses the meaning of 'all around,' it also expresses the meaning of 'near.' Therefore, the meaning is stated as 'sāmantā sāmantā' (near all around). By the repeated word (āmeḍita), the meaning of 'all around' is made clear. Since it is said in the surrounding districts of Nātika village that 'The Blessed One is staying at Nātika village,' the meaning is understood as being in the vicinity of Nātika village. In those surrounding districts of Nātika village, when predicting the destination (gati) of the lay attendants, the prediction for the lay attendants in Nātika village itself is already accomplished automatically. Alternatively, because Nātika village will be directly mentioned in the Pāḷi text, it is simply stated as 'parito parito janapadesu.' 'Paricāraka' refers to the lay followers (upāsakas). Therefore, it is said, 'attendants of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha.' 'Upapatti' refers to the arising in the realms of rebirth. In the phrase 'ñāṇagatipuññānaṃ upapattīsu,' 'ñāṇagatūpapatti' means the arising of the attainment of each path-knowledge (maggañāṇa). With reference to this, it is taught, 'due to the destruction of the five lower fetters,' and so forth. 'Puññūpapatti' means the arising in various groups of devas. This same method applies to the four phrases such as 'Vajjimallesu.' The word 'purimesu' refers to the ten countries mentioned in the Pāḷi, such as Vajjī and Malla. In only those ten countries did He predict the destination of the lay attendants. This is because many people worthy of prediction could be found in those ten countries. Those born in Nātika village are called 'Nātikiyā.' 'Niṭṭhaṅgata' means they have reached a conclusion or certainty.

## Ānandaparikathāvaṇṇanā
Since the good practice of the Saṅgha is due to the excellence of the Dhamma, and the excellence of the Dhamma is due to the perfect enlightenment of the Buddha, praising the qualities of the Dhamma and Saṅgha with 'How wonderful is the Dhamma, how wonderful is the Saṅgha' is, in essence, the praise of the Buddha's qualities. Therefore, the meaning of the phrase 'having the nature of praising the Blessed One' is explained with 'aho dhammo' and so forth.

'Ñāṇagati' is the attainment of path-knowledge (maggañāṇa) that proceeds by way of abandoning what should be abandoned, as mentioned in 'due to the destruction of the five lower fetters (orambhāgiya saṃyojana),' and so forth. By the power of that attainment of knowledge, the distinctions such as the spontaneous rebirth (opapātika) of each noble person (ariya) arise. Therefore, with reference to the future life towards which that noble person is headed, it is said, 'ñāṇābhisamparāyameva.'
206:
The same method applies to monks traveling to distant places, meaning their dangers must be removed. He himself also comes and assembles for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma. 'In such and such' means (provide protection well) in such and such dwelling places of the venerable ones.

'At that time also' refers to the time described as 'Venerable Sir, in the days that occurred previously'. 'For this very reason' means solely because of the occasion of entering the rains retreat. Therefore, it is said in the Pali text: 'On that Uposatha day, the fifteenth, for the sake of entering the rains retreat', and so on. Regarding the seating, in the celestial assembly hall named Sudhammā, after the Tāvatiṃsa devas have first taken their seats, the Four Great Kings sit at the four doors of that Sudhammā hall. This is the established custom for their seating.

'For what purpose' means for what task or for what benefit (they assemble). 'For the purpose of protection' means considering the task of providing protection. Because there is a command spoken (by the devas) to those Great Kings, they are called 'vuttavacanā' (those who receive the spoken command). 'Exceeding' means overpowering (others with radiance), and thus the light appears prominently.

## Sanaṅkumārakathāvaṇṇanā
Being unable to obtain, reach, or see, he is called 'anabhisambhavanīya' (one who cannot be perceived). Therefore, it is explained in the commentary as 'appattabbo' (unattainable), and so on. Since eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) is the path and means for seeing forms, it is called 'cakkhupatha'. To show that he cannot be seen in that eye-path, it is explained as 'in the eye-sensitivity'. Alternatively, the place where the object appears to the eye-sensitivity is called 'cakkhupatha'; thus it is explained as 'in the vicinity of the object'. 'Does not overpower' means he does not come within range; he does not become an object of perception.

'Lower and lower' refers to the devas in the realms below, starting from Tāvatiṃsa. It does not mean starting from Cātumahārājika, nor does it mean starting from the Brahmapārisajja realm. Some teachers say, 'Just as the Cātumahārājika devas can see the natural forms of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, so too the lower Brahmas can see the natural forms of the higher Brahmas'. This is not appropriate. It should be understood that lower Brahmas are indeed unable to see the original rebirth-linking forms (mūla-paṭisandhi-rūpa) of higher Brahmas; they can only see the forms that have been specially manifested.

'Falling into sleep even while listening' means that while (King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī) was investigating and reflecting on the flow of the Pali text, his mind reached a state of stillness and contraction by cutting off externally dispersed thoughts, and thus he fell asleep while listening. 'To my grandfather' is said in reference to the Blessed One.

Because this Brahma has five top-knots of hair, he is called 'Pañcasikha'. It means he is called 'Pañcasikha' because he resembles the deva son Pañcasikha; thus it is explained as 'resembling the Gandhabba Pañcasikha'. 'They cherish' means they are fond of him.
207:
"Sumutto" means being well-freed from the defects of the voice. If the voice were obstructed by bile, phlegm, and so on, it would be impure; to show its clarity due to the absence of those defects, it is said "apalibuddho" (unobstructed). Because it makes the meaning known, it is called "viññeyyo". This word "viññeyyo" is an active derivative (kattu-sādhana) meaning it has the internal cause of making the meaning known, thus it is said "atthaviññāpano" (making the meaning known). The sweetness of the voice means its softness, thus it is said "madhuro mudū" (sweet and soft). Because it is worthy of being heard, it is called "savanīyo". Because it is worthy of being heard and causes pleasure to the ear, it is said "kaṇṇasukho" (pleasant to the ear).

"Bindu" means being compact (rounded). It means being a single mass without being fragmented into pieces like the sound of a struck bronze vessel. Therefore, it is said "ekagghano" (solid/unified). In this way, the non-scattering and non-fragmentation of that voice should be understood as being praised. Because the place of origin of that voice is deep, it has depth; thus it is said "nābhimūlato" (from the base of the navel), etc. "Evaṃ samuṭṭhito" refers to the voice produced merely by the striking of the tongue and so forth. Due to the lightness of the places of origin, it may be unsweet. Because it lacks firmness, it cannot be heard from afar. "Ninnādī" means having a special resonance because it is very extensive, or having a praiseworthy resonance. Therefore, it is said "mahāmegha..." (like a great cloud), etc.

"Pacchimaṃ pacchimaṃ" refers to the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth terms. "Purimassa purimassa" refers to the explanation of the meanings of the first, third, fifth, and seventh terms respectively. The clarity of the voice is known by the ease of understanding the meaning; sweetness is known by its pleasantness to the ear; compactness is known by its non-scattering; and depth is known by its resonance. In the phrase "yathāparisaṃ", the word "yathā" denotes quantity (measure), not variety (manner); thus it is said "yattakā parisā" (how large the assembly is). Therefore, it shows that it is the nature of that Brahmā that the voice issues forth only to the extent of the size of the assembly. Thus it is said "tattakameva" (only that much), etc.

The passage "ye hi keci", etc., is a statement that strengthens the meaning of what was said in "yāvañca so bhagavā", etc., by stating the reason. Because it causes them to attain the bliss of the six celestial realms by making them constantly resort to the refuges and establishing them in the precepts, it is said "ye hi keci...", etc. "Nibbeamatikagahitasaraṇa" refers to those whose refuge is attained through the Path. These people, having completely uprooted doubt, are endowed with unwavering confidence (aveccappasāda) in the Triple Gem. They understand the qualities of the Buddha and others by entering into them through the faith of worldlings. Those who do not have a wisdom that needs to be led by others are to be understood figuratively as those whose refuge is taken without doubt. "Gandhabbadevagaṇaṃ" means the host of Gandhabbas. "Kuṭaja" refers to a resinous tree (the Lin-lun tree). That tree is also called kuṭajarājā.
208:
The resinous tree (Lin-lun tree) is called tukā (khīriṇī); that tree is also called tukā. The powder of that tree is called tukāpiṭṭha (tukā powder). When that powder is pounded and put in, it becomes dense and fills up without gaps.

## Commentary on the Developed Bases of Power

"Supaññattā" means well-made known in various ways. Alternatively, it means placed (in the continuities of those to be taught) without confusion. Since making known and placing without confusion are essentially the teaching itself, it is said "sukathitā" (well-expounded). "Ijjhanaṭṭhena" means because of the sense of success, or because of being the cause of accomplishment (it is called iddhi). "Patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena" means because of the sense of being a foundation (it is called pāda). Because it is the foundation for success, it is called "iddhipāda", meaning the means of attaining success. The reason is that they reach the iddhi (power) called "distinction" (visesa) which occurs later and later through the group of the four preceding mental aggregates which are the means of attainment; therefore, it is called "pāda" (base/foot).

Because it succeeds, it is called "iddhi", meaning it is accomplished or produced. Since iddhi itself is a part/constituent, it is called "iddhipāda", meaning a constituent of success. Thus, first, the meaning in the Pali "cattāro iddhipādā" should be understood. "Iddhipahonakatāya" means due to the ability to produce the power of iddhi. "Iddhivisavitāya" means due to the suitability to produce the power of iddhi. Since roots have many meanings, the word su preceded by vi (visu) has the meaning of suitability (yogya). Alternatively, being able to produce as desired is called "visavitā"; the state of being able to act as desired in producing that power is "visavitā". Therefore, it is said "punappunaṃ" (again and again), etc. "Iddhivikubbanatāya" means for the purpose of creating various forms and appearances through the power of transformation (vikubbaniddhi). Therefore, it is said "for the purpose of showing by making in various ways."

"A bhikkhu, having made intention (chanda) the predominant factor, attains concentration, attains one-pointedness of mind; this is called concentration of intention (chandasamādhi)." According to this Vibhaṅga Pali, it should be understood that the compound was spoken by dropping the word adhipati, meaning concentration where intention is the predominant factor is chandasamādhi. However, by way of showing the meaning of the word adhipati, it should be known that it is explained in the Commentary as "concentration which has intention as its cause, or concentration where intention is excessive, is called chandasamādhi." "Padhānabhūtā" means those (formations) which are energy (viriya), as some teachers say. The term padhāna is used to exclude conditioned formations (saṅkhata-saṅkhāra), etc. Or else, because it accomplishes various specific tasks, all energy is called "saṅkhāra". Among those energies, the term padhāna is used to exclude others from the energy that accomplishes the four tasks (sammappadhāna); therefore, "padhānabhūtā" means those (formations) which are noble/excellent. Because the four types of energy are intended, the plural form (bahuvacana) is used. By way of separate compound construction, taking the previously mentioned meaning of iddhipāda as the meaning of "means" (upāya) and "constituent" (koṭṭhāsa) for the word pāda, as appropriate...
209:
The meaning of the word *pāda* (base) mentioned here should be understood as referring to the agentive sense of *iddhi* and the instrumental sense of *iddhi* regarding the preliminary stages such as *upacāra* (access), etc., which are to be attained later. Alternatively, it refers to the agentive nature of the success (*iddhi*) accomplished through the bases of power such as desire (*chanda*), etc., as taught in the *Uttara-cūḷabhājanīya*, and the instrumental nature of desire, etc. Therefore, in the phrase 'It is *iddhi* in the sense of succeeding,' both the agentive and instrumental senses are taken together. To show the agentive sense first, it says, 'either in the sense of accomplishment or in the sense of succeeding,' and to show the other (instrumental) sense, it says, 'one succeeds by means of this,' and so on. Where is this mentioned? In the *Iddhipāda-vibhaṅga* of the *Vibhaṅga Pāḷi*. 'To one who has become so' means to one who exists having attained those states of desire, etc. By the words 'feeling aggregate' (*vedanākkhandha*), etc., all four aggregates are taught, including desire, etc., within them. 'In the remaining bases of power' means in the remaining bases like the base of energy (*viriyiddhipāda*), etc.

In the description of the base of energy (*viriyiddhipāda-niddesa*), the word 'energy' (*viriya*) appears twice in the phrase 'endowed with concentration of energy and volitional effort' (*vīriyasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ*). There, the first 'energy' is a qualifier for concentration, meaning 'concentration that has energy as its predominant factor is concentration of energy.' The second 'energy' shows the factor of endowment. In all bases of power, only two factors—concentration and volitional effort—are the factors of endowment. Desire, etc., are qualifiers of concentration. Volitional effort, however, is qualified only by the word 'effort' (*padhāna*), not by desire, etc. Therefore, here, the predominance of energy in volitional effort is not taught. Although energy exists qualifying concentration, because it is taught by the word 'volitional effort' (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*) as a factor of endowment, it does not mean endowment with two types of energy. Because concentration is distinguished by desire, etc., and volitional effort and other states are associated with that distinguished concentration, the four bases of power are taught by the power of the qualifiers of concentration. The nature of being a qualifier occurs by showing the respective dependence of desire, etc. Therefore, in this Pāḷi text 'concentration of desire... [pe]... base of power,' although the word *pāda* has the sense of 'dependence' (*nissaya*), it is taught as the nature of the base of power for desire, etc., in the sense of 'means' (*upāya*).

Precisely because the nature of being a base of power in the sense of 'means' is taught, in the *Uttara-cūḷabhājanīya* of the Abhidhamma, the nature of desire, etc., as bases of power is taught as 'The four bases of power: the base of power of desire...' and so on. In the *Pañhapucchaka* (Questionnaire) section, after giving the summary as 'The four bases of power: here a monk [develops] concentration of desire...', the nature of desire, etc., as wholesome, etc., is again analyzed and taught. The description of the base of power as 'dependence' (*nissaya*) is made only to show the base of power as 'means' (*upāya*); otherwise, the fourfold division would not be possible. This should be understood as the decision on the meaning according to the Pāḷi. Now, the statement made to analyze and show the bases of power by way of the preliminary stages is easy to understand. In this *Janavasabha Sutta*, the subject of the bases of power is mentioned only in brief. The details are mentioned in other texts.

The monks residing at the Abhayagiri Monastery say, 'What is called "power" (*iddhi*) is not an ultimate reality (*nipphanna*) accomplished by causes.' Some say, 'The base of power (*iddhipāda*) is not an ultimate reality (*nipphanna*).' In terms of ultimate reality...
210:
The passage starting with 'Api ca' has been taught; it is easily understood. Since the discussion on the bases of power is taught only in brief in this text, it says, 'But in detail... it is taught.'

'Some' refers to the monks residing at the Abhayagiri Monastery. Among those monks, some say, 'What is called "power" (*iddhi*) is not an ultimate reality (*nipphanna*) accomplished by causes.' Others say, 'Only the base of power (*iddhipāda*) is not an ultimate reality.' 'Unproduced' (*anipphanna*) means not established in the ultimate sense, meaning it does not exist. 'Brought' means brought from the Abhidhamma Pāḷi to this Dīgha Nikāya Commentary. It is brought because the teaching proceeds in a different manner from the previous Pāḷi method.

Desire itself is the base of power, thus it is the 'base of power of desire' (*chandiddhipāda*). This same method applies to the remaining terms like the base of power of energy, etc. 'But these states' refers to the bases of power mentioned in this Sutta.

The Elder Raṭṭhapāla thought, 'If there is desire, why would they not give permission?' and after not eating for seven days and getting permission from his parents to ordain, he relied solely on desire and produced the supramundane Dhamma. Therefore, it is said, 'The Elder Raṭṭhapāla... produced [it].'

The Elder Soṇa, while devoted to meditation, possessed stirred-up energy. Although he was very delicate and blisters formed on his feet, he did not relax his energy. Therefore, it is said, 'The Elder Soṇa, making energy the lead...'

The Elder Sambhūta, thinking 'What task cannot be accomplished by one who has mind?', made mind the precursor and succeeded in meditation. Therefore, it is said, 'The Elder Sambhūta, making mind the lead...'

The Elder Mogharāja relied on wisdom. Therefore, the Blessed One taught him the Dhamma of emptiness (*suññatā*), saying, 'Look upon the world as empty [of self].' To subdue the conceit that relies on wisdom and to investigate wisdom, he was asked twice and then answered the question. Therefore, it is said, 'The Venerable Mogharāja, making investigation the lead...'

The repeated production of desire is like giving a command; thus, the similarity of desire to attendance and service is stated.

By the word '*parakkhamena*' (by supreme effort), courage is stated, taking effort as the lead. Because of the nature of strength, the similarity of energy to a courageous person should be seen.

Because thinking is the primary function, the similarity of the mind to the arrangement of a mantra or counsel is stated.
211:
The state of having a distinguished birth is called jātisampatti (perfection of birth). Since it is said, "Among all things, wisdom is the most excellent," the state of vīmaṃsā (investigation) being similar to jātisampatti has been stated. In the Sammohavinodanī Aṭṭhakathā, however, the state of cittiddhipāda (base of power of consciousness) being similar to jātisampatti, and the state of vīmaṃsiddhipāda (base of power of investigation) being similar to the power of a mantra, are explained in connection.

Because this psychic power has many various parts and portions that are performed, it is called "anekavidha" (manifold). Since the word "vidha" is a synonym for "koṭṭhāsa" (portion/part), as in the Pali passages such as "ekavidhena ñāṇavatthu", "iddhividha" is stated to mean "the portions of psychic power".

## Explanation of the Three Types of Okāsādhigama

Because this word "sukhassa" refers to all three types of bliss, it is stated as "bliss of jhāna, bliss of the path, and bliss of the fruit". However, because they reach various types of absorption (appanā) and because they are not primary, the bliss of access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) and the bliss of insight (vipassanā) are not taken here. In the first two types of okāsādhigama (the first jhāna and the fourth jhāna), all three types of bliss are obtained. But how is it in the third okāsādhigama? In that third okāsādhigama, although all three types of bliss cannot certainly be obtained, two types (the bliss of the path and the bliss of the fruit) are indeed obtained. This statement is made according to what is available, similar to the Pali sentences: "One can see the gravel, the schools of fish, those moving, and those standing still." "Saṃsaṭṭha" means one who has reached association or is endowed with. Since that person also has a mind endowed with those qualities, it is stated as "sampayuttacitta" (associated mind). "Ariyadhamma" refers to the Dhamma that makes one a Noble One (ariya). "Upāyato" means by way of method; "pathato" means by way of path; "kāraṇato" means by way of cause. The method by which the practice in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānudhamma-paṭipatti) arises, and because one approaches through that method, it is called "upāya". Because that upāya is the path to the attainment of that Dhamma, it is called "patha". Because it produces that Dhamma, it is also called "kāraṇa".

To explain the meaning briefly stated as "one attends by way of impermanence, etc.", the words beginning with "What is called yoniso manasikāra..." are stated. Among them, "upāya-manasikāra" is the attention that is the cause for the arising of wholesome states (kusala dhamma). "Patha-manasikāra" is the attention that is the path for the arising of those wholesome states. "Anicce" is the construction of meaning as attending to the formations (saṅkhāra) of the three planes of existence, which are impermanent because they have a beginning and an end and because they are not eternal, as "impermanent". This same method applies to the remaining terms. However, this is the distinction: in those same formations of the three planes, one attends to them as "suffering" (dukkha) because they are repeatedly oppressed by the nature of arising and passing away, because they are loathsome, and because they are difficult to endure; and one attends to them as "non-self" (anatta) because they do not follow one's will and because they do not have the nature of a living self (atta)...
212:
Because of its impure nature, it is called asubha (impurity). In truth, all conditioned things (saṅkhata) in the three planes of existence deserve to be called only "asubha" because they pour out the impurities of the defilements (kilesa). "Saccānulomikena vā" means by way of the power that conforms to the realization of the Four Noble Truths. By the words "cittassa āvaṭṭanā" etc., the occurrence of the mind-door wholesome impulsion (manodvārika kusala javana) which is the cause of adverting (āvajjana) and which arises before that adverting, is stated as such by using the name of the effect for the cause. This is because, by the power of that mind-door wholesome impulsion, that adverting becomes a strong dependence (upanissaya) for the arising of the wholesome. Adverting is called "cittassa āvaṭṭanā" because it turns the life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga-citta); it is called "anvāvaṭṭanā" because it turns it repeatedly. It is called "ābhoga" because it attends to an object other than the object of the bhavaṅga. It is called "samannāhāra" because it brings it well to mind. It is called "manasikāra" because it places the object in the mind that arises by following and following itself. This Dhamma, which has the characteristic of upāya-manasikāra, is called "yoniso manasikāra"; by the power of that yoniso manasikāra, a person is able to reflect upon and attend to the Four Noble Truths, such as suffering.

"Asaṃsaṭṭho" means being secluded and separate, not mixed with sensual desires (kāma), etc. The happiness that arises due to the non-mixing with sensual desires, etc., is the joy and bliss born of seclusion (vivekaja pīti-sukha) from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), and thus it is called "paṭhamajjhāna-sukha" (bliss of the first jhāna). Although the bliss of the first jhāna is indeed joy (somanassa), in the Sutta texts, because that bliss of the first jhāna is also the cause of bodily bliss (kāyika-sukha), it is specifically called only "sukha". Therefore, here too, the somanassa that is part of the jhāna is called "sukha", while other somanassa is called "somanassa". Thus it is stated as "sukhā". Because the ablative case is used in the sense of cause (hetu), it means "jhānasukha-paccayā" (due to the cause of the bliss of jhāna). "Aparāparaṃ somanassaṃ" refers to the joy that arises repeatedly by way of reflection (paccavekkhaṇā), etc., due to the cause of attaining jhāna.

Gladness and delight is called "pamuda"; it is tender rapture (taruṇa-pīti); from that, it is called "pamudā". In Pali passages such as "pāmojjaṃ pītatthāya", tender rapture is called "pāmojja". However, here, distinguished delight (pakaṭṭha-muda) is intended as "pamuda", and that is what is meant by "pāmojja". Since that pāmojja cannot exist without joy (somanassa), it is stated as "stronger rapture and joy" (balavatara pīti-somanassa) due to their inseparable nature. With reference to being the direct opposite of jhāna, it is stated as "having removed the five hindrances". In truth, jhāna indeed removes all defilements and all unwholesome states that exist in the same place as those hindrances, and it stands having taken its own opportunity (okāsa) because it cannot be overcome by opposing states. Therefore, from the taking of opportunity, it means "laddhokāsatā" (the state of having gained an opportunity). Alternatively, it is called "okāsa" because it is the opportunity or way for the attainment of the bliss of the path and fruit; the attainment of that okāsa is "okāsādhigama". In the former view, it is called "okāsādhigama" because one attains the opportunity (avasara) by means of this Dhamma.
213:
Because initial and sustained thoughts (vitakka-vicāra) associated with in-breathing and out-breathing have a physical nature, depend entirely on the body, and involve diffusion and movement, [the Teacher], wishing to allow for their coarse state, said: 'Let the bodily formations and verbal formations be coarse first.' Because they are the opposite of those [bodily and verbal formations], he did not wish to allow for the coarseness of certain feelings and perceptions, and thus asked: 'How are mental formations coarse?' Another teacher, giving the reason 'because they have not yet been abandoned,' explained that meaning starting with 'Bodily formations...' These mental formations are unabandoned formations, and because they possess the sign of existing formations, they deserve to be called 'coarse.' However, abandoned formations, lacking that sign, are 'subtle.' Thus, he said: 'In comparison to abandoned states, they are called coarse because they have not yet been abandoned.' Because it is said in the Pali text, 'due to the tranquilization of bodily formations,' it is stated that 'happiness is the happiness of the attainment of fruition associated with the fourth jhāna.' Because it is said, 'due to the tranquilization of mental formations,' it is stated, 'for one emerging from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).' It should be understood that the tranquilization of verbal formations is accomplished by the tranquilization of bodily formations itself. Therefore, he said: 'The second... etc., are not mentioned separately.' In the Pali text, although it is accomplished by way of meaning, it is taken explicitly (sarūpato) to make it very clear. Indeed, in the Noble Discipline (ariya-vinaya), explaining the implication of meaning (atthāpatti) is not the usual practice of the Abhidhamma teaching. Just as the removal of hindrances is the means for attaining the first jhāna, the removal of pleasure and pain is the means for attaining the fourth jhāna; thus it is said: 'The fourth jhāna, having removed pleasure and pain.' The rest is as explained below.

Because it is accompanied by faults such as ignorance and lust, it is called 'blameworthy' (sāvajja), which is unwholesome. Because of the absence of those faults, it is called 'blameless' (anavajja), which is wholesome. Because it should be associated with by one desiring one's own welfare and happiness, it is called 'to be cultivated' (sevitabba), which is wholesome. Because it is the opposite of that, it is 'not to be cultivated' (na sevitabba), which is unwholesome. Because of its low nature, it is 'inferior' (hīna), which is unwholesome. Because of its excellent nature, it is 'superior' (paṇīta), which is wholesome. Thus, these three dyads, such as the blameworthy dyad, should be understood accordingly through these wholesome and unwholesome courses of action (kammapatha). 'All' (sabbaṃ) refers to all phenomena encompassed by the four dyads mentioned. They are called 'dark' (kaṇha) and 'bright' (sukka) because they are opposites, and 'with a counterpart' (sappatibhāga) and 'without a counterpart' (appatibhāga) because of their non-dual nature. Ignorance, which covers the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa), is abandoned through the correct penetration of the Four Noble Truths. Because of that abandonment, the knowledge of the path of arahantship (arahatta-magga-vijjā) arises. 'Happiness' (sukha) here refers to the happiness of the path of arahantship and the happiness of the fruition of arahantship for one who, having investigated the phenomena of the three planes starting with the courses of action, exerts effort in insight and stands in the fruition of arahantship through the sequence of the paths. Other paths are also included therein because they occur without interval.
214:
Regarding 'by way of the thirty-eight objects' (aṭṭhatiṃsārammaṇavasena), it means they are explained in detail by way of the thirty-eight meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) mentioned in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Pali. The intention is that they are explained in detail because they appear by way of the first jhāna and so forth in the Pali text on the attainment of opportunities (okāsādhigama). With the words 'How?' (kathaṃ) etc., he shows the method by which that very attainment of opportunities can be known in detail. What should be said regarding the Pali passages such as 'in twenty-four places' (catuvīsatiyā ṭhānesu) has already been explained by me, the commentator, in the commentary on the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta. By the phrase 'having reached the attainment of cessation' (nirodhasamāpattiṃ pāpetvā), the formless jhanas are also included. This is because it is impossible to enter the attainment of cessation without the formless jhanas, and because those formless jhanas have the nature of the fourth [rupa] jhāna. 'Ten access jhanas' (dasa upacārajjhānāni) refers to the ten access concentrations consisting of the eight recollections (excluding mindfulness of the body and mindfulness of breathing) and the two perceptions (perception of the repulsiveness of food and the analysis of the four elements). What is called 'higher virtue' (adhisīla) leads to concentration. Therefore, because it is said that the lower limit of that higher virtue ends at the first jhāna, it is stated: 'The training in higher virtue reaches the first attainment of opportunity.' What is called 'higher mind' (adhicitta) ends at the fourth jhāna. Because the formless jhanas are included in that fourth jhāna, and because the fruition jhanas end in that fourth jhāna, it is said: 'The training in higher mind is the second.' Because it has reached the summit, what is called 'training in higher wisdom' (adhipaññā-sikkhā) is the knowledge of the path of arahantship; thus he said: 'The training in higher wisdom is the third.' One who extracts the three attainments of opportunity by way of the three trainings should also extract them by way of the various suttas accordingly; to show this, he said 'also in the Sāmaññaphala [Sutta]' etc.

Just as the three trainings reach the three attainments of opportunity in sequence, by that same principle, because those three trainings are primary, the three Pitakas also reach those attainments of opportunity in sequence; to show this, he said 'But in the three' (tīsu pana) etc. 'Having divided the three Pitakas' (tīṇi piṭakāni vibhajitvā) means that we shall have the opportunity to explain the three Pitakas in detail in sequence by way of the three attainments of opportunity. 'Having combined' (samodhanetvā) means having properly connected and brought the meaning taught in those three Pitakas as the meaning of this sutta. It cannot be said that it was poorly spoken due to disconnected speech or excessive elaboration, because such a discourse is indeed well-spoken; therefore he said: 'The Tipitaka... is well-spoken.'

## Commentary on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness

The meaning of 'wholesome' (kusala) should not be taken solely by the method of the Abhidhamma teaching, but also by the method of the Bāhitika Sutta teaching; thus he said: 'And of the wholesome fruition' (phalakusalassa ca). 'In the sense of security' (khemaṭṭhena) means [wholesome] because of the state of being free from danger through the four bonds (yoga). 'Well-concentrated' (sammā samāhito) means...
215:
One is well-concentrated by the power of tranquility (samatha) and by the power of insight (vipassanā). Ekaggacitto means one whose mind has reached one-pointedness and non-distraction because distraction has been driven far away. Attano kāyato means that by the power of contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) in one's own physical body, one has a mind that is well-concentrated, in accordance with the words: "One who is concentrated knows and sees things as they really are."

While producing knowledge and vision in one's own body, one also produces knowledge and vision in the bodies of others external to oneself. Therefore, it is said: "One directs the knowledge towards the bodies of others." Sammā vippasīdati means to enter into the object of one's own physical body with great clarity associated with knowledge, which has well-established concentration as its cause. Sabbattha means in all places. The connection should be made as "mindfulness has been taught." The foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), which are a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane, have been taught. This is because the knowledge and vision of contemplation (anupassanā) are common to both.

## Explanation of the Seven Requisites of Concentration

Ettha means in this discussion. Because virtue (sīla) is taught as the ornament of the chariot of the Noble Path, which has meditative absorption (jhāna) as its axle and energy (vīriya) as its wheels, it is said: "The ornament is called a requisite (parikkhāra)." Sattahi nagaraparikkhārehi means by these seven types of city fortifications: the moat, the rampart, the wall, the gate-pillar, the crossbar, and the circular buildings atop the walls, which are the enclosures made by those who surround and protect the city. In this context, it is called sambhāra (requisite/equipment) because it brings about the result; it is a cause.

Just as medicine is the cause (sambhāra) of life by curing illness. Parivāraparikkhāravasena means by the power of the requisites known as retinues. The Path factors such as Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi) are called requisites because they prepare and construct Right Concentration (sammā-samādhi) by way of conditions such as conascence (sahajāta). It is called upanisā because it is approached and relied upon. Because it exists together with upanisā, it is called saupanisa. Therefore, it is said: "saupanissayo." Here, upanissaya is intended as a group of states that act as a cooperating cause.

Because one possesses good, praised, and excellent wisdom, that person is called sammā-diṭṭhi (one of Right View). For that person who has Right View, [Right Intention arises]. Because that person is established in Right View, it is said: "of one established in Right View." Sammā-saṅkappo pahoti means that just as Right View of the Path, while accomplishing the functions of fully understanding suffering etc., is able to accomplish its own task by uprooting thoughts of sensual desire etc., so too Right Intention arises. To show its occurrence, it is said: "Right Intention arises." This method applies to all terms; by the phrase "for one with Right Intention, Right Speech arises," etc., the meaning already stated is applied to the remaining terms.
216:
In this context, Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi) is of great benefit to the yogi who is practicing to attain Nibbāna. This is true. Right View is also called "the lamp of wisdom" and "the weapon of wisdom." With that Right View, the yogi dispels the darkness of ignorance (avijjā), slays the thieves of defilements (kilesa), and reaches Nibbāna safely. Therefore, in the discourse on the Noble Path, Right View is taken at the very beginning. Here, however, in the teaching according to the person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), it is stated as "for one who has Right View."

Because a person with Right View intends rightly by the power of thoughts of renunciation (nekkhamma-saṅkappa) etc., and does not intend wrongly by the power of thoughts of sensual desire (micchā-kāmasaṅkappa) etc., therefore, for one with Right View, Right Intention arises.

Right Intention is a benefactor to Right Speech. As it is said: "Householder, first one thinks and ponders, and afterwards one breaks into speech," therefore, for one with Right Intention, Right Speech arises.

Because one mostly carries out various actions properly only after first arranging them through speech, saying "I will do this and that," speech (Right Speech) is a benefactor to bodily action (Right Action). Therefore, for one with Right Speech, Right Action arises.

Only in a person who fulfills both types of good conduct by abandoning the four types of verbal misconduct and the three types of bodily misconduct is virtue with Right Livelihood as the eighth (ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla) perfected, and not in others. Therefore, for one with Right Speech and Right Action, Right Livelihood arises.

For one with Right Livelihood that has arisen from purified view, Right Effort (sammā-vāyāma) can occur through wise and proper striving. For one striving wisely, mindfulness is well-established in the four objects such as the body (satipaṭṭhāna). Therefore, for one with Right Effort, Right Mindfulness arises.

Mindfulness thus well-established is able to place the mind well on a single object by investigating the paths of states that are beneficial and unbeneficial to concentration. Therefore, for one with Right Mindfulness, Right Concentration arises.

This method is stated by the power of Right View and so on, which occur at different moments in the preliminary stage (the period of insight). However, at the moment of the Path (magga-khaṇa), the meaning of the terms such as "for one with Right View, Right Intention arises" is appropriate by the power of conascence (sahajāta) etc., of those states like Right View. And this is precisely what is intended here. Therefore, it is said: "But this meaning..." and so on.

"In Path Knowledge" means for one who is established in the knowledge included in the Noble Path, one who is possessed of that. Path wisdom is called "Right View of the Path" (magga-sammā-diṭṭhi) because of its sense of rightly seeing the Four Truths. That same wisdom is also called "Path Knowledge" (magga-ñāṇa) here because of its knowing and penetrating the Four Truths as they really are. "Liberation by the Path" (magga-vimutti) is simply the liberation from defilements by the Path, which is abandonment by uprooting (samuccheda-pahāna). Right View which is the Fruit...
219: The matter stated by the method of extracting the meaning is the same fourfold matter previously mentioned. The Tāvatiṃsa devas and some Cātumahārājika devas observe the five precepts (pañca sīla) for the stability of their attained prosperity and for future purification. To purify those precepts, they perform the act of support through Pavāraṇā. Therefore, it was said, 'By the Great Pavāraṇā,' and so forth. 'Vassasahassa' means a thousand years by human calculation. 'Pannapalāsa' refers to the state when leaves have fallen. 'Khārakajāta' refers to the state where very small buds have appeared. Those very small buds with dark green leaves are called 'khāraka.' 'Jālakajāta' refers to the state where those small buds appear like a complete network of flames. Some teachers, however, explain 'jālakajāta' as appearing like a single mass of flame. It is said that when the Pāricchattaka tree (coral tree) takes on very small buds, the entire tree becomes covered with young shoots; those young shoots shine brilliantly with the color of radiant coral, and thus the entire tree stands glowing. 'Kuṭumalakajāta' refers to the state where large buds have well formed. 'Korakajāta' refers to the state where the leaf-wraps are breaking open and are about to bloom right now. 'Sabbapāliphulla' refers to the state of being in full and wide bloom. 'Kantanaka-vāta' is the wind that cuts the flowers due to the merit of the devas. 'Kantati' means it cuts. 'Sampaṭicchanaka-vāta' is the wind that receives the flowers that have been cut. 'Naccanto' means performing swaying or bending in various forms. 'Aññataradevatānaṃ' refers to devas who are not well-known by name or lineage. 'Reṇuvaṭṭi' is a mass of pollen. 'Kaṇṇikaṃ āhacca' means striking the pinnacle of the Sudhammā assembly hall. The phrase 'on the eight days' refers to the four days in the waxing fortnight and the four days in the waning fortnight, including the Uposatha day (totaling eight days). Listening to the Dhamma occurs regularly on those eight mentioned days. Regarding the listening to Dhamma performed on days other than those eight, it is said, 'One should listen to the Dhamma even at improper times.' The railing made below the parasol on a cetiya is called 'Chattavedikā.' The diamond-patterned wall made by enclosing the area for circumambulation around the cetiya is called 'Puṭavedikā.' The terrace made surrounding the 'belly' (middle part) of the cetiya and connected to the body of the cetiya is called 'Kucchivedikā.' A throne with a base in the shape of a lion is called 'Sīhāsana.' A staircase fitted with lion figures on both sides is called 'Sīhasopāna.'
220:
(The devas) are delighted because it is not a fixed tradition. For this very reason, (the commentator) said, 'Having placed great merit at the forefront,' and so forth. It should be understood that they assemble for the sake of supporting the monks who perform Pavāraṇā by protecting them from danger. This is understood from the words: 'On that Uposatha day, on the full moon night of the fifteenth day, the day of Pavāraṇā, they assemble.'

'Navahi kāraṇehi' means (worshipping and rejoicing) by the nine reasons that manifest the Buddha's power, such as the attribute of 'Arahaṃ,' as taught in 'Itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ,' etc. In the phrase 'Dhammassa ca,' the word 'ca' (and) has the sense of including the unmentioned Saṅgha. Therefore, wishing to show the meaning combined by that 'ca,' he said, 'and the good practice (suppaṭipatti) of the Saṅgha, which is divided into upright practice and so forth.'

## Commentary on Yathābhuccha
Just as in the Pāli, the infinite space itself is called 'ānañca,' and the physician himself is called 'bhesajja,' so too, the attributes that are only as they truly are, are called 'yathābhuccha' in the Pāli; with this intention, he said, 'Yathābhuccha means as it really is (yathābhūta).' Because they are worthy of praise and proclamation, 'vaṇṇa' refers to the qualities or virtues. The question 'How did he practice? (kathaṃ paṭipanno)' is asked with the desire to speak of the practice of the Lord of the World for the benefit of many beings in these three stages: the causal stage, the resultant stage, and the stage of benefiting beings. Indeed, showing that practice of the Buddha from the beginning to the end in brief, he said, 'At the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha,' and so forth. In that context, 'abhinīharamāno' means making the resolve (abhinīhāra). What should be said regarding this great resolve and the perfections (pāramīs) has already been explained in the Brahmajāla Sutta Sub-commentary (Ṭīkā), and should be understood according to the method stated there.
