The phrase 'At the time of being the Khantivādī ascetic,' and so forth, is an explanation of the practice for the benefit of many beings, which is extremely difficult to perform and not shared by others, even in the causal stage. To show that the practice of such actions—without which the desired welfare and happiness cannot be accomplished—is solely for that purpose, he said, 'Even while staying in the Tusita heaven for the full lifespan,' and so forth.

Furthermore, the practice such as the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakkappavattana) is the practice performed for the benefit of many beings. Even the relinquishing of the life-principle (āyusaṅkhāra) is a practice for the benefit of many beings by determining, 'I shall remain for this much time.' The parinibbāna by the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu) is also a practice for the welfare of many beings. Therefore, he said, 'Until his (parinibbāna),' and so forth. The remaining terms refer to words such as 'for the happiness of many beings.' The final term is 'for the purpose, for the benefit (atthāya hitāya)'...
221:
## 
"Sukhāya" refers to the three terms [atthāya, hitāya, sukhāya]. "Purimassa" refers to the three terms preceding those [bahujanahitāya, etc.]. "Attho" means the explanation of the meaning.

Even if there were teachers in the past endowed with [qualities like bahujanahita], since they were also Buddhas, in essence, our Teacher is no different. Thus it is said, "In the past, we do not see anyone other than the Buddha." Just as in the past, so in the future [there is no other than the Buddha]; because this meaning can be inferred, it is said, "In the future also, we do not see [anyone else]." Sakka, the King of Devas, however, did not state this meaning directly but made it an implied meaning, saying only, "But not now." To investigate what Sakka meant, the inquiry "What does Sakka say?" was raised. It is not that Sakka, the King of Devas, did not distinguish that Buddhas appeared in the past and will appear in the future; rather, he grouped them with our Blessed One by their common Buddhahood, and because there is absolutely no other [Buddha] at this time, he spoke thus. To show this, the words beginning with "Etarahi" (now) were spoken. "Svākkhātādīni" refers to terms such as svākkhāta (well-expounded). "Kusalādīni" refers to terms such as "this is wholesome."

Just as the water of the Ganges and Yamuna rivers has different colors where they do not meet, but has the same color where they do meet, it is said, "It coincides and meets even in color." In that place of meeting, the water of the Yamuna is indeed similar to the water of the Ganges. Just as Nibbāna is pure because it is not defiled by any defilement, so too the practice leading to Nibbāna should be understood as pure, being undefiled by any defilement. Therefore, the words beginning with "Na hi" were spoken. Because of the sense of purity by which Nibbāna and the practice leading to Nibbāna are compared to the sky, and because that sense of purity is unattached to anything and undefiled, it is said, "The sky also is unattached and pure." Now, to make that meaning clear with an example, the words beginning with "Candimasūriyānaṃ" (of the moon and sun) were spoken. It coincides and fits because of the mutual suitability between the state of what should be practiced and the actual practice.

"Paṭipadāya ṭhitānaṃ" means [for the sake of] those who are practicing the path of the Noble Way. "Vusitavataṃ" means [for the sake of] those who have lived the holy life. "Laddhasahāyo" means [the Blessed One] who has companions obtained through the power of these practices. In various duties to be performed by disciples for the Teacher, [He has companions]. However, the word "Adutiyo" (without a second/peerless) found in other Suttas is spoken in the sense of being unlike others, not because of a lack of the aforementioned companions. "Apanujja" means having removed or avoided. Since the word "Apanujja" contains an internal limitation (certainty), it is said "Apanujjeva" to refer to the certainty of that removal.
222:
## 
It is called "gain" (lābha) because it is obtained. That gain is highly extraordinary as it is known to have reached an exalted state. Since only widespread and abundant gain is intended here, it is said, "A great gain has arisen." "Ussannapuññanissandasamuppanno" means it has arisen from the flow of extremely widespread and noble merit accumulated over the previously mentioned period of four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons. As if exerting effort with the thought, "These fruits of merit have arisen; after reaching this state of Buddhahood, there will be no further opportunity for my [gain] to arise," it arose increasing successively.

Just as a great twin-cloud rises in all directions and forms a massive storm cloud, all the perfections (pāramīs) combined as if saying, "We shall give fruit in this single existence," and produced this gain, honor, and fame for the Blessed One. Because of that, Khattiyas, Brahmins, and others approached, holding food, drink, clothing, vehicles, flowers, scents, and ointments in their hands, searching for the Blessed One, asking, "Where is the Buddha? Where is the Blessed One? Where is the God of gods? Where is the Bull among men? Where is the Lion among men?" Even though they brought offerings in hundreds of carts, they found no opportunity to donate, and so they stood in the surrounding area for about a league (gāvuta), with the axles of their carts almost touching, and followed him continuously like the Brahmin Andhakavinda and others. All this should be understood according to the method found in the Khandhaka and various Suttas. Therefore, it is said, "Gain and honor are like a great flood," and so on.

"Paṭipāṭibhatta" refers to the meal offered in sequence when many people come forward saying, "We shall give an offering." That offering reached the pinnacle because it was not shared with others. He explained the method to the citizens to enable them to give an offering in a manner they could not otherwise achieve. The Sālakalyāṇီ trees were royal property and not common to others; therefore, a pavilion was built with planks from those trees. Elephants were also royal property and could not be obtained by the citizens; therefore, umbrellas were held by those elephants. Likewise, princesses were made to perform service (veyyāvacca). The phrase "five hundred seats" refers to the seats arranged inside the Sālakalyāṇီ pavilion. Outside that pavilion, however, many seats were arranged. They ground four types of perfume to honor the Sangha headed by the Buddha and to rub the bowls. "Water" refers to the water for washing the bowls. These were invaluable things because they were prepared with priceless gems.

The head will split into seven pieces due to causes such as disrespect. "I shall watch the time" means "I will thus observe the time and ward off the harm that would arise for him."
223:
Kadariya refers to those who turn their backs on performing meritorious deeds and are firmly stingy. Such people do not reach the celestial realms because they have not performed merit and have instead accumulated evil through their stinginess. Bāla refers to those endowed with the characteristics of a fool, such as having evil thoughts. They do not praise giving (dāna); they are not even capable of praising it. Dhīra refers to one who is endowed with steadfast concentration and possesses noble wisdom; by repeatedly rejoicing in the gifts given by others, such a person becomes endowed with both physical and mental happiness in the next world.

Vararoja was the name of the sole khattiya (warrior-noble) at that time. It is meant that for that King Vararoja, because of speaking untruths, his lip would become twisted and his head would split into seven pieces even in his faultless body. Because of his devotion to the physical beauty [of the Buddha], he spoke only in praise of his virtues through more than a thousand words and two hundred and fifty-three verses.

In the phrase "Yāva maññe khattiyā," the word "yāva" is a term indicating a limit or boundary, and the word "maññe" is merely a particle (nipāta). It means that all devas and humans live with affection, taking the khattiyas as the limit. Therefore, he said "Khattiyā brāhmaṇā" and so forth. Madappamatta means being intoxicated and conceited due to gain, honor, and fame, thus becoming negligent, and the subsequent negligence that follows that conceit.

"Tadanvayam eva" refers to the physical actions that follow and conform to the words of the Blessed One. Verbal actions and physical actions do not contradict each other; rather, they truly and certainly conform to one another. Because only goats are the prey, they are called "ajāmiga." Seeing those prey which are goats...

The Blessed One is one who has completely crossed the wilderness of doubt. One might ask: "Do not all Stream-enterers (sotāpanna) also lack doubt?" While it is true that Stream-enterers are free from doubt, what Sakka, the King of Devas, means here is not that kind of freedom from doubt. It is said with reference to the absolute removal of doubt through the decisive realization of all aspects of all knowable things (ñeyyadhamma), as indicated by the words "Yathā hi" and so forth. This occurs due to the excellence of the elements (dhātu). This meaning is also accomplished through the power of the Blessed One's Knowledge of the Various and Manifold Elements (Anekadhātunānādhātuñāṇa). Because he perceives all that is to be known, he is free from doubt in everything. Because he has realized all ultimate realities (paramattha-dhamma) through the knowledge of the realization of the Truths, it is said "by way of conventional expression" or "by way of name and lineage."

Pariyositasaṅkappa refers to one whose desires and intentions are completely fulfilled. One might object: "Is it not that the fulfillment of intentions occurs through the Noble Path by the completion of the sixteen functions of the path, and not by the realization of all knowable things?" To address this, it was said:
224:
Regarding the words "Pubbe ananussutesu" and so forth, it is explained: Just as the Disciple's Knowledge of Perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa) and the Paccekabuddha's Knowledge of Self-Enlightenment (paccekabodhi-ñāṇa) are preceded by the realization of the Four Noble Truths, so too the Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) of the Sammāsambuddhas is preceded only by the realization of the Four Noble Truths. "Ananussutesu" means in things not heard of before. "Sāmaṃ" means by oneself. By these two words, he shows the realization without hearing from another (parato ghosa). The word "tattha" is in the locative case (sattamī) in the sense of cause (nimitta), meaning "because of the cause of the realization of the Truths." It should be understood that the realization of the Truths occurs by the power of the Utmost Path (arahatta-magga). "Balesu ca vasībhāvaṃ" refers to the attainment of mastery to exercise the ten powers of knowledge (bala-ñāṇa) as desired. In saying "Jātattā jātā," he refers to the Sammāsambuddha.

He dwells continuously in various royal capitals and so forth, and wanders for alms in the three circles (maṇḍala) at the appropriate times.

"Assa" refers to the effect (phala). "Taṃ" refers to the cause (kāraṇa). Since there is no cause for two Buddhas to arise simultaneously, how much less could there be for three or four? The passage beginning with "Ettha ca" is undertaken to show the extent and measurement of the world-system (lokadhātu) called "a single world-system."

"Yāvatā" means in as much space. "Pariharanti" means the moon and the sun revolve, encircling Mount Sineru. "Disā" is a nominative form used in the sense of the locative case, meaning "in the directions." "Bhanti" means they shine. "Virocanā" means the moon and the sun shine while spreading radiance or while being beautiful; because the moon and the sun shine in this way, the directions also shine. "Tāva sahassadhā" refers to that thousand-fold world-system (cakkavāḷa).

"Ettakaṃ" means ten thousand world-systems including this world-system at the center. What should be said here has already been stated in the Commentary on the Mahāpadāna Sutta (Mahāpadāna-vaṇṇanā). "Na paññāyati" means it is not evident because it is not included in the Three Piṭakas regarding the future.

## Sanankumāra-kathā-vaṇṇanā

"Vaṇṇena" means by the perfection of physical form. Because it is easily understood, he does not elaborate on that physical form but gives the meaning of the word "yasa" (fame/glory). "Alaṅkāra-parivārena" means by both ornaments and retinue. "Puññasiriyā" means by the power and majesty of merit.

"Sampasādane" means in producing clarity or faith. The word "khā" preceded by "saṃ" has the meaning of knowing, as in "saṅkhāyetaṃ paṭisevati" and so forth. Therefore, it means "let us rejoice having known."
225:
## Commentary on the Story of the Brahmin Govinda

The term 'dīgharattaṃ' refers to a period that is exceedingly long in duration. Therefore, it means 'for this much... for a very long time.' Regarding the statement 'The Blessed One is of great wisdom,' that Brahma spoke it as a question to ascertain the consensus of the devas, saying: 'The Blessed One is of great wisdom; what do you sirs think?' Desiring to answer this question himself, he continued the sequence of words with 'Long ago, sirs,' and so on.

To show that the following meaning is also implied by the sense, he said 'This is not a wonder,' and so on. 'Of the three Maras' refers to Kilesa-māra, Abhisaṅkhāra-māra, and Devaputta-māra. The meaning already stated as 'This is not a wonder' is repeated as a conclusion: 'What wonder is there here?'

He is called a 'purohita' (chaplain) because he places the king's welfare in this life and the next at the forefront, or because he arranges matters beforehand. Thus, it is said, 'the purohita who advises and manages all matters.' 'By the Govinda-consecration' means the consecration into the position of Govinda. It is said that this position was a hereditary rank descending through that Brahmin's family lineage. 'Because of shining' refers to the shining of weapons. 'Because of being able to protect' means being able to protect the king and the immeasurable host of beings from harm.

'Having well relinquished' means giving up or handing over out of respect for that king. He is called 'atthadasa' (seer of welfare) because he sees various benefits and duties.

Prosperity is called 'bhava.' Because one prospers through this cause, it is called 'bhava' (the cause of prosperity). In the compound 'bhavamatthu,' the letter 'ma' is an augment, and 'o' is changed to 'a.' In the phrase 'bhavantaṃ Jotipālaṃ,' the word 'bhavantaṃ' is used in the sense of 'lord' (possessive) but takes the second (accusative) case ending, thus it means 'of the lord.' 'Mā paccabyāhāsī' means 'do not reject.' Since such a rejection is a form of reply, it is said 'mā paṭibyāhāsī' (do not reply back). 'Abhisambhosi' means being capable in the management of tasks, thus it is said 'having managed.' He is called 'Govinda' because he attained (vinda) prosperity (bhava-abhava) and wisdom. A great Govinda is called 'Mahāgovinda.' The word 'go' is a name for wisdom because it understands the meaning.
226:
## Commentary on the Division of the Kingdom

They were younger brothers having the same father but different mothers. 'Ayaṃ abhisitto' means this Prince Reṇu was consecrated in kingship upon the death of his father. 'Rājakārakā' refers to the ministers who establish the prince in kingship.

To show the active sense (kattu-sādhana) that the objects of the five cords of sensual pleasure are intoxicating, he said 'madakarā' (causing intoxication). Since causing intoxication is a specific cause of heedlessness, it is said 'pamādakarā' (causing heedlessness).

Because the area near King Reṇu's kingdom was about ten gāvutas wide and in other parts it was as wide as three hundred yojanas, he established all six kingdoms to be like the front of a cart (sakaṭamukha). Because it was square, King Reṇu's central kingdom was like a ceiling (vitāna).

The word 'sahā' is spoken to complete the verse. To show its meaning, the commentator said 'teneva sahā' (together with him). Alternatively, 'sahā' is an indeclinable in the sense of inseparability, and should be connected as 'saha āsuṃ satta bhāradhā.' This indicates that although those seven kings lived in different regions, they were inseparable in spirit. They bear the burden of the kingdom, carrying it upon themselves; therefore, they are called 'bhāradhā.'

## The Commentary on the First Recitation Section is finished.

## Commentary on the Spreading of the Fame

'Anupurohite ṭhapesi' means appointing them as assistant chaplains, or placing them in the position of assistant chaplains. With reference to listening to the recitation of mantras three times, it is said 'three times a day.' With reference to listening to the recitation during the two junctions of evening and morning, it is said 'evening or morning.' 'Tato paṭṭhāya' means starting from the time he had completed his practice and bathed (snātaka).

'Abhiuggacchi' means it arose or appeared. 'Acinteitvā' means without thinking 'How shall I consult with Brahma?', not even allowing such a thought to arise. Since there was no actual meeting, he remained without consulting. 'Taṃ disvā' means seeing with the eye of wisdom that meditation on the divine abiding of compassion (karuṇā-brahmavihāra-bhāvanā), which is the means for seeing Brahma.
227:
"Evaṃ" refers to the time after reporting to the King in this manner and entering seclusion. "Sabbattha" refers to all the occasions of asking permission from the six Khattiyas, seven Brāhmaṇa-mahāsālas, seven hundred dancers, and forty wives.

"Sādisiyo" means being similar in terms of birth or caste, thus it is said, "those of similar appearance and similar birth."

"Santhāgāra" refers to a house that stabilizes the mind by focusing on jhāna and by stilling the applied thoughts (vitakka) that wander externally; it means a hall for jhāna. "Gahitāva" means that the Bodhisatta has already attained it through the power of generating it within his own mental continuum through the practice of meditation. Because unwholesome states are removed by jhāna alone, there is no dissatisfaction and so forth. Specifically, because he has developed Karuṇā (compassion), there is no dissatisfaction or weariness (ukkaṇṭhanā); because he has developed Mettā (loving-kindness), there is no fear or anxiety (paritassanā). "Ukkaṇṭhanā" is the anxiety or longing to see Brahma, and "paritassanā" is the craving to see that Brahma, as stated in the passage beginning with "Brahmuno pana."

## Description of the Discussion with Brahma

"Cittutrāsa" is merely the trembling of the mind. "Kathaṃ" means in what manner can one be known by way of the residence, name, clan, etc., of the assembly of beings. Therefore, the passage beginning with "Kiṃ" is stated.

He identifies himself, saying, "Among the Brahmas well-known in the world such as Panakana, Sanantabandha, Satana (corrupt text), and Sanaṅkumāra, I am the one named Sanaṅkumāra."

"Aggha" is the food worthy of being offered to those in respected positions. "Madhusāka" is sweet food; it is a metaphorical term for any kind of food that should be offered to a guest. Therefore, it is stated as "Madhusākaṃ pana," etc. "Pucchāma" means asking by way of invitation.

Although the Great Being (Mahāsatta) remained having developed the four Brahma-vihāras, he said "one who has doubt (kankhī)" because he did not yet know without doubt that "this is the path to companionship with Brahma." Some teachers, however, say that his body was weakened due to ascetic practices, and because of the arising of fear upon meeting Brahma, he regressed from the Brahma-vihāras he had just attained; therefore, because of the unremoved doubt (vicikicchā), he said "kankhī." Matters known by others are called "paravediya"; it means those matters were clear and manifest to him.
228:
In the phrase "manifest to others," "paravediya" refers to questions or matters known and manifest to others. The reason for being manifest to others is stated as "because they have been personally realized by others." The act of "mine" is "mamiṅkāra" (mine-making). "Mamatta" means "this is mine... etc... craving." Because one makes the thought "mine" through this state, it is called mamiṅkāra; the craving that functions in that way is mamiṅkāra-taṇhā.

The word "manujesu" is in the locative case (bhummā) in the sense of selection (niddhāraṇa), not in the sense of domain (visaya); to show this, it is said "manujesu yo koci" (anyone among humans). To first show the state of being alone (bhāvattha) for the word "ekodibhūta," it is said "ekībhūta" (become one), and then to explain that meaning in detail, it is said "standing alone, sitting alone." "Tādisa" refers to one who exists being alone. "Bhūta" means one who has become.

"Adhimutti" (resolution) in jhāna can only occur after that jhāna has been produced; if it has not been produced, how could there be adhimutti? Therefore, it is stated to mean "having produced jhāna." "Vissagandha" (foul smell) is the repeated cultivation of defilements such as anger. By removing those defilements, one becomes free from the foul smell. "In these states" refers to the states of monkhood, living in seclusion, Karuṇā Brahma-vihāra, and so forth.

"Avidvā" means one who does not know. "Āvaritā" refers to beings who are obstructed by the prevention of the arising of wholesome superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) such as jhāna, path, and fruition. "Pūtikā" refers to those who are putrid due to a corrupted mind and so forth. Through the power of defilements, they emit a bad smell or a raw, fishy smell. Because they have the nature of being reborn in woeful states such as hell, they are called "āpāyikā"; thus it is said "apāyūpaga" (gone to woeful states). Just as a city is closed by walls, gates, and moats to a person who, being oppressed by thieves and so forth, wishes to enter, so too the Brahma-world is closed and obstructed by defilements such as anger; thus one is called "nivutabrahmaloka" (one for whom the Brahma-world is obstructed). He asks, saying, "By what is it obstructed?"

False speech (musāvāda) itself is "mosavajja," just as a physician (bhisakka) is called "bhesajja" (medicine). Anger (kujjana) is destruction (dussana). Deceiving others by saying one has not seen what was seen is "paravisaṃvādana." Deceiving by showing a similar appearance to lure someone is "vañcana" (deception). Harming friends or destroying friendship is "mittadubbhana" (betraying friends). Intense stinginess is "thaddhamacchariya." Conceit (māna) is thinking of oneself by surpassing one's actual low status or equality. Intolerance and disparagement of others' success is "khīyana." "Vivicchā" refers to various desires, such as the desire to hide one's own success or the intolerance of sharing with others. It is a subtle stinginess (macchariya) caused by miserliness (kadariya). "Yattha katthaci" refers to lustful attachment to any object, whether it be one's own property, others' property, or low objects. Grasping and clinging to an object is "abhigijjhana." Intoxication and self-exaltation with the thought "I am superior" is "majjana." Not understanding the object is "muyhana" (delusion). "In these states" refers to beings who are associated, repeatedly associated, well-associated, and not separated from the evil unwholesome states called defilements (kilesa) because they defile, oppress, and burn the mental continuum of beings, such as the aforementioned anger and so forth.
229:
In this sutta, Sanatkumāra Brahma, having been well questioned by the Great Being (the Bodhisatta) regarding āmagandha (the stench of defilements), explained the evil states that appeared to him by dividing them into fourteen terms. Although these states are mentioned based on that specific occurrence, some are repeated. Some states mentioned in the Āmagandha Sutta (Sutta Nipāta 242) are not entirely mentioned in this sutta. Nevertheless, they should be understood as included in this sutta either by the method of lakkhaṇahāra (conveyance of characteristics), or because they serve the same purpose, or because they reside in the same individual. Therefore, it was said [in the commentary], "This sutta, however," and so on. In that passage, "revealing by means of the Āmagandha Sutta" means that even the āmagandha states not explicitly mentioned in this sutta are revealed and explained by referring to the Āmagandha Sutta, as they share the same characteristics with the states mentioned there, and because those states are explicitly taught in that Āmagandha Sutta. The Āmagandha Sutta is also revealed by this sutta, because some āmagandha states mentioned in this sutta are not found in that Āmagandha Sutta. Since the āmagandha states taught in the Āmagandha Sutta are conceptually included and merged into this sutta, the commentator, while showing the āmagandha states mentioned here for the sake of preservation [of the meaning], stated, "among the fourteen defilements." This is because, in this context, although some states are not defilements by nature according to the Abhidhamma method, they deserve to be called "defilements" (kilesa) because of their nature of oppressing the mental continuum of beings.

Nimmāda means causing to wither or removing; thus, it is said, "to be subdued, to be abandoned." Buddhatantī is the tradition of those who will become Buddhas. Those who will become Buddhas are also called "Buddhas," just as in the example, "The Buddha went to Rājagaha" (referring to the time before full enlightenment). Strengthening the Great Man (Mahāpurisa) means making firm the arising of the thought, "I will renounce," which has occurred in the Great Man.

## Reṇurāja-āmantanā-vaṇṇanā

"Taking away my mind" means removing my mind and not following its desires. "To one who lives having reached the state of being alone" means to one who lives through practice, having reached the state of being alone by cultivating physical seclusion (kāya-viveka). "Spread all around with kusa grass" means the seating area is spread all around with kusa grass. Akāca means being free from breakage or flaws similar to a wound. Therefore, it is said, "not rough."

## Chakhattiya-āmantanā-vaṇṇanā

"We shall cause to learn" means we shall (by persuasion) cause them to be taught. Here, "causing to be taught" means making them possess wealth; therefore, it is said, "we shall persuade."
230:
Due to the absence of the undertaking of effort (vīriya) and the power of patience (khanti), the ascetic practice (samaṇa-dhamma) of those who have renounced cannot be complete or pure. To urge those monks toward the undertaking of effort and the power of patience, it is said, "Exert yourselves," and so on.

Karuṇā-jhāna-magga is the path known as the meditative absorption (jhāna) associated with compassion. Uju-magga is the straight path for going to the Brahma world. Anuttara is the noble path because of its nature as a Divine Abode (brahmavihāra). Therefore, it is called "the noble path." "Guarded by the virtuous" (sabbhi rakkhito) means being guarded and protected by removing opposing states so that there is no decline in the Dhamma of the virtuous. Some read "saddhammo sabbhi vakkhito"; according to them, it means the Dhamma taught and made known by the virtuous ones, such as the Buddhas, because it accomplishes the welfare of oneself and others.

"The nature of perishing in that very moment" (taṅkhaṇa-viddhaṃsana-dhammaṃ) means having the nature of perishing at the very moment of encountering opposing states. Alternatively, it refers to the extremely brief moment of existence that perishes even more quickly than the moment when razor blades, bound to the heads and feet of deities running at full speed toward each other from above and below, collide; it has the nature of perishing in that very moment. Who can know the destination or the end of that life? Mantāya means it should be reflected upon with wisdom. Here, the locative case "mantāya" should be understood in the sense of the instrumental (by means of), like "ñātāya." "All obstacles" (sabba-palibodhe) means all dangers that hinder or obstruct the performance of wholesome deeds.

## Brāhmaṇa-mahāsālā-dīnaṃ āmantanā-vaṇṇanā
Appesakkha means having little influence or power from the time of renunciation onwards.
He is honored like a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti).

## Mahāgovinda-pabbajjā-vaṇṇanā
Knowing the attainments (samāpatti) means personal realization; thus, it is said by the words, "they were unable to produce [them]."
By this phrase "I remember" (sarāmahaṃ), when the Blessed One spoke, it became an admission by the Blessed One of what was spoken by Mahābrahmā, [confirming] "it was just so." Because there was no teaching on the meditation of the Four Noble Truths for the sake of disenchantment with the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa), it was not possible [at that time]. If there is no disenchantment with the round of rebirths, dispassion (virāga) also cannot occur.
232:
## 7. Commentary on the Mahāsamaya Sutta
## Commentary on the Introduction

"Udāna" refers to the inspired utterance made by King Okkāka because of his desire to avoid the mixing of castes. Regarding the single district known as "Sakkā," what should be said here is to be understood according to the method explained in the commentary on the Mahānidāna Sutta. "Unplanted" (aropita) means not planted by anyone (growing naturally).

"By an embankment" (āvaraṇena) means by a dam. "Having it built" (bandhāpetvā) means having the embankment made firm with earth, leaves, stones, clumps of clay, and so forth.

To make the meaning of the summary "they increased the quarrel by insulting each other's birth" clearer, he said, "The Koliya workers said," and so forth.

"Three Jātakas" refers to the Phandana Jātaka, the Pathavī-undriya Jātaka, and the Laṭukika Jātaka. "Two Jātakas" refers to the Rukkhadhamma Jātaka and the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka.

"By him" (tena) refers to the Blessed One. The fact that there was a cause for the quarrel should be understood.

"In an improper place" (aṭṭhāne) means where there is no cause. "Having created enmity" (veraṃ katvā) means having produced a conflict. The Blessed One taught the Phandana Jātaka starting with "A man with an axe in his hand" (kuṭhārihattho puriso). He taught the Pathavī-undriya Jātaka starting with "It makes the sound 'dud-dubha', venerable sirs" (duddubhāyati bhaddante). He taught the Laṭukika Jātaka starting with "I pay homage to you, O elephants" (vandāmi taṃ kuñjarā).

"It is good for relatives to be many,
Even trees growing in the forest (are better if many);
The wind can blow down even a great lord of the forest
If it stands alone."
Starting with these verses, he taught the Rukkhadhamma Jātaka.

"The birds go away in harmony,
Taking the net with them;
When they begin to dispute,
Then they will come under my power."
Starting with these verses, he taught the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka.
233:
"Fear has arisen from the rod of one's own misconduct; look at the people engaged in strife. I shall describe the sense of urgency (saṃvega) just as it was experienced by me."
Starting with this, he taught the Attadaṇḍa Sutta.

Striving with body and speech through various seductive actions, the former wives sent messages saying, "Let them become dissatisfied."

"At the Kunāla Lake" means staying on the banks of the Kunāla Lake. He answered every question asked by the monks, intending, "I shall teach the Kunāla Jātaka in due order in connection with the questioning of the Kunāla bird-king." He dispelled their dissatisfaction by showing the faults of women and by illustrating the disadvantages, vileness, and defilement of sensual pleasures.

By dispelling laziness and increasing manly vigor, the thought arose in them, "We should be like the supreme man."

"Having tasks that are not abandoned" (avissaṭṭhakammantā) means that from the time their dissatisfaction was dispelled, they had the tasks of a recluse and subjects of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) that were not abandoned. The construction of the sentence is: "The Blessed One thought, 'It is proper to sit down.'"

"In the lotus thicket" means in the lotus pond. They blossomed through the penetration of the group of virtues such as the Fruit of Arahantship. By the words "This person... did not tell this person," it is shown that all those monks, having arrived in succession at that moment, did not report to the Blessed One the special attainment they had penetrated because they were shy of one another. He stated the reason for this with the words "Of those whose taints are destroyed" (khīṇāsavānaṃ), and so forth.

"Just as he descended" (osīdamatte) means just as he arrived in the presence of the Blessed One. "In the noble assembly" (ariyamaṇ္ဍle) means in the group of noble ones. "From the eastern enclosure of Yugandhara" means from the eastern side of Mount Yugandhara, not from the Mount Udaya mentioned by outsiders. "For the sake of seeing the delightful" means for the sake of showing the delightful nature of the world, which is especially beautiful because it is adorned by the arising of a Buddha. "Having leaped over" (ullaṅghitvā) means having risen up. The words "at such a moment (khaṇa), instant (laya), or muhutta" were said to show the progression of time at the moment, time, and muhutta when the moon's disk rose.
234:
Similarly, to show that the Buddha had a suitable retinue through the power of those monks' lineage and so forth, he said "Tattha" and so on.

"Samāpannadevatā" refers to deities and Brahmas who have entered meditative absorptions (jhāna-samāpatti) in the vicinity. "Caliṃsu" means they have arisen. A distance of about a gāvuta is the range within which sound can be heard. It is said that in Jambudīpa, sixty-three thousand cities first appeared. Likewise for the second and third times. Referring to the number of cities that appeared three times sixty-three thousand, he said "Tikkhattuṃ tesaṭṭhiyā nagarasahassesu." When combined, these cities total one hundred and eighty-nine thousand. "Navanavutiyā doṇamukhasatasahassesu" means in the nine million nine hundred thousand Doṇamukha cities. A Doṇamukha is a secondary city that serves as a source of revenue for a major city. "Channavutiyā paṭṭanakoṭisatasahassesu" means in the ninety-six hundred thousand crores of coastal towns. In the fifty-six kinds of jewel mines in Tambapaṇṇidīpa (Sri Lanka) and elsewhere, [deities also gathered]. This classification into major cities, Doṇamukha cities, coastal towns, jewel mines, etc., is intended to show the vast number of deities residing in those various places. If deities gathered from ten thousand world-systems, why does the Pali text say "from ten world-elements"? To address this objection, he said "Dasa sahassa... pe... adhippeta." According to this statement, it should be understood that here, one thousand world-systems are meant by one world-element.

"Lohapāsāde" means in the Brazen Palace built at the beginning. "Brahmaloke" means in the lowest Brahma world. To address the objection that if those deities and Brahmas were so densely packed without gaps, there would be no space for those arriving later, he said "Yathā kho pana" and so on. Those born in the group of Pure Abodes are called Suddhāvāsakāyika. Since the Pure Abode realm is their permanent residence, they are called "Suddhāvāsavāsīnaṃ." "Āvāsa" refers to the five Brahma worlds which are their dwelling places. Because these deities have completely cut off the lower fetters and other fetters, and thus have pure dwellings, they are called Suddhāvāsa.

Finding no space elsewhere, they descended at the edge of the eastern world-system. Others did the same. The path directly in front of the Buddhas is called the Buddhavīthi. It is impossible to overwhelm or block it as far as the world-system. "Pahaṭabuddhavīthiyāva" means as far as the path used by those deities and Brahmas approaching the presence of the Buddhas. "Samiti," "Saṅgati," and "Sannipāta" all mean an assembly (samaya). Because it is a great assembly, it is called Mahāsamaya, and thus he said "Mahāsamūha."
235:
"Mahāsamūha" refers to a great assembly. "Vanasaṇḍa" refers to a forest that has grown large, as indicated by the term "Vanasaṇḍa." "Devaghaṭā" means groups of deities.

"Samādahaṃsu" means they have well-established the mind on the object of Nibbāna through supramundane concentration; they have performed it. Alternatively, it is said to be "associated with concentration" just as the mind is placed on the object of Nibbāna; thus it is said, "They associated it with concentration." Because the crookedness of the mind, such as the winding path of cow urine, has been removed far away, they have discarded all crookedness of the mind and made the mind straight. Because horses are led or pulled by these things, they are called "nettāni" or "yottāni" (reins or straps). Bringing horses that are not on the path back to the path is possible by holding the reins. Therefore, after saying "holding all the reins without driving," he said "without driving, without restraining," meaning that such driving is unnecessary.

Just as a stake (khīla) driven into a wall or the ground is difficult to pull out; just as a cross-bar (paligha) prevents entry into a city; and just as an Indakhīla pillar with deep foundations and well-planted is difficult to pull out; similarly, unwholesome states such as greed are difficult to remove from the continuity of beings and prevent entry into the city of Nibbāna. Therefore, those unwholesome states are called "khīla," "paligha," and "indakhīla." Because they lack the shaking of craving, those monks who are unshaken and have the highest contentment can travel without hindrance in the four directions.

"Gatāse" means they have already gone/approached; because they have completed the taking of refuge, there is no need to take refuge again in the future. Because supramundane refuge is intended, it is said, "They have gone with a refuge free from doubt." Those who possess this supramundane refuge will certainly not go to the planes of misery and will fill the heavenly hosts. Those who have gone to the Buddha for refuge with mundane refuge will also not go to the planes of misery, and if they meet with other wholesome conditions, they will leave the human body and fill the heavenly hosts. This is the meaning here.

## Description of the Assembly of Deities

"Etesaṃ" means of those assemblies of deities. "Idāni" means at this time. "Buddhānaṃ" means because of the absence of other Buddhas. "Cittakallatā" means the tenderness of the mind.

If it is asked whether the Blessed One is able to declare the names and clans of those in such a large assembly of deities, it is said "The Buddhas are great" and so on to show that he is indeed able. In that statement, the word "diṭṭha" refers to the base of visible forms (rūpāyatana). The word "သုတ" refers to the base of sounds (saddāyatana). The word "muta" refers to the objects of the senses that receive objects upon contact, namely the bases of odors, tastes, and tangibles (gandha, rasa, phoṭṭhabba). The word "viññāta" refers to the objects remaining after those already mentioned.
236:
An object that has arrived, whether by seeking out all knowable objects or without seeking, is called an 'attained object' (patta). An object that is sought, whether it has arrived or not yet arrived, is called a 'sought object' (pariyessita). 'An object pondered by following with the mind' refers to an object that is contemplated and pondered solely by the mind, independent of seeking or not seeking. Regarding visible-form objects, it should be understood by connecting the meaning thus: in any unspecified visible-form object, such as those distinguished in the Abhidhamma Pāḷi as 'blue, yellow,' etc., there is not even a single visible-form object [remaining unknown]. The same method applies to sounds such as the sound of a drum. 'Yaṃ' refers to which object. 'Etesaṃ' refers to [the knowledge and vision] of those Buddhas.

Now, to complete the aforementioned meaning along with the supporting Pāḷi text, the passage beginning with 'Yathāha' is stated. At that time, to show the state of the act of knowing as not yet exhausted, He said, 'I know' (jānāmi); and because there is nothing among all knowable things that the Blessed One has not known, it is said, 'That I have known through direct knowledge' (tamahaṃ abbaññāsiṃ).

They do not look [at beings who cannot be liberated] because there is no benefit. Beings spoken of by such methods as 'not possessed of the obstruction of kamma' are the opposite of the incapable persons (those who can be liberated). Because there is an abundance of Dhamma discourse on the subduing of lust, starting with 'Yassa maṅgalā samūhatā' and continuing with 'one should subdue lust for the sensual pleasures of humans and devas,' the Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta is a suitable discourse for those of a lustful temperament. Because it extensively clarifies the faults of hatred—showing how quarrels and disputes arise from what is dear and not dear, how that hatred arises from affection, and how that affection arises from desire, both in terms of results and the sequence of causes—the Kalahavivāda Sutta is a suitable discourse for those of a hateful temperament.

"I speak of two fruits of dispute;
that fruit is but little and not enough for peace.
Having seen this disadvantage of dispute,
one should not dispute, seeing Nibbāna as the ground of safety and non-dispute."

Because it destroys delusion and increases wisdom through such methods, the Mahābyūha Sutta is a suitable discourse for those of a deluded temperament.
237:
"If one does not accept the doctrine of another (considering only one's own view as true), then he is a fool, like an animal of little wisdom. If that were so, then all these who hold views would be fools of very little wisdom, because they are all settled in their own views as the truth."

By such methods, primarily removing the wrong consideration of one's own false views and cutting off the discursive thoughts (vitakka) that are scattered in the clinging to doctrines within their own spheres, the Cūḷabyūha Sutta is suitable for those of a speculative temperament (vitakkacarita).

"(The Blessed One said:) One should block with wisdom all the defilements such as ignorance, which are the root of the collection of unwholesome states called papañcasaṅkhā (conceptual proliferation), and the conceit that arises as 'I am.' If any craving, such as craving for forms, arises within oneself, one should train, being ever mindful, to abandon and appease those cravings."

For such instructions, only a person with faith is like a receptive vessel. Since this Dhamma brings welfare to such a person, the Tuvaṭṭaka Sutta is suitable for those of a faithful temperament (saddhācarita).

"(The Blessed One said:) He who has abandoned craving even before the breakup of the body, and therefore does not depend on the past group known as the past as a support for craving, nor can he be called 'one with lust' etc. in the present; for that Arahant, because of the absence of the leading factors of craving and views, there is no longer anything to be led by in the future."

Because of the abundance of such profound words, the Purābheda Sutta is suitable for those of an intellectual temperament (buddhicarita); thus it was said, "Then, having determined what is suitable for them..."

"He did so with the mind (manasākāsi)" means that after taking it into the heart according to the temperaments, He again took it into the heart regarding the suitability of placing His teaching in the continuities of those to be led, in a manner similar to that mental attention. "One should know the desires etc. of others" means...
238:
The Blessed One reflected in his heart on the suitability of establishing his teaching in the mental continuities of those to be guided (veneyya). He contemplated: "Would I be able to know the teaching undertaken solely by my own inclination, without regard for the inclinations and so forth of others?" "By the inclination of others" (parajjhāsayena) means teaching by the inclination of someone among the assembled audience. "Due to an occasion arising" (aṭṭhuppattikena) means teaching due to some occasion that has arisen in this assembly of devas and Brahmās. "By the power of a question" (pucchāvasena) means whether one would know the teaching undertaken in connection with the question of some questioner.

The statement "If there were a Paccekabuddha" was spoken to show that the teaching and questioning of these suttas is a heavy burden for Paccekabuddhas and is beyond their scope. Therefore, it was said: "Even he would not be able to do so."

In this matter, since neither a question for consent (anumati-pucchā) nor a question from a desire to speak (kathetukamyatā-pucchā) is appropriate, what is appropriate is either a question similar to a question for comparing what has been seen (diṭṭhasaṃsandana-pucchā) or a question similar to a question for cutting off doubt (vimaticchedana-pucchā). Only these two types are said to occur by the power of an individual's inclination, not by the power of the Dhamma itself. In that teaching where such questions are raised, if the Blessed One himself were to ask and himself were to answer according to his own wish, the listening devas and Brahmās would become confused, thinking, "The Blessed One first said this, and then he said this again." They would be like those who have entered into darkness. Therefore, it was said: "In this way, these devas will not be able to penetrate [the meaning]." However, in a teaching according to the Dhamma (yathādhamma-desanā), confusion can arise from questioning out of a desire to speak.

That the host of devas said "The sun has arisen" is because the radiance had become particularly close and had become vast and magnificent. According to the method found in the Sutta, "In a single world system," two Buddhas do not appear simultaneously, neither before nor after. For this very reason, it was said: "In the infinite... he saw."

In the verse, with the word "pucchāmi" (I ask), the created Buddha asked for permission to question the Blessed One. "Muni" refers to the Buddha-sage. "Pahūtapañña" refers to the Buddha who possesses great wisdom. "Tiṇṇa" refers to the Buddha who has crossed over the four floods (oghas). "Pāraṅgata" refers to the Buddha who has reached Nibbāna, or who has reached the end and limit of all that is to be known. "Parinibbuta" refers to the Buddha whose defilements are extinguished through Nibbāna with residue remaining (sa-upādisesa-nibbāna). "Ṭhitatta" refers to the Buddha who has a steady mind because of being unshakable by worldly conditions (lokadhamma). "Having gone forth from home and abandoned sensual pleasures" means having gone forth from the household life after discarding sensual objects. "How does that monk fare rightly in the world?" means how does that monk rightly fare, go, and dwell, and how does he transcend the world without being stained [by defilements]?
239:
In the phrase "silokaṃ anukassāmi," what is called "siloka" is a collection of verse-quarters (pāda); a verse recited by ancient seers is also called a siloka. A pāda is a collection of words with a fixed sequence of syllables. To show the meaning "I shall properly perform (proclaim) that siloka (verse)," it was explained as "the syllables... I shall set in motion."

The word "yattha" is a locative case (sattamī-vibhatti) in the sense of location (adhikaraṇa). This indication is given with the elision of the repeated word (āmeḍita), and thus it was explained as "yesu yesu ṭhānesu" (in various places). "Bhummā" refers to the deities residing in connection with the earth, such as in trees. The intention is: "I shall properly perform the siloka together with those deities who reside depending on those various places."

With the verse "Those who dwell in mountain caves," the secluded dwelling of those monks is shown; with the verse "Resolute and concentrated," their application to meditation (bhāvanā) is shown.

Because they numbered five hundred, they are called "many monks." Because they have overcome opposing defilements and because of their intense power, they dwell secluded like lions. "Ekattaṃ" refers to reaching the state of being alone (solitude). "Having become pure with white minds" means they are purified by having attained the Path of Arahatship; it does not mean mere physical purity. "Vippasannā" means they are particularly serene due to the clarity of the Noble Path. They are "undisturbed" (anāvilā) because of the absence of defilements that cause the mind to be turbid.

"Knowing the monks" means knowing that "these monks, who have destroyed defilements, are able to see these hosts of devas with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu)." "Born at the end of the hearing" means being born into the Noble lineage at the conclusion of hearing the Dhamma. "All this" refers to all the Pali text beginning with "more than five hundred."

Those monks also exerted effort and energy to lead toward the attainment of the divine eye. Therefore, it was said: "Not that by them," and so forth. In the word "sattariṃ," the letter 'ta' is replaced by 'ra', and it means seventy. The word "sahassaṃ" (thousand) follows it, and when joined with "sattati," it becomes plural. Therefore, it was explained as: "Some a thousand, some seventy thousand."

"Anantaṃ" means without end or limit; because such limitlessness is exceedingly great (numerous), it was explained as "vipulaṃ" (vast).

"Having looked" (avekkhitvā) means having looked individually with the eye of wisdom. Some also read it as "vavatthitvāna," which has the same meaning. Since that looking constitutes making a determination, it was explained as "vavatthapetvā" (having determined). Regarding the previously mentioned verses, referring to the latter half of the third verse and the first half of the fourth verse, it was explained as "the very verse mentioned before."
240:
Intending that knowing is also seeing, he said "Look, contemplate". Because it is produced by speech, he said "I shall proclaim in due order".

"Satta sahassāni saṅkhāya" refers to seven thousand devas in number. "Yakkhā" are indeed devas of the terrestrial and arboreal classes. "Ānubhāvasampannā" means devas of great power (mahesakkhā). Or, devas possessed of psychic power (iddhimanto). "Jutimanto" means devas of great radiance (mahappabhā). "Vaṇṇavanto" means devas of surpassing beauty (atikkantavaṇṇā). "Yasassino" means those who have a large retinue and widespread fame. With the intention that the word samiti means "nearness", he said "in the presence of the monks".

"Hemavatapabbate" refers to devas dwelling on the mountain situated near the Himavanta.

"Ete sabbepi" refers to all sixteen thousand devas mentioned: the seven thousand from Kapilavatthu, the six thousand from the mountain near Himavanta, and the three thousand from Sātāgira mountain.

"Rājagahanagare" refers to the deva dwelling near the city of Rājagaha. "Taṃ" refers to the deva named Kumbhīra.

Although King Dhataraṭṭha certainly rules the eastern direction, how is he the chief of the Gandhabbas in the four great islands along with their surrounding islands in the four directions? It is because all those Gandhabbas follow the will of King Dhataraṭṭha. The same method should be understood for sentences like "chief of the Kumbhaṇḍas".

The sons of King Virūဠှက (Virūḷhaka) are also similar to the sons of King Dhataraṭṭha in terms of their great number, names, strength, and special qualities such as psychic power.

"Sabbasaṅgāhikavasena" means by way of including all the four Great Kings existing in each of the ten thousand world systems. Therefore, he said "ayañcettha" and so forth.

"Caturo disā" means standing in the four directions, shining, brilliant, and emitting light. If they stand shining in the four directions, how do the Great Kings who came with a large assembly stay in the forest near Kapilavatthu? To answer this, he said "te pana" and so forth.

The construction (yojanā) is that the servants of those Great Kings have come. They are called māyāvī because they are associated with illusion (māyā). They are called vañcanika because they possess deceit or are engaged in deception. They are associated with low, treacherous, and dishonest behavior. Because they have the nature of deceiving both openly and secretly, they are called māyāvī...
241: Māyā is the art of deceiving others. Because those divine servants practice māyā to deceive others, they are called 'māyākārakā' (illusion-makers). 'These many servants' refers to the eight servants of the four Great Kings, starting from Kuṭeṇḍu and ending with Nighaṇḍu. 'Devarājāno' means being devas, they are the kings of their respective groups of devas. The three devaputtas—Citta, Sena, and Cittasena—are referred to in the Pali by a single name using the 'ekasesa' method (as Cittasena). This is explained by the words beginning with 'Citto ca.' Because the Saṅgha of monks gathered in this forest, this forest is called 'Bhikkhusaṅghasamiti' (the forest of the assembly of the Saṅgha of monks). They are the nāgas dwelling in Lake Nāgasadaha. There is a Nāga King in that lake, and because he has lived there for a long time, his retinue has become very large through successive generations. Referring to that retinue, it is called the 'Tacchaka Nāga assembly.' They are the nāgas dwelling in the Yamunā River. The term 'Nāga' is used here in the sense of 'hatthināga' (elephant). Excluding the Kambala and Assatara nāgas, it refers to the other aforementioned nāgas. 'Lobhābhibhūtā' refers to those (garudas) overcome by greed for food. 'Dibbānubhāvatā' means they are called 'dibba' (divine/celestial garudas) because they possess divine power or due to that divine power. The name 'Citrasupaṇṇa' is due to their having variegated and beautiful wings. Approaching closely, they spoke (and took refuge in the Buddha). Even though they have traditional enmity like crows and owls, or snakes and mongooses, they have joyful hearts toward one another like friends or relatives. They took refuge in the Buddha alone, saying, 'Only through the power of the Buddha have we been able to develop loving-kindness toward one another.' They are brothers who are brothers-in-law of Sakka. Therefore, it is said, 'because of the Asura maiden Sujā.' Among those Asuras, they are the ones named 'Kālakañjā.' They have terrifyingly large bodies. 'Abhabbā' means they are incapable of entering the Path of Certainty (sammatta-niyāma). This is because they completely lack the desire (wholesome desire) to attain such a Path.
242:
Since the great Asura named Bali had passed away, the Blessed One, in mentioning only the sons of that Asura Bali, spoke the verse beginning with "Satañca baliputtānaṃ". It is said that this great Asura once created a subtle body and approached the Blessed One.

"Kammaṃ katvā" means having performed the preliminary work (parikamma) [in the jhānas of loving-kindness and compassion]. "Nibbattā" refers to those who were reborn due to access concentration (upacāra-jhāna). Those reborn through absorption concentration (appanā-jhāna), however, are Brahmās; the Blessed One will speak of those Brahmās later with "Subrahmā", etc. This [current] deity is also called a deity of the sensuous sphere (kāmāvacara). Therefore, it is said: "Mettā-karuṇā-kāyikā" refers to the devas reborn after performing preliminary work in the jhāna of loving-kindness and the jhāna of compassion. "Mettā-jhāne karuṇā-jhāne" means because of the sign (nimitta) of mettā-jhāna and the sign of karuṇā-jhāna, or for the sake of that mettā-jhāna and karuṇā-jhāna.

Those water-deities (āpo-devā) and others, being situated according to their respective groups, exist as ten groups. Up to the Karuṇā-kāyikā, there are ten groups of devas. "Nānattavaṇṇā" means those who have various natural complexions.

"Veṇḍu-devatā" refers to the devas named Veṇḍu; likewise, the devas named Sahali, Asama, and Yamaka. Some say "two Ayaniyas", referring to the two groups of devas headed by Asama and Yamaka. "Candassūpanisā devā" are the devas who exist depending on the moon, running in front of, behind, and beside the moon. Therefore, they are called "devas dependent on the moon". The same method should be understood for "Suriyassūpanisā" (dependent on the sun) and "Nakkhattanissitā" (dependent on the stars). Devas who are merely the cause of the wind blowing are called Vāta-valāhaka devas. Similarly, devas who are merely the cause of the movement of cloud layers are called Abbha-valāhaka devas. Devas who are the cause of the occurrence of heat are called Uṇha-valāhaka devas. As for the Vassa-valāhaka devas who are the cause of rain, they are similar to the Pajjuṇṇa devas; they are not mentioned here. Vasu-devatā is the name of a group of devas; because he is their leader and precursor, Sakka is called Vāsava.

"Dasetē" refers to these ten groups of devas beginning with the Veṇḍu-devatā and ending with Vāsava.

"Imāni" refers to these names "Jalamaggī" and "Sikhārivā" which are the names of those devas. However, some teachers say that the letter "ma" is a sandhi consonant for connecting words, and that "Jalā", "Aggī", and "Sikhārivā" are the actual names of those devas. "Etē" refers to some among the aforementioned devas like "Ariṭṭhaka" and "Roja" who are "Umāpupphanibhāsino", meaning they resemble the Umā flower in color. Otherwise, there would be eleven groups of devas.
243:
"Dasetē" refers to these ten groups of devas beginning with the Sahabhū and ending with Vāsavanesi. They appear as ten according to the division of groups. "Samānā", etc., is the collective name for the assembly of those devas. The same applies to the remaining devas.

"Dasetē" refers to these ten groups of devas beginning with the Samāna and ending with the Mahāpāraga. They appear as ten according to that same division of groups. There are also three groups of devas beginning with the Sukka. "Pāmokkhadevā" means the devas who are the leaders and principals. "Disā" means in the directions. "Devo" means the rain cloud. "Dasetē" refers to these ten groups of devas beginning with the Sukka and ending with Pajjuṇṇa. They appear as ten according to the division of deva groups.

"Dasetē" refers to these ten groups of devas beginning with the Khemiya and ending with the Paranimmita. They appear as ten according to the division of deva groups. Among them, it is said that the five groups of devas including Khemiya and Kaṭṭhaka, along with their retinues, are included in the Tāvatiṃsa group. "Nāmanwayena" means following the name, through the similarity of names such as "Āpo-devatā". Therefore, it is said: "by a portion of the name, by a category of the name". "Sabbā devatā" refers to all the devas in the ten thousand world systems. The Blessed One points them out collectively through their respective similar names.

"Pavutthā" means separated, like those who have gone abroad, thus it is said "Vigatā" (gone away). Alternatively, "Pavutthā" means lived out in various ways; thus, one whose birth (jāti) to be lived is finished is called "Pavuṭṭhajāti" (one for whom birth is ended). "Kāḷakabhāvā" refers to the defiling states (kilesa). Because of the total absence of those defilements, the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala) is called "Kāḷakabhāvātīta" (one who has transcended the dark state). Or, like the moon called "Asitātiga" which transcends the dark state due to the absence of spots, it refers to the Blessed One who shines with glory like such a moon.

"Eko Brahmā" refers to the deity Subrahmā who appears in the Sagāthāvagga of the Saṃyutta Nikāya. Ariya-Brahmās are those who, having been reborn in the Brahma world, reside in the lower realms.
244:
They are not the Suddhāvāsa Brahmās. Tissa Mahābrahmā was a worldling (puthujjana) who, having been reborn among humans in later times, became the Elder Moggaliputtatissa.

Regarding "sahassaṃ brahmalokānaṃ" (a thousand Brahma worlds): there exists this world of beings called Brahma for these Brahmās; therefore, the Brahmās are called 'Brahmaloka'. It is said that "a thousand Mahābrahmās arrived," referring to those one thousand worlds of beings who are Brahmās. In this context, the word 'loka' is a synonym for the world of beings (sattaloka). In the subsequent verse, the word "āgatā" (arrived) is stated according to its meaning. "Yattha" means among those thousand Brahmās. "Aññe brahme" refers to other Brahmās besides them. That Mahābrahmā stands surpassing other Brahmās in terms of appearance, retinue, and lifespan.

"Issarā" means (the Mahābrahmās have arrived who are) the lords of the remaining Brahmās because of that very ability to make others follow their will.

Behold the foolishness of the evil Māra, who is endowed with dark, unwholesome states. That Māra strives to exert effort fruitlessly in a domain that is not his own.

By creating an obstacle to the hearing of the Dhamma, which brings about the state of being free from passion, those who are not free from passion are indeed those bound by passion; with this intention, it is said, "Let them be bound by passion."

"Having made a terrifying sound" means having produced a fearsome and great noise (he departed).

Now, wishing to show that sound by way of a simile, he said "yathā" and so forth. "Kañci" means being unable to make any deity or human in that assembly follow his will, he himself became one who could not abide in his own will. Therefore, he said "asayaṃvasī" and so forth.

The phrase "vītarāgehi" (by those free from passion) is the head of the discourse. In truth, the armies of Māra had to retreat far away from the entire assembly that had gathered there. They could not move even a single hair of those people; how then could they cause any harm? Thus, the meaning should be understood in the sense that they could not harm all those who attained distinction (the Dhamma) there. Alternatively, it should be understood that by the term 'vītarāga', both those free from passion and those still with passion are included there. Māra recited this verse, having a mind filled with great wonder and amazement. He thought, "How is it that even though I am performing such a most terrifying and horrific act, all these people remain unperturbed and composed?" Why? Because these are noble persons who have conquered the defilements. Therefore, he said "sabbe" and so forth. Just as the Ariyas'...
246:
## 8. Commentary on the Sakkapañha Sutta
## Commentary on the Introduction
Because it is located near a group of mango trees, that single brahmin village is called "Ambasanda" using the plural form, just as one says "Varaṇā City." 'Vedi' is the same as 'vedika'; 'vedika' becomes 'vediya' by changing the letter 'ka' to 'ya'; in that 'vediyaka' (railing/pedestal). Therefore, it is said in the commentary, "maṇivedikāsadisena" and so forth, meaning with a dark green forest resembling a railing made of gems such as indanīla (sapphire). "Pubbe pi" means that even in the past, before the cave was prepared, it existed in the form of a cave and had an Indasāla tree at the entrance; therefore, it was called "Indasāla Cave" according to its former name.

Desire is called "ussukka". Because that desire arises through the wish to see the Buddha and through exertion, it is called "righteous exertion." Regarding the statement that there is no one equal to Sakka... it is said, "By heedfulness (appamāda), Magha attained the leadership of the gods (the status of Sakka)." "Parittakena" means (being reborn in the celestial realm) by only a small amount of merit, without having performed many repeated meritorious deeds.

Sakka, although certainly one who is fearless due to having performed great merit, became threatened by the fear of death, which was doubled by the sorrow caused by the separation from his superior divine splendor. Therefore, it is said, "Sakka, however, was overcome by the fear of death."

Seeing deities with the divine eye is like penetrating knowledge; thus it is said, "paṭivijjhī" (penetrated). "Pāṭiyekko vohāro" means a distinct and pleasant mode of address. They are called "Mārisa" because they possess splendor that is experienced and manifest. The splendor of those deities is manifest because of their great power; for other deities, however, splendor is not manifest due to unwise attention and lack of power. Because their possession of experienced and manifest splendor is free from suffering, it is also called "niddukkha" (free from suffering). "Ekako" is said because he came without his divine retinue; however, companions such as Mātali were indeed present even then. For this reason, it will be said later, "Indeed, he arose from that concentration because of the sound of the venerable one's chariot wheel."

Opportunity...
247:
The Blessed One, waiting for the maturation of Sakka's knowledge and observing the realization of the Four Noble Truths by many other deities, did not grant Sakka the opportunity (immediately). The word 'so' refers to Sakka.

The word 'evaṃ' is an indeclinable (nipāta) used in the sense of accepting a statement, meaning 'Let it be so' and so forth. The phrase 'bhaddaṃ tava' (may there be goodness to you) was a blessing spoken by those deities addressed to Sakka.

The meaning of being intimate with the Blessed One, approaching him at will, and listening to the Dhamma should be understood through the Mahāgovinda Sutta and others. 'Iminā katokāse' means when this celestial youth Pañcasikha had requested permission from the Blessed One (or when permission was granted).

'Anucariyaṃ' refers to the state of following behind. Since such following is indeed going together, it is said: 'sahacaraṇaṃ ekato gamanaṃ' (going together as one).

'Sovaṇṇamayaṃ' means made of gold. 'Pokkharaṃ' refers to the resonator (body) of the lute (vīṇā). 'Daṇḍo' is the neck of the lute. 'Veṭhakā' are the tuning pegs used for binding and tightening the strings. 'Pattakaṃ' also refers to the resonator of the lute. 'Samapaññāsamucchanā mucchetvā' means having arranged the fifty modes of singing and playing so they could be performed in sequence. This phrase 'playing with fifty modes' is spoken with reference to the fixed method of playing the lute in the celestial realm. In the human world, however, there are only twenty-one modes (mucchanā). Therefore, it is stated in the commentary on the Vīṇopama Sutta:

'Seven notes, three scales, twenty-one modes, and forty-nine tones—these are called the Saramaṇḍala (the circle of notes).'

In that context, there are seven notes: chajja, usabha, gandhāra, majjhima, pañcama, dhevata, and nisāda. There are three scales (gāma), which are groups of notes: chajjagāma, majjhimagāma, and sādhāraṇagāma. According to the playing methods in the human world, by creating three modes for each note, there are twenty-one modes. Since there are seven tone variations (tāna) for each note, from which the most subtle distinctions of a note are determined, there are forty-nine such tone variations. Twenty-two microtones (shuti/suti) are desired, categorized as three, two, four, four, three, two, and four. This celestial youth Pañcasikha, however, played the lute appropriately with fifty modes, consisting of seven modes for each note and one intermediate note (antarasara). Thus it is said:
248:
“Samapaññāsa mucchanā saṃmucchetvā” means having sung and played exactly fifty modes (mucchanā). The construction is that he stood in a certain place, informing the remaining deities and waiting for the time when Sakka's knowledge would mature.

In the word “atiriva,” the letter 'ra' is a euphonic conjunction (padasandhi), meaning 'exceedingly' or 'excessively.' Sakka, being terrified by the fear of death, went in a hurried manner, like a child who is fond of playing in the middle of a village while children are playing during the normal dinner time of people. Therefore, it is said: “nanu ca” and so forth.

Buddhas are of great compassion and arise only for the benefit and happiness of the world including the devas. If that is so, why are they difficult to approach for those who desire to do so? To this, it is said: “ahaṃ sarāgo” and so forth. “Tadantaraṃ paṭisallīnā” means that at the moment Sakka was to approach, the Buddhas were dwelling in the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) or were absorbed in meditation (jhāna). Alternatively, the word “tadantara” is synonymous with “now,” thus meaning “He is now in seclusion.”

## Pañcasikhagītāgāthāvaṇṇanā

“Sāvesi” (made to hear) means that the celestial youth Pañcasikha, having established the desired mode and playing the lute, demonstrated the clear and gentle distinctions of the notes as they arose in various places. With a joyful characteristic like the sound of a honeybee intoxicated by drinking very sweet and tender nectar, and singing clearly, he made the harmonious and pleasant sound of the lute strings heard by the Blessed One.

“The son of the Sakyans, concentrated in meditation, wise and mindful, seeking the Deathless Nibbāna like a sage...
Just as a sage would rejoice, having reached the supreme Enlightenment,” these verses are those connected with the Buddha.

Verses connected with the Buddha are those that proceed by taking the Dhamma-body, which is the fruition of Arahatship of the Buddhas, as their basis. Thus it is said: “dhammo arahatāṃ iva” (as the Dhamma is dear to the Arahats). This should be understood as verses connected with the Dhamma and verses connected with the fruition of Arahatship.

“Sūriyasamānasarīrā” means one whose body has a radiance like the sun. Therefore, it is explained as “tassā kirā” and so forth. Because she was born in the lap of Timbaru, the king of the Gandhabba devas, it is said: “born depending on Timbaru, the king of devas.” Because she is beautiful in all her limbs, she is called “Kalyāṇī,” as stated by “sabbaṅgasobhanā.”
249:
Having first sung the verses beginning with "Gāyanti te pitaram" out of lust, he now sings addressing her as "Agirasi", as if she were standing before him, referring to that same Sūriyavacchasā.

In the word "Thanudaram", it refers to the breasts and the belly, thus "thanavemajjhaṃ udarañca" (between the breasts and the belly) is said. "Kiñci kāraṇam" means not knowing any affliction (pīḷā). Due to intense lust, the mind exists having abandoned its natural stability.

"Vāmūrū" means a sister with beautiful thighs. Therefore, it is said "vāmākārena" and so forth. The words vāma, vikasita, rucira, sundara, abhirūpa, and cāru should be understood as having the same meaning. "Na tikhinam" means not sharp, not harsh, and not coarse. "Mandam" means gentle and smooth.

"Anekabhāvo" means having many natures. Since that sensual desire (kāma) has many varieties, it is said "anekavidho jāto". "Anekabhāgo" means having many parts (koṭṭhāsa).

"Tayā saddhiṃ vipaccataṃ" means: "May that meritorious deed of mine bear fruit only together with you; I wish to experience the fruit of that deed only together with you." Just as the karma that leads to being a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) gives its result only together with the Jewel of a Woman (itthiratana) who is the consequence of that karma, likewise, may that meritorious deed of mine give its result to me only together with you.

"Ekodī" means having reached the state of "ekodibhāva", meaning concentrated (samāhita). "Jigīsāno" means desiring to be. Being in such a state is called seeking (jigīsati); this is the first interpretation. In the second interpretation, the meaning is given by bringing in the verb "vicarati" (wanders).

He speaks the word "Nandeyyaṃ" (I would rejoice) longing for union with the goddess Sūriyavacchasā, who possesses supreme splendor and beauty of form.

"Saṃsandati" means it harmonizes. The meaning is that the sound of the song arises in that very manner, without exceeding the musical scale (mucchanā) and the manner in which the sound of the lute (vīṇā) arose. To clarify all the reasons and purposes for which the Blessed One praised the quality of Pañcasikha's lute, the words beginning with "Kasmā" are said. There is no sensual desire (chandarāga) in the Blessed One, as it was completely eradicated at the foot of the Bodhi tree. The Blessed One is equanimous (upekkhaka) because he is unstained. The Blessed One has a mind well-liberated (suvimuttacitta) from sensual desire.
251:
In the phrase 'Salalamaya-gandhakuṭi', it means [the Buddha was staying] in the perfumed chamber built and offered with salala wood by King Pasenadi of Kosala (or the celestial architect Vissakamma). 'Tena-assā' (to her) means that because she has abandoned gross sensual lust through the attainment of the two lower paths, the goddess Bhunjatī no longer finds delight even in the celestial realm. In the phrase 'He emerged from that concentration because of the sound of the wheel-rim', those who do not understand the intended meaning might think that emergence from attainment occurs due to the intensity of the object. To refute such a notion, it is said: 'It should not be said that one who has entered an attainment hears sound.'

It is said 'he hears' in the sense that if there is an impingement of the object, there must also be a cognition of the sound. The other person, relying merely on the statement 'Sound is a thorn to one who has entered the first jhāna', assumed that sound is a thorn in all jhānas. Unable to bear the refutation, he cited this very sutta passage: 'Did not the Blessed One... say so?' In that cited passage, just as there is no emergence from a formless attainment even by a loud sound because perceptions of resistance (paṭigha-saññā) have been well-abandoned through the power of meditation that opposes the seeing of faults, so too, there is never an emergence from the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) while one is apprehending the object of Nibbāna, because all worldly perceptions have been well-transcended by the Path of Arahantship through the power of meditation that opposes the seeing of faults, such as 'Arising is danger, non-arising is safety.'

Otherwise, because perceptions of resistance have not been well-abandoned, emergence from all fine-material attainments (rūpa-samāpatti) can occur. However, the first jhāna cannot withstand even a slight sound; therefore, it was said of one who has entered it: 'Sound is a thorn.' If there is no emergence from a formless attainment even by a loud sound because perceptions of resistance have been suppressed, how much more so from the attainment of the Path and Fruit? Therefore, it was said: 'By the sound of the wheel-rim,' and so on. In the word 'cakkanemisaddena', the instrumental case is not used in the sense of cause (hetu) or instrument (karaṇa), but rather in the sense of accompaniment (sahayoga). To show this meaning, the phrase 'Bhagavā pana' and so on was spoken.

## Commentary on the Story of Gopaka

'Paripūrakārinī' refers to one who has protected [the precepts] by making them complete and pure. The phrase 'itthitta' (womanhood) and so on shows the manner of disgust for that female state. The meaning is that the censure of the female state is the cause. 'Alaṃ' is a word of refutation, meaning 'there is no use.' 'Virājeti' means she is disgusted. 'Etā sampattiyo' refers to these aforementioned prosperities, such as the glory of a Cakkavatti king. Therefore, through the power of the attachment that arose due to past familiarity, [they arose] in that celestial state. 'Upaṭṭhānasālā' refers to the great celestial assembly hall named Sudhammā.
252:
That person is Gopaka Devaputta. 'Vaṭṭetvā vaṭṭetvā' means repeatedly turning the words of exhortation, just as one might turn a spear or similar object. 'Gāḷhaṃ vijjhitabbā' means they should be struck or prodded very severely.

'Kuto mukhā' means 'Towards which direction is the face of their knowledge turned?' Therefore, it is said: 'Those whose minds are diverted elsewhere.' 'Katapuññe' refers to those who possess well-performed meritorious states.

'Dāya' means the benefit (gain) received. It is called 'dāya' (inheritance) because it is given by those who give, and 'lābha' (gain) because it is received by those who receive. Having [contemplated] formations, they established themselves [in the Fruit of Non-returning] because of their special past meritorious deeds. Their arising [as Brahmas] while staying in that Tāvatiṃsa celestial realm is like Sakka's new arising as Sakka while staying in the Indasāla Cave.

Because he was unable to completely cut off the attachment (nikanti) to that Gandhabba celestial state, [one deva remained behind].

'Attanāva veditabbo' means it should be known by reaching it oneself, not by relying on others. 'Tumhehi vuccamānāni' means [it occurred] only by hearing the Dhamma teachings spoken by you, Venerable Sirs.

'Viyāyāma' means 'We shall exert strong effort in our own continuums.' 'Pakatiyā' means by way of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) state. Alternatively, there is a reading 'anussaraံ'.

Sensual lust (kāmarāga) itself is called 'kāmarāga-saṃyojana' (fetter of sensual lust) in the sense of binding due to the diversity of its occurrence, such as 'desire-lust' (chanda-rāga). It is also called 'kāma-bandhana' (bond of sensuality) due to the diversity of its modes of occurrence as yogas (yokes) and ganthas (ties). In the phrase 'pāpimayogāni', the meaning should be understood by way of the remaining yogas and ganthas.

'Duvidhānaṃ' refers to the two kinds of sensuality: objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and subjective sensuality (kilesa-kāma).

In the two phrases 'ettha kiṃ' and 'tattha kiṃ', the word 'kiṃ' is merely a particle (nipāta). 'Cātuddisabhāva' refers to the state of the three jewels, such as the Buddha, being worthy of the four directions and being unobstructed. The Buddha-jewel is 'cātuddisa' (of the four directions) because of his great compassion, his unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇa-ñāṇa), and his supreme contentment. The Dhamma-jewel is so because it is well-expounded (svākkhāta), and the Sangha-jewel because it is well-practiced (suppaṭipanna). Therefore, it is said: 'One who is unattached in all directions.'

Because they had attained the middle first jhāna, they obtained a Brahma body in the realm of Brahma's Ministers (Brahma-purohita). At that very moment, they regained their previous jhāna-mindfulness. Using that jhāna as a basis and developing insight (vipassanā), they attained the distinction of the Path and Fruit known as the Fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala) by completely cutting off the lower fetters. Some [teachers], however...
253:
Some teachers say that because they attained the paths and fruits while in the sense-sphere existence (kāmāvacara-attabhāva), but had not attained the fifth jhāna, they were not reborn in the Suddhāvāsa (Pure Abodes) realms; however, because they had attained the first jhāna, they were reborn in the Brahmapurohita (Ministers of Brahma) realms.

## Commentary on the Story of Magha Māṇava

'Visuddho' means one with a pure disposition, meaning one endowed with strong supporting wholesome conditions (upanissaya). 'Gāmakammakaranaṭṭhānaṃ' refers to the meeting place or the station of the villagers. 'Tāvatakeneva' means simply because another person came and took possession of the place he himself had cleared (implying the recovery of mindfulness).
