'Satiṃ paṭilabhitvā' means having generated a thought in a wise manner (yoniso), thinking, 'How wonderful! The work I have done has become fruitful.'

'Pāsāṇe' refers to the stones and rocks that stood prominently high in the middle of the road. 'Uccāletvā' means having extracted or removed them. 'Etassa saggassa gamanamaggaṃ' refers to the wholesome merit which is the path leading to this heavenly realm, the place of origin for the moon-deity and others.

'Sugativasena laddhabbaṃ' refers to the reward or prize that should be received due to his service, and 'kahāpaṇaṃ' refers to the silver coins. The offerings or taxes received due to the imposition of fines are called 'daṇḍabali'. 'Gahapatikā kiṃ karissanti' means that the householder class are like those living in the forest, depending on uneven places; they will not be able to do any harm to me. (In response to the question) 'Since you knew this, why did you not tell me?', it means: 'Even if I did not tell you before, I have told you now out of fear; please do not blame me; from the time I have informed you, I am no longer at fault.'

'Nibaddhanti' means occurring constantly and certainly.

'Pisuṇesī' means he committed the act of backbiting; it means 'he brings slanderous speech to me between you all.' Having made a 'brahmadeyyaṃ', which is an absolute gift that cannot be taken back. 'Mayhampī' means 'perform wholesome deeds dedicated to me and for my benefit as well.' A blue lotus (nīluppala) usually rises from the water only when it blooms; however, the meaning here is that just like a blue lotus blooming inside the water, this wholesome merit of ours gives fruit in this very life without passing to another existence. 'Cintāmattakampī' means he did not even have a mere thought of worry or anxiety due to unhappiness.

'Pagevā' means early in the morning, at a very early time. 'Kaṇṇikūpaganti' refers to a tree suitable for making a pinnacle (kaṇṇikā). 'Tacchetvā maṭṭhaṃ katvā' means having completed all the work to be done for the pinnacle. Because it was thus completed, that pinnacle was wrapped with a cloth and set aside.
254:
Binding grass and leaves refers to preparing the foundation of the rest house. Making a platform to stand on when mounting the pinnacle is called binding the pinnacle-frame (kaṇṇikamañcabandhanaṃ).

'On whichever plank it is spread, on that plank it is spread'—this is how the meaning should be construed.

'Avidūre' means in a place not far from the rest house and the koviḷāra (ebony) tree. 'Sabbajeṭṭhikā' refers to Sujātā, who was the eldest among all the wives of the young man Magha.

'Tasseva' means it belongs only to Sakka. 'Santike' means they were reborn as attendants in his presence. The Vejayanta palace, one thousand leagues in height, appeared along with the banner.

'Kakkatakavijjhanasūlasadisa' refers to something like a spit used to poke into a crab's hole in order to catch crabs.

'Maccharūpena' means in the form of a dead fish. 'Osarati' means it floats along. The lifespan of that small female crane was five hundred years. This is because the lifespan of humans, petas, and animals is not fixed, unlike the lifespan of those in the hell realms which is strictly defined.

'Ukkuṭṭhimakāsī' means she made a loud sound.

'Pubbasannivāsena' means due to having lived together for a long time in previous lives. In this way, for some people, affection arises even at first sight. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Through previous association,
Or through present benefit,
Thus is that love born,
Like a lotus in the water.”

'Avasesesu' refers to the deities of the two heavenly realms—Cātumahārājika and Tāvatiṃsa—excluding the Asuras and Sakka.

'Atthanissita' means depending only on the welfare of oneself and others. Since that welfare is the root cause of happiness, it was said to be 'depending on the cause' (kāraṇanissita).

## Commentary on the Explanation of Questions

'Kiṃsaṃyojanā' is a question asking what kind of fetters they have. They are called 'fetters' (saṃyojana) because they bind and join beings to misfortune. Therefore, it was said, 'What fetters do they have? By what fetters are they bound?' 'Puthukāyā' refers to the many groups of beings, hence it is said 'many people.' Enmity (vera) refers to anger (dosa); therefore, it was said, 'Being without enmity means being free from resentment (paṭigha).'
255:
Punishment by striking the body with a weapon is called āvudhadanda. Punishment by compelling the payment of wealth is called dhanadanda. One who is free from both these types of punishment, due to not inflicting them, is called adanda. An enemy is called sapatta because they plunder one's fortune or because they cause misfortune as soon as they are seen. Therefore, it is said: "Asapatta means those without enemies." Mental suffering (domanassa) is called byāpāda (byāpajjha). Meaning those who are free from such mental suffering, it is said: "Those free from mental suffering." Previously, by the word "avera", the absence of a grudge was taught. Therefore, it is said: "Those without enmity." Furthermore, by this word "averino", the non-arising of even a mere spark of anger is intended. Therefore, it is said: "Without giving rise to anger anywhere." The word "viharemu" (may we dwell) should also be connected with the preceding words as "may we dwell without enmity," and so on.

This state of non-enmity and so forth becomes manifest through sharing. To show this, after saying "accharā" and so on, it is said: "Thus it occurs to them." To show that the intention to give arises with greater firmness, it is said: "Having given gifts and performed worship, they aspire." In the phrase "iti ce", the word "ce" connects with the preceding words to provide the sense of reflection; therefore, it is said: "Thus to them."

Because it has the characteristic of disparaging, envying, or being unable to endure the success of others, issā (envy) is called "the state characterized by disparaging the success of others." Because of the limit of being unable to endure others sharing in one's own success, macchariya (stinginess) should also be called "the state characterized by concealment (nigūhana)." Indeed, regarding this, ancient teachers give the definition: "Let this wonder not belong to others, let it belong only to me"—this is macchariya. This has already been explained in the Nikkhepakaṇḍa of the Abhidhamma text Dhammasaṅgaṇī with the words "yā paralābhasakkāra..." and so forth, and also in its commentary, the Atthasālinī. Therefore, the meaning should be understood just as presented in those texts.

Since issā and macchariya have many disadvantages, explaining them is of great benefit to the world. Therefore, although they have been explained in the Abhidhamma commentary, wishing to show the dangers of these states in both the present life and the future, he said "āvāsamacchariyena pana" and so forth. "Ettha" (here) refers to these states of issā and macchariya, or to the five types of stinginess beginning with stinginess regarding dwellings (āvāsa-macchariya). Only by carrying rubbish on the head...
256:
...one wanders, because of a mind attached to that dwelling and because of low intentions. "Mama" means "mayā" (by me); or this "mayā" is the original reading itself. Due to mental distress and a burning heart, blood also issues from the mouth. Diarrhea also occurs for one with an excessively burning internal fire (kammaja-tejo). The Path and Fruit, which are the Dhamma of penetrating the state beyond existence (Nibbāna) other than the scriptural Dhamma (pariyatti), occur only to Noble Ones (ariyas). And those Noble Ones are not stingy with that Dhamma of the Path and Fruit, because they have completely abandoned all stinginess. Since stinginess cannot occur regarding the Dhamma of penetration, it is said: "And through stinginess regarding the scriptural Dhamma (pariyattidhamma-macchariya)." Through stinginess regarding appearance (vaṇṇa-macchariya), one becomes ill-favored. Through stinginess regarding the Dhamma (dhamma-macchariya), one becomes a dribbler (mute) and unwise.

The passage beginning with "api ca" (moreover) shows the results (vipāka) corresponding to the deeds through the power of the five types of stinginess. Through stinginess regarding dwellings (āvāsa-macchariya), one is cooked in the iron-house hell, because of preventing the welfare and happiness of others that depend on a dwelling. Through stinginess regarding families (kula-macchariya), one has few gains, because of preventing the gains that others should receive from families. "Appalābha" (few gains) means no gains at all. Through stinginess regarding gains (lābha-macchariya), one is reborn in the excrement hell, because for the sake of gains, one prevents the enjoyment of gains that others should receive. In truth, the excrement hell is a place without any enjoyment whatsoever. "Vaṇṇo nāma na hoti" means that both physical beauty and the beauty of reputation do not exist even in name. Wherever one is reborn, one is only of an ugly appearance. Due to stinginess, which has the nature of concealing success, qualities (guṇa) generally find no footing in a distorted continuity of mind and body. Even if qualities were to be present, one would not have beauty because of those qualities. For they would not be manifest, like arrows shot at night in the world. Through stinginess regarding the Dhamma (dhamma-macchariya), one is reborn in the ember hell. Because it leads to the states of woe, that issā and macchariya are abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). Just as beings cannot escape birth and so forth, they do not escape from enmity and so forth even if they recite the absence of faults in those without enmity, because it cannot be attained by mere desire for such escape.

In the phrase "tinnā mettha kaṅkhā", the letter "m" is a syllable connector (padasandhi). "Etasmiṃ pañhe" (in this question) means in this matter where one desires to know, "What are the fetters?" "Tumhākaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā" (having heard your words) means having heard your answer which proceeded as, "They are the fetters of envy and stinginess." "Kaṅkhā tinnā" (doubt is crossed over) means that doubt regarding the matter questioned has been crossed over and has vanished merely by following the teaching, not by the power of the Path (magga); thus he said "na maggavasena" and so forth. "Ayampi kathaṃkathā vigatā" (this perplexity has also vanished) means that because doubt has vanished, this perplexity—which is a specific mode of its occurrence as "how is this, how is that"—has also vanished and gone away.
257:
The meanings of the words beginning with 'Nidāna' are exactly as stated in the Commentary on the Mahānidāna Sutta (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.95). Stinginess (macchariya) is rooted in dear beings and formations (piya-satta-saṅkhāra-nidāna) because it arises through the inability to bear sharing one's own cherished beings and formations with others, and through the act of concealment. Envy (issā) is rooted in undear beings and formations (appiya-satta-saṅkhāra-nidāna) because it arises through the inability to bear the possessions of undear beings and formations belonging to others. This is because even an excellent object associated with an undear person is only unpleasant to one who is angry.

'Ubhayā' refers to both stinginess and envy. 'Ubhayanidāna' means having both dear and undear causes. 'Piyā' refers to desirable things. 'Keḷāyitā' refers to cherished things. 'Mamāyitā' refers to things possessed as 'mine'. 'Issāṃ karoti' (one envies) means one is jealous due to the inability to bear another person's acquisition of a dear being, thinking, "What use is this dear thing to this person?" One also envies when another person requests that same dear being. 'Aho vatassa' means performing or producing envy, thinking, "It would be good if this person did not have such a dear object." 'Mamāyantā' means cherishing (and thus being reluctant to use). 'Appiye' refers to undear beings because they cause distress. 'Assa' refers to the person who has acquired those things. 'Te' refers to beings and formations; even if they are unpleasant, envy can still arise because they were obtained from undear persons. 'Viparītavuttitāya' means due to perverted or distorted perception. One envies while exalting oneself, thinking, "Who else but I could obtain such a thing?" Or one envies when such a thing arises for another, thinking, "It would be good if this person did not have such a thing." This method is not adopted here as it has been mentioned below.

Desire arising through the seeking of objects of sensual pleasure is called 'desire for seeking' (pariyesana-chanda). Desire rooted in acquisition is called 'desire for acquisition' (paṭilābha-chanda). Desire arising through enjoyment is called 'desire for enjoyment' (paribhoga-chanda). Desire arising through the hoarding and securing of acquired things is called 'desire for hoarding' (sannidhi-chanda). Desire arising through giving, considering only the benefits of the present life, is called 'desire for giving' (vissajjana-chanda). Therefore, it is said in the commentary, "Katamā," and so forth.

Since these five types of desire are essentially the functioning of craving (taṇhā), it is said, "taṇhā-mattam-eva" (merely craving).

In this context, the 'decisive thought' (vinicchaya-vitakka) mentioned in the Mahānidāna Sutta as "deciding based on gain" is what is meant by 'thought' (vitakka); it does not refer to just any kind of thought. Now...
258:
To demonstrate the aforementioned decisive thought by way of extracting its meaning, the words beginning with "Vinicchayo" were spoken. "Aṭṭhasataṃ" means one hundred and eight (108); to show that this hundred refers specifically to the one hundred and eight mental wanderings of craving (taṇhā-vicarita) and not to just any hundred things, it is said, "taṇhā-vicaritaṃ." It is called 'craving-decision' (taṇhā-vinicchaya) because it decides on an object through the power of craving in the manner to be described. It is called 'view-decision' (diṭṭhi-vinicchaya) because it decides through the power of wrong view, thinking, "This alone is the truth, all else is false."

A sublime object is 'desirable' (iṭṭha), a non-sublime object is 'undesirable' (aniṭṭha), that which should be loved is 'dear' (piya), and that which should be disliked is 'undear' (appiya). The definition of these objects does not occur according to the power of craving. For by the power of craving, one person may consider a certain object sublime, while another considers it inferior; one person may love it, while another does not. Therefore, it is said, "Tadeva hi," and so forth. The word "Dassāmi" (I shall give) should be understood both by the method mentioned in the explanation of the desire for giving and as giving based on the support for the cycle of birth (giving with the hope for future worldly fortune). This is because even such giving based on the cycle is rooted in the desire of craving.

They are called 'proliferations' (papañca) because they arise spontaneously within the continuity of beings and expand (papañcenti) that continuity within the cycle of birth (saṃsāra). Alternatively, they are called proliferations because, having arisen in someone, they manifest (vyañjenti) that person as "one who is lustful," "a being," or "one who is wrongly obsessed." Since craving and views, when they become excessive, lead the person possessed of them to a state of negligence, while conceit leads to a state of intoxication through pride of birth and so on, it is said, "mattapamattākārapāpanaṭṭhena" (in the sense of leading to a state of intoxication and negligence).

A group or category is called 'saṅkhā', because it appears as a portion or part. Because the perceptions of proliferation (papañca-saññā) become the causes for thought (vitakka) in groups according to their respective doors and objects, and not in isolation, it is called 'thought rooted in the categories of perceptions of proliferation' (papañca-saññā-saṅkhā-nidāna). Alternatively, because the perceptions of proliferation are divided into many types, their collection is called 'papañca-saññā-saṅkhā'. By taking 'papañca-saññā-saṅkhā', the entire origin of suffering (dukkha-samudaya) is expressed, as they are the various causes of the suffering of the cycle (vaṭṭa-dukkha).

By the words "Yo nirodho vūpasamo," the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca) is stated. "Tassa sāruppaṃ" means suitable (anucchavika) because it is the means for attaining the cessation and stilling of those categories of perceptions of proliferation; by this, Insight (vipassanā) is meant. "Tatthagāminī" means 'going there' or 'proceeding' by way of making that aforementioned cessation the object; by this, the Path (magga) is meant. Therefore, it is said, "He asks about the Path together with Insight."

## Commentary on the Meditation Subject of Feeling

Only that which was asked has been explained. Because Sakka, the king of devas, asked only about the practice leading to the cessation of the categories of perceptions of proliferation, the Blessed Lord explained the meditation subject of mentality (nāma-kammaṭṭhāna) which is the means for that attainment...
259:
Wishing to teach by making feeling the starting point according to his inclination, he began by teaching the three types of feelings. Thus, he taught the Dhamma with sequence (anusandhi) in relation to the question, teaching only the matter that was asked. Indeed, for the Buddhas, there is no such thing as a discourse without sequence. Now, to show the reason for teaching only the meditation on mentality (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) by making mentality the starting point, the phrase beginning with "Devatānañhi" is stated. By mentioning the subtlety of the physical body (karaja-kāya), it should be understood that its extremely delicate and refined nature is also mentioned. "Kammaja" refers to the fire element born of kamma (kammaja-tejo). The strength of that kamma-born matter is due to being produced by extensive wholesome kamma, and because it can digest extremely sweet and pure nutriment. "Ekāhārampi" refers to even a single turn of taking nutriment. By the word "vilīyanti," it is shown that due to the tenderness of the physical body and the strength of the kamma-born fire element, when the time for food is passed, intense painful feeling arises for those deities and becomes very manifest. This is merely an illustration. In truth, their pleasant feeling also becomes clearly manifest when it occurs successively and without hindrance upon extensive and sublime objects. Equanimous feeling also, when it occasionally arises for them, is peaceful and sublime because it occurs only towards desirable-neutral (iṭṭhamajjhatta) objects. Therefore, the phrase beginning with "Tasmā" is said.

Meditation on materiality (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) means the grasping of matter, the entry into insight (vipassanā) by making matter the starting point. The same method applies to the term meditation on mentality (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna). Among those meditations, entry into serenity (samatha) through meditation on materiality is also included; however, wishing to show that what is intended here is only the entry into insight, it is said: "This is also called the grasping of materiality and the grasping of mentality." In this context of "catudhātuvavatthāna" (definition of the four elements), it means that he teaches meditation on materiality by expanding on the method of defining the four great elements. Having shown the meditation on materiality, he said: "When the meditation on materiality is taught in this way, it becomes well-clarified and manifest." By this statement, they say that in this Sutta as well, meditation on materiality has been partially clarified.

Although meditation on mentality appears in this Sutta by way of feeling, it can also be obtained by way of other mental phenomena. Therefore, to show those mental phenomena by way of analysis, the phrase beginning with "Tividho hi" is stated. Therein, "abhinivesa" means repeated entry or the initial undertaking. This analysis exists only in the initial undertaking. Comprehension (sammasana) through knowledge, however, occurs by grasping the phenomena without remainder. The phrase "when the meditation on materiality has been defined" is said with reference to the entry into insight by making matter the starting point. Entry into insight by making mentality the starting point is generally intended for the person who has serenity as their vehicle (samatha-yānika). That person whose vehicle is serenity, having first grasped feeling and equanimity, then grasps the remaining mental factors such as contact (phassa). In this context of "paṭhamābhinipāto," all mental factors are called the activities of the mind because they are connected with the mind. Contact (phassa) is said to be the phenomenon that first falls upon the object of the mind. Contact, which arises while touching that object already defined by the meditation on materiality, is manifest. When the person or the group of mental factors where contact has arisen touches the object, they experience the object through the feeling that arises together with contact, at the very moment of touching the object.
260:
That practitioner who has tranquility as their vehicle (samatha-yānika) first distinguishes the jhāna factors and thereafter distinguishes the remaining states. Regarding 'the first impact' (paṭhamābhinipāta): since all mental factors (cetasikas) depend on the mind and are described as the activities of the mind, contact (phassa) is called the mind's first impact upon the object. Regarding 'that object': it refers to the object known as the materiality meditation subject (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) which has been distinguished. A person in whom contact has arisen, or the group of mind and mental factors, when touched by the object, experiences it at that very moment of contact through the feeling (vedanā) that arises together with contact. However, contact is said to be like the preceding time because it is a specific condition for feeling and so on, just as a lamp is for light. This refers to the characteristic of contact which directs [the mind] towards the object.

'Touching' (phussanto) means by way of the manner of touching the object. Because this contact is a mental state (nāma-dhamma), although it does not adhere to a single part [physically], it occurs as if touching the mind and the object, or as if striking them, just as matter touches the eye or sound touches the ear. Therefore, contact is said to have 'the function of striking' (saṅghaṭṭana-rasa).

'Experiencing the object' (ārammaṇaṃ anubhavantī) means experiencing the flavor of the object through its sovereignty, capability, and mastery. For associated states such as contact, their occurrence in the object is only partial because they merely touch it, etc. However, feeling occurs in the object without remainder because it occurs by way of enjoying the desired aspect, etc. Taking the object by way of touching, etc., is a partial experience, whereas taking it by way of feeling is a complete experience according to one's desire. Thus, these ways of taking [the object] have distinct natures. Therefore, it should not be argued that contact and so on also experience like a master by performing their own functions, as feeling does.

'Knowing specifically' (vijānantaṃ) means knowing particularly by way of delimiting. Consciousness (viññāṇa) occurs by delimiting and making the object manifest, like a man measuring a measurable substance with a nāḷi measure. It is not merely the act of perceiving like perception (saññā). For this reason, sometimes the manifestation of the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa) also occurs through this consciousness. The nature of the manifestation of these states such as contact should be understood by the power of the preceding part of the state that is accomplished through a specific condition.

Even though those various states are manifest in this way, the Teacher said, 'Monks, everything should be known with higher knowledge,' and 'Monks, when everything is fully known (it is fit for the destruction of suffering),' and so on. Wishing to show that all states fit for contemplation should be distinguished, he said, 'Among those states, to whomsoever...' and so forth. In that statement, the restriction 'only among the five starting with contact' (phassa-pañcamaka) is because the four immaterial aggregates are included within those five starting with contact, and by taking those five, they are already taken. Taking the five starting with contact is because of the fact that all those states follow the mind (are associated with the mind). Among those five starting with contact, by taking contact and volition (cetanā), all states of the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) are grasped. This is because all those formations have volition as their leader. Because volition is the leader, in the detailed analysis (bhājanīya) of the aggregate of formations by the Suttanta method, the aggregate of formations is...
261:
...due to being common to all arisings of consciousness. Among those five starting with contact, by taking contact and volition, all states of the aggregate of formations are grasped, because volition is the primary leader of them. For this reason, in the analysis of the aggregate of formations in the Suttanta-bhājanīya, only volition is analyzed in detail as 'volition born of eye-contact' (cakkhu-samphassajā cetanā) and so on, while the other aggregates are taken only by their own forms.

In the term 'dependent on a base' (vatthu-nissita), the word 'vatthu' (base) refers to the physical body (karaja-kāya), not to the six physical bases. How is this known? He said, 'With reference to which physical body it was spoken.' Where was it spoken? It was spoken in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta. 'So' (he) refers to the physical body. The statement 'There is no mind-and-matter (nāma-rūpa) apart from the five aggregates' was spoken by way of the context of insight (vipassanā). Otherwise, there certainly is a mental state (nāma) that is apart from the [material] aggregates. 'Caused by ignorance, etc.' (avijjādi-hetukā) means having ignorance, craving, clinging, and so on as causes. Having spoken of powerful insight with the words 'one dwells contemplating as impermanent, suffering, and non-self through the sequence of insight,' he then said 'So' (he) and so forth, wishing to show that person's exertion and the attainment of distinction.

'Here' (idha) means in this Sakkapañha Sutta. The reason for teaching the immaterial meditation subject by way of feeling in this sutta should be understood according to the method already mentioned below. Among the three ways of applying the meditation subject mentioned, applying it by way of feeling is easy because of the distinctness (vibhūta) of feelings; to show this, he said 'By way of contact, however,' and so forth. The words 'is not manifest' were spoken with the intention that for those deities, headed by Sakka, feeling appears distinctly, but the other two (contact and consciousness) do not appear so. The distinctness of feeling alone for those deities is because the Blessed One began the teaching in this sutta by using feeling as the starting point. The words 'because of the distinctness of the arising of feelings' were spoken by way of pleasant and painful feelings. The occurrence of those pleasant and painful feelings is coarse (oḷārika), but the other (neutral feeling) is not. However, since the occurrence of the other feeling can also be known by the wise through the taking of those two types, the specific taking of 'pleasant and painful feelings' should be understood. 'When a pleasant feeling arises' and so forth is an explanation of the distinctness of pleasant feeling, and this should be understood by way of the plane of one who has not yet attained concentration (asamāhita-bhūmi). In that context, this pleasant feeling, which has a non-calm nature because its occurrence is coarse as in 'Venerable Sir, the whole body...', is shown to occur only while supporting the associated states and the physical body (karaja-kāya) which is its support, because it has the characteristic of being agreeable. In the words 'When a painful feeling arises' and so forth, the meaning should be understood as the opposite of what was just said.

'Difficult to illuminate' (duddīpanā) means unable to be illuminated by wisdom, meaning difficult to understand. Therefore, he said, 'overwhelmed by darkness.' 'Darkness' (andhakārā) means like being in the midst of darkness.
262:
It creates darkness for those who wish to know (or it is like darkness). Just as a deer's track on a flat rock surface is inferred by means of a well-prepared and well-marked path that is even from beginning to end, it is said, 'That [neutral feeling]... becomes clear' because neutral feeling in neutral objects can be inferred by the experience of pleasure and pain in desirable and undesirable objects. Therefore, he said 'Yathā' and so forth.

In the phrase 'nayato gaṇhantassa' (taking by way of method), this is the method: Since the apprehension of an object that is neither desirable nor undesirable arises from the experience of apprehending desirable and undesirable objects, that [neutral feeling] must not be without experience. Whatever experience is there, that is neutral feeling (adukkhamasukha-vedanā). Thus, neutral feelings experienced through objects such as visible forms, which are not obtained through the experience of desirable or undesirable objects, are seen and can be obtained. A person experiences a neutral object at the time when consciousness of that object arises; therefore, that person cannot remain without experiencing the neutral object. Because it has the nature of apprehending an object, it can be said that the neutral feeling which experiences a neutral object possesses the apprehension of a neutral object. Furthermore, although there is an object that possesses the apprehension of desirable and undesirable things, that neutral feeling which does not experience that object is seen as not taking the desirable or undesirable; such a neutral feeling has the nature of experiencing such an object.

'Nivattetvā' means having extracted. By saying 'I [abandon] joy,' and so forth, he distinguishes it from other mental states of the same class and makes it unmixed, separating it from other immaterial phenomena.

Having taught the meditation on materiality (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna), he then taught the meditation on mentality (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) by extracting it through the means of feeling (vedanā). To show that this teaching, which considers individuals who should be thus disciplined, also appears in other Suttas, he said 'Na kevalaṃ' and so forth. In that context, the fact that feeling is separately extracted and taught in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta will become clear immediately after this Sutta; the Satipaṭṭhāna teaching in the Majjhima Nikāya is also the same. In the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta, it is stated: 'Sakka, lord of devas... it has been heard by a bhikkhu: "All things are not fit to be clung to (through craving and views)"; that bhikkhu fully knows all things with direct knowledge; having known all things with direct knowledge, he fully understands all things; having fully understood all things, whatever feeling he feels—whether pleasant, painful, or neutral—he dwells contemplating impermanence and contemplating fading away in those feelings,' and so forth. Therefore, it is said, 'He showed the meditation on mentality by extracting it through the means of feeling.' In the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta, however: 'That bhikkhu, having thus abandoned favor (anurodha) and opposition (virodha), whatever feeling he feels—whether pleasant, painful, or neutral—he does not delight in that feeling, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it. For him who does not delight in, welcome, or remain clinging to that feeling, whatever delight (nandī) there is in feelings...'
263:
'...that delight ceases,' and so forth (as stated in the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta). In the Cūḷavedalla Sutta, it is stated: 'Lady, how many feelings are there?' and so forth. In the Mahāvedalla Sutta: 'Friend, it is called "feeling"; to what extent, friend, is it called "feeling"?' and so forth. In this way, the occurrences of the meditation on feeling (vedanā-kammaṭṭhāna) should be extracted and stated from the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta and others.

It was said, 'Having first taught the meditation on materiality.' How is that taught here? He said 'rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna' and so forth. It is taught in brief. How is it in brief? It is in brief by showing only the object of feeling. Generally, because feeling arises by way of the five doors, it has material phenomena as its object. Therefore, the object of that feeling is already established previously. The Blessed One, in speaking of feeling, has already taken the objects of that feeling by way of meaning first. By this implication, it is shown that in this Sakkapañha Sutta, the meditation on materiality is taken first; it is not because it is taken directly in its own form. Therefore, he said, 'In that case, it will not appear (directly) in the Pali text.'

'By way of two parts' means by way of the part to be cultivated and the part not to be cultivated. 'Of such a nature' refers to the nature of joy (somanassa) that leads to the increase of unwholesome states and the decrease of wholesome states. Because that joy is connected with sensual desire, it is called 'household-based (gehanissita),' hence he said 'household-based joy (gehasita-somanassa).' 'Iṭṭha' means desirable; 'kanta' means lovely; 'manāpa' means mind-expanding (pleasing); and because they thus expand the mind, they are 'manorama,' delightful things. 'Connected with worldly bait (lokāmisa)' means things connected with sensuality that depend on craving. 'For one who sees by way of obtaining' means for one who enjoys the objects of sight and so forth as they are obtained, thinking, 'Oh, I have obtained these!' 'Past' means gone by; 'ceased' (niruddha) means reached cessation; 'changed' (vipariṇata) means departed from its original nature. [This refers to] one who repeatedly thinks of and remembers such things with enjoyment. 'Gehasita' means depending on the cords of sensual pleasure. The cords of sensual pleasure are intended here as 'geha' (house) because they are like a house for sensual lust (kāmarāga).

'Of such a nature' refers to the nature of joy that leads to the decrease of unwholesome states and the increase of wholesome states. Because that joy arises by way of renunciation and so forth, it is connected with nekkhamma (renunciation); hence he said 'renunciation-based joy (nekkhammasita-somanassa).' Now, to show that according to the Pali text, he said 'In that case, what is it?' and so forth. There, having the characteristic of insight...
264:
When Nekkhamma (renunciation) is shown, other types of joy (somanassa) arising through the power of recollections (anussati), the first jhāna, and so on, are already shown by way of the cause, effect, and meaning of that Nekkhamma-based joy which has the characteristic of Vipassanā (insight). Therefore, desiring to show that Nekkhamma-based joy which possesses the characteristic of Vipassanā, the passage beginning with "Rūpānaṃ tveva" was spoken.

"Vipariṇāma-virāga-nirodhaṃ" should be interpreted as: having known the changeability caused by old age, and the destruction and cessation caused by old age and death. "Uppajjati somanassaṃ" means that an immeasurable joy arises after the gladness (pāmojja), rapture (pīti), and tranquility (passaddhi) that arise sequentially through the practice of the path of Vipassanā. With reference to such immeasurable joy, it was said:

"For the monk who has entered a secluded dwelling,
Who has a peaceful mind,
And who clearly perceives the Dhamma (the nature of things),
There is a joy transcending that of mortals.
Whenever he contemplates the rise and fall of the aggregates,
He gains rapture and gladness;
For those who know the Deathless (Nibbāna), that joy exists."

"Nekkhammavasena" means by way of the state of a monk and so on. All practices such as going to the presence of monks to ordain with the intention "I shall escape the suffering of the round of rebirth," ordaining, following the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla), purifying that virtue, undertaking and practicing the ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa), and performing the preparatory work for kasiṇa (kasiṇaparikamma), are intended here as "Nekkhamma". Considering that access concentration (upacāra jhāna) usually concludes with recollection, it was stated "by way of recollection" and then "by way of the first jhāna and so on."

In this context, just as the state of a monk is called Nekkhamma in the sense of departing from the bond of the household, so too are Vipassanā and other states called Nekkhamma because they are the opposites of that household bond. Therefore, it was said:

"Ordination, the first jhāna,
Nibbāna, and Vipassanā—
All wholesome states
Are called Nekkhamma."

In the phrase "Yaṃ ce", the word "ce" is merely a particle without additional meaning, as only joy (somanassa) is intended. Because the discussion of jhāna in the Suttas is usually taught by way of the fourfold method (catukkanaya), it was stated "by way of the second and third jhānas." "Dvīsu" refers to the two types of joy described as "with initial and sustained thought (savitakka savicāra)" and "without initial and sustained thought (avitakka avicāra)."

"Savitakka-savicāra somanassa" refers to the joy in the lower planes (parittabhūmi) or the joy in the first jhāna. "Abhiniviṭṭha-somanassa" refers to the joys that initiate Vipassanā. By the word "pi", it shows the meaning that rapture (pīti) also exists in the joys that are contemplated.
265:
Insight (vipassanā) that arises by taking joy without initial and sustained thought as its object is superior and more sublime than insight that arises by taking joy with initial and sustained thought as its object. This is because the excellence of insight is achieved even by way of the joy that is contemplated as impermanent and so forth; thus, such excellences are also achieved in the Path (magga). This meaning should be illustrated by the view of the Elder Mahādatta, a resident of Moravāpī, who stated: 'The aggregates which are the objects of insight determine the excellence of the Noble Path, the factors of enlightenment (bojjhanga), and so forth.'

Household-based grief (gehasita-domanassa) is the unhappiness that arises due to the non-attainment of sense pleasures or due to their loss and destruction. 'For one who sees through non-attainment' means due to the repeated distress of thinking 'Only I do not obtain it' because of non-attainment. 'For one who recollects' means for one who thinks by way of repeated recollection such as 'That object was mine, but now it is not mine.' Therefore, it was said in the Commentary, 'Thus in the six doors,' and so forth.

'In the unsurpassed liberations' (anuttaresu vimokkhesu) refers to the liberations of the Noble Fruitions (ariya-phala) such as the fruition of emptiness (suññata-phala). 'Pihanti' means longing or desire (āsā). How can desire (taṇhā) arise in relation to supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma)? This should not be seen as desire occurring there by way of making them a direct object, because supramundane states are not the domain of craving and because the person has not yet attained them. However, because one generates a longing directed toward the unsurpassed liberations known through hearsay, it is said 'one generates longing for those states.' Therefore, He taught: 'When indeed shall I...' and so forth. The construction should be: 'having initiated insight by way of impermanence and so forth when a desirable object (iṭṭhārammaṇa) appears at the six doors.' By the term 'iṭṭhārammaṇe,' it is shown that this grief does not arise only in relation to objects that are undesirable by nature, but rather it can arise in any object whatever due to the frustration of desire caused by not obtaining what is wanted.

Thus, having generated longing in the manner stated as 'When indeed shall I...', the grief that arises in the mind of one who repeatedly grieves, thinking 'I have not been able to reach the distinction of the Noble ones even after striving in insight for this whole fortnight, this whole month, or this whole year,' is called 'by way of renunciation' (nekkhamma-vasena). It is called 'by way of renunciation' with reference to the occurrence of thoughts such as 'I did not get to ordain in this fortnight' or 'I did not get to perform the kasiṇa preliminary work.' In the phrases 'by way of insight' and so forth, the construction should be understood in this same way.

Because the word 'eva' (only/just) restricts the meaning, it was said 'In that also... it is only household-based grief.' For here, the state of being household-based grief is not restricted to having initial and sustained thought; rather, it is the presence of initial and sustained thought within household-based grief that is being restricted.
266:
The word 'eva' (only/just) has the sense of excluding the opposite meaning of 'without initial thought and without sustained thought' (avitakka-avicāra); therefore, the state of being 'with initial thought and with sustained thought' (savitakka-savicāra) is certain. It is said: 'Household-related grief (gehasita-domanassa) is only a state with initial thought and sustained thought, not a state without initial thought and sustained thought.' Furthermore, renunciation-related grief (nekkhamma-sita-domanassa) is in some cases a state with initial thought and sustained thought, and in some cases a state without initial thought and sustained thought. Grief that is the cause of only initial thought and sustained thought is called 'initial-thought-and-sustained-thought grief' (savitakka-savicāra-domanassa). What is that grief? It is household-related grief. That grief which arises by way of renunciation, etc., is the cause for the state without initial thought and sustained thought, and is thus called 'without-initial-thought-and-without-sustained-thought grief' (avitakka-avicāra-domanassa).

Intending that this method is taught figuratively (pariyāya), the phrase beginning with 'nippariyāyena pana' is stated. If that is so, there might be a question as to why it is taught in the Pāḷi text as 'yaṃ ce avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ'; therefore, the phrase beginning with 'etassa pana' is stated. 'Maññanavasena' means by way of conceptualizing. It is taught in the Pāḷi text.

'Tatra' means in that conceptualizing. This is the method that will now be explained. 'Domanassapaccayabhūte' means in those states which are the causes of grief. For one who wishes to produce the Path and Fruition (magga-phala) by making access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) or the first absorption (paṭhama-jhāna), etc., the basis, when grief arises because of not attaining those Path and Fruition states, those states are called the causes of that grief. Therefore, those states of Path and Fruition are figuratively called 'grief' (domanassa) by way of the result's name. If a monk, even though such grief has arisen, does not give up his effort and gradually exerts himself in insight (vipassanā) to produce the Path and Fruition states, those states are figuratively called 'grief' (domanassa) by way of the cause's name. To show this meaning, the phrase beginning with 'idha bhikkhū' is stated.

One might ask: 'At that time, only grief arose for this monk, and the states of insight, Path, and Fruition caused by grief did not arise; if so, why is the name "grief" applied figuratively?' To answer this, the phrase beginning with 'aññesaṃ paṭipattidassanavasena domanassanti gahetvā' is stated. 'Savitakkasavicāradomanasse' means in the grief that has initial thought and sustained thought as its cause. The practice to be accomplished in three months is called 'temāsika'; it refers to the practice performed throughout those three months. These practices, such as the three-month one, should be understood by way of the sharp, medium, or dull faculties (indriya) that have arisen, or by way of superior, medium, or inferior effort (vīriya). 'Jaggati' means one exerts oneself in wakefulness.

## The Explanation of the Story of Mahāsīva Thera

Because they numbered one thousand or two thousand, he wandered among large groups (mahāgaṇa). 'Aṭṭhakathā-therā' refers to the elders who inquire about the meaning of the Commentaries. 'Antarāmagge' means on the path returning from the village to the monastery after receiving alms. 'Tayo... pe... gāhāpetvā' means having him take the warmth [of the sun/fire] three or four times.
267:
The practice to be accomplished in three months is called 'temāsika'. This practice should be understood by way of the sharp, medium, or dull faculties (indriya), or by way of superior, medium, or inferior effort (vīriya). 'Jaggati' means exerting oneself in wakefulness. Because they numbered one thousand or two thousand, he wandered among large groups. There were elders who inquired about the meaning of the Commentaries. On the way back from the village to the monastery after receiving alms, they would have him take the warmth [of the sun/fire] three or four times.

He left the monastery for some long-standing matter of bodily care. At night, not recognizing Mahāsīva Thera who was walking behind him as his teacher, he perceived him merely as a monk who had the same teacher as himself.

Regarding the question of why the Elder Mahāsīva went out of the monastery without informing his resident pupils, the phrase beginning with 'thero kira' is stated. The statement 'What is this called Arahantship?' is said with reference to the fact that the attainment of that Fruition of Arahantship is not something difficult to do. 'By the four postures' (catūhi iriyāpathehi) means: 'The Path and Fruition will not arise for me who remains in the four postures; therefore, until the attainment of Arahantship, I shall renounce the reclining posture'—this is the intention.

'Is this weeping suitable for you?'—feeling a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and energizing his effort, he attained Arahantship. This was because his wisdom had reached maturity due to having practiced insight (vipassanā) well for as long as thirty years.

'Parimajjī' means rubbing or stroking. Some teachers, however, say that 'parimajjī' means that while the Elder Mahāsīva was repeatedly turning and washing his feet, Sakka (the King of Devas) took hold of them and washed them.

The objects of insight (vipassanā) are access concentration (upacāra-jhāna), the first absorption (paṭhama-jhāna), and so on. The explanation to be given for terms such as 'savitakkasavicāradomanassa' should be understood according to the method already stated for 'somanassa' (joy), etc.

'Evarūpā' (of such a kind) refers to that equanimity (upekkhā) which leads to the increase of unwholesome states and the decline of wholesome states; such equanimity is called 'household-related' (gehasita) because it is connected with sensual pleasures. Therefore, it is called 'household-related equanimity' (gehasita-upekkhā). In the terms 'bālassa' (of the fool), etc.: one is a 'fool' (bāla) because of being associated with states that produce foolishness. One is 'deluded' (mūḷha) because of being confused about one's own benefit and the benefit of others. One is a 'worldling' (puthujjana) because of reasons such as producing many (puthu) defilements. One is 'anodhijina' because the limits (odhi) of defilements have not yet been conquered (ajita) by the Noble Paths. (The 'sekha' or learners are called 'odhijina' because they have conquered defilements by way of limits.) By this term 'anodhijina', the state of being a 'sekha' is excluded for that worldling. One is 'avipakajina' because the results (vipāka) that would occur beyond the seventh existence have not yet been conquered. (Arahants are 'vipākajina' because they have conquered the results by having no further rebirth.) By this term 'avipakajina', the state of being an 'asekha' (adept) is excluded for that worldling. One is 'anādīnavadassāvī' (not seeing danger) because of the habit of not seeing the dangers in delusion (sammoha), which is the root of all evil states. One is 'assutavā' (unlearned) because of the absence of learning (āgama) and realization (adhigama). Such a person is certainly called a 'blind worldling' (andha-puthujjana). To show his state as a blind worldling, the word 'puthujjanassa' is said again. 'Evarūpā' means...
268:
The aforementioned variety of equanimity is preceded by delusion. "That equanimity does not transcend form" means it does not become a cause for transcending forms; it means it does not transcend the defilements that take form as an object. Being equanimity of ignorance (aññāṇupekkhā) devoid of wisdom, the equanimity associated with greed (lobha) that occurs by way of indifference toward the object is intended here. Therefore, to show the object suitable for that greed, it is said, "in a desirable object." It cannot be transcended because of not seeing the danger (ādīnava). Because of viewing it with enjoyment (assāda) without seeing the danger, it becomes attached to that very form. It arises as if stuck by that greed, both through the power of the clinging greed and because of the difficulty of being released.

The kind of equanimity that leads to the abandoning of unwholesome states and the increase of wholesome states is associated with renunciation (nekkhamma) because it occurs through the state of monkhood and so on; therefore, it is called "renunciation-based" (nekkhamma-sita). Now, to show that equanimity by way of the Pali text, the passage beginning with "Therein, which is it?" (tattha katamā) is stated. Its meaning should be understood according to the method mentioned below. "That equanimity transcends form" means it is because of seeing the danger in form correctly. It transcends form because it cannot be overcome by the defilements that take form as an object. It arises in the continuity of one who is not lustful, who does not give rise to passion (rāga) toward a desirable object—desirable either by its own nature or by way of intention. The meaning of "one who is not angry at an undesirable object" should also be understood according to the method already mentioned.

Not looking correctly or evenly with a proper cause is called "uneven looking" (asama-pekkhaṇa). Such uneven looking occurs to the foolish in regard to desirable and undesirable objects, just as it does in neutral objects. Therefore, without specifically saying "in desirable, undesirable, and neutral objects," it is said, "of one who is not deluded by uneven looking." It means it arises in the continuity of one who is not deluded by way of uneven looking in all three types of objects. Equanimity associated with insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) is renunciation-based equanimity. It is called "similar to feeling" (vedanā-sabhāga) because it occurs in the manner of indifference and because it is similar to the feeling of equanimity (upekkhā-vedanā). In this explanation of equanimity, what is taken as "equanimity" is indeed tatramajjhattatā (equanimity as mental neutrality). Therefore, in this context, tatramajjhattatā should be taken by the name "equanimity." Referring to that tatramajjhattatā, it is said, "equanimity that arises by way of the first, second, third, and fourth jhānas."

"In that renunciation-based equanimity," the case ending is the locative case (sattamī) in the sense of specification (niddhāraṇa). The passage beginning with "that which by way of renunciation" (yaṃ nekkhamma-vasena) has a clear meaning according to the method already mentioned below.

If Sakka at that time had only the strong supporting condition (upanissaya) for the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), why then did the Blessed One increase the teaching up to the fruit of arahantship? To answer this, the passage beginning with "For the Buddhas..." (buddhānañhi) is stated. "Young Sakka" (taruṇa-sakka) refers to the Sakka who has just newly appeared. It is said "young Sakka" referring to the Sakka who has just become manifest in a new existence. For that Sakka, there is no such thing as being young or old. The cause of his going and coming is also not apparent. When devas pass away, it is not apparent where they pass away. The karma-born matter (kammaja-rūpa) of those devas ceases. Mind-born matter (cittaja-rūpa) and nutriment-born matter (āhāraja-rūpa) also cease because the mind and nutriment, which are their causes, no longer exist.
269:
It is said "young Sakka" (Taruṇa Sakka) referring to the fact that he has just appeared in a new life. For that Sakka, there is no state of being young or old. "Gatāgataṭṭhāna" means the cause of going and coming. It is not apparent or findable. For beings conceived in a womb, when they pass away, the karma-born matter (kammaja-rūpa) ceases, and the mind-born (cittaja) and nutriment-born (āhāraja) matter also cease in succession due to the absence of causes. However, temperature-born matter (utuja-rūpa) may persist for a very long time, continuing the material sequence, or shifting, drying up, becoming soiled, or expanding. This is not the case for devas. Because they are of spontaneous birth (opapātika), when the karma-born matter disappears and ceases, the remaining material sequences also disappear and cease along with the karma-born matter. Therefore, it is said, "It is like the going out of a lamp flame." Because Sakka was reborn in that very same place as Sakka again, the other devas did not know that Sakka had passed away and was newly born. "In the three places" refers to the three concluding places of answering regarding joy (somanassa), grief (domanassa), and equanimity (upekkhā). "Only the resulting fruit that has arisen" means the supramundane Path and Fruit (lokuttara magga-phala), which is the result arising from the practice leading to the Path and Fruit, just as clarified butter arises from butter. It is not something to be taken by flying up, soaring, or leaping, like a bird seizing an object. "Assa" refers to the preliminary practice of the pure Ariya Dhamma called the Path and Fruit.

## Pātimokkhasamvaravaṇṇanā

"Pātimokkhasamvarāya" means the restraint of virtue which is the Pātimokkha; thus it is said, "for the sake of restraining the noble and chief virtue." The Elder Sumatthera, residing at Dīghavāpī Monastery, says, "Pātimokkha virtue is the chief virtue among all virtues." However, his pupil, the Elder Tepiṭakacūḷanāga, says, "Only the restraint of the Pātimokkha is virtue. Although there are places where other restraints are called virtue, he does not wish to permit them as such; restraint of the senses (indriyasamvara) is merely the guarding of the six doors, purity of livelihood (ājīvapārisuddhi) is merely the acquisition of requisites in a righteous and fair manner, and that which is dependent on requisites (paccayasannissita) is merely the reflecting upon and using the acquired requisites for their purpose. In the primary sense, only the restraint of the Pātimokkha is virtue." This is because one whose Pātimokkha virtue is broken is incapable of guarding the other restraints and thus becomes one without virtue. However, one whose Pātimokkha virtue is perfectly healthy is capable of guarding the others and can thus be one endowed with virtue (sampannasīla). Therefore, because the other three types of virtue are the retinue of the Pātimokkha virtue, and because they are included within it either entirely or partially, that alone is called the principal virtue; thus it is said, "for the sake of restraining the noble and chief virtue."

In that passage, just as when the Buddha was asked by Sakka about the practice leading to the cessation of the perceptions and categories of mental proliferation (papañcasaññāsaṅkhānirodha), He analyzed the perceptions of proliferation and the feeling (vedanā) which is the root of the practice, and taught the practice that fulfills the purifying states (vodānadhamma) by abandoning the defiling states (saṃkilesadhamma) according to Sakka's inclination; similarly, when asked about the restraint of virtue (sīlasamvara) which is the root of that practice, the Buddha spoke of "bodily conduct" (kāyasamācara) to explain the purity of that restraint of virtue and the manner of its purification according to Sakka's wish, by fulfilling the purifying states through the abandonment of defiling states.
270: The Buddha spoke starting with "kāyasamācara" (bodily conduct) to analyze and show both why that restraint of virtue is pure and how it is purified, according to Sakka's inclination, by fulfilling the purifying states (vodānadhamma) through the abandonment of defiling states (saṃkilesadhamma). Since the reason for teaching bodily conduct etc. that should not be cultivated has already been stated in the discourse on virtue, "kammapathavasena" means by the power of wholesome and unwholesome courses of action (kammapatha). "Kammapathavasena" also means by the power of investigating the courses of action. Even bodily misconduct etc. that have not yet reached the status of a course of action (kammapatha) are spoken of here as bodily conduct etc. that should not be cultivated. "Paṇṇattivasena" means by the power of the prescribed training rules (sikkhāpada). Whatever abstinence (veramaṇī) from unwholesome states there is, He teaches by the power of the prescription, making both the unwholesome state and the abstinence clear. Therefore, He said "kāyadvāre" (at the body-door) and so on. Because one transgresses the training rule by this, it is called "sikkhāpadavītikkama" (transgression of the training rule). The unwholesome state that arises in the manner of transgressing a training rule is the very nature of bodily conduct etc. that should not be cultivated. Non-transgression, which is the opposite of transgression, is called "avītikkama". Because one does not transgress the training rule by this, it is called "avītikkama", which is virtue (sīla). Because one seeks wrongly or rightly by this, it is called "pariyesanā" (seeking) or "ājīva" (livelihood). In terms of meaning, it is the effort and activity of seeking requisites occurring in the doors of body and speech. If that is so, why is it taken separately? It is said: because the faultless seeking is called "ariyapariyesanā" (noble search). It is also called "ariyapariyesanā" because it is to be sought by the Noble Ones (Ariyas). The seeking that is the opposite of what was said should be known as "anariyapariyesanā" (ignoble search). "Jātidhamma" means having the nature of being born, having birth as its natural state. "Jarādhamma" means having the nature of aging. "Byādhidhamma" means having the nature of illness. "Maraṇadhamma" means having the nature of dying. "Sokadhamma" means having the nature of sorrowing. "Saṃkilesadhamma" means having the nature of being defiled. "Puttabhariyaṃ" means children and wife. This method applies to all other instances as well. They are indicated as a singular through the compound 'samāhāra-dvanda'. In the term "jātarūparajataṃ", gold is called "jātarūpa" because the entire material remains in its original state without undergoing change in color. Silver is called "rajata" or "rūpiya" because of its white nature. Here, however, excluding gold, whatever coins (money) etc. that have come into common usage and are fit for use and consumption are taken as "rajata". "Monks, these children, wives, etc., are the bases of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇūpadhi); all of them are subject to birth (jātidhamma)," thus He showed.
271:
Gold and silver should not be taken in the sections (vāra) concerning things subject to disease (vyādhi-dhamma) and so forth. This is because in gold and silver, there is no such thing as disease like a headache, no death known as passing away (cuti) like that of sentient beings, and no sorrow arises. Death, known as passing away, is the cessation of the aggregates (khandha) included within a single life; such cessation does not exist in gold and silver. However, momentary cessation (khaṇika-nirodha), which occurs at every moment, is indeed found in them. Gold is included in the section on things subject to defilement (saṅkilesa-dhamma) because it can be defiled by impurities like rust. Similarly, it is included in the section on things subject to birth (jāti-dhamma) because it arises due to the seasons (utu), and in the section on things subject to aging (jarā-dhamma) because it decays by accumulating dirt. Because it is not sought by the Noble Ones (Ariya), it is also called ignoble seeking (anariya-pariyesanā).

Now, to show that ignoble seeking also occurs through improper seeking (anesanā), the phrase "api ca" and so forth is stated. In this same way, the meaning should also be understood in the wholesome side (sukka-pakkha).

Seeking requisites (sambhāra-pariyesana) refers to searching for weapons, poison, and so forth. Performing an effort (payoga-karaṇa) means generating the exertion appropriate for acts such as killing (pāṇātipāta) and so forth; it is the bringing about of such an endeavor. Going (gamana) for the purpose of killing and so forth is also included. The word "time" (kāla) should be applied to each: "starting from the time of seeking requisites, starting from the time of performing the effort, starting from the time of going." "The other" (itara) refers to bodily conduct (kāya-samācāra) and so forth, which are stated as "to be practiced." One should also cause the mind to arise. A person with such an arisen mind, when the combination of conditions is complete, performs such effort and exertion and reaches the summit of the practice (the Path and Fruit). Therefore, it was said: "Monks, I say that even the arising of thought (cittuppāda) is of great benefit in wholesome states" (M. Ni. 1.84).

Now, to show what is not to be practiced and what is to be practiced upon reaching that summit, the phrase "api ca" and so forth is stated. In the context of schism in the Saṅgha (saṅgha-bheda) and so forth, the word "ādi" (and so forth) includes causing the Buddha to bleed (lohituppāda) and so forth. Since serving the Dhamma-gem is accomplished only by serving the Buddha-gem and the Saṅgha-gem, it is said: "by way of going to serve the Triple Gem two or three times a day, etc." Sending archers (dhanuggaha-pesana) means urging and commanding archers. The word "ādi" includes asking for the five boons and so forth. It should be understood like the seeking of those who pursue ignoble seeking, such as "Devadatta, whose gain and honor had declined, asking among families by pleasing King Ajātasattu to generate gain."

For the sake of fulfillment (pāripūriyā) means for the purpose of fulfillment. Since the fulfillment of things to be practiced occurs only through the power of the highest Path and Fruit (magga-phala), all preliminary practices (pubbabhāga-paṭipadā) exist for that purpose. The restraint of the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara) is also [fulfilled] only by the highest Path...
272:
Having spoken of the preliminary practice for the sake of the result of the Path of Arahantship, the conclusion is stated: "Pātimokkho... pe... hoti."

## Indriya-saṃvara-vaṇṇanā

"For the closing of the senses" (indriyānaṃ pidhānāya) means for the purpose of shutting out the six senses. The senses are the six doors, such as the eye and so forth. Aiming at the closing, restraining, and guarding of these doors from the arising of unwholesome states, it is said: "by way of guarding the doors" (guttadvāratāya). Lack of restraint (asaṃvara) is the failure to guard the doors of the senses by way of forms and so forth that should not be pursued. The purification of the states of purity is through the abandoning of the unwholesome states of defilement (saṅkilesa). Although forms and so forth that should not be pursued are indeed shown in the Pāli text, Sakka asked only about the practice of sense restraint (indriya-saṃvara). To show that point specifically, it is stated in the Commentary: "Cakkhuviññeyyaṃ rūpampi" and so forth, to show sense restraint by way of forms and so forth that should be pursued. After saying "He remained silent" (tuṇhī ahosi), the phrase "kathētukāmopi" and so forth was stated to clarify the reason for silence through the method of contrast. "Ayaṃ" refers to Sakka, the lord of the devas.

Form (rūpa) refers to the sense base of form (rūpāyatana). Not pursuing that form means not looking at it; with this intention, it is said: "should not be pursued, should not be seen." For one who looks at the forms within the continuity of beings, the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā) may arise through attending to them as repulsive, or faith (pasāda) may arise through the supreme seeing. Alternatively, faith may arise through faith in kamma and its results (kamma-phala-saddhā). Or, one may gain the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā) by reflecting on the nature of disappearing after having come to be.

It is called akkara (letter) or vaṇṇa (syllable) because it cannot be exhausted even when used in various ways (pariyāya). That same letter, when occurring continuously, is called a word (pada) or a sentence (vākya), and because it clarifies the intended meaning, it is called vyañjana (expression). With reference to its beautiful existence in poems, plays, and so forth, through synonyms and through its various modes of pronunciation, it is said: "the sound which has beautiful letters and beautiful expressions, hearing which lust and so forth arise." "Dependent on meaning" (attha-nissita) means dependent on the benefit of the future life. "Dependent on Dhamma" (dhamma-nissita) means dependent on the Dhamma of Nibbāna, which is free from the round of suffering, or dependent on the supramundane Triple Gem. "Faith" (pasāda) refers to faith in the Triple Gem and faith in kamma and its results. "Disenchantment" (nibbidā) means weariness with the round of suffering (vaṭṭa) through the power of the perception of impermanence and so forth.

Although smells and tastes may be pursued without conflict, they are called "not to be pursued" (asevitabba) if practiced with unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra). Smells and tastes that are pursued by reflecting with wise attention are called "to be pursued" (sevitabba) because they are taken with clear comprehension (sampajañña). Therefore, "Yaṃ gandhaṃ ghāyato" and so forth was stated.
273:
The phrase 'yaṃ pana phusato' refers to the contact of an anipphanna (one who does not lie down) person who is to be associated with and contacted. Because of reaching the peak of jāgariyānuyoga (devotion to wakefulness), the destruction of the āsavas (cankers) also occurs. Because of supporting the fourth ariyavaṃsa (noble lineage), energy (vīriya) is also well-supported. The later group of virtuous people is also supported by being urged toward sammāpaṭipatti (right practice).

Those mental objects (manoviññeyyā dhammā) of various kinds, such as desirable objects (iṭṭhārammaṇa), come into the range of one who brings them to mind and reflects on them. The grammatical case of 'manoviññeyyā dhammā' should be modified. The connection is: those mental objects that come into the range of one who reflects through the power of loving-kindness (mettā), etc.—such things should be associated with. By the word 'ādi' (etc.), the inclusion of the brahmavihāras (divine abodes) like compassion (karuṇā) and characteristics like impermanence (anicca) should be understood. 'The mental objects of the three Elders' refers to the mental objects cognizable by the mind of the three Elders who possess the practice currently being described. By the phrase 'did not allow it to run outside,' it is shown that during these three months of the Rains Retreat, a mind devoid of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) never arose even once regarding the visible forms (rūpa), etc., that came within the monastery precinct; and because there were no disagreeable (visabhāga) visible forms within the precinct, he did not allow the mind to run outside through the power of distracted thought (vitakka). 'Nivāsagehato' means from the living quarters. It means not going outside from the object of insight (vipassanā), which is one's own five aggregates. The Elder practiced all his duties by making the meditation subject the priority.

Because of the power of clear comprehension without delusion (asammohasampajañña), there is no duality, thus it is 'one-sided' (ekanta). Because they have a single doctrine, they are 'ekantavādā' (proponents of a single doctrine). Therefore, it is said, 'They speak only one thing.' It means they have an undivided doctrine. 'Ekācārā' means having the same conduct; 'ekaladdhikā' means having the same view; 'ekapariyosānā' means having the same final conclusion.

Thus, Sakka, the King of Devas, having known through the penetration of the Truths that the various doctrines, conduct, views, and conclusions of many recluses and brahmins he had heard before were without essence, now remains firm. Desiring to know the cause of such diversity, he asks about that very cause through the method of contrast (vyatireka), starting with 'Sabbēva dhammā nu kho' (Are all teachings...).

'Dhātu' refers to the dispositional element (ajjhāsayadhātu), mentioned by dropping the latter word. Since in meaning it is just 'disposition' (ajjhāsaya), it is said, 'anekajjhāsayō nānajjhāsayō' (of various dispositions, of different dispositions). The phrase 'ekasmiṃ gantukāme' (when one wishes to go) is said by way of illustration. Even in postures (iriyāpatha), it is rare to find beings with the same disposition.
274:
To show the finality in views, it is said 'pageva laddhīsu' (how much more so in views). 'Yaṃ yadēva ajjhāsayaṃ' means whatever disposition such as the eternalist view (sassata), etc. 'Abhinivisanti' means they enter into those various views with the power of firm mental adherence called wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi), facing them and being in a state where they are difficult to relinquish; they grasp them with a strong grip. 'Thāmena ca parāmāsena ca' means through the strength of wrong view and through the misapprehension of wrong view. 'Sutthu gaṇhitvā' means grasping very firmly. 'Voharanti' means they make known the wrong views they have firmly adhered to in various ways; they make others grasp them and establish them. Therefore, it is said, 'They speak, they illustrate, they praise,' which means they proclaim.

Because they have transcended destruction, they are called 'accanta' (absolute/final). Because the final goal, Nibbāna, belongs to these people, they are called 'accantaniṭṭhā' (having the absolute goal). 'Sabbesaṃ' refers to the Nibbāna of all recluses and brahmins. Nibbāna is also called 'yogakkhema' (security from bondage) because it is not corrupted by the four bonds (yogas). Although it should be said 'accantayogakkhemā,' it is taught as 'accantayogakkhemī' using the 'i' suffix; or it means 'accantayogakkhemī' because the absolute security from bondage, which is Nibbāna, belongs to them. 'Caranti' means they approach the Noble Path, they attain it. 'Pariyosāna' is also a name for Nibbāna because it is reached at the end of the suffering of the round of rebirths and exhausts it.

'Saṅkhiṇāti' means the Noble Path exhausts craving by cutting it off completely. 'Vināseti' means because of such exhaustion, it brings craving to total disappearance. 'Vimuttā' are those who are specially liberated by the absolute departure from the suffering of the round of rebirths.

Why is it said, 'Envy (issā) and avarice (macchariya) are one question'? Are envy and avarice not the answer (vissajjana)? This is true, but the meaning desired to be known is called the 'question' (pañha). Since that very meaning to be known is what is answered, there is no fault in saying this; otherwise, it would be like answering 'breadfruit' to someone asking about 'mango.' Thus, it refers to the answer to the question by focusing on the meaning to be known. Therefore, only the terms of the answer such as 'dear and not dear' are taken. In places like 'dear and not dear is one question,' it should be understood in this same way. In the Pali 'papañcasaññā,' because only the papañca (proliferations: craving, view, conceit) are taught by making 'perception' (saññā) the head, it is said, 'papañca is one question.'

In this context, just as the question on the restraint of the Patimokkha (pātimokkhasamvara) becomes three questions because it is answered by dividing it into bodily conduct (kāyasamācāra), etc., so too the question on the restraint of the senses (indriyasamvara) would become six questions because it is answered by dividing it into the six objects like visible forms (rūpa), etc. If that were the case, there would be nineteen questions. If it were made into one question because of the commonality of being 'restraint of the senses,' then the questions on the restraint of the Patimokkha would also be just one question because of their commonality, and all questions would be only twelve. But it is not so. This is because when bodily conduct, etc., are explained in detail, there would be an immeasurable division due to the vastness of the field.
275:
It is possible to answer (that restraint of the Pātimokkha). The entire Vinaya Piṭaka is indeed the commentary on that restraint of the Pātimokkha. However, when describing forms (rūpa) and so forth in detail, it is not possible to answer with such detailed classification because the scope is narrow. Thus, because the scope is vast, three questions were made regarding the restraint of the Pātimokkha (pātimokkhasamvara), whereas only one question was made regarding the restraint of the sense faculties (indriyasamvara) because its scope is narrow. Therefore, it is said, "The fourteen great questions."

In the sense of shaking means in the sense of moving. Because craving (taṇhā) is unstable in its occurrence by way of sensual lust, lust for fine-material existence, and lust for immaterial existence, it shakes by itself; it also causes the continuity of beings in whom it has arisen to move by dragging them through existences and so forth. Therefore, craving is called "ejā" (motion/shaking) in the sense of shaking. In the sense of afflicting means in the sense of oppressing because it is the cause of various sufferings. In the sense of being corrupted means it is like a "boil" (gaṇḍa) because it corrupts in various ways: through unrighteous lust, whether in one's presence or absence, and by the oozing of the impurities of defilements. In the sense of piercing means it is like a "dart" (salla) because it pierces in a way that is difficult to extract from its resting place. It drags according to its own desire. High and low (uccāvaca) refers to the state of being noble and the state of being base. Among those recluses and brahmins. There is also a Pali reading "yesāhaṃ," which some interpret as "of whom I am (the servant)." "In this way" means in accordance with what was heard and what was learned. "Venerable Sir, although I am a teacher of other recluses and brahmins, I am a disciple of the Blessed One... one whose destination is the three higher paths (sambodhiparāyaṇa)," thus he makes known his state of being a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna).

## Commentary on the Acquisition of Joy
"Attained" means having well entered into the midst of battle, like an intense engagement. "They conquered" means the gods conquered the Asuras so that they could not raise their heads again; to show this, it is said, "The gods conquered the Asuras so that they would not return again." Such a victory resulted in an extraordinary acquisition of joy for Sakka. "Two kinds of essence (ojā)" means both the divine essence and the Asura essence. Only the gods will consume it because the Asuras no longer have access. Warding off the enemy by wielding a staff is called "daṇḍāvacara"; "together with the daṇḍāvacara" means it is to be accomplished either by striking with a staff or by warding off.

"In this very place" means in this very Indasāla Cave. "To me who has become a god" means to me who was previously Sakka, a god. "Being" means even while currently existing as Sakka, I have regained my life span.
276:
The bodies known as the collection of the five aggregates belonging to the celestial realm are called 'dibba-attabhāva' (divine bodies). By the words 'I shall enter the womb without confusion,' he shows that for the noble disciples (ariya-sāvaka) of the Buddha, there is no dying in confusion or entering the womb without mindfulness, as is the case with blind worldlings (andha-puthujjana); rather, there is only dying without confusion and entering the womb with clear comprehension and mindfulness. Noble disciples, having a fixed destiny, are reborn only in happy destinations (sugati). Even among those happy destinations, if they are reborn as humans, they will take rebirth only in high-ranking and prosperous families. Sakka also has such an inclination. Therefore, it is stated in the Pali, 'In whatever place my mind finds delight'; referring to that, it is said 'yattha me' and so forth. Sakka, by his own divine power, is indeed capable of knowing such future circumstances of his.

'By a reason' (kāraṇena) means by a reason that is suitable and appropriate for the state of being a noble disciple. Therefore, it is said 'righteously' (samena).

He speaks with reference to the Path of Once-returning (sakadāgāmi-magga) because he will speak about the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-magga) in the sixth point. 'Desiring to know' (ājānitukāmo) means desiring to penetrate the extraordinary Dhamma not yet attained. It will be the final birth in the human world because there will be no further rebirth as a human. 'Again' (punadeva) means after being born among humans and passing away from that human life, he will again become a noble being in this Tāvatiṃsa heaven. As to what kind of noble being he will be, it is said 'Sakka' and so forth.

'In the final existence' (antime bhave) means in the very last existence of all my existences. By the word 'by life-span' (āyunā), he includes all qualities such as appearance (vaṇṇa) and so forth that coexist with that life. By the word 'by wisdom' (paññāya), he includes all qualities such as faith (saddhā), mindfulness (sati), energy (vīriya), and so forth. In that existence, which is the final state of being Sakka, without becoming an 'attainer of Nibbāna in the interval' (antarā-parinibbāyī) and so forth, he will certainly become one who 'goes upstream to the Akanittha realm' (uddhaṃsota-akaniṭṭhagāmī). From there, by sequence, being reborn in the Pure Abodes such as Avihā and so forth, he will attain Parinibbāna in the Akanittha realm. Therefore, he said, 'That abode shall be my dwelling.' To expand on the meaning briefly stated as 'he will be reborn in Avihā and so forth,' it is said 'esa kira' and so forth. To show that this sequence of existence is not only for Sakka but also for the great treasurer (Anāthapiṇḍika) and the great female lay follower Visākhā, it is said 'Sakka, the king of gods' and so forth. Because his aspiration is not yet fulfilled by way of the attainment of existence and the attainment of Nibbāna, he remains with an uncompleted desire, wishing to attain those respective attainments. And those (recluses and brahmins) who...
277:
