"Samaṇe" refers to those who have gone forth. "Pavivittavihārino" means "I consider that they dwell having cultivated the three kinds of seclusion, namely, bodily seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion from the substrates of existence, in various and manifold ways."

"Sampādanā" means the fulfillment of the Path, the proper attainment of that Path. "Virādhanā" means the failure to attain the Path, the practice of the wrong way. "Na sambhonti" means they are not able (they do not reach). Since inability (anabhisambhuṇana) regarding the meaning of what is asked is simply the incapacity to speak well, it is said, "They are unable to speak so as to fulfill [the meaning]."

"Tasmā" (Therefore) is because he belongs to the same lineage as the sun. For that very reason, it is said, "By the lineage named Ādicca." Because the sun is his kinsman, he is called "Ādiccabandhu" (Kinsman of the Sun). Or else, it refers to the Blessed One who is called "Ādiccabandhu" because he is a relative of the sun. In fact, because the sun is a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), he is the Blessed One's own breast-born son. Therefore, it is said:

That sun who makes light in the dark gloom,
The radiant one, circular in form, of fierce power;
O Rāhu, do not swallow my son, the sun,
Who moves in the sky; Rāhu, release him!

"Sāmaṃ" refers to one's own effort. Since the effort made by a disciple of the Teacher is simply the act of paying homage, it is said, "They pay homage."

"Parāmasitvā" (Having touched) means touching the earth, either with joy, thinking, "Sitting on this very earth, I have attained this wonderful Dhamma," or with a sense of wonder, thinking, "On this very earth, such a wonderful and marvelous Buddha-treasure has appeared." "Patthitapañhā" (The desired question) refers to the question that was greatly longed for, thinking, "When shall I get the opportunity to ask the Blessed One?" in order to uproot the doubts that had been latent for a long time. Here, the passage that has not been analyzed in detail according to its meaning is easily understood.

## The Explanation of the Subtle Meanings (Līnatthappakāsanā) of the Commentary on the Sakkapañha Sutta is finished.
278:
## 9. Commentary on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta
## Commentary on the Section of the Summary (Uddesavāra)
"Why did the Blessed One preach this sutta?" Thus, he asks about the specific origin (asādhāraṇa-samuṭṭhāna) that does not apply to other suttas. Since the general origin (sādhāraṇa-samuṭṭhāna) applicable to all suttas is obvious, without considering that, the words beginning with "of the inhabitants of the Kuru country" are spoken. Origin (samuṭṭhāna) means the source (nidāna) of the teaching. That source is of two kinds: general (sādhāraṇa) and specific (asādhāraṇa). The general is also of two kinds: internal (ajjhattika) and external (bāhira).

Among those two, the internal general origin is the Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā) of the Blessed One. Urged by that Great Compassion, the intention to preach the Dhamma to those who are to be guided (veneyya) arose in the Blessed One. It is as stated: "Out of compassion for beings, he surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye." The external general origin is the request and invitation of the Great Brahma Sahampati, who has a retinue of ten thousand. It is as stated: "Having known the request of the Brahma." After that request, having subsided the inclination to remain inactive (appossukkatā) which had arisen from reflecting on the profundity of the Dhamma, the Blessed One became enthusiastic to preach the Dhamma.

Just like the Great Compassion, the Ten Powers (dasabala-ñāṇa) and so forth should also be mentioned as internal origins of the teaching. Having truly known all things to be known, the methods by which those things should be taught, and the inclinations (āsaya) and latent tendencies (anusaya) of beings, the Blessed One, through his skill in what is possible and impossible (ṭhānāṭhāna), set forth the teaching in various ways according to the dispositions of those to be guided.

The specific origin is also of two kinds: internal and external. Among these two, the internal origin should be understood as both the Great Compassion and the Knowledge of Teaching (desanā-ñāṇa) that brought about this sutta. To show the external origin, the words beginning with "of the inhabitants of the Kuru country" are spoken. Therefore, it is said that he asks about the specific origin. By asking thus, it amounts to asking about the delivery of the sutta (sutta-nikkhepa): "Among the four types of sutta delivery, such as by one's own inclination (attajjhāsaya), which one is this?" The other (the commentator) shows by the words beginning with "of the inhabitants of the Kuru country" that "this sutta is one delivered according to the inclination of others (parajjhāsaya)."

At that time, the Kuru country was endowed with favorable weather and so forth, mostly due to the proper practice of the beings living there, such as having wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), and due to the power of merit performed in the past. Therefore, it is said, "Because of being endowed with favorable weather and so forth." By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the abundance of food and so on is included. Some teachers, however...
279:
It is said that because of the habitual tendency (vāsanā) of consistently observing the ancient practices of the Kuru country (the five precepts), it was generally endowed with favorable weather and other conditions, like Uttarakuru; during the time of the Buddha, that country was exceptionally endowed with suitable weather and other favorable conditions. 'Cittasarīrakallatāya' means due to the health and freedom from disease of both mind and body. 'Anuggahitapaññābalā' refers to those who possess the power and influence of acquired beneficial wisdom, or the power and majesty of wisdom that has been repeatedly practiced. 'In twenty-one places' means in twenty-one places as follows: fourteen places by way of mindfulness of the body (kāyānupassanā), one place by way of mindfulness of feeling (vedanānupassanā), likewise [one] by way of mindfulness of the mind (cittānupassanā), and five places by way of mindfulness of mental objects (dhammānupassanā); thus it occurs in twenty-one places. 'Incorporating the meditation subject into Arahantship' means that just as the meditation on the Four Noble Truths leads to Arahantship, so it is incorporated into Arahantship by the power of the teaching.

Just as various flowers such as jasmine (sumana) and champak (campaka), or the seven kinds of gems such as rubies and pearls, when placed in golden baskets or golden caskets, shine exceptionally and fulfill their purpose because of the excellence of the container and their pleasing nature; similarly, this teaching of the Blessed One, taught to the audience of the Kuru country who are special vessels due to their excellence in virtue, vision, and so on, shines exceedingly and fulfills its purpose of enabling beings to attain the benefits of the Path and Fruition. This meaning is shown by the words beginning with 'Yathā hi puriso'. 'Ettha' means in the Kuru country.

'Pakatiyā' means by their own nature, or even before the teaching of this Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta. [The inhabitants of that country] lived constantly devoted to the practice of meditation in accordance with the Buddha's teaching.

'Vissaṭṭha-attabhāvena' means that one should not have a mind let loose according to the desire for delight in sense objects such as forms, without applying the mind to wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) by way of impermanence and so on; it means that one should abandon negligent living and be diligent.

In the term 'ekāyano', the word 'ayana' is a synonym for 'path' (magga). To show that not only 'ayana' but there are also many other synonyms for 'path', he said 'Maggassa hi', etc. If the word 'ayana' is a synonym for 'path', why is the word 'magga' mentioned again? Addressing this objection, he said 'Tasmā', etc. In that context, 'ekamaggo' means the only path. This is because there is no other path that leads to Nibbāna. If it is asked: 'Is it not Satipaṭṭhāna that is intended as the "path" here? Are there not many other path-factors (maggadhamma) besides Satipaṭṭhāna?' It is true, there are; however, they are included by the mention of Satipaṭṭhāna itself, as they are inseparable from it.
280:
This is because although wisdom (ñāṇa), effort (vīriya), and so forth are included in the detailed exposition (niddesa), in the summary (uddesa), only mindfulness (sati) is taken, according to the disposition of the beings to be guided (veneyyajjhāsaya). By the phrase 'not a two-way path' (na dvidhāpathabhūto), he shows that this path is not multiple, and it is not a path that does not lead to Nibbāna. 'Eka' means alone, without a companion. This solitude is of two kinds: physical solitude (vūpakaṭṭhakāyatā), which is the absence of another person as a companion; and mental solitude (pavivittacittatā), which is the absence of craving (taṇhā) as a second companion. Therefore, he said, 'one who is physically secluded and mentally solitary.' In the world, a noble person is also called 'eka,' as in 'I will make you the foremost (eka) among others,' etc. Thus, he said, 'Ekassa means of the noble one.' If the word 'ayana' means the way of escape from Saṃsāra, since it is common to others who are endowed with the necessary conditions (upanissaya), one might ask why it belongs only to the Blessed One. To address this, he said 'kiñcāpi' and so forth. In the phrase 'imasmim kho,' the word 'kho' is used for emphasis. Therefore, it means 'only in this Dispensation (Sāsana).' The distinction between 'magga' (path) and 'ayana' (way) is merely a difference in the teaching (desanā). Alternatively, the word 'ayana' has meanings divided by object (kamma), instrument (karaṇa), etc. Therefore, he said, 'But in meaning, it is only one.'

'Proceeding by way of development through various portals' means proceeding by the method of development starting with the portals such as mindfulness of the body (kāyānupassanā), and therein, starting with portals such as mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna). 'Ekāyana' means leading to the one [Nibbāna], or leading to Nibbāna. Nibbāna is called 'eka' (one) because it has no equal second and because of its nobility. As the Blessed One said: 'Truth is one, there is no second' (Sn 890); and 'Monks, whatever things there are, conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (virāga) is said to be the foremost among them' (AN 4.34). Nibbāna, being the end of destruction, is called 'khayanta.' Because he has seen the end of birth, which is Nibbāna, he is called 'Jātikhayantadassī' (Seer of the end of birth). Because he compassionately seeks the welfare of all beings impartially, he is called 'Hitānukampī' (Compassionate for welfare). 'Atariṃsu' means they have crossed over. 'Pubbe' means the Buddhas of the past, or in the past time.

The statement of those teachers, or the interpretation of it as a verbal action, is not appropriate. For the word 'eka,' which refers to a being by way of emphasizing the countable, does not have the meaning of a verbal action. It should be expressed with the syllable 'sakiṃ ayano' (going once), as in 'it might go upwards even once' (AN 7.72). 'Thus connecting the meaning' means connecting the meaning of the compound word as 'he has one way.' Both ways (the former and the latter) are inappropriate. Why? Because the path intended here has the nature of occurring many times. Therefore, he said 'kasmā' (why) and so forth. The phrase 'it goes many times' shows the inappropriateness of the former method, and 'he has many goings' shows the inappropriateness of the latter method.
281:
In this word, it refers to this sentence: "Monks, this path is the only way," or to this word of classification: "The preliminary path, the supramundane path." The mixed path (missakamagga) is the supramundane path mixed with the mundane path. The teacher, the Elder Cūḷasumana, who wished to encompass the direct cause of the purification of beings and so forth, said "mixed path." The other, the disciple Elder Cūḷanāga, considering that in this context insight (vipassanā) as a figurative cause is intended, said "preliminary path."

"Having heard the sound" means hearing, either directly or by report, the sound announcing the time, saying: "Venerable sir, it is time for the Dhamma talk." "Lifting up thus" means not discarding these words, thinking, "How can we discard these words which are so excellent and heart-captivating?" but rather upholding one's words and not wandering about, like one carrying a bundle of sugarcane. "Āluḷeti" means it is stirred or becomes confused. By the statement "The only way is called the preliminary path of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)," the intended meaning in this context is accomplished; however, for the sake of adorning that preliminary path, and to show that the preliminary path is the precursor to which supramundane path, the verse beginning with "Maggānaṭṭhangiko" is brought from the Paṭisambhidāmagga and placed here.

"In the sense of going to Nibbāna" means it is called Nibbānagamana because one goes to or attains Nibbāna by this path. That very Nibbānagamana is called 'attha' (sense/purpose) because of its unerring nature; thus, it means by the nature of the sense of reaching Nibbāna, or as the means for the attainment of Nibbāna. "Magganīyaṭṭhena" means by the state of being sought after. Alternatively, there is a reading "gamanīyaṭṭhena," which means by the state of being approached. By the phrase "by greed, etc.," only greed (rāga), hatred (dosa), and delusion (moha) should be taken. This is because it was taught: "Greed is a stain, hatred is a stain, delusion is a stain." By the phrase "by covetousness, abnormal greed, etc.," however, those three—greed and so forth—are extracted separately for the purpose of encompassing all defilements (upakkilesa). To show the certainty of the meaning taught as "for the purification of beings," he said the words beginning with "Tathā hi." Indeed, although the word "visuddhiyā" (for purification) is a general indication, to show that only the purification of the mind (cittavisuddhi) is intended here, he taught the words beginning with "Rūpamalavasena pana." To show that this is not merely the word of the Commentaries, but is the word directly spoken by the Blessed One in this context, he said the words beginning with "Tathā hi."

Since this purification of the mind, when accomplished, leads to the non-arising of sorrow and so forth, it is taught: "for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation," etc. Therein, sorrow (soka) is the burning of the mind, an internal smoldering, caused by the loss of relatives and so forth. Lamentation (parideva) is the verbal wailing and distraught speech, such as "Where is my only son? Where is my only son?" by one who is overcome by sorrow due to that same cause of the loss of relatives and so forth.
282:
Lamenting is lamentation (parideva). Because it refers here to the non-arising [of sorrow and lamentation] in the future, he said "pahānāya" (for the sake of abandoning). To demonstrate how that surmounting is brought about by way of an example, he said the words beginning with "Ayañhi."

In that verse, by the words "Yam pubbe tam visodhehi" (Purify what was before), the purification of the defilement of craving in the past aggregates (khandhas) is taught. "Pacchā" means in the future. "Te" means for you. "Mā ahu" means let it not be. "Kiñcanaṃ" refers to the oppressive defilements (kiñcana) such as greed and so forth. By this, the purification of defilements in the future aggregates is taught. "Majjhe" means in the present, which is between those two, the past and the future. "No ce gahessasi" means if you do not grasp or seize [with the notion of 'I' or 'mine']. By this, the occurrence of clinging (upādāna) in the present continuity of aggregates is taught. "Upasanto carissasi" means if the defilements occurring in the three periods of time are thus purified, one will live as one who is peaceful, with all fevers extinguished. Thus, he concluded the verse with the peak of Arahantship. Therefore, he said the words beginning with "Imaṃ gāthaṃ."

"Sons" (puttā) means biological sons, or any other kind such as adopted sons or famous sons. "Father" (pitā) means the progenitor, or others standing in the place of a father. "Relatives" (bandhavā) means kinsmen. The meaning here is: sons, fathers, or relatives are not able to protect one who is overcome by the Ender, Death, from dying. Why? Because there is no protection among relatives. There is no protection from death by the power of relatives. Therefore, the intention is: "Do not lament in vain, O Paṭācārā, thinking 'both my sons are dead,' but rather see the Dhamma as it really is."

"Established in the fruit of Stream-entry" (sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhitā) means being established in the fruit of Stream-entry, adorned with a thousand methods, at the conclusion of the special Dhamma teaching (sāmukkaṃsikā dhammadesanā) which was delivered in accordance with the temperaments of beings. But how did she become established in the fruit of Stream-entry by way of the path of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)? He said the words beginning with "Yasmā pana," because there is no attainment of the Noble Path for disciples without the discourse on the meditation of the Four Noble Truths. The statement "having heard this verse" is said in reference to hearing first the verse delivered for the purpose of dispelling sorrow. For that [verse] also, by showing impermanence, is merely an accompaniment to the teaching of the Truths. In the other verse, there is nothing more to be said. "Bhāvanā" here refers to the development of insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā-bhāvanā), which is what is intended. Therefore, because the repeated contemplation of form and so forth as impermanent and so on is also the development of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā), he said "Therefore." In the words "they too," [it implies that] the Minister Santati and Paṭācārā are also included.
283: Five great bandits, each with a retinue of a hundred bandits, were sent in succession. Those bandits entered the forest and, while searching for the Elder, eventually arrived near him. Therefore, it is said: "They went and sat surrounding the Elder." "Dispelling the feeling" means removing the painful feeling caused by the breaking of the thigh bone by not attending to it. Because there was not even a hint of remorse, joy and gladness arose. Therefore, it is said: "Depending on pure virtue." When the Elder reflected on his own virtue, great joy and gladness arose based on that pure virtue, and that joy dispelled the painful feeling caused by the breaking of the thigh bone. The phrase "throughout the three watches of the night" is in the accusative case indicating duration of time; by this, the Elder's diligence in insight meditation and his exertion in practice are shown. "Pādāni" means the feet. "Saṃyamessāmi" means I will make known, I will control. "Aṭṭiyāmi" means I am repelled. "Harāyāmi" means I am ashamed. "Vipassisaṃ" means I have seen clearly. "Pacalāyantānaṃ" refers to those who are nodding off and falling asleep. "Agatiṃ" means an unsuitable place for wandering. "Vatasampanno" means one endowed with the dhuta-practices. The word "pamādaṃ" is spoken with reference to nodding off. "Oruddhamānaso" means one with a restrained noble mind. "Pañjarasmiṃ" means in the body. Because the body is a collection of bones bound together by sinews, it is called a "cage (pañjara)" here. One who was known as "Pītamalla (The Yellow Wrestler)" because he wrapped his body in yellow-colored cloth and had a mind for wrestling, became known as "Pītamalla Thera" when he ordained. Having heard that in the three kingdoms of Paṇḍu, Coḷa, and Goḷa, "all wrestlers receive honor and respect in the island of Sri Lanka," he came to the island of Tambapaṇṇi. "Making that very Dhamma a goad" means making the meaning revealed in the Na Tumhāka Vagga—that "form and so on should not be taken as mine"—into a goad for the great elephant of his own mind. When he was unable to step or walk with his feet due to excessive walking meditation, he thought, "If I sit, there will be an opportunity for nodding off," and so he practiced walking meditation on his knees. By announcing the fruitfulness of his own energetic effort, he spoke of another benefit to inspire his fellow monks in that Dhamma. "Bhāsitaṃ" means the word; if asked whose word it is, it is "the word of the Buddha, the foremost in all the world." The words beginning with "Na tumhākaṃ" show the manner in which that Dhamma arose. Intending to show that "This Nibbāna is the cause for the absolute cessation of my formations (saṅkhāra)," he recited the verse beginning with "Aniccā vata." By that verse, he shows: "Now, being free from the disease known as the moment-to-moment breaking up [of formations], I attain Parinibbāna, free from disease."
284:
"Assa" refers to the (becoming) of Sakka. "Upapatti" means rebirth as a deva. Since he was reborn in the state of Sakka itself, he returned to his original condition.

"Subrahmā" is the name of that young deva. From the time he saw his retinue of goddesses being reborn in hell, he spoke the verse beginning with "This mind is always terrified," referring to his own constantly arising mental trepidation. In that verse, "utrastaṃ" means greatly terrified or fearful. "Ubbiggaṃ" means agitated. Or, "utrastaṃ" means terrified, and "ubbiggaṃ" means greatly trembling along with the physical basis due to fear. "Anuppannesu" means in those that have not yet arrived; "kiccesu" means in various duties to be done. There is also a variant reading "kicchesu," meaning in sufferings; here the locative case is used in the sense of cause, meaning "due to the cause of future suffering." "Uppatitesu" should be connected as "in duties that have arisen." At that time, he speaks with reference to the suffering in hell that had arisen for his retinue of five hundred goddesses.

"Bojjhā" means from bodhi, or from the Noble Path. In relation to the word "aññatra," it is in the ablative case, meaning "except for the Noble Path." The same method applies to the remaining words. "Tapasā" means from the practice of austerity; by this, he shows the practice of effacement (sallekha-paṭipadā), such as the dhuta-practices, which is the means for attaining the Path. "Indriyasaṃvarā" means from the restraint of the senses, with the mind as the sixth. By this statement, with mindfulness-restraint (sati-saṃvara) at the head, all virtue of restraint (saṃvara-sīla) is shown. Or, by the method of the "Hāra of Characteristics" (lakkhaṇa-hāra), all fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhi-sīla) is shown. "Sabbanissaggā" means from the relinquishment of everything, from the abandoning of all defilements. For when defilements are relinquished, the round of kamma and the round of result are also relinquished. "Sotthiံ" means safety, the absence of calamity.

It is called "Ñāya" because it leads to Nibbāna through certain determination, or because Nibbāna is realized through this [Path]. Therefore, it is said: "Ñāya refers to the Noble Eightfold Path." It is called "taṇhā-vāna-virahita" because it is devoid of the "vāna" (weaving/bond) known as craving. For craving is called "vāna" because it weaves together aggregate with aggregate, kamma with result, and beings with suffering. In this Nibbāna, that "vāna" does not exist; or, when this Nibbāna is attained, the person no longer has "vāna," thus it is the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) called Nibbāna (the state without vāna). "Attapaccakkhatāya" is said because realization (sacchikiriyā) is the act of witnessing for oneself without depending on another's cause.

Regarding the question: "Since mental purification is intended by the word 'visuddhiyā,' are not the overcoming of sorrow and so on already included by taking the word 'visuddhi'? Why are they taken again?"—the passage beginning with "Tattha kiñcāpi" is spoken. "Sāsanayuttikovida" means one who is skilled in the logic of the Dhamma, characterized by the Truths, Dependent Origination, and so on. That (to the venereable persons)...
285:
'He makes that meaning known' means that the Blessed One, through the elegance of His teaching, makes known that meaning to whichever individuals capable of being enlightened should be enlightened in such and such a way, whether briefly or in detail. 'Showing that meaning clearly' means showing that meaning clearly without regard for the implication of the meaning. For indeed, the Fully Enlightened One possesses speech that accomplishes the making known of the implication of meaning and so forth.

'It leads to' means it arises or it comes to be. Because for one who has not yet transcended sorrow and lamentation, there is never purification of mind; since purification of mind can only be achieved through the transcendence of sorrow and lamentation, it is said: 'It occurs through the transcendence of sorrow and lamentation.' Furthermore, because sorrow and so forth overwhelm the worldling who is touched and oppressed by painful states that are the causes of grief, and when those states are fully understood, those sorrows and so forth no longer occur; therefore, it is said: 'The transcendence of sorrow and lamentation occurs through the passing away of pain and grief.'

'The Way' (Ñāya) refers to the Highest Path (Arahattamagga) and the Third Path (Anāgāmimagga). By the attainment of those paths, there is the passing away of pain and grief in due order. The other realization (Path-knowledge), which occurs together with the realization that is the witnessing of Nibbāna, is spoken of as if it were caused by the realization of witnessing, because it is inseparable from that realization of witnessing. 'The attainment of the Way is for the witnessing of Nibbāna' is said with reference to the direct realization through Fruition-knowledge (Phala-ñāṇa); the phrase 'for the witnessing of Nibbāna' should be understood in the sense of the dative case (sampadāna).

'Speaking of praise' means words of commendation. To show that such praise is not only in this Sutta but is indeed the Teacher's custom in other Suttas as well, He said 'Just as indeed' (Yatheva hi) and so forth. In that context, it is called 'good in the beginning' (ādikalyāṇa) because it is good at the start or because its beginning is good. The same method applies to the remaining two terms (good in the middle, good in the end). It is called 'with meaning' (sāttha) because it is endowed with the accomplishment of meaning. It is called 'with phrasing' (sabyañjana) because it is endowed with the accomplishment of phrasing. It is called 'entirely complete' (kevalaparipuṇṇa) because it is fulfilled by the five aggregates of Dhamma such as virtue (sīla) and so forth, and because there is nothing to be added. It is called 'pure' (parisuddha) because it is free from defilements and because there is nothing to be removed. It means: 'I shall proclaim to you the holy life (brahmacariya) of the Dispensation and the holy life of the Path, because it is the noblest conduct.' This is the summary here; the detailed explanation should be understood according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga.

'Noble lineages' (Ariyavaṃsa) refers to the lineages and traditions of the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas and others. They should be known as 'foremost' (agga) because they are the noblest among all lineages. They should be known as 'of long standing' (rattaññū) because they have existed for a long time. They should be known as 'lineages' (vaṃsaññū) because they are the lineages of the Buddhas and others. They are called 'ancient' (porāṇa) because they are old and not of recent origin. They are called 'unadulterated' (asaṅkiṇṇa) because they are not scattered and have not been discarded. The Noble Ones have never discarded them in the past, thinking 'What is the use of these lineages?'; they do not discard them now, and they will not discard them in the future. It means they are not discarded or reviled by wise ascetics and brahmins in the world.
286:
The Noble Ones (Ariyas) have never abandoned [these lineages] in the past, thinking, 'What is the use of these lineages?' Even now, those Noble Ones do not abandon them. In the future, those Noble Ones will not abandon them. 'Not censured by the wise' means they are not rejected, not blamed, and not reproached by the wise recluses and brahmins in the world. 'By the words beginning with visuddhiyā' means by sentences that reveal the purification of beings from defilements, or by groups of Dhamma categorized by meanings such as purification. 'Upaddave' refers to misfortune, which is the opposite of welfare. 'Visuddhi' means purification or the abandonment of defilements (saṃkilesa). Making it proficient in the mouth is called learning (uggaha). Repeated study is called familiarization (paricaya). Establishing the meaning in the heart is called retention (dhāraṇa). Repeated recitation or teaching is called recitation (vācanā).

'Gandhāro' refers to one born in the country of Gandhāra. 'Pahonti' means they are able. 'Aniyyānikamaggā' refers to wrong paths, or paths that are certain to lead to misery and those whose results are uncertain. The word 'suvaṇṇa' (gold) is also used for counterfeit gold. Since 'maṇi' (gem) is used for glass gems, 'muttā' (pearl) for bamboo pearls, and 'pavāḷa' (coral) for young sprouts, they are qualified with terms like 'rattajambunada' (red gold from the Jambu river) to distinguish genuine gold, pearls, etc., from imitations.

'Not below that' is said because the body (kāya), etc., intended here do not have the nature of feeling (vedanā), etc., and because the mundane phenomena (tebhūmaka-dhamma) apart from body, feeling, and mind are taken as separate objects of perversion (vipallāsa); thus, it is spoken regarding the incompleteness of the objects of perversion in the lower classifications. Since there is no fifth object of perversion, it says 'not above that.' Here, the classification of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) should be understood by the classification of objects. 'Tayo satipaṭṭhānā' (three foundations of mindfulness) is an exposition of the meaning of the term satipaṭṭhāna and does not show the meaning of the term satipaṭṭhāna as taught in this Pali text. In the words beginning with 'satigocaro,' the word 'ādi' (etc.) includes sutta passages that reveal the objects of mindfulness, such as: 'With the arising of contact, there is the arising of feelings; with the arising of name-and-form, there is the arising of mind; with the arising of attention, there is the arising of mental objects.' Similarly, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali, the word 'ādi' should be understood as indicating the remaining Pali passages. 'Satiyā paṭṭhānaṃ' means the place where mindfulness should be established. For one performing acts of giving (dāna), etc., forms (rūpa), etc., are the places of mindfulness. To exclude those, it says 'padhānaṃ ṭhānaṃ' (the principal place). Here, the prefix 'pa-' indicates the meaning of 'principal' (padhāna), as in 'paṇītā dhammā' (exalted dhammas).

By the word 'Ariyo,' it refers to the Fully Enlightened Buddha, the most excellent of all beings. 'Ettha' (herein) refers to this Saḷāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta. A part of the sutta is used to represent the whole sutta. In that sutta:

The Blessed One frequents the three foundations of mindfulness. Because he frequents these foundations of mindfulness, the Blessed One, as a teacher, is worthy of instructing a group of disciples. For what reason is this said? Monks, in this Dispensation, the Teacher, the Blessed One, out of compassion and seeking their welfare, teaches the Dhamma to the disciples, saying: 'This is for your benefit and happiness.' Those disciples of the Blessed One do not wish to listen, do not lend an ear, do not apply their minds to knowledge, and they practice by turning away from the Teacher's instruction. Monks, in such non-compliance, the Tathāgata, the Blessed One, does not become displeased, does not experience displeasure, but dwells mindful and clearly comprehending.
287:
“There are three foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) which the Noble One [the Buddha] cultivates; by cultivating these foundations of mindfulness, the Teacher is worthy of instructing the assembly of disciples.” Thus it was said. For what reason was this said?

Monks, in this Dispensation, the Teacher, being compassionate and seeking their welfare, out of compassion, teaches the Dhamma to the disciples: “This is for your welfare; this is for your happiness.” Those disciples of the Teacher do not wish to listen, do not lend an ear, do not apply their minds to knowledge, and they practice by deviating from the Teacher’s instruction. Monks, in that situation, the Tathāgata is not displeased, nor does he experience displeasure; he dwells unpolluted (anavassuta), mindful and clearly comprehending. Monks, this is the first foundation of mindfulness. Which the Noble One cultivates... is worthy.

Furthermore, monks, the Teacher... [teaches]: “This is for your happiness.” Some disciples of the Teacher do not wish to listen... and they do not practice by deviating from the Teacher’s instruction. Monks, in that situation, the Tathāgata is not displeased, nor does he experience displeasure; he is not pleased, nor does he experience pleasure. Avoiding both displeasure and pleasure, he dwells equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending. Monks, this is called the second foundation of mindfulness.

Furthermore, monks... [teaches]: “This is for your happiness.” The disciples of the Teacher wish to listen... and they practice [according to the instruction]. Monks, in that situation, the Tathāgata is pleased and experiences pleasure; he dwells unpolluted, mindful and clearly comprehending. Monks, this is called the third foundation of mindfulness. (M. Ni. 3.311).

Thus, the state of being unpolluted by aversion (paṭigha) and attraction (anunaya), and the state of transcending both through constantly established mindfulness, is called “Satipaṭṭhāna.” Only the Buddhas possess this state of constantly established mindfulness because it is a unique quality (āveṇika-dhamma), and it does not occur in Paccekabuddhas and others.

The prefix “pa-” illuminates the meaning of beginning or undertaking (ārambha). Since undertaking is the same as setting in motion (pavattī), it is said to have the meaning “because of being set in motion.” The state that is to be established by means of mindfulness is called Satipaṭṭhāna. The suffix “-ana” in the word “paṭṭhāna” can also have the sense of the object (kamma) by the rule of plural usage (bahulaṃ-vacana). Similarly, since the sense of the agent (kattu) is also obtained for that suffix, it is said: “It is paṭṭhāna because it establishes (paṭṭhāti).” In this word “paṭṭhāti,” the prefix “pa-” indicates a distinguished plunging into; thus it is said: “It has the meaning of occurring by entering into, plunging into, and spreading out.” Again, explaining the word “sati” which has the sense of state (bhāva)...
288:
In explaining the word “paṭṭhāna,” it is said “Atha vā” (Or else), and so on. According to that statement, it should be understood that in the previous alternative, the words “sati” and “paṭṭhāna” have the sense of the agent (kattu). By the sense of “saraṇa,” it means the act of repeatedly recollecting (anussaraṇa) what was done or said long ago. “Idaṃ” refers to the meaning stated as “Mindfulness itself is the foundation of mindfulness.” This is the intended meaning in this scriptural passage.

If it is asked: “If mindfulness itself is the foundation of mindfulness, and mindfulness is a single phenomenon, why is the plural 'satipaṭṭhāna' used?” The answer is: “Because of the many varieties of mindfulness.” If it is asked: “If those mindfulnesses are many, why is the singular 'maggo' (the path) used?” The explanation is: The sense of “magga” is the sense of deliverance (niyyāna) from the suffering of saṃsāra. Because the path-dhamma is the means of deliverance, it reaches a state of unity through that very nature of deliverance and goes exclusively to Nibbāna. Also, because it is sought after for that purpose by those who desire [Nibbāna], it is called “magga.” The commentator brings back the statement previously made as evidence. In that statement, “catassopi cetā” refers to these four types of mindfulness by way of contemplation of the body, etc. “Aparabhāge” means at the moment of the Noble Path (ariyamagga). “Kiccaṃ sādhayamānā” means that in the preceding stage, having occurred separately by way of dispelling the perversions (vipallāsa) such as the perception of beauty (subha-saññā) in the body, etc., at the moment of the path, mindfulness itself goes to Nibbāna by taking it as an object while accomplishing the task of abandoning (pahāna-kicca) by way of the total eradication of the four perversions in the body, etc. It is only because of accomplishing these four tasks that the plural designation is used here. Thus, since it can be called “maggo” in the singular by taking unity in the sense of the path, and “cattāro” (four) in the plural by taking the fourfold nature based on the difference of objects, the teaching beginning with “Ekāyano ayaṃ” (This is the only way) is indeed connected in its sequence and not disconnected.

To demonstrate this meaning with an illustration, the scriptural passage “Mārasenappamaddanaṃ” (Crushing the army of Māra) is brought forward and compared with the illustration beginning with “Yathā.” The passage beginning with “Tasmā” is the concluding statement.

Specifically, because the body and feelings are causes of gratification (assāda), for the purpose of abandoning that craving (taṇhā), the contemplations of foulness (asubha) and suffering (dukkha) in those gross and subtle bases of craving—the body and feelings—are easy for those of craving-temperament (taṇhā-carita) with dull or sharp wisdom. Therefore, those contemplations are called the “Path of Purification” (visuddhimagga) for them. Likewise, the contemplations of impermanence (anicca) and non-self (anatta) in the mind and phenomena (citta-dhamma), which are the special causes of the view (diṭṭhi) that takes them as “permanent and self,” are easy for those of view-temperament (diṭṭhi-carita) with dull or sharp wisdom in those mind-phenomena which are categorized as very diverse or not very diverse by way of being with lust, etc., or by way of perception, contact, etc., or by way of hindrances, etc., for the purpose of abandoning that view. Therefore, those contemplations are called the “Path of Purification” for them. In this context, just as mind and phenomena...
289:
Just as the state of being a base for craving exists in the mind (citta) and mental objects (dhamma), so too the state of being a base for views (diᅡᅡhi) exists in the body (kāya) and feelings (vedanā). Although the state of being a base for craving and views exists in all four—body, feeling, mind, and mental objects—it should be understood that the Teacher has made a specific selection to show which is the predominant condition for which craving or view.

It is said, "Because of not being established in a coarse object," that a person of sharp wisdom who has serenity as their vehicle (samatha-yānika) discerns a coarse object, but without remaining there, enters into a meditative absorption (jhāna); then, emerging from the jhāna, they discern and contemplate feelings. For a person who has insight as their vehicle (vipassanā-yānika), however, the mind enters into the subtle mind and mental objects. Therefore, the way of purification for those with dull or sharp wisdom who have insight as their vehicle is stated as the contemplation of the mind (cittānupassanā) and the contemplation of mental objects (dhammānupassanā).

In the phrase "tesaᅃ tattha," the word "tattha" should be construed with the word "pahānatthaᅃ." The same method applies to the "tesaᅃ tattha" that appears later. The five cords of sensual pleasure are specifically obtained in the body; therefore, the body is specifically the base for the flood of sensuality (kāmogha). By perceiving happiness in existences, there is delight in existence; therefore, feeling is the base for the flood of existence (bhavogha). By perceiving a continuity or a mass, there is specifically the adherence to a self in the mind; therefore, the mind is the base for the flood of views (diᅡᅡhogha). Because of the difficulty in distinguishing mental objects and because of the difficulty in penetrating them as mere phenomena, delusion occurs; therefore, mental objects are the base for the flood of ignorance (avijjogha). Thus, only these four are taught for the sake of abandoning those floods in those respective bases.

By thus explaining the state of the body and so on as the bases for the flood of sensuality and so on, the state of being bases for the yoke of sensuality (kāmayoga) and the taint of sensuality (kāmāsava) is also explained, because those yokes and taints are not different in essence from the floods. To the extent that the body is the base for the flood of sensuality and so on, to that same extent it is the base for the bodily tie of covetousness (abhijjhā-kāyagantha). Since it is said, "The underlying tendency to resistance underlies painful feeling," feeling which consists of the suffering of pain (dukkha-dukkhatā), the suffering of change (vipariᅇāma-dukkhatā), and the suffering of formations (saᅃkhāra-dukkhatā) is specifically the base for the bodily tie of ill-will (byāpāda-kāyagantha). By perceiving the mind as permanent, there is the wrong handling of a stable self, such as "one is purified by virtue"; therefore, the mind is the base for the clinging to rites and rituals (sġlabbataparāmāsa). For one who does not see reality as it is through the discernment of mind and matter, there is the dogmatic adherence to the truth expressed as "this alone is the truth," which is known as the view of existence (bhava-diᅡᅡhi) and the view of non-existence (vibhava-diᅡᅡhi); therefore, mental objects are the base for that adherence. The state of the body being the base for clinging to sensuality (kāmupādāna) is according to the method already stated. To the extent that the body is the base for the flood of sensuality, to that same extent it is the base for clinging to sensuality, because they are not different in essence. Through delight in pleasant feeling, without regard for the next world, one produces wrong handling such as "there is no giving"; therefore, feeling is the base for the clinging to views (diᅡᅡhupādāna)...
290:
...base. The state of the mind and mental objects being the bases for other types of clinging should be understood in the same way as mentioned in the third and fourth connections of the bodily ties (gantha). The state of the body and feelings being the bases for the bias of desire (chandāgati) and the bias of hatred (dosāgati) should also be understood in the same way as mentioned in the connections of the flood of sensuality (kāmogha) and the bodily tie of ill-will (byāpāda-kāyagantha). Because delusion often occurs in a mind accompanied by lust due to perceiving it as a continuous mass, the mind is called the base for the bias of delusion (mohāgati). Because fear often occurs due to not understanding the nature of phenomena, mental objects are called the base for the bias of fear (bhayāgati).

In accordance with the words: "With the arising of nutriment, the body (kāya) arises; with the arising of contact, feelings arise; with formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, mind-and-matter," the four nutriments—physical food (kabaᄷġkāra), contact (phassa), mental volition (manosacetanā), and consciousness (viāᅇa)—which are the causes for the arising of the body and so on, become fully understood through the full understanding of the body and so on. Therefore, it is said, "For the sake of the full understanding of the four nutriments." The term "pakaraᅇanayo" refers to the method of explaining the Suttanta by way of the Nettippakaraᅇa.

"Saraᅇavasena" means by way of maintaining (mindfulness) so that the body and so on, and the wholesome states and so on, do not perish. Because of the meaning "they go to Nibbāna by this (dhamma)," it is called mindfulness (sati). In that mindfulness, the convergence into Nibbāna, which has a single nature, is called "ekatta-samosaraᅇa" (convergence into unity). To show this very meaning, the passage beginning with "yathā hi" is stated.

Alternatively, because it is the cause for entering the single Nibbāna, the single nature of the foundations of mindfulness is called "ekatta" (unity). The convergence in that foundation of mindfulness is called "ekatta-samosaraᅇa." This is simply being of the same nature as that foundation of mindfulness. To show the state of being the cause for entering the single Nibbāna, the passage beginning with "yathā" is stated. In this sense, "saraᅇa," "ekatta," and "samosaraᅇa" should be understood as being stated together as the cause for the single nature of the foundations of mindfulness. In the previous sense, they were separate. If "saraᅇavasena" is taken in the sense of "going" (attaining), then that going itself is "samosaraᅇa." Or, if "samosaraᅇa" is not stated as the meaning of the word "sati," then since the nature of maintaining (dhāraᅇa) is alone mindfulness and there is no other meaning, the first term is the cause for the state of mindfulness, and the latter term is the cause for the state of unity. Therefore, even in the convergence into Nibbāna, those terms are stated together as the causes for the single nature of the foundations of mindfulness.

"In 14 ways, 9 ways, 16 ways, 5 ways" is stated by way of the sections on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānapabba) and so on that appear later in the Pali text. However, by way of other divisions of those sections and by way of the divisions following them, the manifold nature of meditation is indeed obtained. The similarity to goods appearing from the four directions should be seen in the power and influence of the respective meditations on the foundations of mindfulness, such as the contemplation of the body.
291:
The question asked with the desire to explain (kathetukamyatāpucchā) is stated in this way (as "What are the four?") because other types of questions are not possible here, and because of the desire to teach by way of detailed exposition (niddesa). The word "idha" (here) indicates the support (sannissaya) of the monk who fulfills the practice to be taught. Since there is no other support for that monk besides the Dispensation (sāsana), it is said, "idha—in this Dispensation."

The address "O monks" (bhikkhave) is for the purpose of making those monks face him and to make them listen to the Dhamma respectfully. In accordance with the words, "Monks, roam in your own ancestral domain, your own resort (gocara)," these dhammas, namely mindfulness of the body and so forth, are the resorts of monks. Because one becomes a monk by practicing mindfulness of the body and so forth, and because that practice is established only in a monk, he points out the monk with the words "dwells contemplating the body" (kāyānupassī viharati), etc. Therefore, the teacher said, "Because of showing the state of being a monk through practice."

Because he follows the conduct of the Teacher and because he accepts and upholds the entire Dispensation, the monk is the vessel (bhājana) for all forms of instruction. When the monk is taken, since the assembly of monks is the chief, other assemblies are also included by implication, just as when a king arrives, his retinue is also included. Therefore, he said, "the rest (of the assemblies)," etc. Having thus analyzed the first reason, he said "And he who this..." etc., to analyze the other reason.

"Should live evenly" (samaṃ careyya) means abandoning uneven conduct of body and so forth, and living evenly in accordance with the Dhamma through body, speech, and mind. One who is peaceful (santa) due to the subsiding of lust etc., disciplined (danta) due to the restraint of the faculties, certain (niyata) through the certainty of the four paths, a liver of the holy life (brahmacārī) due to noble conduct, and one who has laid down the rod (nidhāya daṇḍaṃ) by laying down the rod of punishment towards all beings—standing in the state of an Ariya, such a person is to be known as a "Brahmin," a "Samana," and a "Bhikkhu" because of having discarded evil, calmed evil, and destroyed the defilements.

In places such as "this body and the mentality-materiality outside," the term "body" (kāya) is used for the five aggregates; in places such as "he experiences happiness with the body," it refers to the mental aggregates of feeling and so forth. To distinguish from those meanings, he said, "Body means the physical body (rūpakāya)." "Of the dhammas such as hair etc." means the collection of primary elements (bhūta-rūpa) and derived matter (upādā-rūpa) designated as hair and so on. Having thus shown the word "kāya" by way of the meanings of "accumulation" and "body," he now says "And as..." etc., to show it by way of etymology (nirutti). "Āyanti" means they arise (uppajjanti).
292:
"Asammissato" means without mixing. Although feeling and so forth are dependent on and connected to this physical body, when one repeatedly contemplates feeling and so forth in the body, it means one should contemplate without mixing them with those feelings. Because the word "kāya" has the meaning of a collection, and because it takes the collection of foul aspects, it is spoken in the singular as "kāye" (in the body). Similarly, although the mind has many divisions by way of objects etc., it is taken as one by the commonality of the nature of mind and spoken in the singular as "citte" (in the mind). But feeling is spoken in the plural as "vedanāsu" (in feelings) to show that it should be contemplated separately by way of its divisions such as pleasant feeling etc.; it is also presented this way in the Niddesa section. Since dhammas have more than fifty divisions and are of many types by way of the modes of repeated contemplation, they are also spoken in the plural.

To prohibit the perception of a distinct substance apart from the whole (avayavī) in a collection of parts, the overstepping (atidhāvana) into designations like "woman" or "man," and the firm adherence to the idea of a core essence, he analyzes the body into major and minor limbs, those limbs into hair etc., and hair etc. into primary and derived matter, saying "Not so in the body," etc. Even those who speak of a "whole" in the collection of parts of a city like a palace etc., do not perceive the "whole" as something separate. However, since some might overstep into the designation "there is a certain thing called a city," the example of a city is given regarding the overstepping into designations like "woman" or "man." There is no such thing as a "body" apart from the aforementioned collections—the collection of limbs, the collection of hair and fur, and the collection of primary and derived matter—much less "woman" and so on. Therefore, he said, "Neither a body, nor a woman, nor a man, nor any other dhamma is seen." By the words "any other dhamma," he rejects concepts like "being" (satta) or "soul" (jīva). The "whole" is already rejected by the rejection of the "body." If it is thus rejected, how can there be overstepping into designations like "body" etc.? To address this, he said, "In the aforementioned dhammas... they act." "In such and such a way" means they wrongly cling by way of the modes of "body" etc.

"What one sees" means whatever woman or man one sees. If one asks, "Is it not that there is no seeing of a woman or man with eye-consciousness?"—this is true. However, it is said "what one sees" by the power of the perception (saññā) that arises as "I see a woman, I see a man." Or, what one sees through wrong vision or wrong view—that seen object is not the base of visible form (rūpāyatana). This is because it is a form wrongly conceptualized through perverted grasping. Or, that seen object is not what is called the collection of primary and derived matter like hair etc., because it is not cognizable by eye-consciousness, or it is not the seen object. "One does not contemplate what is seen" means that although the rūpāyatana called the collection of primary and derived matter like hair etc. is seen, one does not see that rūpāyatana as it really is with the eye of wisdom. "Bound without seeing" means one who does not see this individual existence (attabhāva) as it really is with the eye of wisdom...
293:
“This is mine, this I am, this is my self”—thus one is bound by the fetters of defilements. “Does not contemplate other natures” means one does not contemplate the nature of beauty (subha) and such, but rather contemplates the nature of the unattractive (asubha) and so forth. By the words “What is meant?” etc., he makes that same meaning clear. “Earth-body” (pathavīkāya) refers to the parts such as hair, etc.; it is called “body” (kāya) because it is a collection of phenomena (dhammasamūha). Alternatively, it refers to the characteristic of earth (lakkhaṇapathavī) found throughout the entire body in its various forms, which exists in a continuous sequence of preceding and succeeding states; taking this as a group, it is called “body.” The same method should be understood for “water-body” (āpokāya) and so forth. This refers to what is grasped by blind fools as “I” and “mine,” in the sense of self and what belongs to self (atta-attaniya).

Now, to show the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) by way of the seven modes of contemplation, he begins with the words “Moreover” (api ca), etc. Therein, “contemplates as impermanent” means repeatedly contemplating the body originated from the four causes as “impermanent.” One who sees thus is said to contemplate the mode of impermanence of that body. For such a person, not even a trace of the grasping of permanence remains in that body; therefore, it is said “not as permanent.” Because there is no such grasping, it is said “he abandons the perception of permanence” (niccasaññaṃ pajahati). Here, the word eva (only) is implied in the phrase “contemplates only as impermanent.” To show the meaning excluded by that word eva, it is said “not as permanent.” Here, one should not suspect that the word eva excludes contemplation as suffering (dukkha) and so forth, because the purpose of the word eva is to exclude the opposite, which is permanence, and because the contemplations of suffering, etc., are taught further on. The same method applies to the words “contemplates as suffering,” etc. Specifically, because the impermanent body is suffering, he contemplates that very body as suffering. Because the body that is suffering is not-self, he contemplates it as not-self. Since that which is impermanent, suffering, and not-self should not be delighted in, and since that which should not be delighted in should not be craved, it is said: “he becomes disenchanted, he does not delight; he becomes dispassionate, he does not lust.” One who thus does not lust causes lust to cease; he does not produce it, meaning he does not create its origin. One who practices thus relinquishes and does not grasp. This contemplation of impermanence, etc., is called “relinquishment as giving up” (pariccāga-paṭinissagga) because it abandons defilements through the respective factors of insight along with the body and the formations associated with it, and “relinquishment as entering into” (pakkhandana-paṭinissagga) because, seeing the faults of the conditioned, the mind leans and enters into Nibbāna, which is the opposite. Therefore, a bhikkhu endowed with that contemplation abandons defilements in the manner described and enters into Nibbāna. Such a bhikkhu does not grasp defilements by way of producing them, nor does he grasp the object of formations (saṅkhārārammaṇa) because he sees the faults of the conditioned. Therefore, it is said “he relinquishes, he does not grasp.” To show which of the seven contemplations abandons which state, it is said: “by contemplating as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence,” and so forth.
294:
He does not grasp defilements, nor does he grasp the object of formations by way of seeing the faults of the conditioned. Therefore, it is said “he relinquishes, he does not grasp.” Now, to show which states are abandoned by those contemplations of that bhikkhu, it is said: “contemplating as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence,” and so forth. In that text, “perception of permanence” (niccasaññā) refers to the perverted perception that “formations are permanent.” The mention of “perception” (saññā) should be understood as the abandonment of the perversion of perception (saññā-vipallāsa) preceded by the abandonment of the perversions of view (diṭṭhi-vipallāsa) and mind (citta-vipallāsa). Or, by taking perception as the head, those others are also included. “Delight” (nandi) refers to craving accompanied by joy (pīti). The rest is as previously explained.

By the word “dwells” (viharati), he refers to the abiding in postures of one endowed with the contemplation of the body; thus he says “he moves” (iriyati), meaning he carries out the postures. Because it pervades by way of making them objects, it is said “in the three realms.” However, by way of arising, the defilements belong only to the sense sphere (parittabhūmaka). If it is said that the abandoning of defilements is “ardor” (ātapana), then that ardor also exists in right view and so forth. However, just as the word ātappa, the word ātapa is established only for energy (vīriya); thus it is said “this is a name for energy.” Alternatively, because the “burning” of energy, which occurs by way of encouraging the associated states in abandoning the opposing defilements, is exceedingly intense, energy alone is called so, not other states. In the word “ardent” (ātāpī), the suffix “ī” is used in the sense of praise, or it indicates excellence. By the term “ardent,” he shows the possession of right striving (sammappadhāna).

One is “clearly comprehending” (sampajāna) because one knows rightly (sammā), entirely (samantato), and by oneself (sāmāṃ). It means knowing rightly and without distortion because there is no contemplation of other states when defining things without confusion; knowing entirely because of knowing all modes; and knowing by oneself because of proceeding in a way that brings about higher and higher distinction. If one contemplates with wisdom (paññā), why is it called a foundation of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna)? To answer this, he says “Not indeed,” etc. “Useful in all circumstances” (sabbatthika) is said because it occurs in all places, and because it is desired when the mind is shrunken or agitated. Or, it is called sabbatthikā because all the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) to be developed during shrinkage or agitation must seek help from this mindfulness. Only with wisdom that has received the assistance of mindfulness does the bhikkhu, a practitioner of meditation on the aforementioned body, dwell contemplating the body (kāyānupassī). “Internal contraction” (antosaṅkhepo) means internal shrinking or sloth (kosajja). In the phrase “grasping the means” (upāyapariggaha), the “means” (upāya) refers to the purification of virtue, counting, skill in learning, and so forth. Its opposite should be understood as “non-means” (anupāya). Since one who is established in mindfulness does not abandon the aforementioned means and does not grasp the non-means, it is said “one who is forgetful... is unable.” The word “by that” (tena) means because of being unable to grasp the means and avoid the non-means, or to relinquish and not grasp. “Of him” (assa) means of that meditator (yogī).
295:
In this teaching of Satipaṭṭhāna, since the Blessed One taught mindfulness alone as Satipaṭṭhāna, the associated states such as energy (vīriya) and wisdom (paññā) are called factors (causal factors). To show this, it is said: "Showing its associated factors" (*sampayogangañcassa dassetvā*). Here, the word *anga* should be understood as a synonym for the word *kāraṇa* (cause). In this context, by taking mindfulness, concentration (*samādhi*) is also taken; because that mindfulness is included within the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*).

Alternatively, this teaching is one taught with mindfulness as the head. Indeed, the abandonment of defilements is not possible through mere mindfulness alone without concentration, nor is the realization of Nibbāna possible, nor does mere mindfulness even occur. Therefore, just as in the teaching of the *jhānas*, the words such as *savitakka* (with initial application) show the associated factors, so too here it shows the associated factors of that mindfulness. Thus, the word *anga* should be understood as a synonym for *avayava* (part/constituent). "*Pahānaṅga*" (factor of abandonment) is for the purpose of showing the unwholesome parts to be abandoned, namely covetousness (*abhijjhā*) and grief (*domanassa*), as in the Pāḷi texts such as "Quite secluded from sensual pleasures" (*vivicceva kāmehi*). Since in this Sutta Pāḷi only the mundane path (*lokiya-magga*) is intended and not the supramundane path (*lokuttara-magga*), desiring to show only the removal (*vinaya*) of covetousness and grief that occurs in the preliminary stage, it is said: "Either by the removal through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-vinaya*) or by the removal through suppression (*vikkhambhana-vinaya*)." "*Tesaṃ dhammānaṃ*" means of the states such as feeling (*vedanā*). Since those states such as feeling are not intended in that Vibhaṅga Pāḷi, the teacher said: "This is said by way of the method of extracting the meaning" (*atthuddhāranayenetaṃ vuttaṃ*). "*Tattha*" means in the Vibhaṅga. "*Ettha*" means in this word "*loke*."

Having stated the abandonment of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) generally through both the removal of covetousness and the removal of grief without distinction, it is said "specifically" (*visesena*) to show the specific way of abandonment stated by each of covetousness and grief. Alternatively, desiring to show the benefit of teaching the removal of covetousness and grief instead of saying "having removed the hindrances," the words beginning with "specifically" are said. Indeed, showing the abandonment of attraction (*anurodha*) and aversion (*virodha*), which are the direct opposites of the development of mindfulness of the body (*kāyānupassanā-bhāvanā*), is the benefit of teaching the abandonment of this covetousness and grief. "*Kāyasampatti-mūlakassa*" means the attraction rooted in the perfection of the body, such as beauty of form, physical strength, youthfulness, and health. By the reverse of the aforementioned perfection of the body such as physical strength, aversion (*virodha*) rooted in the decay and ruin of the body should be understood. "*Kāyabhāvanāya*" means in the development of mindfulness of the body (*kāyānupassanā-bhāvanā*). Here, *kāyabhāvanā* is intended as that mindfulness of the body. In the phrase "*subhasukhabhāvādīnaṃ*," by the word *ādi* (etc.), the inclusion of states such as being pleasing to the mind and being permanent should be understood. Furthermore, in this text "*asubhasukhabhāvādīnaṃ*," by the word *ādi*, the inclusion of states such as being unpleasing to the mind and being impermanent should be understood. "*Tena*" means by the statement showing the abandonment of attraction (*anurodha*) and so forth. The words beginning with "*yogānubhāvo hi*" are for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of the abandonment of attraction, aversion, and so forth already mentioned. Indeed, the power of yoga (*yogānubhāva*) is the power of the development of meditation (*bhāvanā*). "*Yogasamattho*" means being capable of repeatedly practicing the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) that has been undertaken. By the earlier statement beginning with "*anurodhavirodhavippamutto*," the benefit of the monk who has already practiced meditation has been shown. By the second statement, "*yogasamattho*," the practice of the monk who is currently practicing meditation is shown. Indeed, the meditation of a monk who is oppressed by attraction, aversion, and so forth cannot reach fulfillment.
296:
In the term "Anupassī," the meaning should be understood as referring to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) that illuminates the contemplation (anupassanā) obtained here. Otherwise, the instrumental case "by contemplation" (anupassanāya) would not be appropriate. Contemplation itself is the meditation subject; here, the object (ārammaṇa) is not intended, or it may be appropriate. It should be connected as "carrying the body (kāyapariharaṇaṃ) has been stated." Since the meaning of carrying the meditation subject is automatically accomplished here, it is stated only as "carrying the body." For the person practicing meditation, carrying the body is solely for the purpose of carrying the meditation subject. Alternatively, because the carrying of the meditation subject will be taught through terms like "ardent" (ātāpī), it is stated only as "carrying the body." Or, by the word "body" (kāya), the mental body (nāmakāya) is also taken, not just the physical body (rūpakāya); thus, carrying the meditation subject is also included. By doing so, the use of the word "ettha" in "dwells (viharati) by the dwelling (vihāra) mentioned here" is also established, because the dwelling is specifically taught as "contemplating the body, he dwells" (kāyānupassī viharati). The words beginning with "ardent" (ātāpī) are an elaboration, along with the means of accomplishment, of the carrying of the meditation subject which was stated in brief. "By ardency" (ātāpena) means by taking ardency (referring to right effort/sammappadhāna). The same method applies to "with mindfulness and clear comprehension" (satisampajaññena), etc. "Universal meditation subjects" (sabbatthaka-kammaṭṭhāna) are: recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati), loving-kindness (mettā), mindfulness of death (maraṇassati), and meditation on foulness (asubha-bhāvanā). These four are called "universal meditation subjects" because they must always be maintained by the yogi. They are mentioned by taking mindfulness and clear comprehension because they serve as protection for all meditation practices and must be maintained continuously through the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension. Alternatively, by mindfulness, serenity (samatha) is meant, as mindfulness is included in the concentration aggregate (samādhikkhandha).

In the Vibhaṅga, the meaning is explained—this should be construed. "By that" (tena) means together with the Vibhaṅga text, which proceeds by way of analyzing the essential meaning (bhāvattha) without prioritizing the literal meaning (saddattha). "The method of the Commentary" (aṭṭhakathānayo) is the method of explaining the meaning which also clarifies the literal meaning as appropriate. "As it tallies" (yathā saṃsandati) means it should be understood as tallying and agreeing perfectly in terms of meaning and intention without contradiction.

Regarding "the repeated mention of feelings, etc.": because mental phenomena (cittadhamma) depend on feeling as a support condition (nissaya-paccaya), and because in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava) immaterial phenomena proceed in connection with matter, even though the contemplation of the body, etc., might be mistakenly applied to feeling, the second mention of the word "feeling" (vedanā) is made to show the determination [of feeling] without confusion with those [other phenomena], and to show the resolution of the compact (ghana-vinibbhoga), etc. Therefore, in feeling, one is not a contemplator of the body or a contemplator of mental phenomena, but rather one is a contemplator of feeling alone. By the repeated mention of the word "feeling," by showing only the mode of repeatedly contemplating feeling, the determination [of feeling] without confusion with mental phenomena is shown. Alternatively, at the time there is a pleasant feeling, at that time there is no painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Or, at the time there is a painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, at that time another pleasant feeling does not occur. Thus, feeling...
297:
By the word "contemplating feeling" (vedanānupassī), by seeing only the mode of contemplating feeling in the basis (vatthu) called feeling, the determination [of feeling] without confusion with other phenomena is shown. Likewise, "At the time there is a pleasant feeling, at that time there is no painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. At the time there is a painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, at that time there is no other feeling." By seeing each specific feeling distinctly, rather than remaining in the generality of "being a feeling," the resolution of the compact (ghana-vinibbhoga) and the detachment from the notion of permanence (dhuvabhāva-viveka) are shown. By showing this, through seeing the existence of those feelings for only a moment, the characteristics of impermanence (aniccata), and because of that impermanence, suffering (dukkhata) and non-self (anattata) are made clear. In the term "ghana-vinibbhogādi," this meaning should also be understood by the word "ādi." This monk is one who repeatedly contemplates feeling in feeling, not one who contemplates other phenomena. What is meant? Just as a fool sees the appearance of a gem in a water bubble which is not a gem, this monk does not see a pleasant aspect in feeling which is [actually] unstable and not delightful—let alone in the other [painful feelings]. Rather, he contemplates it in terms of impermanence, non-self, and foulness, because of its momentary dissolution, its being beyond control, and its oozing with the impurities of defilements. He contemplates it specifically as suffering because of the suffering due to change (vipariṇāma-dukkhatā) and the suffering due to formations (saṅkhāra-dukkhatā). In the same way, the purpose of the repeated mention in the case of mind (citta) and phenomena (dhamma) should be stated as appropriate. This is because the intention is the range of mundane (lokiya) investigation. By the words beginning with "kevalaṃ panidha," the delimitation of what should be known is shown: "In this place, this much should be known." By the words "esa nayo" (this is the method), the meaning is indicated: "Just as the mind and phenomena should be contemplated, so one who contemplates them should be known as a contemplator of mind in the mind, and a contemplator of phenomena in phenomena." "As suffering" (dukkhato) means it should be contemplated as "suffering" by its nature of suffering. The same method applies to the remaining two terms.

The monk who sees pleasant feeling as "suffering" with the eye of wisdom because of the suffering due to change. He sees painful feeling as a dart (salla) because it produces affliction, stabs within, and is difficult to extract. He sees neither-painful-nor-pleasant (equanimous) feeling as "impermanent" (anicca) because, although it is peaceful like pleasant and painful feelings because of its lack of grossness and its nature of being calmed by conditions, it does not exist after having been, it has rise and fall, it is temporary, and it is the opposite of permanent. That monk is indeed one who sees rightly (sammaddaso), meaning he sees feeling correctly and clearly.
298:
It is also called suffering. All these feelings are called suffering because of the nature of suffering in formations (saṅkhāra-dukkhatā). I [the Buddha] say, "Whatever feeling there is, it is included within suffering," because all these feelings do not transcend the nature of suffering in formations. It is understood that these feelings should be repeatedly contemplated as suffering, both by way of pleasant suffering and because they are described through the nature of pleasure and the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-dukkha). The seven contemplations (anupassanā) have already been clearly explained below. The remaining divisions, such as worldly (sāmisa) and unworldly (nirāmisa), should be explained in the contemplation of feelings (vedanānupassanā).

"By way of the diversity of objects and so forth" means it should be understood that one should contemplate by way of the diversity of objects such as visible forms, the diversity of types such as blue and so forth, the diversity of predominances (adhipati) such as desire (chanda), the diversity of types such as inferior and so forth, the diversity of conascent states (sahajāta) such as wisdom (ñāṇa) and jhāna, the diversity of types such as with-prompting (sasaṅkhārika), without-prompting (asaṅkhārika), with initial thought (savitakka) and so forth, the diversity of planes (bhūmi) such as the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), the diversity of types such as superior (ukkaṭṭha) and middle (majjhima), the diversity of kamma such as wholesome kamma, the diversity of types such as that leading to the deva realm, the diversity of results (vipāka) such as black and white, the diversity of types such as that to be experienced in the present life (diṭṭhadhamma-vedanīya), the diversity of functional (kiriya) states occurring in the limited plane (paritta-bhūmi), and the diversity of types such as functional states with three roots (tihetuka). By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the diversity of states with a physical basis (savatthuka) and without a physical basis (avatthuka), and the diversity of types common to the three kinds of persons should be included. "By way of individual characteristics (salakkhaṇa) and common characteristics (sāmañña-lakkhaṇa)" means it should be understood as contemplating by way of individual characteristics such as touching (phusana) and common characteristics such as impermanence (aniccata). "Of the state of emptiness" (suññata-dhamma) means by way of the nature of emptiness known as non-self (anattā). To clarify this state of emptiness, the teaching on the section of emptiness (suññatā-vāra) was given in the Abhidhamma, starting with, "At that time, there are states (dhammā), there are aggregates (khandhā)."

That covetousness and displeasure (abhijjhā-domanassa) have already been abandoned during the previous contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā), and thus they are indeed abandoned. Therefore, it should not be said that those respective defilements are abandoned again. This is because, in the abandonment of defilements, they are not abandoned by distinguishing objects, but rather, only those defilements capable of arising in the future are to be abandoned. Therefore, once covetousness and the like are said to be abandoned in one state, it should not be said again in another state. This meaning is shown by the words beginning with "Kāmañcettha." Alternatively, at the moment of the path-consciousness (maggacitta), a defilement abandoned in one foundation of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) is abandoned in all foundations of mindfulness. Therefore, it should not be said that they are abandoned separately in each path-moment. In truth, it should only be said that they are abandoned once by the path. Between these two answers, the former is an explanation regarding various individuals; the abandonment by one person is not the abandonment by another. The latter is an explanation regarding various moments of consciousness. "Various moments of consciousness" refers to the moments when the mundane path-consciousness of mindfulness arises. Here, the mundane path (pubbabhāga-magga) that precedes the supramundane path is intended. Covetousness and displeasure abandoned in the material body (rūpa-kāya) through mundane development (lokiya-bhāvanā) are not yet abandoned in feelings and so forth.

Even if they are not yet abandoned, because they have been well-abandoned by the opposing development, it should only be said that covetousness and displeasure no longer arise in those feelings and so forth. Therefore, it is indeed appropriate to speak of abandoning that covetousness and displeasure once more. The teacher stated the words "abandoned in one place" (ekattha pahīnaṃ) with reference to the supramundane development of mindfulness. Or, it was stated with reference to the mere non-arising of covetousness and displeasure in all objects—body, feelings, mind, and mental objects—due to mundane development. It should be understood that the Blessed One taught in the Vibhaṅga, regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, that the five aggregates and the five aggregates of clinging are "the world." This is the sub-commentary (ṭīkā) explaining the hidden meaning of the commentary on the summary section (uddesavāra).

## Commentary on the Section on Mindfulness of Breathing in the Contemplation of the Body

One understands well and repeatedly by way of the diversity of objects such as the body which should be repeatedly contemplated. This is the division of the foundations of mindfulness shown in brief.
299:
Covetousness and displeasure, though abandoned in the body, are not yet abandoned in feelings and so forth. Even if they are not yet abandoned, because they have been well-suppressed (vikkhamhita) by the opposing development, it is not that it should not be said, "covetousness and displeasure do not occur" there; rather, it should indeed be said. Therefore, it is appropriate to speak of their abandonment once again. The statement, "What is abandoned in one place is abandoned in the rest," was made by the teacher with reference to the supramundane development of mindfulness, or with reference to the mere non-occurrence of defilements in all objects during mundane development. It should be understood that in the Vibhaṅga, in all four instances, it is stated: "The five aggregates of clinging are the world."

## Illumination of the Hidden Meaning of the Commentary on the Summary Section

## Contemplation of the Body

## Commentary on the Section on Mindfulness of Breathing

"By way of objects" (ārammaṇavasena) means by way of objects such as the body which are to be repeatedly contemplated. "Having divided into four" (catudhā bhinditvā) means having divided into four types by way of the summary (uddesa). The remaining meaning of the text is that, taking each foundation of mindfulness from those four, he analyzes the body (the group of materiality).

In the word "Kathañca," "kathaṃ" is a word asking about the manner. By that word, he asks about the various modes of the contemplation of the body being pointed out. The word "ca" shows a distinction. By that word "ca," he highlights a specific detail that was not clear in the summary section (uddesavāra) but is made clear in the detailed exposition (niddesavāra). Since even in external systems a small portion of this might exist, the phrase "of one who produces all modes of the contemplation of the body" is used to include every mode. By this, the fourteen modes that appear by way of the section on mindfulness of breathing and so forth, the modes of internal contemplation and so forth included therein, as well as the modes of the four jhānas having kasina objects based on the color and shape of hair and so forth as taught in the Kāyagatāsati Sutta, and the mundane modes and so forth—all these are included without exception.
