It is said, "all modes... and the negation," to mean that these modes exist only in this Dispensation (Sāsana) and not outside of it. In that context, "negation of such a state" (tathābhāva-paṭisedhano) means the negation of any other teaching as a support for a person who produces all modes of the contemplation of the body. By this, he shows that in the Pali "Idha bhikkhave," the word "idha" (here) has the meaning of the word "eva" (only) contained within it. There are indeed single words that carry a restrictive meaning, such as "vāyubhakkho" (one who eats only air). Therefore, he said, "Only here" (idheva).
300:
Monks, the term 'samaṇa' and so forth refers to that person who possesses the Dhamma that brings about the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) in every aspect and fulfills the state of a complete recluse in various ways. 'Parappavāda' refers to the various doctrines of other sectarians outside the Buddha's dispensation and the birthplaces of false views.

The words beginning with 'imassa hi' are spoken to show the suitability of the lodging for a monk living in places such as the forest for meditation. An ox that is difficult to tame and has not reached the state of being disciplined is called a 'kūṭagoṇa' (a rogue ox). A cow that hinders milking by not letting the milk flow completely from the udders during milking is called a 'kūṭadhenu' (a rogue cow). The pleasurable taste that arises depending on visible forms, sounds, and so forth is called 'rūpārammaṇādirasa'. 'Pubbe āciṇṇārammaṇa' refers to an object practiced either in the time before becoming a monk or in the beginningless saṃsāra. 'Nibandheyya' means 'should be tied'. 'Satiyā' means by means of mindfulness that arises through the power of properly noting the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). 'Ārammaṇe' means in the object of meditation. 'Daḷhaṃ' means firmly; it means making it powerful so that the concentration of a monk who is constantly mindful, consisting of access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi), becomes fulfilled.

'Visesādhigamadiṭṭhadhammasukhavihārapadaṭṭhāna' refers to [mindfulness of breathing] which is the proximate cause for the attainment of distinction by all Buddhas, some Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha, as well as for the pleasant dwelling in the present life of those virtuous ones who have attained distinction through other meditation subjects besides mindfulness of breathing.

The Blessed One is like a teacher who knows the science of site selection (vatthuvijjā) because he points out suitable places for meditators. The meditating monk is like a leopard because, by living alone in the forest and suppressing opposing defilements, he achieves the desired goal of the paths and fruits. The phrase 'phalamuttama' is spoken with reference to the fruits of the ascetic life (sāmaññaphala). 'Parakkamazavayoggabhūmi' is the ground made suitable for the momentum of meditative exertion.

The construction is: 'breathing in long' according to the long duration of in-breaths and out-breaths, or 'breathing in short' according to the brief duration of in-breaths and out-breaths. 'Evaṃ sikkhato' refers to a monk who practices the meditation on mindfulness of breathing by way of knowing the long and short breaths, experiencing the whole body [of breath], and calming the gross bodily formation. Or, it refers to a monk who, being such a practitioner, develops the three trainings: virtue, concentration, and wisdom.

'Assāsapassāsanimitte' means in the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) that appears based on the in-breaths and out-breaths. One who discerns the in-breaths and out-breaths by applying insight (vipassanā) with a focus on materiality is called 'assāsapassāsakammika' (one whose work is in-breaths and out-breaths). One discerns the jhana factors by applying insight with a focus on mentality. What is called 'vatthu' (basis) is the physical body (karajakāya) because it is the place where consciousness and mental factors occur. The realization that there is no being or person other than causes and effects is the purification of view (diṭṭhivisuddhi).
301:
'This phenomenon is merely a phenomenon; it is not without a cause, nor is it caused by an uneven cause such as a creator god; in reality, it arises due to causes such as ignorance (avijjā).' Thus, by overcoming doubt regarding the three periods of time, one becomes free from doubt. By applying the three characteristics through the method of 'whatever materiality, monks...' and so forth, by way of comprehension of groups (kalāpasammasana), and developing insight by way of contemplating arising and passing away, one gradually [reaches the fruit of Arahantship] through the sequence of the paths.

This Pali passage, 'in the body of in-breaths and out-breaths of another,' is stated considering the turn of comprehension (sammasana). However, by way of serenity (samatha), there is no occurrence of the absorption sign (appanānimitta) in the in-breaths and out-breaths of another. 'Without stopping' means without stopping in between. 'The time of wandering repeatedly' refers to the time when meditation occurs continuously even regarding internal and external phenomena. Since both cannot be obtained at the same time, it means these two phenomena called 'internal' and 'external' cannot be obtained as a single object at the same time; they cannot be taken as an object simultaneously.

Because it arises from this cause, it is called 'samudaya' (origin). That cause itself is 'samudayadhamma' because it is a phenomenon in the sense of being a cause. One who habitually contemplates the physical body (karajakāya) and so forth, which are the causes for the arising of in-breaths and out-breaths, is called 'samudayadhammānupassī' (a contemplator of the nature of arising). Wishing to show that 'samudayadhamma' by way of a simile, he said 'just as' and so forth. There, 'bhasta' means a leather bag (bellows). 'Gaggaranāḷi' means the nozzle of the bellows. 'Te' refers to the physical body and so forth. Just as the body of in-breaths and out-breaths is connected to the physical body and so forth because of being caused by them, so too the physical body and so forth are connected to the body of in-breaths and out-breaths by being their cause. Therefore, because it is appropriate to say 'the nature of arising in the body,' it is said 'samudaya...pe... is said'. Alternatively, the word 'dhamma' expresses 'inherent nature' (pakati), as in 'subject to birth' (jātidhamma) and so forth. One who repeatedly contemplates the body, which has the nature of arising when causes meet, is also called 'samudayadhammānupassī'. Therefore, he said 'and the physical body' and so forth. In this case, the locative case 'in the body' is even more appropriate.

In this context of 'contemplator of the nature of passing away' (vayadhammānupassī), although passing away is without a cause, it is said by way of metaphor (upacāra) that the absence of the physical body and so forth is the cause of the passing away of the body of in-breaths and out-breaths, because when certain causal phenomena are absent, the effect does not occur, and that absence is spoken of as the cause of that non-existence. Therefore, he said 'just as' and so forth.
302:
"Bhastāyā" etc., is the explanation of the meaning here according to the first alternative (vikalpa). According to the second alternative, the meaning should be understood only by way of metaphorical usage (upacāra).

Just as in the case of internal and external contemplation (ajjhatta-bahiddhā-nupassanā), because the objects are different, the insight contemplation of the nature of arising and passing away (samudaya-vaya-dhammānupassanā) also cannot be attained at the same time. Therefore, it is said, "contemplating arising at times, and contemplating passing away at times." In the phrase "Atthi kāyo" (There is a body), the word *eva* (only) is elided. Thus, it means "Only the body exists." To show the exclusion [of a being] by this determination, he said "not a being," etc.

The meaning of that is: One is conceived by others as a "being" (satta) because of being attached to forms, etc., or because of causing others to be attached, or because of being endowed with the quality of a being (sattva-guṇa). It is called a "person" (puggala) because of filling the group of beings or because of the nature of falling away through death and rebirth. It is called a "woman" (itthī) because the embryo is deposited and gathered here. It is called a "man" (purisa) because he exists or proceeds in the front part. It is called "self" (attā) because the conceit "I" is placed in this life. It is called "belonging to self" (attaniya) as being one's own property. One says "I" (ahaṃ) considering it not to be another. One says "mine" (mama) considering it to be one's own property. One says "someone" (kocī) considering it to be another distinct from the aforementioned types. One says "someone's" (kassacī) as being that person's property. [In reality], there is no one to be so conceived; there is only "the body exists." Even with these ten terms, he clarifies only the emptiness (suññata) of the body from self and what belongs to self. "Evam" (Thus) refers to the manner stated as "only the body exists," etc.

"Ñāṇapamāṇatthāya" means for the purpose of bringing the knowledge of body-contemplation to its limit. "Satipamāṇatthāya" means for the purpose of bringing the mindfulness that grasps the body to its limit. For this yogi, the mindfulness that is established through repeated occurrence as "the body exists" in the manner described, leads to the further increase of knowledge and mindfulness in that body beyond measure. Therefore, he said, "for the growth of mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña)." Because this meditation is the direct opposite of the graspings of craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi), he said, "craving... pe... dwells." Such a person does not see anything in the world to be grasped as "I" or "mine." Thinking "where would one grasp?" he said, "he does not cling to anything," etc. In the word "evampi," the word *pi* has the sense of including what is not mentioned, because the kind of meaning indicated below does not exist. Thus, he said, "depending on the meaning above." For example, in the Pali "ayampi pārājiko hoti," the word *pi* includes the unstated meaning. The word "evam," however, is used to reflect on the indicated manner by way of conclusion. Thus, he said, "In this way (he shows that mindfulness is the truth of suffering, as the mindfulness of the preliminary path is intended in this sutta)," etc.
303:
Because the mindfulness of the preliminary path (pubbabhāga-satipaṭṭhāna) is intended here in this Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, it is said, "Mindfulness is the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca)." That mindfulness occurs in a certain individual existence (attabhāva); the craving (taṇhā) that produces that individual existence is also said to be the producer of that mindfulness. This is because in the absence of that individual existence, mindfulness cannot exist. Therefore, he said, "The producer of that mindfulness is the preceding craving." For example, in the Pali "saṅkhārapaccayā" (conditioned by formations), the entire sequence of mundane consciousness arising from the seed of consciousness conditioned by those formations is simply called "consciousness conditioned by formations" according to the Suttanta method.

"Appavatti" (non-occurrence) refers to Nibbāna, which is the cause of non-occurrence. It means Nibbāna (the truth of cessation/nirodha-sacca) is the cause of the non-occurrence of both the truth of suffering and the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca). Alternatively, it is called *appavatti* because both suffering and origin do not occur in this truth of cessation. The words "dukkhaparijānano" (comprehending suffering), etc., are said to show the occurrence of the Noble Path solely by way of accomplishing the four functions: full understanding (pariññā), abandonment (pahāna), realization (sacchikiriyā), and development (bhāvanā). The penetration through development (bhāvanā-paṭivedha) of that Noble Path is accomplished as if stated, though not explicitly mentioned. "Catusaccavasena" means by way of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) for penetrating the Four Truths. "Ussakkitvā" means ascending through the successive purifications such as purification of virtue (sīla-visuddhi) and carrying the development of insight (vipassanā-bhāvanā) upwards. "Niyyānamukha" means the means of exit from the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha).

## The Explanation of the Section on Mindfulness of Breathing is Finished.

## The Explanation of the Section on Postures

"Iriyāpathavasena" refers to *iriyā* and *kiriyā*, which are movements or actions. Here, it should be understood as bodily movements. It is called *iriyāpatha* because it is the cause or the path of occurrence of bodily movements. It is the bodily state occurring by way of walking, etc. Indeed, a being performs the actions to be done by the body while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down. It means by way of those postures, or by way of the division of the four postures: walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.

"Puna caparaṃ" means "and again, I shall speak of another meditation subject." The intention is: "I shall speak of another meditation subject of body-contemplation which is additional to the previously mentioned meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing; listen." The words "gacchanto vā" (or when walking), etc., are common to both the mere knowing of walking, etc., and the knowing of the specific material process (rūpa-pavatti) within the movements of walking, etc. Among these two, the mere knowing of walking is not intended here; only the knowing of the specific material process within the movements of walking, etc., is intended. Therefore, to show that specific knowledge in detail, he said "tattha kāmaṃ," etc.

"Sattūpaladdhi" means the perception that "a being exists," the clinging to a being. Because there is the clinging "I walk, my walking," one cannot abandon that view. Because of not being able to abandon the view that a being exists, one cannot discard the perception of self (attā-saññā) which occurs as "there is a self who is the doer and the feeler"...
304:
Because of the absence of an opposing state or because of the lack of cultivation, one cannot abandon or remove the distorted perception. For such a person, how could meditation and so forth occur? With this intention, it is said: "Neither meditation nor the development of the foundations of mindfulness occurs." The phrase "Imassa pana" etc., belongs to the "white side" (the wholesome side), and its meaning should be understood as the opposite of what was previously stated. To clarify that very meaning, the phrase "Idañhi" etc., is stated.

In that context, the question "Who goes?" is an inquiry into the agent of the action of going, without distinguishing the agent from the action. This question has the sense of negating a distinct self (atta) as the agent, by showing that the accomplishment of going is merely a phenomenon (dhamma). The phrase "Whose is the going?" expresses the same meaning in another way. It distinguishes the agent from the action to clarify that there is no agent related to the action of going. The word "kiṃ" (what/who) occurs in both phrases "Ko gacchati?" and "Kassa gamanam?" with the sense of negation implied within. The question "For what reason?" asks for the undistorted cause of the action of going after the agent has been negated. This so-called "going" is a specific mode of the occurrence of phenomena (dhamma) arising from suitable causal conditions, free from false causes such as "the self is joined with the mind, the mind with the senses, and the senses with the self," and so forth. Therefore, "Tattha" etc., is stated.

No being (satta) or person (puggala) goes, because the accomplishment of going is merely a phenomenon, and because there is no one else apart from that phenomenon. Now, to show that the accomplishment of going is merely a phenomenon, "cittakiriyā vāyodhātu vipphārena" etc., is stated. In that context, the mental activity and the expansion or vibration of the air element is called "cittakiriyā-vāyodhātu-vipphāra" (expansion of the air element caused by mental activity). Here, by taking "cittakiriyā" (mental activity), the movement of the inanimate air element is excluded. By taking "vāyodhātu-vipphāra" (expansion of the air element), the mental activity consisting of volition and vocal intimation is excluded. By both together, bodily intimation (kāya-viññatti) is clarified. To show how the conventional term "goes" arises in relation to the body as it proceeds, "Tasmā" etc., is stated. "Taṃ" refers to the mind that arises with the desire to go. "Vāyaṃ janeti" means it produces a group of material qualities (rūpa-kalāpa) in which the air element is predominant. Here, predominance is in terms of capability, not in terms of quantity. With reference to the air element occurring through a specific mode that is the cause for the propping, supporting, and moving of the group of co-nascent material qualities produced by the mind of going, it is said: "The air element produces intimation (viññatti)." Indeed, the specific mode of movement that occurs together with the intention is called intimation. The term "air element" (vāyo) is used only because of the aforementioned predominance of capability, not because the air element alone is the producer. By other means...
305:
The status of intimation-materiality as derived materiality (upādā-rūpa) would be difficult to establish (if it were ineffectual). Moving forward means the proceeding of the body in the forward direction; this moving forward is called "abhikkama."

Having stated it briefly by way of the indication "In the same way," the phrase "Tatrāpi hi" etc., is stated to explain the meaning in detail. "Starting from the edge" means starting from the lowest edge, the soles of the feet. "The state of being lifted up" means the state of being raised high.

"One who knows thus" refers to a yogi who knows that going and so forth occur only through the expansion of the air element caused by mental activity. To make that yogi's conclusion firm, the reflection "It happens thus" is stated. In the world, those who do not know according to reality speak by way of wrong adherence or by way of worldly convention (that a being goes). "Does it exist?" is a question asked by way of one's own investigation. "It does not exist" is a statement of negation of a being by way of a firm conclusion. "Just as," etc., is the clarification of that same meaning by way of a simile, which is easily understood.

"The boat by the force of the wind" means: just as an inanimate boat goes to another place by the force of the wind, and just as an inanimate arrow goes to another place by the force of the bowstring, so too the inanimate body, carried by the mind-born air mentioned above, goes to another place. Thus the comparison with the similes should be understood. If someone should say, "Just as the boat and the arrow go to another place by the power of a man who exerts effort, so too is the body," let it be so. The desired meaning is this: just as the boat and the arrow go by the power of a man who has the characteristic of coordinating them, and not by the power of a man who lacks the characteristic of coordinating them, so too is the body. What loss is there for us? Even more so, the mere state of phenomena (dhamma-mattanā), which is not a person or a being, gains a footing, while the doctrine of a person (purisa-vāda) cannot find a footing. Therefore, "By the power of the machine-strings" (yanta-sutta) etc., is stated.

In that verse, "joined" means the machine of the body coordinated by causal conditions through the modes of going and so forth in the manner stated above. "Stands" means it remains still. "Herein" means in this world. "Without causal conditions" means without causal conditions such as the mind desiring to go and the air element born of that mind. "Who indeed would stand or go?" is how the meaning is connected. Here, the word "kiṃ" (who/what) has the sense of negation. Therefore, by being devoid of causal conditions...
306:
Starting with the rejection of standing and walking as being independent of causal conditions, it should be understood that by demonstrating that the occurrence of all phenomena is dependent on causes, impermanence and suffering are made manifest, just like the emptiness of self.

Paṇihito means that which is produced and established by causes such as the mind and the air element, through various modes like walking and standing. Sabbasaṅgāhikavacanaṃ is a term that collectively encompasses all four postures: walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. Since the postures were previously taught individually, it means that here they are taught collectively. Alternatively, in the first method, the posture was made primary; in that method, the material body was secondary, following as a result. In this second method, the material body is made primary, and the non-primary posture is shown as a result. Thus, the distinction between the two methods should be understood here. Ṭhito means "occurred" (exists).

The discernment of postures is also the discernment of the body that possesses those postures. Because it is a specific state of that body, such as walking, it is said, "By discerning the postures, one dwells contemplating the body in the body." For that reason, in this section on postures, the origin and so on are extracted only in terms of the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha). This method applies to the remaining sections as well. In the word "ādi" (and so on), the four modes are included: seeing the origin of the aggregate of matter by seeing the origin through craving, the origin through kamma, the origin through nutriment, and seeing the origin of the aggregate of matter when seeing the mere characteristic of arising without cause. Similarly, it should be understood that the five modes, such as "due to the cessation of ignorance," are also included. The rest is as previously explained.

## The Explanation of the Section on Postures is finished.

## The Explanation of the Section on the Fourfold Clear Comprehension

By way of the fourfold clear comprehension means: one is "sampajāna" (clearly comprehending) because one knows in all aspects and modes, or knows distinctly and specifically. The state of a clearly comprehending person is "sampajañña" (clear comprehension). It refers to the knowledge that occurs in such a way. Because it is divided into various parts such as the movement of hands, the four types of clear comprehension brought together are called "catusampajañña." One contemplates by way of those four types of clear comprehension. Since the terms "abhikkante" (in going forward) and so on have already been explained in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, they will not be explained again. Therefore, the clarification of the hidden meanings in those respective explanations should be taken according to the method shown in the sub-commentary (ṭīkā) of that Sāmaññaphala Sutta. Because of the words, "In going forward and in returning, he acts with clear comprehension," and so on, it is intended here that by discerning the four types of clear comprehension in going forward and so on, one contemplates the nature of the arising of the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) alone. Thus, it is said, "The arising and passing away of the aggregate of matter alone..."
308:
Jīvanako refers to one who slaughters cows for a livelihood. Vinivijjhitvā means piercing through or separating at a single place. The place described as the center of the great roads is called the center because it is the location where four great roads intersect in such a manner. Because those four great roads come from the four directions and meet there as if unified, that place is called a four-way crossroads (catumahāpatha); at that four-way crossroads (as if standing).

The word 'ṭhita' (standing), in Pali passages such as 'ṭhito vā' (or standing), indicates being endowed with the posture known as standing; or, because the root ṭhā has the meaning of ceasing from movement, it indicates being endowed with the remaining postures, excluding walking, in other contexts. However, in this context, because it is intended to show the mode of occurrence of the material body, the teacher said, 'Because it is situated in any one of the four postures, it is yathāṭhitaṃ (as it is situated).' In that phrase, 'by way of mode' means by way of the mode of occurrence of the material body, such as standing. It has already been stated that standing and so on are called 'postures' (iriyāpatha) because they are the path of occurrence for the activity known as posture.

Yathāṭhitaṃ means as it occurs; since the aforementioned standing itself is intended here as the positioning (paṇidhāna), it was said, 'both as it is situated and as it is positioned.' Alternatively, 'ṭhita' shows the connection with the posture known as standing, while 'paṇihita' shows the connection with other postures. Or, 'ṭhita' shows the firm persistence of the material phenomena known as the body in each moment by way of their own function, while 'paṇihita' means placed in various ways by way of their respective conditions; thus should the meaning be understood. Paccavekkhati means he reflects repeatedly; he sees each part separately, having distinguished them with the eye of wisdom.

Now, to clarify the meaning already stated by way of explaining the essence, the passage beginning with 'Just as a butcher' (yathā goghātakassa) was said. In that phrase, 'to one who raises' means to one who nourishes the cow with rice-bran, cooked rice, cotton seeds, etc., to increase the growth of flesh. 'Killed and dead' means dead after being harmed. 'Dead' also means just recently dead. Therefore, it was said, 'at that very moment.' 'The perception of a cow does not disappear' means that because the major and minor limbs are still situated as they were, the designation 'cow' remains even in a recently dead cow as long as the arrangement of those limbs is not destroyed.

'Vilīyanti' means they perish or are divided; thus they are called 'bīlā' (portions), by changing the letter 'v' to 'b' and 'i' to 'ī'. 'Bīlaso' means having made them portion by portion. 'Having divided' means having separated the flesh from the mass of bones, or having made the flesh so separated into portions. Therefore, it was said, 'the perception of meat arises.' This also applies to a monk who has not yet grasped the meditation subject. 'Ghana-vinibbhoga' means the breaking down or separation of the compactness of continuity (santati-ghana), the compactness of group (samūha-ghana), and the compactness of function (kicca-ghana).
309:
"Contemplating by way of elements" refers to a yogi who contemplates by separating each element, such as the earth element, by breaking down the compactness. "Perception of a being" refers to the perception of a being that occurs by the power of the view of self (atta-diṭṭhi), so the teachers say. It is also appropriate that the perception of a being that occurs by way of worldly convention disappears at that time, because of the accomplishment of the breaking down of compactness according to reality. Only when it is so does the meaning of the object of comparison (upameyya) truly coincide and agree with the meaning of the aforementioned simile. Therefore, it was said, "The mind becomes established only by way of the elements."

"Skilled" means one who is expert in the respective names of the parts. This is because he understands: "As long as the cow is as it was born, with its neck, tail, hooves, horns, etc., and the collection of parts like bones and flesh is not divided, the designation 'cow' exists; it does not exist when divided. When divided, there are only the designations of parts like 'bones' and 'flesh'."

The four postures like the four great crossroads refers to the fourfold postures which are the path of occurrence for the body, just like the four great crossroads where the butcher stands. This should be understood as explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga and its commentary. The remaining words are to be understood in the same manner as already stated.

## The Explanation of the Section on Attention to Elements is Finished.

## Explanation of the Section on the Nine Cemetery Contemplations

The words occurring in sections related to the bloated corpses, etc., discarded in the cemetery, and the parts of the foulness (asubha) such as bloatedness which are the meanings expressed by those words, were given the designation "Sivathikapabba" (Cemetery Sections) by the Elders who performed the Recitation (Saṅgītikāra). Therefore, it was said, "to divide by way of the cemetery sections."

A corpse that has passed one day after death is called "ekāhamata" (dead for one day). "After the end of life" means beyond the end of life, the period after death. "Samuggata" means having risen or become bloated. "Uddhumāta" means becoming swollen and bloated upwards after death.

A bluish-black corpse mixed with white and red colors is called "vinīla". Or, a bluish-black color that is a transformation of the original color is "vinīla". "Vinīla" itself is called "vinīlaka" by adding the letter 'ka' to lengthen the word without a difference in meaning, just as in "pītaka" and "lohitaka". Alternatively, this letter 'ka' is said to show the meaning of loathsomeness, to indicate "the loathsome bluish-black color," because it is disgusting. For example, as in "An evil (pāpaka) reputation spreads."

A corpse with pus trickling from places torn by crows, vultures, etc., is called "vissandamānapubba". It means pus is oozing and trickling here and there. "Tathābhāvaṃ" means reaching the state of oozing pus.
310:
"That monk" refers to the monk mentioned in the phrase, "one should see a body cast away in a cemetery." That monk compares his own body to the state of that corpse. The words beginning with "Ayampi kho" show the manner of comparison. "Life" (āyu) refers to the physical life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya). As for the mental life-faculty (nāma-jīvitindriya), in this context, it follows the course of consciousness. "Heat" (usmā) refers to the fire element born of kamma (kammaja-tejo). In this way, it is of a nature that is extremely foul-smelling, loathsome, disgusting, and putrid. The meaning is that it is not just a slight nature as when life and so on have not yet departed. "It will be of such a nature" means it will become so through various states such as bloating (uddhūmātaka); thus it is said, "evaṃ uddhūmātādibhedo bhavissati."

"Luñcitvā luñcitvā" means tearing and pulling apart. "Sāvasesamaṃsalohitayuttaṃ" means being joined with flesh and blood that remains here and there because it has not been entirely devoured. By the Pali "aññena hatthaṭṭhikaṃ," the Buddha wished to show the scattered state of hand-bones and so on without distinction; thus, desiring to show their being scattered without remainder, he said "catusaṭṭhibhedampi" and so on.

"Terovassikāni" refers to bones that have reached a period of more than a year. Because those bones have passed a year, they are called "atikkantasaṃvaccharāni." The state of being crumbled into powder due to the loss of solidity through old age and decay is here called "putrefaction" (pūtibhāva). Desiring to show how that putrefaction occurs, he said "abbhokāse" and so on. "Terovassikāneva" means they have indeed passed the measure of one year. Because the second cemetery section and others are defined by the way they are devoured by crows, vultures, and so on, it is said, "khajjamānatādīnaṃ vasena yojanā kātabbā."

## The Explanation of the Nine Cemetery Sections is Finished.

In the phrase "imāneva dve," the restriction with the word "eva" (only) is because there is no attainment meditation (appanā-kammaṭṭhāna) in the other sections; thus, attainment meditation is restricted only to these two sections (mindfulness of breathing and reflection on repulsiveness). Where the word "eva" follows a term, it restricts it from others. However, even with such restriction, it should be understood that the status of these two sections as insight meditation (vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna) is not prohibited, as one observes impermanence and so on. Because the cemetery sections clearly show the danger in conditioned things (saṅkhāra), it is said, "sīvathikānaṃ ādīnavānupassanāvasena vuttattā." Since it is well-known that the remaining twelve sections, such as the section on postures, can lead to attainment, it is said, "sesāni dvādasapi." Whatever is not explained by way of meaning in this chapter is easily understood.

## The Explanation of the Contemplation of the Body is Finished.
311:
## Explanation of the Contemplation of Feeling
In the phrase "sukhaṃ vedanaṃ," it is called 'sukha' (pleasant) because it causes ease. The meaning is that it produces a pleasurable taste in the associated states and the physical body. Alternatively, it is called 'sukha' because it well consumes or digs up physical and mental painful affliction. Others say, "It is called 'sukha' because the giving of opportunity for this feeling is easily done." It is called 'vedanā' (feeling) because it experiences the flavor of the object. "Vedayamāno" means experiencing (the one who is experiencing). In the phrases beginning with "kāmaṃ," what should be said is exactly as explained in the section on postures. Experiencing while knowing in every way is called 'sampajāna-vediyana'.

"Vatthu-ārammaṇa" refers to objects such as visible forms. Here, objects like visible forms are intended as "vatthu" (basis) because they are the place where feeling arises. "Assa" means it should be. Since there is no experiencer (agent) apart from the phenomena, he said, "Feeling alone feels," desiring to show that only the phenomenon is the agent. By the words "vohāramattaṃ hoti," he shows that saying "experiencing a pleasant feeling, I experience a pleasant feeling" is merely a worldly convention.

"Nitthunanto" means groaning by way of giving vent to that feeling, having seen the danger in suppressing the force of powerful feeling. Because very great suffering arises when the force is restrained, it could produce other distortions; therefore, that Elder rolled to and fro. "Vīriyasamathaṃ yojetvā" means, because the energy of endurance was excessive, he balanced energy and concentration by reducing that energy to a state where it had a function equal to concentration. "Saha paṭisambhidāhi" means together with the supramundane analytical insights. In the moment of the Noble Path, the analytical insights are attained by way of non-delusion; however, the analytical insight of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā) can also be attained by way of making it an object. Alternatively, he said "saha paṭisambhidāhi" referring to the mastery in those analytical insights at the time of their arising even for mundane states. "Samasīsī" means being one who attains the end of defilements and life simultaneously (vāra-samasīsī), meaning he attained Parinibbāna in the stage immediately following the stage of reviewing.

Just as it was said regarding experiencing with full awareness in the case of pleasant feeling, such as "Who experiences pleasant feeling?", the same is said for painful feeling. In that context, it is called 'dukkha' (painful) because it causes suffering. The meaning is that it hurts and oppresses the associated states and the body. Alternatively, it is called 'dukkha' because it badly consumes or digs up physical and mental pleasure. Others say, "It is called 'dukkha' because the giving of opportunity for this feeling is difficult to do." "Arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna" means the discernment of the non-material (mentality), the entry into insight by way of non-material phenomena. Because contact and consciousness have unmanifest characteristics, they are not clear. Therefore, he said, "It appears like darkness." Regarding the phrase "na pākaṭaṃ hoti"...
312:
This statement is made with reference to such a person (for whom contact and consciousness are not prominent); for those individuals, at the beginning, only feeling (vedanā) arises more prominently. In this way, it is consistent and not contradictory with the statement in the commentary on the Sakkapañha Sutta and others, which says, "Contact is prominent, consciousness is prominent." The construction should be understood as: the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) taught by way of feeling is prominent. The phrase "because of the prominence of the arising of feelings" is spoken by way of pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) and painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā). Only the occurrence of those pleasant and painful feelings is gross and prominent; the occurrence of the other (neither-painful-nor-pleasant) feeling is not gross (not prominent). Alternatively, because the occurrence of the other feeling is also indeed prominent to the wise by way of taking those two types (pleasant and painful), it should be understood that the term "of feelings" is taken generally without specification. It should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Sakkapañha Sutta; therefore, the specific meaning stated in that Sutta should be taken according to the method stated in the Līnatthappakāsanī.

Previously, it was stated how one perceives the dependence of feeling on an object and its non-self nature, saying, "Depending on the base and object, only feeling feels." Now, wishing to show the perception of its impermanence and so on, he says, "This is another method of perception." Just as two consciousnesses cannot occur simultaneously in a single moment, two types of feelings also cannot occur at the same time because they occur with distinct objects; thus he says, "Because of the absence of painful feeling at the moment of pleasant feeling." This is merely an illustration; it is because at that time, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (upekkhā-vedanā) is also absent. Therefore, by perceiving the absence after having occurred of other feelings that existed before the moment of pleasant feeling, the absence after having occurred of the pleasant feeling itself is also known. Wishing to show the prominence of that pleasant feeling, he says, "Because this pleasant feeling did not exist before this (moment of occurrence)." By this statement, it should be understood that the prominence of those other feelings is also shown. Therefore, he says, "Feeling is indeed impermanent, unstable, and subject to change." By the term 'impermanent' (anicca), the nature of destruction of feelings is shown, because impermanence is easily understood in destruction. By the term 'unstable' (adhruva), the nature of prominence is shown, because it shows the nature of not existing forever. By the term 'subject to change' (vipariṇāma), the nature of suffering (dukkha) is shown, because it indicates transformation into another state. By that term 'vipariṇāma', if even pleasant feeling is suffering, there is no need to mention that other feelings are suffering; thus the nature of suffering of all three feelings is shown. In this way, it should be understood that the perception of the three characteristics in all three feelings is illuminated, as in "Whatever is impermanent is suffering; whatever is suffering is certainly non-self." Therefore, he says, "Thus, one is clearly comprehending in that feeling."
313:
Now, in order to establish that meaning by the Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 2.205), he says "This too has been said," and so on. In that Sutta, "at that time, one does not feel a painful feeling" means that at the time when one is endowed with that pleasant feeling, one does not feel a painful feeling because the past painful feeling has ceased and the future painful feeling has not yet arisen, respectively. As for the impossibility of present feelings [occurring simultaneously], it has already been stated.

They are called impermanent (anicca) because they exist only for the moment of performing their own function. They are called conditioned (saṅkhata) because they are produced and prepared by a combination of causes. They are called dependently arisen (paṭiccasamuppanna) because they arise depending on causes such as the base and the object. They should be understood as subject to exhaustion (khayadhamma), subject to passing away (vayadhamma), subject to fading away (virāgadhamma), and subject to cessation (nirodhadhamma) because their nature is to be exhausted, to pass away, to break up, and to cease.

Because they are to be touched by defilements, the five cords of sensual pleasure are called 'carnal' (āmisa). Because it occurs together with those carnal things by way of making them an object, it is called 'with carnal' (sāmisa). Therefore, he says, "dependent on the carnal things which are the five cords of sensual pleasure."

Regarding the text from here onwards, with reference to the Pali starting with "There is feeling," he says, "It is in the same manner as stated in the Contemplation of the Body."

## The Explanation of the Contemplation of Feeling is Finished.

## Explanation of the Contemplation of the Mind

It is called 'with lust' (sarāga) because it occurs together with lust by way of association (sampayoga). Therefore, he says, "associated with greed (lobha)." In this term 'without lust' (vītarāga), although it should certainly be the opposite of the term 'with lust', because the scope of investigation (sammasana) is intended, only the consciousness belonging to the three planes should be taken; thus he says, "mundane wholesome and indeterminate," and explains that very intention with "But this..." and so on.

As for the remaining four unwholesome consciousnesses—the two rooted in hatred and the two rooted in delusion—they are not 'with lust' because they are not associated with lust. However, because they can arise due to that lust, they are also not 'without lust' at the time they are accompanied by it. Therefore, since they are only found to be free from the two dyads (of with lust and without lust) in this context, he says, "They belong neither to the former term nor to the latter term." If it is so, does it not lead to a partial understanding? No, it does not, because those consciousnesses are included in other dyads.

Some teachers, however, desire that "when the state of being an opposite is not taken, the mere absence of association is the standard here, as in the case of some indeterminate states." According to the view of those teachers, the remaining unwholesome consciousnesses should also be understood as included in the second term (without lust).
314:
It should be understood. In the second dyad as well, the meaning should be understood according to the method already mentioned.

Among the unwholesome roots, the mind called "with delusion" (samoha), because it occurs only together with delusion, refers to the "mind accompanied by doubt and the mind accompanied by restlessness." Why is this? Because in these unwholesome roots, the restriction (avadhāraṇa) in the previous term—"it is called samoha because it occurs only together with delusion"—is also obtainable; therefore, it is said "Yasmā pana" and so forth. However, because it is said to be a "deluded mind" (momūhacitta) due to being extremely bewildered and having a distinct type of delusion according to the way it occurs in specific individuals, the two minds accompanied by doubt and restlessness are specifically called "with delusion" (samoha), whereas the remaining unwholesome minds are not called so. Therefore, he speaks with a sense of doubt, saying "they indeed occur."

It is called "followed by sloth and torpor" (thinamiddhānupatita) because it is followed by sloth and torpor by way of association. The five types of prompted (sasaṅkhārika) unwholesome minds are called "shrunken mind" (saṅkucitacitta). A shrunken mind is so called because it occurs by way of shrinking in relation to the object. It is called "mind accompanied by restlessness" (uddhaccasahagata) because it is mixed and occurs together with restlessness that has become powerful by way of a specific cause; otherwise, all unwholesome minds would be accompanied by restlessness. It is called "scattered mind" (pasaṭacitta) because it occurs in a state of being spread out by way of a specific distraction regarding the object.

It is called "exalted" (mahaggata) because it has reached a great state due to its ability to suppress the defilements, its abundant results, and its long continuity; or because it is practiced with great and noble desire (chanda) and so forth. That exalted mind occurs in the fine-material and immaterial spheres, for there is nothing greater than that in the world. Therefore, it is said to be "of the fine-material and immaterial spheres." Since the opposite of this term "exalted" is only the limited (paritta), it is said that "the unexalted (amahaggata) refers to the sense sphere."

It is called "surpassable" (sauttara) because it occurs with states nobler than itself that are capable of surpassing it. It is called "unsurpassable" (anuttara) because it is the opposite of that. Both should be understood by comparing one with the other; thus it is said, "the surpassable refers to the sense sphere," and so forth. It is called "concentrated" (samāhita) because it is well-placed on the object by means of concentration capable of suppressing the opposing defilements. Therefore, it is said "yassa" and so forth. "Yassa" means "of which mind." It is called "unconcentrated" (asamāhita) because it is not well-placed on the object by the aforementioned concentration. Therefore, it is said to be "devoid of both types of concentration (access and absorption)."

Referring to both the sense-sphere wholesome mind liberated by "liberation by substitution of opposites" (tadaṅgavimutti) and the exalted mind liberated by "liberation by suppression" (vikkhambhanavimutti), it is said: "the mind liberated by liberation by substitution of opposites and liberation by suppression." If one considers that a mind where these two types of liberation are absent is a mind "devoid of both types of liberation," there might be doubt regarding the supramundane mind. To remove that doubt, it is said: "there is no opportunity for the occurrence of liberations such as liberation by destruction (samuccheda), etc." The absence of opportunity should be understood because the range of the investigation of insight (sammasanavipassanā) is intended here. What is not explained here in terms of meaning is quite clear, as it follows the method already mentioned below.

## The Explanation of the Contemplation of the Mind is finished.
315:
## Contemplation of Phenomena
## Explanation of the Section on Hindrances

By way of showing the classification of things to be abandoned and so forth, the contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanā) is indicated in five ways; since this meaning can be understood from the Pali text itself, he said, "to teach the contemplation of phenomena in five ways," extracting that meaning. If it is indicated in five ways by way of showing things to be abandoned, why is it indicated only by way of the hindrances and so forth? It is indicated according to the inclinations of those to be led (veneyya). For those to be led who should first be taught the hindrances by way of classification among the things to be abandoned, the Blessed One first taught the contemplation of phenomena regarding the hindrances in this sutta.

Accordingly, the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) was also taught as being preceded by tranquility (samatha). Thereafter, the higher teaching was given regarding the five aggregates which should be fully understood, the bases (āyatana), the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) which should be developed, and the four truths which have divisions such as things to be fully understood. Therefore, in this sutta, tranquility meditation (samatha-bhāvanā) is also desired only for the sake of insight (vipassanā). The teaching of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) has insight as its primary focus and insight as its culmination. To clarify that it is taught by way of classifying the application of insight in that Satipaṭṭhāna teaching, he said "Api ca" and so forth.

In that context, it should be noted that the teaching of the mixed grasp (of phenomena) is by way of the aggregates, bases, and the truth of suffering. In the phrase "the grasping of the aggregates of perception and mental formations as well," the word "api" (as well) includes the grasping of all five aggregates of clinging, because the other aggregates are included within those five aggregates of clinging.

When it is known that "there is no yoking together of dark unwholesome states and bright wholesome states," because of the absence of those states, it is said "by way of frequent occurrence." "Existing" (saṃvijjamānaṃ) means that which is obtained within one's own continuity (such as sensual desire). "As" (yathā) means in whatever manner it occurs. Since it is said that "the arising of sensual desire occurs," that manner is indeed the cause of sensual desire; because in meaning it is just the cause, he said "by whatever cause." The word "ca" (and) has the sense of aggregating the meaning that will be spoken.

In that context, "tatthā" refers to the word mentioned as "yathā ca" and so forth. "Subhampi" means sensual desire is also (called the sign of beauty). Indeed, that sensual desire is called "beauty" (subha) by way of its own manner of grasping, and it is also called a "sign" (nimitta) because it is the cause for another sensual desire occurring in that manner. An object such as a visible form which is desirable by nature, or is grasped as being desirable, is called an "attractive object" (subhārammaṇa). Attention that is not a means for attaining the desired welfare and happiness is called "unskilful attention" (anupāya-manasikāra). By that term, unwise attention (ayonisomanasikāra) is meant. "Tattha" (therein) refers to the two types of signs of beauty: those by nature and those by way of the object. It is called "nutriment" (āhāra) because it brings about its own fruit, meaning it is a cause.
316:
"Asubha" (impurity) refers to "asubha-jhāna" by dropping the latter part of the word. This asubha-jhāna should be understood as occurring in the ten types of inanimate impurities and in animate impurities such as hair and so forth. In the Girimānanda Sutta, the perception regarding hair and so forth is called "asubha-saññā" (perception of impurity). Here, the mention of the four types of unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) and wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) is intended to show them without omission. However, in this context, the attention directed towards these impurities as "beautiful" (subha) or "not beautiful" (asubha) is what is intended. Other types of attention occur in accordance with this attention to beauty or impurity.

Learning the aspect of loathsomeness in the eleven types of impurities, or practicing in such a way that the learning sign (uggaha-nimitta) arises therein, is called "learning the sign of impurity." Repeatedly practicing asubha-bhāvanā, which can lead to access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and attainment concentration (appanā-samādhi), is called "devotion to the development of impurity."

Teachers say, "For one who knows the measure in food and eats moderately, sensual desire (kāmacchanda) is abandoned without finding an entrance because of the absence of being overcome by sloth and torpor (thina-middha)." This same meaning is also stated in the Niddesa. One who well knows the loathsomeness of food, its transformation, its basis, the extreme loathsomeness of the body which is its support, and how the body exists only because of nutriment—such a person is called "one who knows the measure in food" by knowing the limit in food in every way. For such a person, sensual desire is indeed abandoned.

The Elder Tissa, who practiced asubha meditation, was one who saw the teeth-bone as an impurity. "Pahīnassa" refers to sensual desire that has been abandoned by way of suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna). In other similar instances that follow, the same method should be understood. According to the Abhidhamma method, since all greed (lobha) is called the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa), it is said to be "abandoned by the path of Arahantship."

Former aversion (paṭigha) is called "paṭigha-nimitta" because it is the cause for aversion that will arise later.

One is called "mitta" (friend) because of being affectionate; it refers to a person who desires the welfare of others. The desire for welfare occurring in that friend or belonging to that friend is called "mettā" (loving-kindness). Since the word "mettā" is a general term, it can apply to both attainment (appanā) and access (upacāra). However, when "ceto-vimutti" (liberation of mind) is mentioned, only attainment should be taken, because before reaching attainment, there is no complete liberation from the opposite state, ill-will (byāpāda). "Taṃ" refers to wise attention (yoniso manasikāra). "Tattha" refers to being in loving-kindness. For one who frequently develops (loving-kindness), ill-will is abandoned.
317:
The arising and occurrence of the development of loving-kindness and the offering of welfare towards beings is called "learning the sign of loving-kindness" (uggaha). The initial wise attention to loving-kindness is itself the "sign of loving-kindness" because it is the cause for the loving-kindness that will arise later. Beings have kamma as their own property; this state is called "kamma-ssakatā" (ownership of kamma) and "kamma-dāyādatā" (heirship of kamma). Investigating and reflecting on the faults and benefits of ill-will and loving-kindness as they truly are is called "paṭisaṅkhāna" (reflection) here. Having a good friend who dwells in loving-kindness is called "kalyāṇa-mittatā" (good friendship) here.

Radiating (loving-kindness) specifically towards oneself, a very dear person, a neutral person, and an enemy is called "odisaka" (specified radiation). Radiating by breaking down the barriers between beings is called "anodisaka" (unspecified radiation). Radiating towards each direction is called "disā-pharaṇa" (directional radiation). These points should be understood in the learning of loving-kindness. Alternatively, radiating with reference to a monastery, a road, or a village is "odisaka-disā-pharaṇa." Radiating according to directions like the East without specific reference to a monastery etc., is "anodisaka-disā-pharaṇa." With reference to these two types of learning, it is said "odisaka-anodisaka-disā-pharaṇānaṃ." This learning (uggaha) should be understood as reaching up to access concentration (upacāra). The repeated cultivation of the learned loving-kindness is called "bhāvanā" (development).

Therein, unspecified (anodisaka) radiation of loving-kindness is of 20 types, occurring through the 5 categories of beings (satta), breathing things (pāṇa), creatures (bhūta), persons (puggala), and individuals (attabhāva-pariyāpanna), and through the 4 modes for each: "May they be free from enmity, free from mental suffering, free from physical suffering, and may they maintain themselves happily." Specified (odhiso) radiation of loving-kindness should be understood as follows: 7 types through the 7 groups of women, men, noble ones, ordinary persons, deities, humans, and those in states of deprivation (vinipātikā) (or 28 types when multiplied by the 4 modes); 10 types through the 10 directions; and 480 types when the 5 categories of beings and 7 groups like women etc., are multiplied by the 4 modes like "free from enmity" etc., for each direction. These varieties of specified radiation of loving-kindness should be understood.

The unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) by which discontent (arati) and so forth arise is called "unwise attention regarding discontent etc." In the following terms like "ārambha-dhātu" (element of initiative), it should be understood in the same way. Discontent in secluded monasteries or in superior wholesome states is called "ukkaṇṭhitā" (boredom/dissatisfaction). Bending the body in an ungraceful manner is "kāya-vinamanā." A shrunken or sluggish state is "līnākāra" (sluggishness).

Effort that occurs through the element of initiative (ārambha-dhātu) etc., because of its nature of initiating the practice of wholesome states and its nature of drying up opposing states, is called "paṭhamārambha-viriya" (initial effort). Because mere initial effort cannot destroy laziness or reach higher states, it is said "kosajja... balārambha."
318:
In the initial effort (ārambhadhātu), which is merely the beginning of exertion, there is no power to destroy laziness or to reach higher states. Therefore, it is said, "Because of emerging from laziness, it has more power than that initial effort (ārambhadhātu)." Furthermore, the effort called striving (parakkama), through repeated and successive occurrence, gains the quality of cultivation and, bringing about distinction in higher stages, reaches extreme power. Therefore, it is said, "Because of being able to step onto successive stages, it has more power even than that exertion (nikkamadhātu)."

"Taking up the sign in overeating" (atibhojane nimittaggāho) means taking up the sign of sloth and torpor (thina-middha) in eating excessively. The meaning is that one notes the cause or non-cause of sloth and torpor, thinking, "If I eat this much food, it will be a cause for sloth and torpor; if I eat this much, it will not be." This statement is made by way of negation (vyatireka). Therefore, it should be understood that by saying, "If I eat this much, that food will not be a cause for sloth and torpor," moderation in eating (mattaññutā) is also shown by implication. Thus, it is said, "Four or five [mouthfuls]... does not occur."

"The light of the sun by day" (divā sūriyālokaṃ) means that the meaning should be understood thus: even for one who reflects at night on the light of the sun as perceived during the day, sloth and torpor can be dispelled. Because ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) are based on energy (vīriya), it is said, "also by suitable talk connected with the ascetic practices."

Remorse (kukkucca) also, occurring by way of grieving over what has been done and what has been left undone, has the same characteristic as restlessness (uddhacca) because it brings about lack of peace in the mind. Therefore, it is said, "Lack of peace (avūpasama) is the state of being unpeaceful; in essence, this is just restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca)."

For one of great learning (bāhusutta) who investigates the Suttas and so forth by way of text and meaning, and who dwells frequently in that practice, distraction does not occur because of the attainment of the knowledge of the meaning and so forth. Due to practicing according to the rules and applying appropriate remedies, there is no more grieving over what was done or not done. Therefore, it is said, "By great learning (bāhusacca) also... restlessness and remorse are abandoned." Just as restlessness and remorse are abandoned by great learning to such an extent, it should be understood that they are also abandoned to that same extent by frequent questioning and by being one who knows the nature of the Vinaya. Furthermore, attending on elders is said to be a cause for abandoning restlessness and remorse because it brings about the practice of great virtue and produces peace of mind. However, it should be understood that masters of the Vinaya (vinayadhara) who can dispel remorse regardless of their age are also called spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitta). Since distraction for monks is mostly caused by remorse, questioning and so forth are pointed out according to the method of the Vinaya, starting with "for one who frequently questions about what is allowable and what is not."

In the phrase "when restlessness and remorse are abandoned" (pahīne uddhaccakukkuce), the locative case is used in the sense of specification (niddhāraṇa). Because remorse is associated with displeasure (domanassa), its future non-arising through the path of non-returning (anāgāmimagga) is stated.
319:
Doubt (vicikicchā) stays or occurs in this [state], therefore it is called a ground (ṭhānī). Things that are the grounds for doubt are vicikicchāṭhānīyā; they are the things that are the causes of doubt. Or, it stays, therefore it is called a ground; doubt is the ground of this, thus it is vicikicchāṭhānīya. In terms of meaning, it is just doubt itself. For that doubt which arose previously is the uncommon cause for the doubt that arises later, by being a cause of the same kind.

Regarding "wholesome and unwholesome" (kusalākusala): they are called wholesome (kusala) because they are produced by wisdom (kosalla); they are called unwholesome (akusala) because they are the opposite of that. Those which are unwholesome are blameworthy, not to be cultivated, and inferior. Those which are wholesome are blameless, to be cultivated, and superior. Or, wholesome states are inferior if undertaken with inferior desire (chanda) and so forth, and superior if undertaken with superior [desire and so forth]. "Dark" (kaṇhā) means dark states because they make the mind lack radiance. "Bright" (sukkā) means white states because they make the mind radiant. Or, they are called dark because they are the cause of a dark rebirth; they are called bright because they are the cause of a bright rebirth. These very states have their counterparts. Dark states have bright states as their counterparts because they are direct opposites; likewise, bright states have the others as their counterparts. Alternatively, dark, bright, and their counterparts are called kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgā. Just as pleasant feeling is the counterpart of painful feeling, and painful feeling is the counterpart of pleasant feeling.

Indeed, through great learning and questioning, all eightfold doubt is abandoned; nevertheless, because the remaining doubts have their root in doubt regarding the Three Jewels, it is said, "referring to the Three Jewels." When the qualities of the Three Jewels are realized, doubt such as "he doubts the Teacher" cannot occur. Knowing the nature of the Vinaya is said to abandon the doubt stated as "he doubts the training (sikkhā)," hence it is said, "also for one who has mastery through practice in the Vinaya."

"For one who is full of resolution (adhimokkha) known as conviction-based faith (okappanīyasaddhā)" means the state of one who has much resolution and decision through the resolution known as faith that enters into the object worthy of faith; it should be understood that resolution is just the production of adhimokkha. Or, adhimokkha is the resolution that is the leaning or inclining through faith.

"Arising and passing away" (samudayavaya) means states that have the nature of arising and passing away. In the phrase "in the sign of beauty, the sign of foulness, etc." (subhanimitta-asubhanimittādīsu), the word "etc." (ādi) should be applied to each term: "in the sign of beauty, etc., in the sign of foulness, etc." There, by the first "etc.," the sign of resistance (paṭighanimitta) and so forth are included; by the second, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (mettācetovimutti) and so forth are included. Whatever else remains to be said here has already been stated in the manner mentioned before.

## The explanation of the section on hindrances is finished.
320:
## Explanation of the Section on Aggregates
The aggregates that are clung to by means of making them objects of clinging and so forth, or those that are the products of clinging, are called the aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā).

In the phrase "iti rūpaṃ," the word "iti" is used with the same meaning as "idaṃ" (this), thus it means "This is form." This word, by way of encompassing the specific nature, implies an exhaustive inclusion; hence it is said, "Form is only this much; there is no form beyond this." Alternatively, "iti" is an indeclinable used in the sense of variety (manner). Therefore, by the phrase "iti rūpaṃ," it shows the exhaustive inclusion of all varieties of form, such as primary form (bhūta-rūpa) and derived form (upādā-rūpa). The phrase "by way of its nature" means by way of the nature of being deformed (ruppana-sabhāva), and by way of the nature of the eye-sensitivity, color, and so forth. Regarding feeling and the others, it should be applied in the same way: "This is feeling; feeling is only this much; there is no feeling beyond this; he understands feeling by way of its nature," and so forth. "By way of its nature" here should be applied as "by way of the nature of experiencing, and by way of the nature of being pleasant," and so forth. The remaining parts are easy to understand as they follow the method already described.

## The Explanation of the Section on Aggregates Ends.

## Explanation of the Section on Sense Bases
In the phrase "in the six internal and external [bases]," the word "six" should be applied to each (i.e., six internal and six external). Why are both of these taught as only six? It is because of the determination of the doors and objects for the arising of the six classes of consciousness. For the class of consciousness included in the eye-consciousness cognitive process, the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) alone is the door of arising, and the form-base (rūpāyatana) alone is the object. Likewise, for the others, their respective doors and objects apply. For the sixth, the mind-consciousness, a part of the mind-base (manāyatana) known as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is the door of arising, and the mental-object base (dhammāyatana), which is not shared with others, is the object.

It is called the eye (cakkhu) because it enjoys or manifests; the meaning is that it enjoys and manifests the form-object. It is called the ear (sota) because it hears. It is called the nose (ghāna) because it smells. Taste-object is called "jīvita" (life) because it is the cause of life; it is called the tongue (jivhā) because it calls out that life. It is called the body (kāya) because it is the place of origin for the loathsome states associated with the taints (āsava). It is called the mind (mano) because it knows the object. It is called form (rūpa) because, while undergoing change in color, it manifests the state of what has reached the heart. It is called sound (sadda) because it is brought by its own conditions and is made to reach the state of being cognizable by ear-consciousness. It is called smell (gandha) because it indicates its own foundation; therefore...
321:
...smell (gandha). It is called taste (rasa) because beings enjoy it. It is called the tangible (phoṭṭhabba) because it is touched. They are called mental objects (dhammā) because they bear their own nature. All twelve, such as the eye-base, are called sense bases (āyatana) in the sense of expanding the mind and mental factors that occur in the doors and objects. This is a summary of the explanation of the section on sense bases; the details should be understood according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga commentary.

In the passage "he understands the eye," the term "eye" refers only to the sensitive eye (cakkhu-pasāda), not the physical eye-ball (sasambhāra-cakkhu), nor the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) and so forth. Thus, the teachers said "eye-sensitivity" (cakkhu-pasāda). Referring to this eye-sensitivity, the Blessed One taught: "That eye which is the sensitivity derived from the four great elements." The word "ca" (and) has the sense of aggregating the meaning that will be stated later. "By way of true function and characteristic" means understanding by way of one's own true function (rasa) and characteristic. The meaning is: by way of the function of pulling in the forms, and by way of the characteristic of sensitivity of the elements capable of being struck by forms, and by way of the characteristic of sensitivity produced by karma rooted in the desire to see. Alternatively, "by way of true function and characteristic" means by way of true function and by way of characteristic; "true function" should be understood as the unerring nature. That nature is called "rasa" (function/taste) because it is tasted, enjoyed, and delighted in by way of unerring penetration; therefore, it means "by way of its own characteristic" (salakkhaṇa). "By way of characteristic" means by way of general characteristics (sāmaṇya-lakkhaṇa) such as impermanence.

In passages such as "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises," the use of the plural "forms" (rūpe) is to clarify the meaning that only the collection of form-bases is the cause for the arising of eye-consciousness, not each one separately. According to that same method of teaching, it is also said here, "he understands the forms." However, because they are similar in the nature of form, taking them all together, the meaning should be interpreted in the singular as "the form produced by the four causes that is external." "By way of its own function and characteristic" should be applied as: by way of the function of being the object of eye-consciousness, and by way of the characteristic of being struck in the eye.

"Dependent on both" means dependent on the eye, which is a condition by way of the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya), and on forms, which are conditions by way of the object-predominance and object-decisive support conditions. Although this is a commentary on the Suttas, what is called a direct discourse (nippariyāya-kathā) must rely on the Abhidhamma; therefore, showing the fetters according to the Abhidhamma method, it is said: "sensual lust (kāmarāga)... pe..." Attachment to the objects of sensual pleasure is called sensual lust. That sensual lust itself is called a fetter (saṃyojana) in the sense of binding. That state binds the person in whom it arises to the suffering of the round of rebirths. It is called a fetter because it binds the being to suffering, the resultant (vipāka) to new existences, and the resultant to the causal karma. In this way, the cause and meaning of the fetter of aversion (paṭigha-saṃyojana) and so forth should be understood as appropriate. Another meaning is: in this context, "by way of its own function and characteristic" should be applied as: by way of its function of not releasing the being from the suffering of the round, and by way of its characteristic of binding inseparably. To exclude attachment to existence and views, the word "kāma" (sensual) is used to take attachment to sensual pleasures. "Greatly delighting" means occurring together with rapture (pīti).
322:
The teacher says "Avijjāsaṃyojanaṃ" (the fetter of ignorance). Among those ten fetters, attachment to the objects of sensual pleasure, and because it is a state that both desires and is the desire itself, it is called "Kāmarāga" (sensual lust). This sensual lust itself is called a "fetter" (saṃyojana) in the sense of binding. If this sensual lust exists in a person's continuum, it binds that person to the round of suffering (vaṭṭa). Because of this binding, it is called a fetter because it binds the being with suffering, with other existences and births, and binds the result (vipāka) with the causal kamma. The meaning of the fetter of aversion (paṭighasaṃyojana) and others should also be understood accordingly in this manner. In the phrase "sarasa-lakkhaṇa-vasena" (by way of its own essence and characteristic), it should be understood as being connected by the power of its own function, which is the non-relinquishing of the being from the round of suffering, and by the power of the characteristic, which is the aforementioned binding.

The inclusion of enjoyment in sensual pleasures is to prevent enjoyment in existence (bhava) and enjoyment in views (diṭṭhi). "Assādayato" means one who greatly enjoys. "Abhinandato" means one who delights by the power of craving accompanied by joy (pīti). By these two words, the arising of sensual lust, which is the cause of strong sensual lust, is stated. In the remaining words, it should be understood in the same way. In the text "aniṭṭhārammaṇe" (in an undesirable object), the word "āpāthagataṃ" should be brought in and connected by changing the case ending of "āpāthagate". "Etaṃ ārammaṇaṃ" refers to an object that is so subtle and difficult to perceive. The words "niccaṃ dhuvaṃ" (permanent and stable) are merely given as an example. The views of one who holds "it will be cut off, it will perish," etc., should also be included. First, by way of conforming to identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), the fetter of doubt (vicikicchā) arises in the continuum of one who doubts, "Is it a being?" or, by way of conforming to another identity view, "Is it the form of a being?" Since doubt cannot exist without the view that grasps at "self" (atta) and "what belongs to self" (attaniya), doubt follows view. One who longs for existence means one who desires existence, thinking, "In such a prosperous existence, we have easily obtained this desired form-object; therefore, in the future too, let there be such an existence, or one even more prosperous than this." "Evarūpaṃ" means a form of such a nature. In things similar to the original form, the same designation is used. Just as the original designation is used for similar things, such as "that very same partridge" or "those very same medicinal plants." "Usūyato" means one who gives rise to envy (issā). "Aññassa maccharāyato" means one who practices stinginess (macchariya) to make something not shared with others. It occurs together with all the nine aforementioned fetters.

"Tañca kāraṇaṃ" refers to the cause of each respective fetter, namely the desirable or undesirable form-object, which is the analyzed cause such as the sign of beauty (subhanimitta) or the sign of aversion (paṭighanimitta), and the unwise attention (ayonisomanasikāra) caused by that sign. Referring to the state of being not suppressed (avikkhambhita), not eradicated (asamūhata), and having gained ground (bhūmiladdhuppanna), it is stated as "arisen because of not being abandoned." The state of the fetter being currently present is taken by way of active manifestation (samudācāra). "Yena kāraṇena" means by whatever cause, namely insight (vipassanā) and serenity (samatha) meditation...
323:
...by which cause, non-arising occurs in the future; that cause is the reason for abandoning that fetter by way of substitution of opposites (tadaṅga) and by way of suppression (vikkhambhana). Because envy (issā) and stinginess (macchariya) are states leading to the states of deprivation (apāya), the Blessed One stated that they are to be abandoned by the first path (the Path of Stream-entry). If that is so, how does it agree with the Sutta passage: "With the destruction of three fetters, one becomes a stream-enterer"? It should be answered that the passage was spoken according to the Suttanta method. Because the Suttanta teaching is a teaching that disciplines according to the inclinations of beings, while this commentary is according to the Abhidhamma method, there is no fault of contradiction.

"Oḷārika" (coarse) means having a gross nature, which is the intensity of active manifestation (pariyuṭṭhāna) due to constant arising. "Aṇusahagata" (subtle) means having reached a minute or subtle state without the aforementioned coarse nature. Here, the non-arising of the fetter of restlessness (uddhaccasaṃyojana) should also be understood as being stated, because restlessness is inseparable from and occurs together with the aforementioned fetters, thus having a single meaning. Knowing the ear-sensitivity (sotapasāda) and so on by way of their own nature, function, and characteristic, and knowing the arising and so on of the fetters caused by those ear-sensitivity and so on, should be understood in the same way as previously stated; to show this, he refers back saying, "This is the same method."

"Or in one's own dhammas" means knowing in one's own internal sense bases (ajjhattikāyatana), or in both one's own internal and external dhammas. In this context, the meaning is by way of taking the internal sense bases as the starting point. By explaining in this way, the grasping of sense bases in one's own continuum and the continuum of others without remainder is accomplished. In the phrase "or in the dhammas of others," the method is the same. The form-base (rūpāyatana), which has eleven types of form-nature, should be brought in and connected to the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) according to the method stated. "In the remaining aggregates" refers to the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations. By this reference "according to the method stated," he explains this distinction: "arising due to nutriment" in the aggregate of form, "arising due to mind-and-matter" in the aggregate of consciousness, and "arising due to contact" in the remaining aggregates. Other explanations are the same in all places. Just as in the section on aggregates (khandhapabba), in the section on sense bases (āyatanapabba) as well, it is stated that "supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma) should not be taken," meaning that the exclusion of supramundane states is not included in the Pali text. The remaining Pali sentences are just as previously stated.

## Conclusion of the Explanation of the Section on Sense Bases.

## Explanation of the Section on Enlightenment Factors

"Of the awakening being" means a being who awakens from the sleep of defilements, or a being who penetrates the Noble Truths. "In the factors" means in the causes or in the constituent parts. They are called enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga) because they are parts of the Path that arises and awakens from the sleep of defilements. The Suttanta teaching is a discourse known as figurative exposition (pariyāyakathā).
324:
Alternatively, from the arising of the knowledge of arising and passing away (udayabbaya-ñāṇa) onwards, one is said to be established in the path of enlightenment (sambodhi-paṭipadā). Thus, it is said: "Starting from one who has begun insight (vipassanā), the practitioner (yogāvacara) is called 'enlightenment' (sambodhi)." What is known as a Suttanta teaching is a figurative discourse (pariyāya-kathā), and since this teaching on the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) proceeds by way of the mundane path, it is said: "The practitioner is called 'enlightenment'." Otherwise (if referring to the supramundane path), it would have been called a "noble disciple" (ariya-sāvaka).

The meaning of the term "basis for the enlightenment factor of mindfulness" (sati-sambojjhaṅga-ṭṭhānīya) should be understood in the same manner as explained for the term "basis for doubt" (vicikicchā-ṭṭhānīya). "Taṃ" refers to wise attention (yoniso-manasikāra). "Tattha" refers to being in mindfulness, or the locative case is used in the sense of accomplishment.

Mindfulness and clear comprehension are called "mindfulness and clear comprehension" (sati-sampajañña). Alternatively, it is the knowledge that discerns the purposefulness of moving forward and so forth, with mindfulness being predominant. Because that mindfulness and clear comprehension brings about the state of acting with mindfulness in all matters, it serves as a support for the arising of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness.
