Just as the abandoning of opposing states and the cultivation of suitable states serve the arising of unarisen wholesome states, so too the avoiding of unmindful persons, the association with mindful persons, and the commitment to that mindfulness serve the arising of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness; this meaning is shown by the words "mindfulness and clear comprehension" and so forth.

Tissadatta Thera is the elder who, holding a golden voting-ticket at the Bodhi-maṇḍa, invited the assembly, saying: "In which of the eighteen languages shall I preach the Dhamma?" Abhaya Thera refers to Dattābhaya Thera.

The investigation of states, or investigation into states (or into the Four Noble Truths), is "investigation of states" (dhamma-vicaya); that itself is an enlightenment factor, thus "the enlightenment factor of investigation of states" (dhamma-vicaya-sambojjhaṅga). Regarding the words "wholesome and unwholesome states" (kusalākusala dhammā) and so forth, what should be said is to be understood in the same manner as previously stated. In that context, "making much of wise attention" (yoniso-manasikāra-bahulīkāra) is the arising of consciousness and mental factors associated with knowledge, which arises by way of understanding the respective natures, functions, and individual characteristics of wholesome states and so forth as they truly are. Indeed, because it is an act of attention that is non-perverted, it is called "wise attention" (yoniso-manasikāra); because it has that same focus, the advertence (āvajjana) is also of the same nature. The constant occurrence of that wise attention is "making much of it" (bahulīkāra). "For further increase" (bhiyyobhāvāya) means for the sake of repeated occurrence. "For expansion" (vepullāya) means for the sake of becoming vast. "For fulfillment" (pāripūriyā) means for the sake of cultivation.

"Inquisitiveness" (paripucchakatā) is the state of asking questions by delving deep. It means approaching teachers, delving into the five Nikāyas together with the commentaries, and asking about various difficult points therein: "Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?"
325:
For one who asks about the meaning of the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), and so forth, the enlightenment factor of investigation of states arises. Therefore, it was said: "The aggregates, elements... [pe]... abundance."

In the phrase "making the bases clear" (vatthūnaṃ visadabhāva-karaṇaṃ), the body is intended as a "basis" (vatthu) because it is the locus for the occurrence of consciousness and mental factors, as are the robes and other requisites connected with it. Making those bases in such a way that they bring happiness to the mind is "making them clear." Therefore, it was said: "of internal and external [bases]" and so forth. "Excessive fault" (ussanna-dosaṃ) means having excessive faults due to wind and so forth. "Smeared with sweat and dirt" (seda-mala-makkhitaṃ) means smeared with sweat and the dirt of the body known as grime. By the word "ca" (and), other things that bring affliction to the body and mind are also included. In the phrase "or the lodging" (senāsanaṃ vā), the word "vā" (or) should be understood to include the alms-bowl and so forth.

When the internal or external basis is not clear, or when it becomes an object, [the knowledge is also not clear]. How do these become objects for one devoted to meditation? This is said by way of the consciousnesses that arise in the intervals of the meditative mind. Those consciousnesses lead to the impurity of the mind's one-pointedness. In the consciousness and mental factors which are the conditions such as the support (nissaya), [the knowledge is also not clear]. In the term "knowledge also" (ñāṇampi), the word "pi" (also) has the sense of inclusion. By that word "pi," it shows that not only is the basis itself [unclear], but if that basis is impure, the knowledge is also impure. Just as the state dependent on a support is impure because the support is impure, it shows the impurity of the possessor of the object (the knowledge) because the object is impure.

"Balancing" (samabhāva-karaṇaṃ) means making the faculties neither deficient nor excessive in terms of their function. When the function of decision (adhimokkha) is exceptionally sharp by way of the condition in an object of faith, the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) becomes powerful because wisdom is not clear and effort and so forth are slack. Therefore, it was said: "the others are weak." "From that" (tato) means because of that power of the faculty of faith and the weakness of the others. Upholding the associated states without letting them fall into the side of sloth, and providing further strength, is "exertion" (paggaha). Since that exertion is itself the function, it is called the "function of exertion" (paggaha-kicca). [Effort] should be connected with the phrase "is unable to perform" [that function of exertion]. Reaching the object and staying there, or not letting go, is "presence" (upaṭṭhāna).

The rejection of distraction is "non-distraction" (avikkhepa). Or, that function by which the associated states are not distracted is "non-distraction." Just as one sees a form with the eye, the function by which one sees the nature of the object as it truly is, is the "function of seeing" (dassana-kicca). Because it is overwhelmed by the powerful faculty of faith, [effort cannot perform the function of exertion, and faith cannot perform the function of seeing]. For among the co-nascent states, the accomplishment of the purpose occurs only by way of the single flavor of the states occurring together while performing their respective governing roles, and not otherwise. By the word "therefore" (tasmā), the aforementioned meaning is reflected upon as the cause. "Taṃ" refers to that faculty of faith. "Through reflection on the nature of states" (dhamma-sabhāva-paccavekkhaṇena) means that the faculty of faith becomes powerful because of the excessive occurrence of conviction in the noble qualities of the object of faith; this is because of showing the state of cause and effect in that object of faith.
326:
The faculty of faith (saddhindriya) becomes strong. This strength arises from investigating, in accordance with reality, the nature of cause and effect and so forth of the object of faith. Thus, when faith is grasped according to its natural essence through the method of natural law, an expansive conviction (adhimokkha) does not occur. This is because the activity of wisdom (paññā) is excessive in the mode of discerning, 'This is the nature of these phenomena.' Indeed, among the leading mental factors, just as wisdom is weak when faith is strong, so too is faith weak when wisdom is strong.

Therefore, it is said: 'It should be diminished either by reflecting on the nature of those phenomena, or by not attending to it in the same manner that it was attended to when it became strong.' The phrase 'by not attending to it in that manner' means not engaging in the meditation in the same way that the yogi engaged in it when the faculty of faith became strong. Here, the strength of the faculty of faith is of two kinds: either due to its own specific cause exceeding its function, or due to the weakness of the functions of energy (vīriya) and the others. In the first case, the method of diminishing it has already been shown. In the second case, however, in the same way that the faculty of faith became strong because energy and the others were weak due to a certain way of attending, it should be diminished by attending in a way that brings about the sharpness of energy and the others, thereby making the faculty of faith equal in essence with those phenomena. In this same way, the method of diminishing the remaining faculties should also be understood.

## The Story of Elder Vakkali

That Venerable Vakkali, having performed meritorious deeds to attain the rank of foremost (etadagga) among those who are released through faith (saddhādhimutta), lived solely devoted to gazing upon the physical body of the Teacher. Although the Teacher admonished him, saying, 'Vakkali, what is the use of seeing this foul body? Vakkali, he who sees the Dhamma sees me,' and urged him toward the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), he did not apply himself. When he was eventually dismissed, he climbed a cliff to throw himself down. At that moment, the Teacher, while remaining seated, emitted a radiance to show himself and spoke this verse:

'The monk who is full of joy and has confidence in the Buddha's teaching, may attain the peaceful state, the bliss of the stilling of formations.'

Having spoken this, He said, 'Come, Vakkali.'

Venerable Vakkali, as if sprinkled with the nectar of the Deathless (amata), joyfully began his insight meditation (vipassanā). The Blessed One, knowing that Vakkali could not enter the path of insight because his faith was too strong, purified and gave him a meditation subject to bring about the equilibrium of the faculties. That Venerable Vakkali, the Teacher...
327:
...standing in the method given by the Teacher, applied himself to insight meditation and reached Arahantship through the sequence of the paths. Therefore, it is said: 'The story of Elder Vakkali is an illustration here.' The phrase 'here' refers to the situation where the other faculties cannot perform their functions when the faculty of faith is excessive.

'The distinction of other functions' refers to the specific functions such as established mindfulness (upaṭṭhāna) and so forth. In the phrase 'tranquility and so forth' (passaddhādi), the word 'and so forth' should be understood to include the enlightenment factors of concentration (samādhi-sambojjhaṅga) and equanimity (upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga). 'Should be diminished' means that just as the strength of the faculty of faith is diminished by reflecting on the nature of phenomena, the excess of the faculty of energy is diminished by developing tranquility and so forth, because those factors belong to the side of concentration. Indeed, just as the development of energy and so forth protects the faculty of concentration from falling into sloth (kosajja), the development of tranquility and so forth protects the faculty of energy from falling into restlessness (uddhacca) and certainly diminishes it. Therefore, it is said: 'It should be diminished by the development of tranquility and so forth.'

'The story of Elder Soṇa' refers to the story of the delicate Elder Soṇa. That Venerable, having taken a meditation subject from the Teacher, lived in the Sīta Forest. Thinking, 'My body is delicate, and it is not possible to attain bliss through ease; I must practice the ascetic life even if it exhausts me,' he resolved only on the postures of standing and walking. Although blisters broke out on the soles of his feet, he disregarded the pain and exerted firm energy. However, due to over-exertion of energy, he was unable to attain any distinction. The Teacher went there, admonished him with the 'Simile of the Lute' (vīṇūpama), showed him the path of balancing energy, purified his meditation subject, and then went to Gijjhakūṭa Hill. The Elder, balancing his energy according to the method given by the Teacher, applied himself to insight meditation and was established in Arahantship. Therefore, it is said: 'The story of Elder Soṇa should be shown.' The phrase 'in the remaining cases also' refers to the faculties of mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

'Equilibrium' (samata) means the state of mutual non-deficiency and non-excess between faith and wisdom, and likewise between concentration and energy. Indeed, since faith and wisdom are each leading factors, their mutual non-transgression in terms of function is specifically desired, for when they have equal weight, absorption (appanā) is accomplished. Similarly, when concentration and energy—which are prone to sloth and restlessness respectively—are equal in essence and support each other, the associated mental states do not fall into either of the two extremes, and absorption is properly achieved. The passage beginning with 'Strong faith' (balavasaddho) is a confirmation of the meaning already stated through the method of negation. Its meaning is: one who possesses strong faith but has unclear wisdom is 'blindly devoted' (mudhappasanno); he does not have 'wise confidence' (aveccappasanno). Thus, he becomes confident in what is not a proper object, just like the disciples of other sects.
328:
"The side of deceit" (keraṭikapakkha) means taking the side of craftiness. One who thinks excessively with wisdom devoid of faith is deceived by counterfeit reasons and imagines such things as, "Even without relinquishing a gift, merit consisting in giving (dānamaya-puñña) occurs by the mere arising of a thought." Being so, one whose mind is ruined by dry logic does not take the words of the wise and does not reach conviction. Therefore, it was said (in the Commentary), "Like a disease caused by medicine, it becomes incurable."

In this context, just as the imbalance between faith (saddhā) and wisdom (paññā) does not bring benefit but only harm, so too the imbalance between concentration (samādhi) and energy (vīriya) does not bring benefit but only harm. Likewise, it does not bring non-distraction but only distraction. (If concentration is excessive), sloth (kosajja) overcomes it; the meaning is that because of such overcoming, one does not reach absorption (appanā). In the case of "restlessness (uddhacca) overcomes it," the method is the same. "Those two" refers to the pair of faith and wisdom, and the pair of concentration and energy. "Should be made equal" means they should be made to have an equal function.

"One whose work is concentration" (samādhikammika) refers to one whose meditation subject is serenity (samatha). "Thus" (evaṃ) means when it is so, when faith is slightly strong. "Believing" means without thinking, "How can jhāna arise by the mere attention to 'earth, earth'?" but believing that "The method taught by the Fully Enlightened One will surely succeed," thus generating faith. "Placing faith" (okappento) means entering into the object, as it were, and placing faith by way of decision, thus leaping forward. Since concentration is the primary factor of jhāna, a strong one-pointedness (ekaggatā) is appropriate. "Of both" means of concentration and wisdom. Since the excessiveness of wisdom is also desired for the concentration of one whose work is concentration, he said "also by equality," meaning by way of an equal state. "Absorption" (appanā) refers to mundane absorption. This is why he speaks with doubt, saying "it just is." But in supramundane absorption, their equal state is definitely desired. As it is said, "He develops serenity and insight yoked together."

If the equality of faith-wisdom and concentration-energy is specifically desired, what about mindfulness (sati)? He said, "Mindfulness, however, is appropriate to be strong in all instances." "In all instances" means in the five faculties which belong to the sides of sluggishness (līna) and restlessness (uddhacca). Taking a part belonging to the side of restlessness, he said, "of faith, energy, and wisdom." It should also be taken in another way. For this reason, it was only said, "by concentration belonging to the side of sloth," and not "by tranquility, concentration, and equanimity." "That mindfulness" refers to mindfulness. Just as a minister appointed to all the king's affairs is called "all-purposeful" (sabbakammika), so it is stated in the Commentary because it is desired in all instances. Mindfulness is called "all-desirable" (sabbatthika) because it is desired when the mind is sluggish and when it is restless.
329:
Whether the mind is sluggish or restless, the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) to be developed at all times exist in this mindfulness; therefore, mindfulness is called "sabbatthika" (mindfulness that can bring all benefits). "Mind" refers to the wholesome mind. For that wholesome mind, mindfulness is the only refuge and resort for reaching the unreached and attaining the unattained. Therefore, it was said, "having protection as its manifestation" (ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhāna), and so on. 

Those who have wisdom that does not penetrate the various divisions such as the aggregates (khandha) refers to those whose intellect is not yet established in the aggregates, bases (āyatana), etc., even through scriptural learning. Associating with those of great learning brings about knowledge based on learning (sutamaya-ñāṇa). One endowed with tender insight is also called a wise person because they stand in knowledge based on development (bhāvanāmaya-ñāṇa). Therefore, it is said, "associating with a person endowed with the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa) which perceives the fifty characteristics." Because of the profound nature of the things to be known, the profound nature of the knowledge that distinguishes them should be taken; intending this, it is said, "with profound wisdom occurring in profound things such as the aggregates." Since that which is to be known is the range of such wisdom, it is called "gambhīra-ñāṇa-cariya" (the range of profound knowledge). Alternatively, the diverse occurrence of that wisdom in those profound things is called "gambhīra-ñāṇa-cariya." Intending the reflection on the occurrence of that wisdom, it is said, "reflecting on the diversity of profound wisdom." Just as one who has reached the fullness of mindfulness is an Arahant, so too one who has reached the fullness of wisdom is that same Arahant. Therefore, it is said, "the fulfillment of development occurs through the Path of Arahantship." The same principle should be understood for energy (vīriya) and so on.

"They drive a red-hot iron stake into the hand," etc.—these fivefold bindings and tortures are mostly performed first of all on a being born in hell. Since these tortures are mentioned at the beginning in the Devadūta Sutta and others, it is said, "starting from the fivefold binding and torture." In the phrase "at the time of pulling a cart, etc.," the word "etc." (ādi) includes times when they are oppressed by other humans or animals. "For the interval between two Buddhas" is said with reference to beings born repeatedly only in the realm of hungry ghosts (peta). Or, it is said intending that some hungry ghosts, like some animals, may have such a long life. This statement is true. "Kāla the Naga King, having lived to see four Buddhas, will also see the Blessed One Metteyya." By this statement, the Naga King's life for an entire aeon (kappa) is mentioned. 

"One who habitually sees the benefit" refers to one who has the nature of seeing the benefit in energy, thinking, "The attainment of all mundane and supramundane distinctions depends only on energy." "The path to be traveled" refers to the practice leading to Nibbāna in the preliminary stage along with insight (vipassanā).
330:
The sequence of the Noble Path or the sequence of the Seven Purifications is called *gamanavīthi* (the path of travel). This practice is called *gamanavīthi* because it is the path that must be traveled by monks for the sake of deliverance from the suffering of the round of rebirths.

'*Kāyadaḷhībahulo*' means being habitually devoted to and striving in the strengthening of the body for a certain purpose. '*Piṇḍa*' refers to the alms-food (*raṭṭhapiṇḍa*) donated by the people of the country. The honoring of alms-food by making the merit performed by the donors of the four requisites great through one's own right practice is called '*piṇḍāpacāyana*'.

'*Nīharanto*' means taking out from the bowl-bag. '*Taṃ saddaṃ sutvā*' means hearing those words of the laywoman with the divine ear (*dibbasota*) while standing at the door of his leaf-roofed hut, because he is endowed with the five supernormal knowledges (*abhiññā*). Human prosperity, divine prosperity, and the prosperity of Nibbāna are these three types of prosperity. '*Dātuṃ sakkhissasi*' means the Elder asks himself: "Through the merit consisting in giving (*dānamaya*) and the merit consisting in service (*veyyāvaccamaya*) performed for you, and by becoming like a special field of merit, you will be able to give the prosperity of devas and humans repeatedly, and finally the prosperity of Nibbāna." '*Sitaṃ karonto*' means smiling with the power of joy that arises after reflecting: "I have crossed over the suffering of the round without difficulty."

'*Vippaṭipanna*' means practicing wrongly by transgressing the customs of one's birth and family. Just as a son who practices wrongly is excluded from the family lineage due to that wrong practice and does not receive the father's inheritance, so too a lazy person, practicing wrongly due to that laziness, does not receive the inheritance of the noble wealth (*ariyadhana*) that should be obtained from the Teacher. Only one who has aroused energy (*āraddhavīriya*) receives it because of practicing rightly. The construction is: "The energy factor of enlightenment (*vīriyasambojjhaṅga*) arises," and it is the same in other places.

'*Mahā*' means being great, extensive, and unique due to virtues such as morality (*sīla*). To show that the greatness of the Teacher's virtues is well-known in the world through the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world system, he said "*Satthuno hi*," etc.

Because the status of being a son of the Sakyans (*sakyaputta*) arises for one ordained in the Teacher's Dispensation through the undertaking of ordination, he said "*Asambhinnāya*," etc., to show the status of being a son of the Buddha.

Avoiding from afar those who are lazy, who do not even know the name of meditation (*bhāvanā*), who are devoted only to strengthening the body, who eat as much as they want and indulge in the pleasure of sleep, etc., and who engage in animal-talk (*tiracchānakathā*), is called *kusītapuggalaparivajjanā* (avoidance of lazy persons). "Walking during the day..."
331:
"...walking during the day, sitting at night," etc. Approaching at the appropriate time those who have aroused energy and firm effort through the power of undertaking meditation is called *āraddhavīriyapuggalasevanā* (associating with persons of aroused energy). Therefore, he said "Having filled the belly," etc. In the *Visuddhimagga*, however, these two—reflecting on the greatness of birth and reflecting on the greatness of fellow practitioners—are not taken; instead, these two—dispelling sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*) and reflecting on the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*)—are taken. There, reflecting on the right efforts is included by way of seeing the benefits, because of seeing that the attainment of mundane and supramundane distinctions depends on energy. Dispelling sloth and torpor is included by way of being inclined towards that energy, because for a person who is properly devoted to arousing energy, the dispelling of sloth and torpor is naturally accomplished. Among those causes for energy, dispelling sloth and torpor, avoiding lazy persons, associating with persons of aroused energy, and being inclined towards that energy should be understood as producers of the energy factor of enlightenment (*vīriyasambojjhaṅga*) by way of bringing about the means to remove opposites; while reflecting on the danger of the states of deprivation (*apāyabhaya*), etc., do so by way of stimulation.

The joy (*pīti*) that arose previously is the specific cause and similar cause for the joy that will arise later; therefore, it is said, "Joy itself is the states that are the basis for the joy factor of enlightenment (*pītisambojjhaṅga*)." The use of the plural is based on its occurrence many times. Practicing according to the manner in which that joy arises is the attention (*manasikāra*) that produces that joy.

The words said in terms like "recollection of the Buddha" (*buddhānussati*) should be understood according to the method already stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.

Because the recollection of the Buddha ends only in access concentration (*upacārasamādhi*), it is said "up to access concentration." "Pervading the whole body" means pervading the whole body with refined material forms produced by joy. For one who recollects the virtues of the Dhamma as well, the construction is: "the joy factor of enlightenment arises, pervading the whole body up to access concentration." The same method applies to the remaining recollections. It should also be applied to the reflection on suttas that inspire confidence (*pasādanīyasuttanta*), because reflecting on those suttas is also a basis for liberation and is similar to the recollection of the Buddha, etc. Even in the partial cessation of formations, as in the complete cessation, because of the occurrence of wisdom in that way, the attention of meditation (*bhāvanāmanasikāra*) becomes capable of suppressing defilements and brings about access concentration. Being endowed with such joy and happiness, it leads to the arising of the joy factor of enlightenment; thus he said, "also for one reflecting on the attainment... etc." There, the text is "the defilements are suppressed." Indeed, they do not occur. The word "*iti*" has a causal meaning: because they do not occur, therefore (the joy factor of enlightenment arises) for one reflecting on their non-occurrence.
332:
The interpretation (yojanā) is as follows: The interpretation should be made that the enlightenment factor of joy (pīti-sambojjhaṅga) arises for one who reflects on the non-arising of defilements. This is because it is not appropriate for joy to arise in one who reflects on defilements that have arisen. Due to the absence of the moisture of devotion toward the inspiring Triple Gem and so forth, the heart is like coarse chaff, and there is a state of roughness. That state of roughness is known by the lack of respect and reverence. Therefore, it is said: "In the state of roughness indicated by disrespectful action" (asakkaccakiriyāya saṃsūcitalūkhabhāve).

Tranquility (passaddhi), characterized by the subsiding of the distress of body and mind, is itself the enlightenment factor of tranquility (passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga), which is a factor of the aforementioned enlightenment (bodhi). The interpretation should be made that the arising of this enlightenment factor of tranquility occurs in this way.

Partaking of choice and suitable food means partaking of food that is both excellent and beneficial. By the taking of comfortable climate and postures, it should be understood as taking a suitable climate and suitable postures. When these three kinds of suitability (sappāya) are cultivated, they bring about the health of the body and thereby bring about the health of the mind, thus becoming the cause for both kinds of tranquility (tranquility of body and mind). The extreme view that the happiness and suffering found in beings occur without a cause is one extreme. The view that happiness and suffering occur due to an uneven cause such as a creator (Issara) and so forth is the second extreme. Without approaching these two extremes, the view that they occur according to one's own kamma is the middle way (majjhimā paṭipadā). One who has an effort or application situated in the middle is one who has equanimous application (majjhatta-payoga). The state of such a person is equanimous application (majjhatta-payogatā). This equanimous application, by abandoning the state of an agitated body and being the cause for the state of a tranquil body, brings about the two kinds of tranquility. By this very equanimous application, it should be understood that the avoiding of persons with agitated bodies and the associating with persons of tranquil bodies are described as bringing about those two kinds of tranquility.

Serenity (samatha) that occurred previously and is grasped by way of noting its concentrated manner is itself the sign of serenity (samatha-nimitta). Distraction (vikkhepa) is called 'byagga' because it has various (vi-) points (agga) due to wandering among various objects. Indeed, that distraction is said to have the function of instability and the manifestation of wavering. Concentration (samādhi), being the opposite of 'byagga' because of the state of one-pointedness (ekaggatā), is called 'abyagga'. That very 'abyagga' concentration is the sign (nimitta), as stated previously. Therefore, it is said: "And the sign of non-distraction in the sense of non-wavering" (avikkhepaṭṭhena ca abyagganimittaṃ).

It has been stated that the cleansing of internal and external bases and the balancing of the faculties bring about wisdom. They also bring about concentration. It is precisely because they bring about concentration that they also bring about wisdom. Therefore, it is said: "The cleansing of the bases... should be understood."

Because the skill in producing and developing the sign (karaṇa-bhāvanā-kosalla) are inseparable, and because the skill in protecting it (rakkhana-kosalla) is rooted in them, it is simply called "skill in the sign" (nimitta-kusalatā). The phrase "of the kasiṇa sign" (kasiṇanimittassa) should be understood as a mere illustration. This is because skill in grasping the sign for the arising of any jhāna whatsoever, such as the foulness sign (asubha-nimitta), is also called skill in the sign. In the phrase "by very lax energy and so forth" (atisithilavīriyatādīhi), the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes the weakness of the application of wisdom and the lack of joy.
333:
It is stated only as "skill in learning" (uggahaṇa-kusalatā). The phrase "of the kasiṇa sign" should be understood as a mere example. This is because skill in learning the sign for the arising of any jhāna, whether it be the foulness sign (asubha-nimitta) or any other, is indeed skill in the sign (nimitta-kusalatā). In the phrase "by very lax energy and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes the weakness of the application of wisdom and the lack of joy. Uplifting the mind (paggaṇhana) means pulling the mind out from the state of sluggishness by arousing the enlightenment factor of investigation of states (dhamma-vicaya-sambojjhaṅga) and so forth when that mind is shrunken. Regarding this, the Blessed One said: 

"Monks, at whatever time the mind is sluggish, that is the time for developing the enlightenment factor of investigation of states, the time for developing the enlightenment factor of energy, and the time for developing the enlightenment factor of joy. For what reason? Monks, a sluggish mind is easily uplifted by these states. Monks, suppose a man wanted to make a small fire blaze up. If he were to throw into it dry grass, dry cow-dung, and dry wood, and were to blow on it with his mouth, and did not sprinkle it with dust, would that man be able to make that small fire blaze up?" "He would, venerable sir," (they replied). (SN 5.234).

In this context, it should be understood that the development and arousing of the enlightenment factor of investigation of states and so forth occur by the power of their respective nutriment (āhāra); this has been explained just previously. In the phrase "by energetic effort and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes the strength of the application of wisdom and the heightening of joy. Restraining the mind (niggaṇhana) means preventing the mind from the state of restlessness by arousing the enlightenment factor of tranquility (passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga) and so forth when that mind is agitated. Regarding this, the Blessed One also said:

"Monks, at whatever time the mind is agitated, that is the time for developing the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the time for developing the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the time for developing the enlightenment factor of equanimity. For what reason? Monks, an agitated mind is easily calmed by these states. Monks, suppose a man wanted to extinguish a great mass of fire. If he were to throw into it wet grass... and were to sprinkle it with dust, would that man be able to extinguish that great mass of fire?" "He would, venerable sir," (they replied). (SN 5.234).
334:
## Commentary on the Factors of Enlightenment in the Contemplation of Phenomena. In this context also, it should be understood that the development and arising of the factor of enlightenment of tranquility (passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga), etc., occur by way of their respective causes. Among them, the development of the factor of enlightenment of tranquility has already been mentioned. The development of the factor of enlightenment of concentration (samādhi-sambojjhaṅga) will be mentioned immediately after. 'Paññā-payoga-mandatā' (slowness in the application of wisdom) means due to the lack of exertion of wisdom. Just as giving (dāna) is based on non-greed (alobha) and virtue (sīla) is based on non-hatred (adosa), so meditation (bhāvanā) is based on non-delusion (amoha, i.e., wisdom). In that meditation, when wisdom is not strong, it cannot bring about progress from the preceding to the succeeding stages. Just as unprepared food does not provide enjoyment to the consumer, it does not generate delight in the yogi's mind and thus becomes tasteless. Furthermore, because the meditation does not correctly enter the right path and thus does not attain the bliss of peace (upasama-sukha), the mind becomes tasteless. Therefore, it is said: 'Paññā-payoga... becomes tasteless.'

To show the remedy for this by causing urgency (saṃvega) and clarity (pasāda), he mentioned 'the eight grounds of urgency' (saṃvega-vatthu), etc. Among them, birth, aging, sickness, and death occur as appropriate in the happy and unhappy realms. Besides these, the suffering of the lower realms caused by the five kinds of bondage, hunger and thirst, and mutual oppression, etc., should also be noted. All of this is taken in connection with the present life of those various beings. The sufferings rooted in the cycle of rebirth (vaṭṭa) occurring in the past and future are taken separately. For those beings who live depending on food, and among them, those who live depending on the fruits of their exertion, the 'suffering of livelihood' (jīvika-dukkha), which is not shared with others, is taken as the eighth ground of urgency. 'Samaye sampahansanā' (gladdening at the proper time) means gladdening and delighting the mind of meditation well by generating urgency and clarity in the manner mentioned when it is time to gladden it.

'Sammāpaṭipattiṃ āgamma' (having arrived at the right practice) means arriving at the correct practice of meditation without deviation, following the path of tranquility (samatha), free from sluggishness and agitation. Because factors associated with laziness are not excessive, it is 'not sluggish' (alīna). Because factors associated with agitation are not excessive, it is 'not agitated' (anuddhatā). Being endowed with the application of wisdom and attaining the bliss of peace, the mind is flavorful (not tasteless), and thus proceeds evenly on the object, having entered the path of tranquility. At that time, because it is not sluggish, there is no need for exertion in uplifting (paggaha); because it is not agitated, no need for restraint (niggaha); and because it is flavorful, no need for gladdening (sampahansana). This is called 'equanimity at the proper time' (samaye ajjhupekkhana-tā) towards the meditation mind.
336:
## Commentary on the Section on the Four Truths

'Yathāsabhāvato' means according to the undistorted nature. It means (knowing) through the individual nature of each, such as the nature of being deformed and the nature of hardness, from whatever nature is individual by way of the characteristic of oppression. 'Janikaṃ samuṭṭhāpikaṃ' refers to (the state) that produces suffering characterized by continuous occurrence and gives rise to the mark of the cause of suffering. 'Purimataṇhaṃ' means (knowing) the craving that has already occurred prior to the time of the arising of the suffering that has been defined. Indeed, when the cause is completed, the arising of suffering, which is the effect of that cause, occurs. The phrase "He knows: 'This is the origin of suffering'" is the connection of the words. In the case of "This is the cessation of suffering," the same method applies.

'Ubhinnaṃ appavattiṃ' means (knowing) the cause of the non-occurrence of these two: suffering and craving, which is the origin of suffering. Through this Dhamma, both suffering and origin do not occur; the nature of the unconditioned element (asankhata-dhatu), which is the cause of the non-occurrence of both suffering and origin, is called 'appavatti'. 'Dukkha-parijānano' refers to the Noble Path (ariya-magga) because it delimits and knows the Truth of Suffering by way of the realization of full understanding (pariññābhisamaya). (Knowing) that Noble Path which fully understands the Truth of Suffering. In the remaining two phrases, the meaning should be understood in this same way.

## Commentary on the Description of the Truth of Suffering

'Evaṃ vuttā' refers to (that birth which) is thus spoken of by way of summary indication. It is a statement that encompasses all beings entirely, because it is a repeated description with the intention of pervading all beings. 'Sattanikāye' means in the group of beings, in the assembly of beings. In various existences such as devas and humans, the assembly of beings distinguished by their respective births, such as earth-dwelling devas, kings, elephants, and hungry ghosts (peta) suffering from hunger and thirst, is called 'sattanikāya'.

Considering that the first arising of the aggregates (khandhas) in the ultimate sense is birth (jāti), and defining it as 'jananaṃ jāti' (birth is the producing), the phrase 'savikārānaṃ' (of those with modifications) and so forth is stated to show those aggregates together with the mode of arising (uppāda-vikāra), which is not a finished product but is desired in those aggregates. 'Savikārānaṃ' means (the first arising) together with the mode of modification called arising. It is true that the three characteristics, such as birth, are specific modifications (vikāra-rūpa) of the eighteen types of concrete matter (paramattha-rūpa). By the phrase 'upasagga-maṇḍita-vevacanaṃ', it is shown that the word is expanded solely by the prefix 'saṃ' without being mixed with the original root 'ja'. 'Anupaviṭṭhākārena' means by way of entering and dwelling in the egg-shell or the womb. 'Nibbattisankhātena' means by way of the completion and accomplishment of the sense bases (āyatanas) (the completion of the task of forming organs like the eyes).

Alternatively, by the explanation 'jananaṃ jāti', birth with incomplete sense bases is meant. 'Sañjāti' is birth with complete sense bases. It is true that complete birth is called 'sañjāti'. Because of the meaning of descending, it is called 'okkanti'...
337:
...referring to birth by way of egg-born (aṇḍaja) and womb-born (jalābuja) beings. Those beings take rebirth as if entering the egg-shell or the womb. Because of the meaning of distinct arising by way of moisture-born (saṃsedaja) and spontaneously born (opapātika) beings, it is called 'abhinibbatti'. Those beings are born with their physical limbs and organs clearly manifest. A very distinct arising is called 'abhinibbatti'. The teaching 'jananaṃ jāti' and so forth is spoken to show birth by encompassing all beings through two pairs of terms: by way of sense bases and by way of modes of birth (yoni). The phrase 'of those various beings... arising' is conventional discourse (sammuti-kathā) because it is spoken by way of 'beings'. In the term 'pātubhāvo', the word 'iti' means 'beginning' or 'manner'. Therefore, it should be noted that the meaning of the phrase 'acquisition of the sense bases' (āyatanānaṃ paṭilābho) is also included. This statement is also ultimate discourse (paramattha-kathā).

When there is the manifestation of those aggregates in one-constituent existence (fine-material realm), four-constituent existence (immaterial realm), and five-constituent existence (sensual realm), the acquisition of sense bases occurs. It should be noted that this encompasses: by way of two sense bases each in one-constituent and four-constituent existences; by way of five sense bases arising at the moment of rebirth in the remaining fine-material Brahma realms; and by way of seven, nine, ten, ten again, and eleven sense bases in the sensual realm, depending on whether the beings have deficient or non-deficient organs. Those sense bases simply manifest; they do not come from anywhere. They are called 'acquired' because they exist in the continuity of that being. Alternatively, 'āyatanānaṃ paṭilābho' should be understood as the self-acquisition of the sense bases.

'Sabhāva-niddeso' means the description of the intrinsic nature. The reality of 'jiṇṇatā' (decay) is 'jarā' (old age) or 'vayohāni' (decline of life). Decay itself is 'jīraṇatā'. Alternatively, the mode of one who is decaying is expressed by the suffix 'tā', hence it is called 'ākāra-bhāva-niddeso' (description of the state of the mode). In the word 'khaṇḍita-dantā' (one with broken teeth), the latter word 'danta' is dropped and it is called 'khaṇḍitā'. The modification by which a being is called 'broken' is 'khaṇḍiccaṃ' (brokenness of teeth). Similarly, one with gray hair is called 'palito', and that grayness is 'pāliccaṃ'. One is called 'valittaco' because of having wrinkled skin.

'Phalūpacārena' means speaking by way of the metaphorical usage of the effect. Passing away itself is 'cavanatā'. Alternatively, the suffix 'tā' expresses the mode of one passing away. 'Aggregates break up' means the aggregates that are the end of the continuity of aggregates belonging to a single existence break up. Because of that breaking, they reach cessation and invisibility. Therefore, breaking and disappearance are called 'maraṇa' (death). 'Maccu-maraṇaṃ' is death which is the cutting off of the life faculty (jīvitindriya) belonging to a single existence, known as 'maccu'. Therefore, it is taught as 'not momentary death' (na khaṇika-maraṇaṃ).
338:
In the term 'maccu-maraṇa', it is also appropriate to connect them separately without forming a compound, where 'maccu' refers to the breaking up of the aggregates and 'maraṇa' refers to the relinquishing of life. 'Kālakiriyā' (passing away) means making the 'time' (kāla), which is specifically called 'time' because the time of death cannot be surpassed. In terms of its essence, it is simply the aggregates of falling away (cuti-khandha) reaching destruction. Alternatively, it means the falling away or death which is called in the world as making an end of time. All these passages starting with 'yaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ' (of those various beings) are merely conventional discourse (sammuti-kathā) because they are taught in terms of beings. This passage is ultimate discourse (paramattha-kathā) because it points to the destruction of phenomena (dhamma) which have the nature of being deformed, etc., as found in the ultimate sense.

The collection of aggregates is called 'attabhāva' (individuality) because the mind arises there as 'self' (attā). Laying down that individuality means its destruction. In the Commentary, however, it is shown that the falling down of one who has reached death is called 'nikkhepa' (laying down) by way of metonymy (phalūpacāra), where the result is named after the cause. 'Khandhānaṃ bheda' (breaking up of the aggregates) is partially ultimate discourse because it points to the destruction of the continuous collection of phenomena. In this passage, 'jīvitindriyassa upaccheda' (interruption of the life faculty), since there is not even a trace of conventional usage, it is stated that 'the interruption of the life faculty is indeed death in the ultimate sense in every aspect.' Even so, the breaking up of aggregates due to which the conventional expressions 'Tissa is dead, Phussa is dead' occur in the world, is worthy of being called 'conventional death' (sammuti-maraṇa) because the continuity of the aggregates is not yet [completely] cut off; thus it is said, 'this breaking up of aggregates itself is also called conventional death.' Therefore, it is said, 'jīvitindriyupacchedameva hi' (for it is only the interruption of the life faculty), and so on. The complete cutting off of the continuity in every way is called 'final death' (samuccheda-maraṇa).

'Byasaneṇa' means by ruin or misfortune. As in the passages such as 'dhamma-paṭisambhidā', the word 'dhamma' is a synonym for cause; thus it is said, 'by the cause of suffering.' 'Socana' (sorrow) has the characteristic of grieving because it is to be noted as such. The state of the grieving person or of the mind is called 'socitabhāva'. 'Abbhantare' means inside the individuality (body). Drying up by its own harsh nature, and drying up all around (parisosento) by reaching its full strength, it occurs.

'It is called ādeva (lamentation) because by this sound they cry out and wail repeatedly (referring to children, etc.)'; thus, having formed the word 'ādevana', for those who reach the transformation such as the shedding of tears...
339:
Because of reaching such transformation as the shedding of tears, that sound is spoken of as the cause (of lamentation). 'Taṃ taṃ vaṇṇaṃ' means praising various qualities. 'Tasseva' means only of that lamentation and wailing. 'Bhāva-niddesa' (descriptions of the state) refers to the words indicating the nature of the meaning, such as 'ādevitattaṃ' (the state of lamenting) and 'paridevitattaṃ' (the state of wailing).

The sensitive body (kāyapasāda) which is the basis of this suffering exists; therefore, it is called 'kāyika' (bodily). Thus the teachers said, 'having the sensitive body as its basis.' The difficult endurance of this bodily suffering exists; therefore, it is called 'dukkhamana'. Since that very nature of difficult endurance is the meaning, it is called 'dukkhamanaṭṭha'. It is called 'asāta' (disagreeable) because it is the opposite of what is pleasant.

It is called 'cetasika' (mental) because it arises in the mind. Since that mental suffering is associated with the mind through various modes such as arising together, it is said to be 'associated with the mind' (cittasampayutta).

Sinking down all around by way of preventing the approach to all objects is 'saṃsīdana'. Sinking that is very powerful or distorted by way of making one unable even to rise is 'visīdana'. Fatigue of the mind (citta-kilamatha) is the exhaustion of the mind in the mode of distress. Despair (upāyāsa) is not suffering (feeling) itself because it is anger (dosa), or because it is a different phenomenon included in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). Those teachers who say that despair is only mental pain (domanassa) should be refuted by this Dhātukathā Pali: 'Despair is associated with three aggregates...' The word 'upa' has the sense of 'excessive' (bhusa); thus it is said, 'excessive distress is despair.' These are descriptions of the state (bhāva-niddesa) which illuminate the mere nature of phenomena, showing the absence of an agent other than the phenomena; and when there is no agent, there is the absence of what is to be done or what is to be grasped by that agent; thus it is said, 'descriptions of the state which illuminate the absence of self and what belongs to self.'

In the term 'jātidhammānaṃ', the word 'dhamma' is a synonym for nature (pakati); thus it is said, 'jātisabhāvānaṃ', which means those who have the nature of being born. The state of desiring to develop the path because of the development of the path should be desired; wishing to prohibit such a desire (to be free from birth without the path), it is said, 'without developing the path.' Another way: 'na kho panetaṃ' refers to the state of non-birth found in the Noble Ones who have abandoned the origin (of suffering), and the non-coming of birth found in those who have attained Parinibbāna; although one desires that, without developing the path...
340:
The meaning here should be understood thus: it is not something that can be attained merely by wishing, because it cannot be attained without developing the Path, and because it can be attained by developing the Path even if one does not wish for it. The word 'pi' (also/even) has the sense of including the meanings that will be mentioned later; thus it is said, "The word pi occurs by taking up the remaining terms above." The word 'yaṃ' (which) is a nominative case used in the sense of an instrumental cause; thus it is said, "even by which state (dhamma)." This word 'dhamma' has the sense of cause; here, the state of being unobtainable should be understood as the cause. Alternatively, 'taṃ' (that) refers to the non-attainment of the desired object; thus, the meaning of "yampi" is stated here as "yenapi" by way of change of case-ending. When the word 'yaṃ' refers to 'icchaṃ' (desire), then it refers to desire characterized by non-attainment. But when it refers to 'na labhati' (does not get), then it refers to non-attainment characterized by desire. Although that state is not another state in terms of meaning, it nevertheless refers only to the desire (craving) regarding an unobtainable object. "Sabbattha" (everywhere) refers to all the occurrences beginning with "jarādhammānaṃ" (of the nature of aging) and so on.

## Description of the Exposition of the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering

It is called 'punobbhava' (further existence) because it creates further existence; it should be noted that the first word ends in 'o' after dropping the latter word, as in the word 'mano'. Alternatively, because the meaning is made known by the suffix '-ika' in the sense of habit (sīla), the word expressing the action is not seen, just as it is said, "One who habitually eats cakes is called asūpika." In the Sammohavinodanī Commentary, however, the meaning is stated: "It is called ponobbhavikā because it gives further existence, it leads to further existence, and it causes rebirth in existence again and again." That meaning is stated with the intention that the word 'ponobbhavika' can be established in those senses because of the indication by the plural "taddhitā", because of the variety of the derivative (taddhita) meanings, or because derivatives have the characteristic of expressing the meaning of a sentence. Among those meanings, craving (taṇhā) that arises together with kamma gives further existence; craving that does not arise together with kamma but is a companion to kamma leads to further existence; both types should be understood as causing rebirth in existence again and again.

It is called 'nandīrāga' (delight and lust) because of the sense of delighting and the sense of lusting. Whatever is 'nandīrāga' and whatever is 'taṇhā' (craving) in the sense of longing—both are identical in meaning and differ only in phrasing; therefore, craving is said to have "attained identity in meaning with nandīrāga." Here, the word 'saha' (with) has the sense of 'being of that nature,' as in "sanidassanā dhammā" (states with visibility) and so on. Therefore, 'nandīrāga-sahagatā' means (craving) that has attained the state of delight and lust, because it occurs without discarding the state of delight and lust in all stages. It is said "uppannassa" (of what has arisen) because it occurs in connection with lust. Since lust for fine-material and immaterial existence is mentioned separately, it should be understood that the arising of longing for existence in the sense-sphere (kāmabhava) alone is meant.
341:
In those various things of a pleasant nature, it is said to "arise" by way of its first occurrence, and it is said to "settle" by way of its repeated occurrence. Alternatively, arising and settling should be understood in connection with the power of obsessive craving (pariyuṭṭhāna) and latent craving (anusaya). "In prosperity" (sampattiyam) refers to the glory and wealth of humans and the state of being a deva. "One's own eye" refers to the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) together with its physical base, or else it refers to the lump of flesh together with the eye-sensitivity. The eye with five clear colors refers to the eye possessing the five colors—blue, yellow, red, black, and white—which are pure and very clear. Because it is white inside, they perceive the eye-socket like a silver tube. They also perceive it like an ornamental cord (pāmanga) hanging from the ear. They also perceive their own nose which has acquired the designation of being a high or long nose. Alternatively, there is the reading "laddhavohārā"; in that case, the connection should be made as: those beings who have high noses are called "tuṅganāsa" (high-nosed ones), and such beings perceive their own noses.

The tongue is perceived as being like a red woolen blanket in terms of its color and shape, and in terms of its function, as that which provides sweet and cool tastes. The body is perceived as being like a sal tree or a golden pillar because of its perfection in height and circumference. The mind is perceived as being excellent, unlike other minds, because of its ability to think about past and other matters. They perceive the bodily odors and so forth within their own continuity that they have acquired, as well as external scents such as perfumes applied to the body. In the phrase "the craving that is arising, arises," when craving is in the process of arising, the action of "arising" taken in a general sense is stated as the characteristic (lakkhaṇa), while the action "arises" as specified by the object where craving arises is stated as that which is to be characterized (lakkhitabba). Indeed, the usage of distinction between the general and the specific is not non-existent; it certainly exists. Alternatively, "arising" is stated as the cause in the sense of an indefinite arising, and "arises" is stated as the result in the sense of a definite arising. If it is in the process of arising, then it arises here in this (eye) as the result.

## Explanation of the Exposition of the Truth of Cessation

Having stated that "all these are synonyms for Nibbāna," the phrase beginning with "Nibbānañhi" is undertaken to make that meaning clearer. In that passage, "āgamma" means having made Nibbāna the cause. For the complete fading away and cessation of craving occurs because of Nibbāna as the cause. It fades away by way of reaching exhaustion. It ceases by way of reaching non-occurrence. It is given up by way of abandoning due to lack of regard, or by way of decrease. It is relinquished by way of throwing it far away so that it cannot occur again, in a manner that it cannot occur again. It is released by way of liberation from craving, which is a bond. It does not cling because it is not defiled. Why is this Nibbāna, being only one, spoken of by various names? To show that it is because of the variety of opposites, he said "ekameva hi" and so on. Since Nibbāna has a nature contrary to conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhamma), the names of Nibbāna, being given based on qualities, are also contrary to conditioned phenomena. Therefore, it is said, "by way of being the opposite of the names of all conditioned phenomena." In this (Nibbāna), craving fades away without remainder; therefore, it is called "asesa-virāga." This same method applies to the remaining terms. This is the distinction: for this (Nibbāna), by its nature, there is no arising.
342:
In another way, when this nature of Nibbāna is realized and witnessed, the arising of that person no longer exists; thus it is called anuppāda (non-arising), which is the asaṅkhata-dhamma (unconditioned reality). In terms such as "appavatta" (non-occurrence) and others, the meaning should be understood in this same way. Āyūhana (striving/accumulation) is samudaya (the origin of suffering), and by way of its opposite, it is called anāyūhana (non-striving).

The statement "to show its non-existence in that very place" is made to clearly demonstrate that although craving (taṇhā) tends to arise in pleasant and agreeable objects like the eye before it is abandoned, it no longer exists in those objects once it has been abandoned. Apannatti means making non-manifest (non-designation) or the absence of the conventional expression "there is a bitter gourd." The Noble Path (ariya-magga) should be understood like a man who desires the non-occurrence of a bitter gourd vine. The abandoning of craving by the Path which takes Nibbāna as its object is like cutting the root of the bitter gourd vine, and Nibbāna, being the state where craving does not occur, is like the non-occurrence of that vine.

In the second analogy, Nibbāna should be understood as the south gate, and the Path as the executioner of thieves. Just as thieves are killed at the south gate but are later described as "thieves were killed in the forest," so too craving, which has reached Nibbāna and ceased, is said to have "ceased in the eye, etc.," because it no longer performs the function of attachment in those objects. The previous analogy (the bitter gourd vine) is given to show that craving ceased by the Path is fit to be called "ceased in pleasant and agreeable objects," while the latter analogy (the thief) is given to show that craving ceased upon reaching Nibbāna is fit to be called "ceased in those objects." This is the distinction between these two analogies.

## Explanation of the Description of the Truth of the Path

"Aññamaggapaṭikkhepanatthaṃ" means to reject the notion that the practice conceived by those outside the Dispensation is the way to the cessation of suffering, or to reject the path-status of any other practice. The word "ayaṃ" (this) refers to a direct, present experience because this Dhamma is personally realized by the Blessed One Himself and by some of those bhikkhus. It is called "ariya" (noble) because it is far (ārakattā) from defilements, according to the method of etymology. It is called "ariya" because it produces the state of being noble (ariyabhāvakara). Alternatively, it is "ariya" because it makes a person noble, or because it causes one to obtain the Noble Fruit (ariyaphala). It should be understood that the name "ariya" is acquired through its own function in the former sense, and through the power of the Fruit in the latter sense. The meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) that can bring about the penetration of the Four Truths is called catusaccakammaṭṭhāna. Alternatively, the practice of meditation (bhāvanā) aimed at realizing the Four Truths, which is the ground for the special happiness of yogis, is called catusaccakammaṭṭhāna. The first two truths...
343:
...are called vaṭṭa (the round) because they are the cause of the occurrence of the round. The latter two truths are called vivaṭṭa (the ending of the round) because they are the cause of turning away from the round and the means of attaining that ending. Application of the meditation subject to the round exists because it involves grasping and observing the actual characteristics. In the ending of the round (vivaṭṭa), however, there is no such application because it is not the object (of mundane insight), or even if it were, there would be no purpose. The phrase "having learned the first two truths" is connected thus: In the text of the meditation subject, "learning" (uggaha) means mastering by heart through noting the meaning of that text. Therefore, it is said, "reciting repeatedly with the voice." By the words "pleasant and agreeable," He shows the inclination of the mind toward the Truth of Cessation and the Truth of the Path, not sensual delight; and that very inclination should be understood as the practice of meditation upon those truths.

"By a single penetration only" means penetrating with a single knowledge. Penetration (paṭivedha) is the act of piercing through, characterized by moving without attachment or obstruction in the object. Realization (abhisamaya) is the understanding characterized by the attainment of the object without fail. Knowing by defining, "This is suffering, this much is suffering, there is no more than this," is penetration by the aforementioned method, and is thus called "penetration by full understanding" (pariññā-paṭivedha). By that (one knows). This statement is made by taking the occurrence of knowledge in such a way that, once that knowledge has arisen, there is no more delusion in defining the nature and characteristics of suffering thereafter; it is not because the Path-knowledge occurs with the thought "This is suffering," etc. The superior abandoning, relinquishing, and cutting off of defilements such that they need not be abandoned again is penetration by the aforementioned method, and is thus called "penetration by abandoning" (pahāna-paṭivedha). By that (one knows). This "penetration by abandoning" is also spoken of in reference to the knowledge that acts as an obstruction to those defilements—which, if not abandoned, would prevent the development of the Path, and which would arise in the absence of Path-development—bringing them to a state where they cannot arise again, by way of moving without attachment and without obstruction in its occurrence. Realization (sacchikiriyā) means making it manifest to oneself. It is the taking of the object according to its actual nature, saying "This is it," having let go of thinking about what has been heard and so on. That realization is penetration by the aforementioned method, and is thus called "penetration by realization" (sacchikiriyā-paṭivedha). By that (one knows). This is also spoken of because, as long as the obstruction is not completely cut off, knowledge cannot take Cessation as its object; but because that obstruction is completely cut off, knowledge arises making that Cessation manifest in its actual nature. Development (bhāvanā) means producing and increasing. Therein, in the first path, it is understood in the sense of producing; in the second path and so on, in the sense of increasing; or in both cases, in both senses. For even in the first path, development can be understood in the sense of increasing, as it proceeds by increasing the full understanding and so on that occurred in the insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā). In the second path and so on, development can be understood in the sense of producing, because of the abandoning of defilements not yet abandoned and because of the achievement of the status of a different noble person. That producing or increasing is penetration by the aforementioned method, and is thus called "penetration by development" (bhāvanā-paṭivedha). By that (one knows).
344:
This development (bhāvanā) is also spoken of in terms of the manner in which confusion does not occur regarding the specific nature of the Path-factors after the Path-knowledge has arisen, just as confusion does not occur when knowledge is proceeding.

Let the Path-factors as they have been attained stand for now; even in the Fruition-dhammas (phala-dhamma) as they occur, there is indeed an absence of confusion, just as in the Truth-dhammas (sacca-dhamma) as they have been attained. For this very reason, it was said: "One who has seen the Dhamma, reached the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, plunged into the Dhamma." Because for that person of Fruition, the reviewing knowledges (paccavekkhaṇāñāṇa)—which are prompted by the nature of things and have as their object the Truth-dhammas as they have been attained—arise after the Path-process (magga-vīthi), reviewing the Path, the Fruition, the defilements abandoned, the defilements remaining, and Nibbāna. Reviewing also occurs for the Truth of Suffering, personality-belief (sakkāya-diṭṭhi), and so forth. This explanation of meaning should also be understood in the context of "realization through full understanding" (pariññābhisamaya) and so on.

Regarding the statement, "He realizes through a single realization (ekābhisamaya)," the Vitandavādin (sophist) says: "The Noble Path-knowledge performs its function by way of separate realizations of the four Truths." He should be convinced by the Odhisokathā in the Kathāvatthu of the Abhidhamma. Now, in order to clarify that very same single realization in detail, the passage beginning with "evamassa" is stated.

Why is it said, "In the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga)... penetration (paṭivedha) occurs"? Is it not true that penetration does not occur in the preliminary stage? This is true in the literal sense (nippariyāyato). However, here, the understanding that occurs by way of learning (uggaha) and so forth is spoken of in that way figuratively (pariyāyato). Or, because it is the cause of penetration, the knowledge in the preliminary stage regarding the Truths such as suffering, which occurs by way of learning and so forth, is called "penetration"; it does not mean penetration by its actual nature.

"By way of function" (kiccato) means that the function to be performed by the knowledges of suffering and so forth in the preliminary stage is completed here in this Path; or it refers to the function of this very knowledge in manifesting suffering and so forth, meaning full understanding (pariññā) and so on. By the term "penetration of the object" (ārammaṇa-paṭivedha), the penetration that is the realization (sacchikiriyā) of Nibbāna is meant. That reviewing knowledge is not mentioned here because it is not the occasion for it while learning and so forth are being discussed. Indeed, only when there is attainment (adhigama) would there be an occasion for it.

To show that very lack of occasion, the passage beginning with "imassa ca" is stated. There is no penetration prior to the discernment of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). The discerning of the four Truths by way of learning and so forth is called "discernment" (pariggaha). Because of such discernment, due to the firmness of attention, the full understanding of suffering and so forth in the preliminary stage certainly occurs. Therefore, it is said, "It occurs starting from discernment." "In the subsequent stage" (aparabhāge) means at the moment of the Path.

Because they are difficult to see—even though they are evident by way of their own moment of occurrence—they cannot be seen according to their intrinsic nature and function by ordinary knowledge. They must be seen according to reality only by the deep knowledge of development (bhāvanā-ñāṇa), and even then, only by the Noble Path-knowledge that has reached its peak.
345:
(Those two Truths) are deep. Therefore, the Teacher said: "Both are deep because of the penetration of their characteristics." The other two (the Truth of Cessation and the Truth of the Path) are extremely deep because they are untainted (asaṃkiliṭṭha) and not objects of defilement, because they have reached ultimate happiness, because they do not lead to further birth, because they have never occurred before, and because their occurrence is not evident. Likewise, they are difficult to see because they must be seen only with extremely deep knowledge and cannot be seen with ordinary knowledge. Therefore, the commentator said the passage beginning with "itareasaṃ pana."

"Effort" (payoga) means action or exertion. He shows the great desirability and the extreme difficulty of that effort through metaphors such as "for the sake of grasping the peak of existence" (bhavaggaggahaṇatthaṃ). "At the moment of penetration" (paṭivedhakkhana) means at the moment of the simultaneous penetration of the four Truths by the Noble Path. "That knowledge is only one" means that the Path-knowledge is only one by way of accomplishing the functions of full understanding (pariññā) and so forth regarding suffering and the other Truths.

"In these three instances" refers to the three objects of sensual thought (kāma-vitakka), ill-will thought (byāpāda-vitakka), and cruel thought (vihiṃsā-vitakka), which are shown as things to be abstained from. In the phrase "by the cutting off of the path" (padapacchedato) regarding the three types of unwholesome intentions that have arisen separately, the path of approach is called "pada." The means or cause by which sensual thought arises is its path of approach (gatamagga). The cutting off or destruction of that path is "padapaccheda." By way of accomplishing the non-arising (anuppatti) through such cutting off, a single wholesome intention arises, fulfilling the Path-factor while accomplishing the function of the Path. Here, the total eradication of the three types of unwholesome intentions should be understood as the accomplishment of the three functions. In this same manner, the meaning of the passages beginning with "in these four instances" should be understood.

Regarding "abstinence from false speech and so forth," since it is stated in the Sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga that the volition of abstinence (virati-cetanā) and all associated dhammas are training rules (sikkhāpada), the Sammohavinodanī Commentary states, "There are abstinences (virati) and there are also volitions (cetanā)," by way of the primary volitions of abstinence. Therefore, some teachers say: "By the word 'ādi' (and so forth), not only are abstinences from slanderous speech and so forth included, but such volitions are also included." This would be appropriate if spoken regarding the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga). Abstinence (virati) should be applied at the time of abstaining from false speech and so forth, and volition (cetanā) at the time of speaking well-spoken words and so forth. However, at the moment of the Path, only abstinences (virati) are desired, because volitions are not Path-factors. Just as a single Path-knowledge is the knowledge of suffering and so forth, and just as a single abstinence is the nature of abstaining from false speech and so forth, a single volition does not have the nature of accomplishing the three functions of Right Speech and so forth. Therefore, the status of Right Speech and so forth cannot be established through volition, and if that is not established, the status of the three Path-factors cannot be established.
346:
The bodily and verbal misconduct of a bhikkhu rooted in livelihood can only arise through the search for nutriment by improper means; thus it is said, 'edible... etc... misconduct.' The reason for mentioning only bodily and verbal misconduct is to demonstrate that the corruption of livelihood occurs only in the bodily and verbal doors, not in the mind door. Therefore, it is said, 'only in these [seven] places.'

'Unarisen' refers to those that have not arisen either by way of habitual practice or by way of experiencing an object not previously encountered. Otherwise, in the beginningless saṃsāra, there would be no such thing as evil, unwholesome states that have never arisen. Therefore, it is said, 'in this single existence,' and so forth. In whichever existence this practitioner arouses this energy, it is in that single existence [that he strives to prevent unarisen unwholesome states from arising].

'Generates' means he brings into being. By producing such desire, he is said to 'generate desire.' 'Makes an effort' means he applies exertion and endeavor. 'Arouses energy' means he exerts bodily and mental energy in various ways. 'Upholds the mind with energy' means that with that same co-nascent energy, he lifts up the mind and upholds it by preventing it from falling into sloth. 'Exerts striving' means he applies the energy known as the four right efforts. In sequence, these four terms should be connected with frequent practice, development, repetition, and constant application.

'Those that have previously arisen' is stated by way of similar usage. Such usage is common for things similar to the original, as in 'that same partridge' or 'those same medicines.' Therefore, it is said, 'now, such as those.' 'Arisen' refers to those unwholesome states that have reached a condition where they cannot be called 'unarisen.' 'For the sake of abandoning' means for the purpose of giving them up.

In the phrase 'unarisen wholesome states,' 'wholesome' refers to the states of superior men (jhāna, path, and fruit). The 'arising' of these states means their attainment or acquisition, and 'non-arising'—as their opposite—means not yet having acquired them. Thus, it is said, 'of the first jhāna, etc., which have not yet been acquired.'

When it is said, 'he arouses energy for the sake of maintenance,' it does not refer to momentary maintenance, as there is no need to arouse energy for that; rather, it refers to maintenance in the sense of continuous duration. Thus, it is said, 'for the sake of maintenance by way of the sequence of repeated arising.'

'Forgetfulness' means falling into non-perception by way of opposing states. Its opposite, non-forgetfulness, is 'asammosa' (non-confusion). Thus, it is said, 'for the sake of non-disappearance.' 'Bhiyyobhāva' (increase) means repeated occurrence. This repeated occurrence is arising higher and higher. Thus, it is said, 'for the sake of arising further.' 'Abundance' means reaching a state of proficiency and strength through constant occurrence. Thus, it is said, 'for the sake of abundance means for the sake of becoming vast.' 'For the sake of fulfilling development' means for the purpose of increasing the development of jhāna, and so forth.
347:
'In the four instances' means in the four instances such as the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states. 'By way of accomplishing the task' means by way of fulfilling the fourfold task as a single unit.

Jhānas are various both in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the path. Even if Right Concentration (Sammā-samādhi) is classified by way of the four jhānas—which occur with excellence of development through association with jhāna factors such as initial application (vitakka), which have the nature of peaceful happiness and which perform functions like directing onto the object, rubbing the object, being fond of the object, and intensifying associated states—nevertheless, just as energy fulfills the fourfold task of energy such as the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states, and just as Right Mindfulness (Sammā-sati) fulfills the fourfold task of mindfulness such as abandoning the perception of beauty in the body, etc., which are actually unattractive, painful, impermanent, and non-self, a single concentration cannot fulfill the concentration-tasks of the four jhānas. Therefore, the first jhāna concentration in the preliminary stage is the very one that occurs at the moment of the path; likewise, the fourth jhāna concentration in the preliminary stage is the very one that occurs at the moment of the path.

'By way of various paths' means jhānas are various according to the various paths such as the first path. The second path, etc., also occur by way of the second jhāna, etc. In the phrase 'ayaṃ panassa,' although there are four types by way of the path, they are taken together as one, and it is said 'of it' (assa), meaning 'of this path.' 'Ayaṃ' (this) refers to this distinction of being entirely similar, entirely dissimilar, or partially similar in relation to the jhāna.

'It occurs by the rule of basis jhāna' means it is stated here making the rule of basis jhāna (pādakajjhāna) the primary focus. This is also stated in the Sammohavinodanī Commentary. In the Atthasālinī Commentary, however, the rule of insight (vipassanā) is stated so as not to contradict any tradition. Here, the rule of basis jhāna is stated to refute the views and inclinations of those who focus on the jhāna scrutinized by insight. It should be understood that the rule of insight is not rejected here either, as it is universal. Other teachers' views will be mentioned later and should be analyzed accordingly. Therefore, analyzing the aforementioned rule of basis jhāna, he said, 'firstly, by the rule of basis jhāna.'

It is associated with the first jhāna. This is because an attainment (samāpatti) that has arisen in close proximity makes the path similar to itself, just as the color of the ground makes the color of a lizard similar to its own. 'They are indeed complete' means there are eight or seven factors. There are seven factors due to the absence of Right Thought (Sammā-saṅkappa). There are six factors due to the absence of the Enlightenment Factor of Joy (Pītisambojjhaṅga). He points out the sevenfold or sixfold nature of the path factors and enlightenment factors by saying, 'this is the method.'

The meaning is that in the formless sphere (arūpa), the jhāna consisting of four or five factors is only a supramundane jhāna and not a basis jhāna, as stated in the Atthasālinī. One might ask: 'Is it not stated in that Atthasālinī that three or four jhānas arise in the formless sphere, and not four or five jhānas?' This is true. However, for those who have doubts...
348:
By showing the arising in the formless realm (arūpabhūmi), it should be understood that it is said that, in terms of meaning, "the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise." Considering the collection as a whole, it is said, "That collection is only supramundane (lokuttara), not mundane (lokiya)." This means that "the single state of a partial jhāna is the distinguishing factor of the whole collection of jhānas." In that formless realm, only the fourth jhāna arises as mundane; the fourfold or fivefold jhānas do not arise as mundane.

In this context, "how is it?" means: since there is no basic jhāna (pādakajjhāna), how should it be understood? The meaning is that for that person in the formless realm, the three paths associated with a jhāna similar to that basic jhāna arise. By making the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) etc., associated with that jhāna, the basis, they arise for the sake of developing the higher paths. Furthermore, by developing the path associated with the threefold and fourfold jhāna, for a person born in that formless realm, the fourth formless jhāna and the fruit associated with that jhāna are made the basis. Due to the insight (vipassanā) that develops the higher paths, other paths associated with jhānas also arise. The paths that have the determination of jhāna factors etc., are states based on the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) which is prepared in the preceding stage of the path to bring about the path. Since they are not to be contemplated as impermanent etc., the state of the fruit being the basis for the higher path should also be noted.

The phrase "some teachers" refers to the Elder Moravāpī Mahādatta. Again, the phrase "some teachers" refers to the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya. In the third instance, the phrase "some teachers" refers to the remaining elders, excluding the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga, who says "it only determines the basic jhāna," and the two elders mentioned immediately before.

Cessation (nirodha), which is defined by the non-occurrence of suffering (dukkha) and the origin of suffering (samudaya) included within one's own continuity, is spoken of as "one's own four truths," as if it were a state included within one's own continuity. In the case of "the truths of another," the same method applies. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "In this very fathom-long body, endowed with perception and mind, I make known the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the practice leading to the cessation of the world."

How does a beginner define the truth of cessation and the truth of the path? One defines them through the manner accomplished by tradition (anussava) and so forth. By defining them in this way, defining them with reference to the supramundane factors of enlightenment (lokuttara-bojjhaṅgas) is also not contradictory. "According to possibility" means according to what is possible; the meaning is that, excluding the truth of cessation, the arising and passing away should be understood by the power of the remaining truths.

## The Explanation of the Section on the Four Truths is finished.
