## The Explanation of the Contemplation of Phenomena is finished.
349:
The seven types of charnel ground (sivathika) meditations, such as "a skeleton with flesh," are mentioned as meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) capable of producing absorption (appanā) because they are skeleton meditations, and the others, such as the bloated (uddhumātaka), are so by their own nature. "Only two" refers to these two: mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna) and the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra). "Immersion" (abhinivesa) means the immersion of insight (vipassanā); that immersion is the defining of states that should be contemplated as impermanent etc.

Postures (iriyāpatha) and clear comprehension such as looking (ālokita) etc., do not reach the state of being (directly) contemplated because they are merely specific moments of material states, like intimation (viññatti) etc. With the intention that the hindrances (nīvaraṇas) and factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅgas) should not be grasped at the beginning, it is said: "postures...pe... do not arise." Just as by pointing out hair etc., the states that cling to those hairs are grasped, so too, by pointing out the postures etc., the material states existing in those moments of posture are defined. Furthermore, starting with the hindrances etc., the associated states (sampayutta-dhamma) conjoined with those hindrances, and the material states that are the basis for those hindrances, are also defined. With this meaning, the Elder Mahāsiva said that "immersion (abhinivesa) arises" even in the postures etc. The passage beginning with "Is there in me?" shows that, by nature, the postures etc., are not desired for a beginner practicing meditation. This is because full understanding (pariññā) cannot occur without prior defining knowledge.

"Here, monks, a monk..." and so forth in the brief instruction (uddesa) and detailed explanation (niddesa), the term "monk" (bhikkhu) is used in various places to show the state of being a monk through that practice of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). However, to show that this teaching is common to all, it is said, "Monks, whoever..." and not just "a monk." To show that it does not mean only a monk, it is said, "Whether it be a monk or anyone else," and so forth. The wisdom of the highest path (aggamagga-paññā) which has reached its peak, knowing without overstepping the boundaries of the four truths already known through the path of seeing (dassana-magga), is called "Aññā" (highest knowledge). Since it is the fruit of that highest path, the highest fruit (aggaphala) is also called "Aññā"; thus it is said, "Aññā means Arahantship (arahatta-phala)."

The connection of the text is such that it shows the liberating nature of the Dispensation (Sāsana) even within a very short period. "Niyyātento" means speaking with the intention of concluding.

## The Exposition of the Hidden Meaning (Ṭīkā) on the Explanation of the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta is finished.
350:
## 10. Payāsi Rājañña Sutta Vaṇṇanā
Since the Blessed One took the name in this way as 'Kumāra Kassapa', this grammatical connection is made. In the world, princes are addressed as 'Kumāra'. This Venerable Kumāra Kassapa was also the adopted son of the King; therefore, the teacher said, 'The King's... they knew.'

While performing meritorious deeds, that Elder arose in the realms of gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, but because his faculties (indriya) were not yet mature, he was unable to produce the special attainment of the Paths and Fruits. 'On the third day' means on the third day from the day he climbed the mountain.

Because those (Elders) were destined for the Enlightenment of a Disciple (Sāvakabodhi) and because their accumulation of merit was superior, they did not go to the states of deprivation (apāya), but while enjoying bliss for the interval between two Buddhas... 'Devatā' refers to a deity of the Suddhāvāsa realm who was a former companion in the Dhamma.

After saying 'He was born in the womb of a young lady of good family,' the phrase beginning with 'Sā ca' is stated to show the fact of his birth in that womb from the very beginning. In that phrase, 'Sā' refers to the young lady of good family. The word 'ca' has a sense of distinction (vyatireka); by that word, it highlights the special meaning that is about to be stated. 'Kulaghara' means the home of the husband's family. 'Gabbhanimitta' refers to the physical sign or appearance of the establishment of the pregnancy. Although Visākhā belonged to a family residing in Sāvatthī, the phrase 'Visākhā also' is mentioned to show her primary role in the investigation of that pregnancy. It is like saying, 'The Brahmins have arrived, and Vāseṭṭha has also arrived.' 'Devatā' here also refers to that same Suddhāvāsa deity. 'Pañhe' refers to the fifteen questions that appear in the passage beginning with 'Monk, monk, this anthill...' (M. Ni. 1.249).

'Setabyā' is the name of that city in the feminine gender. In the word 'uttarena', because it is associated with the suffix '-ena', the second accusative case 'Setabyaṃ' is stated in the Pāḷi text. However, in explaining the meaning, in consideration of the word 'uttara', the connection with the ablative case as 'Setabyato' is made. 'Anabhisittakarājā' refers to a king of the Khattiya caste who has not yet received the royal consecration (abhiseka).

## Payāsi Rājañña Vatthu Vaṇṇanā
In the phrase 'Only a view is diṭṭhigata', the word 'gata' is said to be an augmentation of the term. Alternatively, 'diṭṭhigata' means the mere occurrence of a view. Because it is not grasped according to reality, there is no objective truth to be reached, thus it is merely the grasping of a view. It is purely a wrong reflection away from the truth. Nevertheless, that wrong view came to be manifested in that person due to unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) and so forth.
351:
It is merely a grasping, meaning it is entirely a wrong obsession. That 'diṭṭhigata' (view) arose through his unwise attention and so forth, and because of the absence of encountering its opposite (Right View) and because of obtaining suitable nourishment (conditions), it reached the state of habitual practice (samudācāra); thus it is said in the Pāḷi, 'it has arisen.' The phrase 'without pointing to various causes' means that because he cannot point to one who comes here from another life or one who goes there from this life, he points to various false causes such as 'beings are annihilated right there in those respective lives.'

This use of the word 'purā' is intended for a meaning that is not desired but has arrived; thus, in the phrase 'purā...pe... saññāpeti', it means 'as long as he does not make it known.'

## Candimasūriya Upamā Vaṇṇanā
Just as the moon and the sun, having grand and extensive radiance, cannot be overcome by any other light, so too this Elder will be one who cannot be overcome by others due to the light of wisdom; showing this, he said the phrase beginning with 'Candima...pe... aññena'. By the word 'ādi' in 'ādīhi', he includes challenges such as 'In how much space do these (moon and sun) travel? To how much space does their radiance spread?' 'Paliveṭhessati' means he will entwine or bind, meaning he will cross-examine. 'Nibbeṭhetuṃ' means to unravel or to solve that challenge. 'Therefore' means because he is unable to solve the aforementioned challenge. Acknowledging a side (argument) that is not desired by himself (which challenges his doctrine), he said, 'It exists in the other world, not in this one,' and so forth.

As to why this person with a nihilistic view (natthikadiṭṭhi) admits to 'Devas', the passage beginning with 'Bhagavā pana' is stated to show the reason. His view might be: 'Devas are annihilated only as Devas, and humans are annihilated only as humans.' By holding this view, the statement 'They are Devas, not humans' does not contradict his own doctrine. Similarly, in the word 'Sande', it refers to the moon-mansion (vimāna), and even if it is not spoken of as the moon-deity, it does not contradict his doctrine.

Those who have illness are called 'ābādhika'. Those in whom suffering has arisen are called 'dukkhitā'. Those who should be followed with faith, or who are the ground for the occurrence of faith, are called 'saddhāyikā'. Therefore, he said 'Ahaṃ tumhe' and so forth. Those who have trust (pattiyāyana) are called 'paccayikā'.
352:
## Explanation of the Simile of the Thief

'Uddisitvā' means approaching and showing. 'Kammakāraṇikasattesu' refers to those beings who inflict torture upon the beings in hell. 'Kammameva' refers only to the unwholesome kamma committed by those hell-beings themselves. 'Kammakāraṇaṃ karoti' means performing various tortures in accordance with the kamma performed, thus meaning to cause such suffering. In this context of 'Nirayapālā', the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'and so forth' (ādi-attha); by this word 'iti', the entire Nirayakaṇḍa Pāḷi is included in that teaching. Having thus shown the existence of hell-wardens through the Sutta Pāḷi, the phrase beginning with 'manussaloke' is now stated to show it through logic as well. In that context, they are called 'Nirayapāla' (hell-wardens) because they keep the hell-beings in hell and because they guard them without allowing them to leave that hell. Further points to be discussed here should be taken from the Papañcasūdanī-ṭīkā.

## Explanation of the Simile of the Man in the Cesspool

'Nimmajjatha' means to clean without leaving any residue, to make pure. Since such thorough cleaning and removal of that excrement is indeed an act of taking away, it is said 'apanetha' (remove it).

'Asuci' means impure; since that excrement does not increase the mind's delight nor is it attractive, it is called 'amanāpo' (disagreeable). 'Asucisaṅkhāta' means having reached a portion of impurity or having reached its own impure nature, thus it is called 'asucikoṭṭhāsabhūto' (consisting of a mass of impurity). 'Duggandha' means having a bad smell, an undesirable smell; since that smell is not just any kind but a putrid smell, it is called 'kuṇapagandho' (smell of a corpse). 'Jigucchitabbayutto' means being associated with what is loathsome and blameworthy. 'Paṭikūlo' means having a nature that is repulsive to the sense of smell (ghānindriya). 'Ubbādhati' means to oppress repeatedly. The smell of humans oppresses even the devas living a hundred leagues away, like a rotting carcass hung around the neck; this is because of its extremely impure nature, because of being born and raised only in impurity, and because the devas' sensitive organ of smell (ghānapasāda) is extremely sharp and clear.

Devas such as the Paranimmita-vasavatti and others who are born far away.

'Sundaradhamme' means in beautiful qualities. 'Sugatisukha' means the happy destination (sugati) and the happiness included within that state.
353:
## Explanation of the Simile of the Pregnant Woman

Happiness is called 'aya' because it arises from meritorious kamma. Suffering is called 'anaya' because it is the opposite of that happiness. 'Apakkaṃ' means something that is not yet finished or has not yet reached the end. 'Na paripācenti' means they do not bring it to completion. They do not cut off life in the middle because committing suicide is blameworthy. 'Āgamentī' means they wait for the time of maturity. 'Nibbīsanti' means experiencing the result of that kamma while being associated with it; or it means waiting, just as a hired servant expects his wages. In the word 'ubbhinditvā', the prefix 'u' is merely for word-augmentation, so it means 'bhinditvā' (having broken open).

## Explanation of the Simile of the Dream

'The soul (jīva) that goes out or comes in'—this statement is made according to the inclination of King Pāyāsi. For he held such a wrong and perverted view: 'When beings dream, the soul goes out from the body and wanders here and there to see various pleasant things like gardens, and then re-enters the body.' Then the Elder Kumāra Kassapa, wishing to remove the view of annihilation (uccheda-diṭṭhi) by using the designation 'soul' (jīva)—like removing a large peg with a small peg—said: 'Do they see your soul entering or leaving?' To show that the activity of the mind is designated as 'soul', it is said: 'Taking the activity of the mind as the soul, he spoke.'

'Veṭhetvā' means wrapping by binding tightly to kill. 'Cavanakāle' means at the time when one has reached the point of passing away, not while one is in the process of passing away. 'Rūpakkhandhamattameva' means only a small collection of material phenomena. This is because at that time, only the collection of material phenomena born of temperature (utu) is obtainable; or, the word 'matta' has the sense of excluding distinction, thus it excludes the special material phenomena of the three continuities such as those born of kamma. 'Appavattā honti' means the mental aggregates do not occur, they are not found. In consciousness (viññāṇa), however, there is the perception of a soul; therefore, it is said 'the aggregate of consciousness goes.' This is the intention because consciousness is not found in that dead body.

## Explanation of the Simile of the Heated Iron Ball

'Vūpasantatejaṃ' means the subsiding of heat and glow. In the word 'āmato', the syllable 'ā' has the meaning of 'half' like the word 'āmisa', so it means 'a half-dead person.' Or, 'āmato' means one who is dying, associated with slight burning, heat, and death.
354:
It means one who is in the process of dying, associated with death, with a slight burning and vital heat. A dying being is not yet devoid of vital heat, unlike one who is dead. Therefore, it is said, "He has begun to die (is dying)."

Similarly, the shaking of the physical body (odhuna) means turning it to this side (the inner side); thus it is said, "Turn it to this side." The repeated turning (sandhuna) of one who wishes to turn to this side is actually turning to the other side; thus it is said, "Turn it to that side (the outer side)." Turning a person who has been faced outward to this side and that side (niddhuna) is called "Turn it this way and that way." With the meaning that the faculties (sensitive matter) are not yet destroyed, it is said, "He does not experience that base (āyatana)."

## Explanation of the Simile of the Conch Blower
One is called a conch blower (saṅkhadhama) because he blows the conch himself or makes another blow it. "Upalāpetvā" means making a sound by repeatedly connecting with sound, making it associated with sound. Since making it associated with sound is essentially blowing, it is said, "having blown."

## Explanation of the Simile of the Fire-worshipping Ascetic
He is called "aggika" (fire-worshipper) because he has fire that is to be honored. The state of being a fire-worshipper is desired for the purpose of attending to that fire by preparing the altars for fire-offerings, by offering requisites such as fuel, sacrificial grass, ghee, and oil, and by making offerings such as flowers, incense, and scents; thus he is called "a fire-attendant." "If I could reach the end of life" means just as one who lives long, so if I could reach the final stage of life (it would be good). "If I could reach growth" means if I could reach prosperity in the parts of the body and in the parts of virtue. "A pair of fire-sticks" refers to the two fire-sticks: the upper stick and the lower stick.

"Thus" refers to the manner such as "Prince Pāyāsi is foolish," etc. (implying reproach). The word "you" is spoken referring to the Elder (Venerable Kumāra Kassapa). "By the characteristic of destroying the stated logical reason" means by the nature of concealing and destroying the stated logic. "By the characteristic of taking up an equal burden" means by the characteristic of competing as an equal. In the phrase "with rivalry (palāsa)," he is called "palāsa" because he competes as an equal. It means that he discards the superior qualities of others as if biting them off, and makes them equal to his own qualities. Rivalry (palāsa) has the function of making things equal; thus, "with that rivalry."
355:
## Explanation of the Simile of the Two Caravan Leaders
"Haritakapatta" means green leaves or a few leaves. Therefore, it is said, "at the very least," and so on. In the term "sannaddhadhanukalāpa," "kalāpa" refers to a quiver. Since a quiver cannot be prepared without a bow when being equipped, it is said, "sannaddhadhanukalāpa" (equipped with bow and quiver). "Āsittodakāni vaṭumāni" means that because the rain has fallen well and thoroughly on the paths where people travel and on the watercourses, water is flowing in those various places. Therefore, it is said, "the roads and ravines are full of water."

"Yathābatena" means as it was placed in the carts. It is like when it is said, "Dear daughter, put it here," and she puts it. This is because the verb "to do" (karana-kiriyā) can denote actions in general. Therefore, the meaning is given as "as it was loaded" or "as it was taken."

## Explanation of the Simile of the Gambler
"Parājayaguḷa" refers to the die or the casting-stick which, when present, causes defeat; it means swallowing that die or casting-stick so that it cannot be seen. "Pajjohana" refers to various kinds of sacrificial acts. Since that sacrifice is performed by the loser as a payment, it is called "balikamma" (offering).

## Explanation of the Simile of the Hemp-carrier
"Gāmapatta" refers to a place that has become a village but is not to be inhabited because it is deserted. Therefore, it is said, "a deserted village site." In the term "gāmapad," just as the place where a man sets his foot is called a "pada" (footprint/step), so the place where the houses of the villagers were located is called "gāmapada" (village-site). Therefore, it is said, "This is the very meaning." "Susannaddha" means well-prepared so as to be suitable for carrying easily. Since such good preparation is only through firm binding, it is said, "subaddha" (well-bound).

Although iron and other metals are also "loha" (metal), in the Dispensation (Sāsana), the word "loha" is traditionally used for copper; thus it is said, "loha means copper (tambaloha)."
356:
## Explanation of Going for Refuge (Saraṇagamana-vaṇṇanā)

*Abhiraddho* means having a mind that is satisfied. Since the state of having a satisfied mind in the Dispensation (Sāsana) occurs by way of devotion, it is said, "*abhippasanno*" (greatly devoted). *Pañhuppaṭṭhānāni* means the manifestations of knowledge in questions; it refers to the manifestations in knowledge by way of your answers to the meanings I have asked.

## Explanation of the Talk on Sacrifice (Yaññakatha-vaṇṇanā)

In the word *saṅghātaṃ*, the syllable "*saṃ*" is merely an augment to the word, and therefore it is said, "*ghātaṃ*" (slaughter). *Vipākaphaleṇa* means by way of a result that is similar to the cause. Because it is defiled by the killing of animals such as cattle, it does not have great fruit. *Guṇānisaṃsena* means by way of the subsequent increasing benefit. *Ānubhāvajutiyā* means by the power of majesty, which is the natural state produced by the removal of opposing unwholesome states. Because it is impure, it does not have great splendor. *Vipākavipphāratāyā* means by the pervasiveness and abundance of the fruit of result; it means completeness.

*Duṭṭhukhette* means in a field spoiled by defects such as salt-earth (alkali). Since that field is unfit for sowing and is without essence, it is called "*nissārakhette*" (a field without essence). *Dubbūme* means in a contemptible part of the ground. That contemptible state may be due to a lack of essence or due to defects such as being low-lying or hollow. Between these two, the first part is shown by the first word "*duṭṭhukhette*," and therefore, wishing to show the remaining part, it is said, "*visamabhūmibhāge*" (in an uneven part of the ground). *Daṇḍābhighātādinā* refers to seeds that are broken and destroyed by being struck with a stick and so forth. *Pūtīni* refers to seeds that have reached a state of rot because they were not dried by pleasant means such as being smeared with cow dung. Since those seeds have no essence, it is said, "*nissārāni*." *Vātātapahatāni* refers to seeds whose potency has been destroyed by wind and the heat of the sun. Therefore, it is said, "*pariyādinnatejāni*" (those whose vitality is exhausted).

In natural paddy and so forth, the potency of the seed suitable for producing a sprout from the grain is called the essence of the grain (*taṇḍulasāra*). Taking that essence of the grain means the arising of such potency. However, these seeds do not have such potency because of defects such as being broken. Bringing a stream of water into the field means raining; showing this by way of negation, it is said, "*na sammā vasseyya*" (it would not rain properly). In the phrase *aṅkuramūlapattādīhi*, the construction should be: growth upwards by way of sprouts and tubers, etc.; flourishing downwards by way of root-fibers, etc.; and expansion all around by way of leaves and flowers, etc.

*Aparūpaghātena* means by harming and killing others. *Uppannapaccayato* means from the gift-objects such as food and clothing that have arisen. Even by the killing of animals such as cattle, it causes doubt regarding the food of the recipients in that offering. This statement, "*aparūpaghātita-yā*," is because of being virtuous—
357:
—a word that shows the cause. *Guṇātirekaṃ* means one who is superior in virtue, meaning one who is distinguished by supramundane virtues such as morality. *Vipulā* means abundant and extensive by way of the fulfillment of faith and so forth.

## Explanation of the Story of the Young Man Uttara (Uttaramāṇava-vatthu-vaṇṇanā)

At that time, the meal prepared with rice mixed with broken grains was undercooked; therefore, it is called "*uttaṇḍulabhattaṃ*." *Bilaṅga* refers to sour gruel (vinegar) because it is produced from *bilaṅga*. That same sour gruel is called *kañjiya* because it is produced from rice water. Since that sour gruel is the second (dish) for this meal of broken rice, it is called "*bilaṅgadutiyaṃ*." That same *bilaṅgadutiya* is also called "*kañjikadutiya*." *Dhorakāni* means clothes that are washed. Since even very coarse things deserve to be called "*thūlāni*" (coarse), it is said, "*thūlāni ca*." *Guḷadasāni* means that the fringes (of the cloth) are clumped together in masses due to the thickness of the threads and the density of the rice water. Therefore, it is said, "*puñjapuñja... dasāni*." *Anuddisati* means speaking repeatedly.

*Asakkaccaṃ* means acting without respect and with disregard. Since that occurs because of the absence of faith in action and its result, it is said, "*saddhāvirahita*" (devoid of faith). *Acittīkataṃ* means not done with respect as the primary focus. Therefore, it is said, "*cittīkāravirahita*" and so forth. Alternatively, *acittīkataṃ* means not done in a way that would cause wonder in others. The expansive and noble state of the mind is hindered by the very act of giving disrespectfully. *Apaviddhaṃ* means giving by discarding it like a thing to be thrown away; by this, it means the lack of respect in that gift. *Serīsakannāma* means the mansion named "Serīsaka." *Tucchaṃ* means empty because it is devoid of a specific retinue of attendants.

## Explanation of the Deva Pāyāsi (Pāyāsidevaputta-vaṇṇanā)

*Tassānubhāvena* means by the power of that gift. *Sirīsarukkho* is a divine Sirīsa tree (Acacia lebbeck) that is pleasant to behold, endowed with a radiant trunk, forks, branches, twigs, and foliage. *Aṭṭhāsi* (it stood) means it manifested and stood at the door of the mansion, wishing to show that the result is similar to the action. *Pubbāciṇṇavasena* means by way of the habit of having lived there in a previous life. It is not only by way of former habit, but also to show that it was due to the comfort of the season, it is said, "It is said that there is the comfort of the season in that mansion."
358:
That person refers to the young man Uttara. If King Pāyāsi was reborn in that Sirīsa mansion despite giving gifts disrespectfully, one might ask why the retinue of King Pāyāsi was reborn in that same place despite giving gifts respectfully; therefore, it is said, "*pāyāsissa pana*." *Nikantivasena* means (being reborn in his vicinity) by way of the power of craving that is concerned with King Pāyāsi. Alternatively, it is because they had lived in that place in a previous life. *Disācārikavimānaṃ* means a mansion that stays in the sky and can travel through the directions; it is not a mansion attached to trees, mountain peaks, and so forth. *Vaṭṭaniaṭaviyam* means on the path of the mansion.

## Clarification of the Implicit Meaning of the Explanation of the Pāyāsi Rājañña Sutta.

## The Clarification of the Implicit Meaning of the Mahāvagga Commentary is finished.
